ui.meta.titre: {marque} — around the world in 3 curiosities a day
ui.meta.description: Every day, three picture puzzles about the world's curiosities: dishes, monuments, festivals, instruments. Which country do they belong to? Free, no account needed, and your atlas fills up day after day.
ui.meta.partage: A dish, a monument, a festival, an instrument… Which country do they belong to? One free challenge a day, the same for everyone.
ui.statique.titre: Around the world in 3 curiosities a day
ui.statique.texte: {marque} is a free daily game: three picture puzzles about the world's dishes, monuments, festivals, traditions and objects, each to match with its country. No account, just a few minutes.
ui.nav.label: Main menu
ui.commun.detail_alt: Detail of the curiosity to guess
ui.commun.photo_alt: Photo of the curiosity to guess
ui.commun.erreur_chargement: This page could not be loaded. Please check your connection.
ui.intrus.encore_pays: No: this one comes from {pays}, like two others. One more try.
ui.signaler.corps:
Hello,

Here is what seems wrong or unclear to me:
ui.accueil.titre: Three picture puzzles, one discovery of the world
ui.accueil.texte: A dish, a monument, a festival, an instrument… Which country do they belong to? A few minutes a day, and every answer teaches you something.
ui.accueil.minuit: Midnight passed during your game: a new challenge is waiting for you.
ui.accueil.a_revoir_texte: The ones you missed come back here so you can remember them.
ui.accueil.premiere_visite: First visit? Try an easy challenge first, nothing at stake.
ui.accueil.gratuit: Free, no account. Your progress stays on this device.

joker.utilise.other: Joker used: it comes back in {n} days.

ui.resultat.copie: Result copied, now just paste it

resultat.nouvelles.other: {n} new curiosities have been added to your album.

ui.resultat.joker: You had missed a day: your joker saved your streak.

joker.stock.other: {n} jokers in reserve: up to {n} missed days will be forgiven.

ui.joker.gagne: 7 days in a row: you earn a joker.
ui.rappel.texte: Add the challenge to your calendar: an alert every day, at the time of your choice.
ui.ami.bandeau: A friend scored {score}/300 on this challenge. Your turn to beat it.
ui.ami.perdu: You {vous} · your friend {ami}: your friend wins this time.
ui.ami.egal: You {vous} · your friend {ami}: it's a tie.
ui.bonus.titre: Sunday bonus: the week in review
ui.bonus.texte: Find the country of each of the week's featured curiosities. This bonus does not count toward today's score.
ui.jour.titre: {marque} #{n}: where does this close-up come from?
ui.installer.bouton: Add the game to your home screen
ui.installer.ios: To find the game every day: tap Share, then “Add to Home Screen”.
ui.origine.etiquette: Where's it from? · clue {n} of 4 · {points} points
ui.origine.consigne: Which country does this curiosity belong to?
ui.origine.indice.1: Here's a detail of the photo. Each mistake unlocks a clue, but costs points.
ui.origine.indice.4: Last chance: it's one of these four countries.
ui.origine.trouve.1: First try, from just a detail: {pays}.
ui.origine.aussi: Answer accepted: it is also linked to {pays}, but first and foremost to {principal}.
ui.intrus.consigne: Three of these curiosities come from the same country. Which one comes from somewhere else?
ui.intrus.encore: No, this one does come from the same country as two others. Try again.
ui.intrus.explication: The odd one out was “{nom}” ({pays}); the other three come from: {trio}.
ui.liens.consigne: Give each curiosity its country. Careful: there's one country too many.
ui.liens.aide: Tap a curiosity, then its country.
ui.liens.groupe: Country to assign to the selected curiosity
ui.atlas.bilan: {decouverts} of {total} countries discovered, including {connus} known and {maitrises} mastered.
ui.atlas.regle: Discovered: 1 correct answer. Known: 3, on at least 2 different curiosities. Mastered: 6, on at least 3 different curiosities, with at least 3 correct answers out of 4. An answer counts when it's found without help: before the name is given, or on the first try.
ui.album.texte: Every curiosity you meet in a challenge goes into your album, with its card. Tap one to read it again.

revision.attente.one: A missed curiosity will come back in the next few days.
revision.attente.other: {n} missed curiosities will come back in the next few days.

ui.revision.explication: Curiosities you miss in the challenge come back here the next day, then 3 days and 7 days later, until you know them.
ui.revision.note: Review doesn't change your score for the day, but it helps your atlas grow.
ui.revision.bilan: {n} of {total}. The others will come back tomorrow.
ui.regles.jour: One challenge a day, the same for everyone. It changes at midnight, your device's time.
ui.regles.semaine: The week gets harder as it goes: easy on Monday and Tuesday, hard on Saturday, a big challenge on Sunday, followed by a bonus to find the week's featured curiosities again.
ui.regles.origine: Where's it from? Four clues to find the country: a detail of the photo (100 points), the whole photo (70), the name (40), then a choice of four countries (20). After each mistake, the game tells you whether you're on the right continent.
ui.regles.intrus: Odd One Out. Three curiosities come from the same country, the fourth from another country on the same continent. 100 points on the first try, 50 on the second.
ui.regles.liens: Matchups. Four curiosities, five countries, so one country too many. 100 points for four correct matches, 70 for three, 45 for two, 20 for one.
ui.regles.serie: Playing every day extends your streak. You start with one joker and earn another every 7 days in a row (2 at most): each joker forgives one missed day.
ui.regles.rattachement: A curiosity belongs to the country where it was born or with which it is most associated. The expected answer is the one in the Wikipedia article shown after each round.
ui.regles.couverture: The game covers {pays} countries and {curiosites} curiosities. Spotted a mistake? Every answer links to its source.
ui.langue.texte: The game is available in several languages. Your progress is the same in all of them.
ui.sauvegarde.texte: No account: your streak, atlas and album stay on this device. To switch phones or avoid losing them, keep this code.
ui.sauvegarde.confirmer: Replace this device's progress with the one from the code?
ui.sauvegarde.rappel: Your progress only exists on this device. Keep your backup code so you don't lose it.
ui.sources.textes: The texts link to Wikipedia articles. The photos come from Wikimedia Commons, under free licenses.
ui.sources.vie_privee: The game doesn't ask for an account: your progress stays in your browser.

sushi.fait: Originally, fermented rice was used to preserve fish; today's form, nigiri, was born in Edo (Tokyo) in the 19th century.

shamisen.fait: This three-stringed lute is played with a large plectrum called a bachi and accompanies kabuki theater.

hanami.fait: Every spring, people gather under the cherry trees in bloom for picnics; the weather service even publishes blossom forecasts.

himeji.fait: Nicknamed the “White Heron” for its brilliant white walls, it is the largest surviving feudal castle in the country.

kintsugi.fait: This art repairs broken ceramics with lacquer dusted with gold, to highlight the cracks instead of hiding them.

taj-mahal.fait: This white marble mausoleum was built in the 17th century by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal.

holi.fait: To celebrate the arrival of spring, people throw colored powders at each other in the streets.

sitar.fait: This long-necked lute has sympathetic strings that vibrate on their own; Ravi Shankar made it known around the world.

kathakali.fait: In this dance theater from Kerala, the actors' makeup can take several hours.

jantar-mantar.fait: This 18th-century observatory has the largest stone sundial in the world.

grande-muraille.fait: Built and rebuilt over nearly two thousand years, it is not visible to the naked eye from the Moon, contrary to legend.

canard-laque.fait: The duck is roasted until its skin turns crispy, then served in thin slices rolled up in a pancake.

erhu.fait: This fiddle has only two strings, and the bow stays wedged between them.

armee-terre-cuite.fait: Thousands of life-size clay soldiers, all different, guard the tomb of the first emperor; farmers discovered them in 1974.

cite-interdite.fait: This palace of nearly a thousand buildings was home to twenty-four emperors; ordinary people were not allowed to enter.

kimchi.fait: The communal preparation of these fermented vegetables before winter, kimjang, is inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.

hanbok.fait: This traditional costume consists of a short jacket and, for women, a full skirt tied high.

gayageum.fait: This zither traditionally has twelve silk strings, set on movable bridges.

bibimbap.fait: Its name means “mixed rice”: all the ingredients are stirred together with the chili paste just before eating.

haenyeo.fait: On Jeju Island, these women divers, often elderly, gather shellfish while holding their breath, without air tanks.

tom-yam.fait: This sour and spicy soup is flavored with lemongrass, galangal and makrut lime leaves.

songkran.fait: The traditional New Year, in April, is celebrated with gigantic water fights in the streets.

loy-krathong.fait: On the full moon of November, people set small rafts decorated with flowers and candles on the water.

wat-arun.fait: This “Temple of Dawn” is covered with pieces of colorful porcelain.

khon.fait: In this masked dance theater, the actors do not speak: a chorus recites the text.

pho.fait: This rice noodle soup with a long-simmered broth is often eaten as early as breakfast.

baie-along.fait: Nearly 2,000 limestone islands and islets rise from the sea; its name means “where the dragon descends.”

ao-dai.fait: This long tunic, slit up the sides, is worn over loose trousers.

marionnettes-eau.fait: The puppeteers, hidden behind a curtain, work the figures while standing waist-deep in water.

banh-mi.fait: This sandwich combines a baguette inherited from the colonial era with pâté, pickled vegetables and cilantro.

borobudur.fait: The largest Buddhist temple in the world, built in the 9th century, long lay buried under volcanic ash and vegetation.

gamelan.fait: This orchestra of bronze gongs and metallophones is tuned as a whole: instruments cannot be swapped from one ensemble to another.

wayang.fait: In this shadow theater, a single puppeteer, the dalang, moves all the leather figures and does all the voices, sometimes for an entire night.

angklung.fait: Each bamboo instrument produces only one note when shaken: several players are needed to make a melody.

kriss.fait: The wavy blade of this dagger is forged from layers of different metals; it is said to have powers.

angkor-vat.fait: The largest religious monument in the world appears on the national flag.

ta-prohm.fait: Giant tree roots grip the walls of this temple, left almost as the forest had covered it.

bayon.fait: Its dozens of towers each bear large stone faces with an enigmatic smile.

krama.fait: This checkered scarf is used for everything: turban, towel, baby hammock or bag.

tonle-sap.fait: Twice a year, the river that links this lake to the Mekong reverses its flow.

petra.fait: The Nabataeans carved this city directly into the pink sandstone; it is reached through a narrow gorge more than a kilometer long.

mansaf.fait: This dish of lamb cooked in a dried yogurt sauce is traditionally eaten by hand, around a large shared platter.

wadi-rum.fait: This red sand desert has stood in for the planet Mars in several films.

jerash.fait: It is one of the best-preserved Roman cities, with its oval plaza surrounded by columns.

qusair-amra.fait: This small desert castle, built in the 8th century, is decorated with frescoes of hunting and bathing scenes.

sainte-sophie.fait: Inaugurated in 537, it has been in turn a basilica, a mosque, a museum, then a mosque again in 2020.

derviche.fait: Their whirling dance, the sema, is a religious ceremony of the Mevlevi Sufi order, founded in Konya.

cappadoce.fait: Erosion has sculpted “fairy chimneys” here, into which the inhabitants dug houses, churches and underground cities.

pamukkale.fait: Its name means “cotton castle”: hot springs have deposited pools of white limestone here.

ebru.fait: For this marbled paper, the colors are laid on the surface of water before the sheet is placed on it.

parthenon.fait: This temple dedicated to Athena was completed in the 5th century BC; its columns bulge slightly so they look straight to the eye.

bouzouki.fait: This long-necked lute with a metallic sound is the emblematic instrument of rebetiko.

sirtaki.fait: This dance is not ancient: it was created in 1964 for the film Zorba the Greek.

meteores.fait: Monasteries were built on top of rock pillars; people once went up in nets hoisted by rope.

komboloi.fait: This small string of beads has nothing religious about it: people spin it between their fingers to pass the time.

colisee.fait: Inaugurated in the year 80, this amphitheater could hold about 50,000 spectators.

pizza-napolitaine.fait: The art of Neapolitan pizzaiuoli has been inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list since 2017.

gondole.fait: This boat is asymmetrical: its left side is wider, to offset the weight of the rower standing at the stern.

palio.fait: Twice each summer, the city's districts compete in a bareback horse race that lasts barely a minute and a half.

tour-pise.fait: It began to lean during its construction, in the 12th century, because the ground was too soft.

flamenco.fait: Born in Andalusia, this art combines singing, guitar, dance and handclapping.

paella.fait: Originally from the Valencia region, it takes its name from the large pan in which it is cooked.

sagrada-familia.fait: Begun in 1882, this basilica by Antoni Gaudí has been under construction for more than 140 years.

tomatina.fait: On the last Wednesday of every August, in Buñol, thousands of people pelt each other with tons of overripe tomatoes.

castells.fait: These human towers can reach ten levels; a child climbs to the top.

fado.fait: This melancholy song, accompanied by a twelve-string guitar, expresses saudade, a blend of nostalgia and longing.

pastel-de-nata.fait: This custard tart in puff pastry is said to have been created by monks of the Jerónimos Monastery, in Belém.

tour-belem.fait: Built in the 16th century at the mouth of the Tagus, it guarded the entrance to the port from which the great navigators set sail.

palais-pena.fait: This palace with yellow and red facades blends Gothic, Moorish and Renaissance styles on a hill in Sintra.

coq-barcelos.fait: This colorful ceramic rooster recalls a legend: a roast rooster is said to have started crowing to prove a condemned man innocent.

tour-eiffel.fait: Built for the 1889 World's Fair, it was supposed to be taken down after twenty years.

baguette.fait: The artisanal know-how and culture of the baguette have been inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list since 2022.

mont-saint-michel.fait: During the highest tides, the sea completely surrounds the rock and its abbey.

petanque.fait: This game of boules was born in the early 20th century in La Ciotat; its name comes from the Provençal “pèd tanca,” meaning feet planted on the ground.

viaduc-millau.fait: Its tallest pylon reaches 343 meters, higher than the Eiffel Tower.

stonehenge.fait: Some of its stones were transported from Wales, more than 200 kilometers away.

cornemuse.fait: It has three drones that hold a continuous note while the piper plays the melody.

fish-and-chips.fait: This dish of battered fried fish and fries was traditionally served wrapped in newspaper.

big-ben.fait: Big Ben is actually the nickname of the great bell, not of the tower, which is called the Elizabeth Tower.

tower-bridge.fait: This bascule bridge, completed in 1894, still opens several hundred times a year to let boats through.

bodhran.fait: This frame drum is struck with a small double-headed stick, while the other hand changes the sound by pressing on the skin.

saint-patrick.fait: On March 17, people wear green and a shamrock, which the saint is said to have used to explain the Trinity.

hurling.fait: This very old stick-and-ball sport is one of the fastest field sports in the world.

livre-kells.fait: This illuminated manuscript of the Gospels, made by monks around the year 800, is kept at Trinity College Dublin.

falaises-moher.fait: These eight-kilometer-long cliffs drop into the Atlantic from a height of more than 200 meters.

oktoberfest.fait: The world's largest folk festival actually begins in September; the first one celebrated a princely wedding in 1810.

neuschwanstein.fait: This castle of King Ludwig II of Bavaria inspired the one in Disney's Sleeping Beauty.

porte-brandebourg.fait: During the Cold War, it stood in the restricted zone at the foot of the Wall, and no one could pass through it.

currywurst.fait: This sausage topped with curry tomato sauce is said to have been invented in 1949 by Herta Heuwer, in Berlin.

cathedrale-cologne.fait: Its construction, begun in 1248, lasted more than six centuries.

kapellbrucke.fait: This 14th-century covered wooden bridge in Lucerne is decorated with triangular paintings under its roof.

chillon.fait: Built on a rocky islet in Lake Geneva, it inspired a famous poem by Lord Byron.

aletsch.fait: About twenty kilometers long, it is the largest glacier in the Alps.

rosti.fait: This grated potato cake gave its name to the “Röstigraben,” the cultural border between the country's two main language regions.

combat-reines.fait: In Valais, Hérens cows face off head to head to choose the “queen” of the herd.

kinderdijk.fait: These nineteen 18th-century windmills were used to pump water to keep the land dry.

stroopwafel.fait: This thin syrup-filled waffle, born in Gouda, is placed on top of a hot cup to soften.

delft.fait: This blue and white decoration emerged in the 17th century to imitate porcelain imported from China.

koningsdag.fait: On April 27, everyone dresses in orange and the streets turn into a huge flea market.

rijksmuseum.fait: It houses Rembrandt's “The Night Watch”; a bike path runs under the building.

cheval-dalecarlie.fait: This small painted wooden horse, originally carved by lumberjacks during winter evenings, is often red.

fika.fait: This coffee break with a pastry is an institution, at work as well as among friends.

vasa.fait: This warship sank in 1628 a few minutes after setting off; raised in 1961, it is almost intact.

surstromming.fait: This fermented herring smells so strong that the can is usually opened outdoors.

icehotel.fait: Every winter, it is rebuilt with ice from a river, then melts in the spring.

goulash.fait: Originally, it was the soup of herdsmen, cooked in a cauldron and seasoned with paprika.

parlement-budapest.fait: This neo-Gothic building on the banks of the Danube has 691 rooms.

rubiks-cube.fait: Invented in 1974 by an architecture professor, Ernő Rubik, it has more than 43 billion billion combinations.

szechenyi.fait: In these open-air thermal baths, people play chess in the hot water, even in winter.

bastion-pecheurs.fait: Its seven white towers represent the seven founding tribes of the country.

matriochka.fait: The first of these nesting dolls was made around 1890, inspired by a Japanese toy.

balalaika.fait: This three-stringed instrument is recognizable by its triangular body.

saint-basile.fait: Ivan the Terrible had it built in the 16th century; each of its colorful onion domes is different.

lac-baikal.fait: It is the deepest lake in the world: it holds about one fifth of the planet's surface fresh water.

ermitage.fait: It holds about three million works; cats have lived there since the 18th century to hunt mice.

jemaa-el-fna.fait: Storytellers, musicians and snake charmers gather there every evening; it is the square that inspired UNESCO's concept of intangible heritage.

ait-ben-haddou.fait: This fortified mud-brick village has served as a set for many films, including Gladiator.

chefchaouen.fait: The alleys of its old town are painted blue, from the steps to the walls.

mosquee-hassan-ii.fait: Built partly over the ocean, it has one of the tallest minarets in the world, at about 200 meters.

koutoubia.fait: Its 12th-century minaret is said to have inspired the Giralda in Seville and the Hassan Tower in Rabat.

timgad.fait: This Roman city founded by Emperor Trajan around the year 100 has kept its grid plan almost intact.

tassili.fait: This Saharan plateau is home to thousands of rock paintings showing a time when the region was green.

djemila.fait: This Roman mountain city had to adapt its layout to the slopes, which gives it two forums.

karakou.fait: This velvet jacket embroidered with gold thread is the traditional festive attire of the women of Algiers.

mzab.fait: Five fortified towns built nearly a thousand years ago in the desert, whose architecture inspired Le Corbusier.

kheops.fait: It is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing; it remained the tallest human-made structure for nearly 4,000 years.

sphinx.fait: Carved directly from the bedrock, it spent much of its history buried in sand up to its shoulders.

kochari.fait: This street food mixes rice, lentils, pasta and chickpeas, with a tomato sauce and fried onions.

abou-simbel.fait: In the 1960s, the temples were cut into blocks and reassembled higher up to escape the waters of the Aswan Dam.

vallee-rois.fait: More than sixty tombs are dug into the rock there, including that of Tutankhamun, found almost intact in 1922.

lalibela.fait: These eleven churches were not built but dug downward, each from a single block, into the rock.

injera.fait: This large fermented flatbread made from teff, shared with neighboring Eritrea, serves as both plate and utensils.

timqet.fait: For this Epiphany festival, in January, processions carry replicas of the Ark of the Covenant to a body of water.

fasil-ghebbi.fait: This fortified compound in Gondar, residence of the emperors in the 17th and 18th centuries, looks like a medieval castle.

dallol.fait: This hydrothermal site below sea level, with its yellow and green colors, is one of the hottest places on the planet.

djenne.fait: It is the largest mud-brick building in the world; every year, the inhabitants replaster it together during a festival.

tombouctou.fait: A crossroads for Saharan caravans, it was a great center of learning and preserves tens of thousands of ancient manuscripts.

bogolan.fait: This cotton cloth is dyed with fermented mud, which produces brown and black patterns.

bandiagara.fait: Dogon villages cling to this sandstone cliff, which stretches more than 150 kilometers.

tombeau-askia.fait: This earthen pyramid bristling with wooden stakes was erected in Gao at the end of the 15th century.

thieboudienne.fait: This dish of rice with fish, born in Saint-Louis, has been inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list since 2021.

goree.fait: This small island off Dakar is a place of remembrance of the slave trade.

lac-rose.fait: A microscopic alga gives its very salty waters a pink hue, more or less vivid depending on the season.

sabar.fait: This drum is played with one hand and a stick; it gave its name to the dance and the celebration it accompanies.

lutte-frappe.fait: Before the bout, wrestlers cover themselves with amulets and dance to the sound of drums; the champions are stars.

kilimandjaro.fait: The highest peak in Africa, at nearly 5,900 meters, is an isolated volcano capped with glaciers, very close to the equator.

stone-town.fait: The old town of Zanzibar is famous for its carved wooden doors; Freddie Mercury was born there.

serengeti.fait: Every year, more than a million wildebeest set out there on a great migration in search of fresh grass.

tingatinga.fait: This brightly colored style, originally painted with bicycle paint, is named after its creator, Edward Saidi Tingatinga.

ngorongoro.fait: This collapsed volcano forms a basin more than twenty kilometers wide, where thousands of animals live.

vuvuzela.fait: This long plastic horn became famous around the world during the 2010 soccer World Cup.

table-mountain.fait: Its perfectly flat summit is often covered by a cloud that locals call “the tablecloth.”

biltong.fait: This dried, spiced meat was originally a way to preserve game during long journeys.

robben-island.fait: Nelson Mandela spent nearly 18 of his 27 years in prison on this island, which has become a museum.

bo-kaap.fait: The houses in this neighborhood are painted in bright colors, a legacy of Cape Town's Malay community.

allee-baobabs.fait: These giant trees, about thirty meters tall, line a dirt road; some are said to be several centuries old.

valiha.fait: This zither is made from a bamboo tube around which the strings are stretched.

tsingy.fait: This “forest” of sharp limestone needles bears a Malagasy name often translated as “where one cannot walk barefoot.”

famadihana.fait: During this “turning of the bones,” families take their ancestors out of the tomb, wrap them in new shrouds and dance with them.

lamba.fait: This large cloth draped over the shoulders accompanies a person throughout life, even serving as a shroud.

chichen-itza.fait: At the equinoxes, the shadows form a serpent that seems to slither down the stairs of the great pyramid.

jour-des-morts.fait: In early November, families set up flower-covered altars and share a meal with their departed, in a joyful atmosphere.

mariachi.fait: These bands of violins, trumpets and guitars play in embroidered costumes and wide-brimmed hats.

taco.fait: It is a corn tortilla folded around a filling; the traditional cuisine it belongs to has been inscribed by UNESCO since 2010.

lucha-libre.fait: The wrestlers wear colorful masks; losing one's mask is the worst of dishonors.

machu-picchu.fait: This Inca city perched at 2,430 meters, long forgotten, was only revealed to the world in 1911.

ceviche.fait: The raw fish is “cooked” by the acidity of lime juice.

nazca.fait: These huge drawings traced in the desert about 2,000 years ago can only be clearly seen from the sky.

vinicunca.fait: Minerals have striped this “Mountain of Seven Colors,” located more than 5,000 meters above sea level.

marinera.fait: In this courtship dance, the partners circle each other, each waving a handkerchief.

christ-redempteur.fait: This 30-meter statue, inaugurated in 1931, towers over the city from the top of Mount Corcovado.

capoeira.fait: This martial art created by enslaved Africans is disguised as a dance and practiced to music, in a circle.

carnaval-rio.fait: The samba schools spend a year preparing their parade for a passage of about an hour through the Sambadrome.

berimbau.fait: This single-stringed musical bow, fitted with a gourd, sets the rhythm of capoeira circles.

theatre-amazonas.fait: This opera house was built in the middle of the forest during the rubber boom, with materials brought from Europe.

mojito.fait: Rum, lime, mint, sugar and soda water: Ernest Hemingway is reputed to have been a great fan of it.

capitole-havane.fait: Completed in 1929, it closely resembles the Capitol in Washington.

habano.fait: The finest are rolled entirely by hand by torcedores, to whom, by tradition, a reader reads novels and newspapers aloud.

vinales.fait: Rounded limestone hills, the mogotes, rise in the middle of tobacco fields.

trinidad.fait: This colonial town with cobbled streets grew rich from sugar, then froze in time.

statue-liberte.fait: A gift from France in 1886, it was originally copper-colored: the green comes from oxidation.

mont-rushmore.fait: The faces of four presidents, 18 meters high, were carved into the granite between 1927 and 1941.

golden-gate.fait: Its color, “International Orange,” was chosen so that it would remain visible in the fog.

jazz.fait: This music was born in the early 20th century in New Orleans, from the meeting of blues, ragtime and brass bands.

grand-canyon.fait: The Colorado River carved this gorge, more than 1,600 meters deep.

poutine.fait: Fries, cheese curds that “squeak” between your teeth, and brown gravy: this dish was born in Quebec in the 1950s.

tour-cn.fait: At 553 meters tall, it was the world's tallest freestanding structure for more than thirty years.

inuksuk.fait: These stone stacks serve as landmarks for the Inuit in the tundra; one of them appears on the flag of Nunavut.

lac-moraine.fait: Its turquoise color comes from the “rock flour” that glaciers grind up and pour into its waters.

frontenac.fait: This hotel overlooking the St. Lawrence is said to be the most photographed in the world.

didgeridoo.fait: This Aboriginal instrument is traditionally made from a eucalyptus branch hollowed out by termites.

opera-sydney.fait: Its sail-shaped roofs are covered with more than a million tiles; its architect, Jørn Utzon, never saw it completed.

uluru.fait: This rock, sacred to the Anangu people, changes color with the time of day; climbing it has been banned since 2019.

boomerang.fait: Not all of them come back: hunting models, which are heavier, were made to fly straight.

grande-barriere.fait: At 2,300 kilometers long, it is the largest structure built by living beings.

haka.fait: This Maori chanted dance is known worldwide thanks to the All Blacks rugby team.

hangi.fait: The food cooks for several hours in an oven dug into the ground, on heated stones.

ta-moko.fait: This Maori tattoo tells the genealogy and rank of the person who wears it; it was once carved with a chisel.

sky-tower.fait: From the top of its 328 meters, you can jump into the void, held by a cable.

milford-sound.fait: This steep-walled fjord is one of the rainiest places in the world, which multiplies its waterfalls.

sachertorte.fait: This chocolate cake filled with apricot jam was created in 1832 by a sixteen-year-old apprentice pastry chef, Franz Sacher.

schonbrunn.fait: The summer residence of the Habsburgs, it has 1,441 rooms; Mozart played there at the age of six before the empress.

valse-viennoise.fait: Considered scandalous at first because the dancers held each other close, it still opens hundreds of balls every year.

grande-roue-prater.fait: Built in 1897, it long remained the tallest operating Ferris wheel in the world.

atomium.fait: Built for the 1958 World's Fair, it represents an iron crystal magnified 165 billion times.

manneken-pis.fait: This bronze statuette, about fifty centimeters tall, has a wardrobe of more than a thousand costumes.

carnaval-binche.fait: On Mardi Gras, the Gilles, wearing tall ostrich-feather hats, throw oranges to the crowd.

gaufre-liege.fait: Its yeast dough contains pearl sugar that caramelizes during baking.

pierogi.fait: These half-moon dumplings are filled with potato and farmer's cheese, meat, cabbage or even fruit.

mine-wieliczka.fait: Worked for seven centuries, it houses, more than a hundred meters underground, a chapel carved entirely out of salt.

wawel.fait: The residence of kings for centuries, it overlooks a cave where, according to legend, a dragon lived.

malbork.fait: Built by the Teutonic Knights, it is the largest brick castle in the world.

horloge-prague.fait: Installed in 1410, it still works: every hour, the twelve apostles parade past its windows.

pont-charles.fait: Legend has it that eggs were mixed into the mortar to make this 14th-century bridge stronger.

cristal-boheme.fait: This cut and engraved glass rivaled that of Venice as early as the 17th century.

cesky-krumlov.fait: This small medieval town nestles in a bend of the Vltava, below a castle with an intact Baroque theater.

lagon-bleu.fait: Its milky waters, at nearly 38 °C, come from a nearby geothermal power plant.

hakarl.fait: This shark, fermented and then dried for months, smells so strongly of ammonia that beginners hold their noses.

geysir.fait: This jet of hot water gave its name to all the geysers in the world.

hallgrimskirkja.fait: The facade of this church recalls the basalt columns formed by lava as it cools.

stavkirke.fait: Built around 1130, this all-wood church is decorated with carvings inherited from Viking art.

brunost.fait: This caramel-flavored “brown cheese” is made by slowly boiling down whey.

geirangerfjord.fait: Waterfalls such as the “Seven Sisters” plunge into this narrow fjord framed by mountains more than a thousand meters high.

preikestolen.fait: This perfectly flat rock platform towers 604 meters above the fjord, without any railing.

nyhavn.fait: The colorful houses of this old harbor line a canal dug in the 17th century; the writer Andersen lived in several of them.

smorrebrod.fait: These open sandwiches of buttered rye bread are eaten with a knife and fork, so generously are they topped.

lego.fait: Its name comes from “leg godt,” which means “play well”; today's bricks still fit together with those from 1958.

tivoli.fait: Opened in 1843, this amusement park right in the city center is said to have inspired Walt Disney.

bodnath.fait: The eyes of the Buddha painted on its four sides look in every direction.

kumari.fait: A girl chosen at a very young age is worshipped as a living goddess until she reaches puberty.

swayambhunath.fait: It is called the “Monkey Temple,” because hundreds of macaques live there freely.

durbar-katmandou.fait: This ensemble of palaces and temples in carved wood faced the former royal palace.

sigiriya.fait: In the 5th century, a king had his palace built on top of this rock, nearly 200 meters high, which is reached between the paws of a giant lion.

temple-dent.fait: It houses a tooth attributed to the Buddha; every year, a replica of its reliquary is paraded on the back of an elephant.

the-ceylan.fait: Tea plantations replaced coffee plantations, which were destroyed by a disease in the 1870s.

esala-perahera.fait: For ten nights, dozens of elephants adorned with lights parade with dancers and drummers.

yourte.fait: Called a “ger” in Mongolia, this round felt tent can be taken down in a few hours and carried on camelback.

morin-khuur.fait: The neck of this two-stringed fiddle ends in a carved horse's head.

naadam.fait: Every summer, this festival brings together the “three manly games”: wrestling, archery and horse racing.

khoomii.fait: The singer produces two notes at once: a low drone and a whistled melody.

registan.fait: Three Koranic schools covered in blue mosaics frame this square, the heart of Samarkand on the Silk Road.

itchan-kala.fait: The old town of Khiva has remained enclosed within its mud-brick ramparts, like an open-air museum.

suzani.fait: These large hangings embroidered with flowers and suns were traditionally part of the dowry.

minaret-kalon.fait: At 46 meters tall, this minaret in Bukhara is said to have been spared by Genghis Khan, who was impressed by its beauty.

khatchapouri.fait: In its boat-shaped version, this cheese bread is served with an egg and butter that you mix in yourself.

kvevri.fait: In these large clay jars buried up to the neck, wine has been made for about eight thousand years.

ouchgouli.fait: This mountain hamlet, one of the highest in Europe, bristles with medieval defensive towers.

guergueti.fait: Isolated at an altitude of 2,170 meters, it stands out against the snows of Mount Kazbek.

shwedagon.fait: Its stupa, nearly a hundred meters high, is covered with gold plates and crowned with thousands of diamonds.

bagan.fait: More than two thousand temples and pagodas built from the 11th to the 13th century dot this plain.

thanaka.fait: This yellow paste made from tree bark is worn on the cheeks, both as makeup and as sun protection.

pont-u-bein.fait: At 1.2 kilometers long, it is the longest teak bridge in the world; it was built around 1850.

masai-mara.fait: Every summer, hundreds of thousands of wildebeest cross the crocodile-infested Mara River there.

lamu.fait: In this car-free Swahili town, donkeys and dhows remain the main means of transport.

fort-jesus.fait: The Portuguese built this fort in Mombasa in 1593; seen from above, its layout resembles a human body.

amboseli.fait: Its elephants are photographed in front of Kilimanjaro, which actually lies on the other side of the border.

kente.fait: This cloth made of narrow strips sewn together was reserved for Ashanti kings; each pattern has a name and a meaning.

elmina.fait: Built by the Portuguese in 1482, it is the oldest European building south of the Sahara; it was used in the slave trade.

cercueils-figuratifs.fait: A fish, an airplane or a cocoa pod: craftsmen make coffins in the image of the trade or dreams of the deceased.

adinkra.fait: Each of these symbols printed on fabrics sums up a proverb or an idea.

el-jem.fait: This Roman amphitheater could hold about 30,000 spectators: only those of Rome and Capua were larger.

sidi-bou-said.fait: The whole village is painted white and blue, from the studded doors to the mashrabiyas.

chechia.fait: Making this red wool cap involves many steps: knitting, fulling, dyeing, carding.

kairouan.fait: Founded in 670, it is one of the oldest mosques in the Muslim world; its minaret served as a model for the whole Maghreb.

perito-moreno.fait: This glacier advances about two meters a day and drops chunks of ice as tall as buildings into the lake.

cueva-manos.fait: For thousands of years, prehistoric hunters stenciled hundreds of hands on the walls of this cave.

caminito.fait: The houses on this alley are made of sheet metal painted in bright colors, originally with leftover boat paint.

obelisque-buenos-aires.fait: At 67 meters tall, it was erected in 1936 in barely two months.

moai.fait: Easter Island has nearly nine hundred of these giant statues; most of them have their backs to the sea.

torres-del-paine.fait: Three granite towers more than 2,000 meters high overlook turquoise lakes and glaciers.

valparaiso.fait: To climb its hills covered with colorful houses, this port city uses old funiculars that are over a century old.

atacama.fait: It is the driest desert in the world outside the poles: some weather stations there have never recorded rain.

cano-cristales.fait: Every year, an aquatic plant colors this river red, yellow and green: it is called “the river of five colors.”

cumbia.fait: Born on the Caribbean coast from a blend of African, Native American and Spanish traditions, it is danced with small gliding steps.

cathedrale-sel.fait: This church was dug nearly 200 meters underground in a salt mine.

carthagene.fait: Its dozen or so kilometers of ramparts protected the galleons' gold from pirates.

reggae.fait: Born in the late 1960s, it has been on UNESCO's intangible heritage list since 2018.

jerk.fait: The meat is marinated in a mixture of very hot peppers and spices, then cooked slowly over a wood fire.

rastafari.fait: Born in the 1930s, this spiritual movement sees Emperor Haile Selassie as a messiah; reggae made it known throughout the world.

port-royal.fait: This pirate haven, reputed to be “the most depraved city in Christendom,” was partly swallowed up by an earthquake in 1692.

chambord.fait: This château, the largest of those in the Loire Valley, stands at the heart of the largest enclosed forest park in Europe, surrounded by a 32 km wall.

pont-du-gard.fait: Probably built in the first half of the 1st century, this three-tiered bridge is the highest known aqueduct bridge in the Roman world.

versailles.fait: Commissioned by Louis XIV to glorify the monarchy, this palace has 2,300 rooms, and its grounds cover 815 hectares, including 93 of gardens.

arc-triomphe.fait: Its construction, ordered by Emperor Napoleon I, began in 1806 and was not completed until 1836, under the reign of Louis-Philippe.

carcassonne.fait: This medieval citadel owes its fame to its double wall nearly 3 km long, lined with fifty-two towers, which overlooks the Aude valley.

dune-pilat.fait: Located in Gironde, at the entrance to the Arcachon Bay, it is the highest dune in Europe: its height was 103.6 meters in 2023.

croissant.fait: Its ancestor is the Austrian kipferl, but the first recipe for the modern croissant, made with puff pastry, was created by a French chef in 1915.

cassoulet.fait: This specialty of Languedoc takes its name from the cassole, a glazed earthenware pot; originally, it was made with fava beans.

camembert.fait: This soft cheese with a bloomy rind is the second most consumed cheese in France, behind Emmental (2022 figures).

macaron.fait: This almond petit four, derived from meringue, contains as much almond as powdered sugar: this is called “tant pour tant.”

champagne.fait: As early as the Middle Ages, the region produced still wines, without bubbles; its name comes from an old word meaning “large expanse of flat land.”

pastis.fait: This spirit is flavored with anise and licorice; some recipes add other plants, notably fennel.

beret.fait: This round, flat cap, made of soft felt or knitted and felted wool, originated in Béarn; its name comes from the Gascon “berret.”

santon.fait: These small, brightly colored clay figurines populate the Christmas nativity scene and also depict the inhabitants of a Provençal village and their trades.

fete-lumieres.fait: Launched by the city of Lyon in 1999, it continues a tradition whose origins date back to 1852: placing small candles in windows.

alhambra.fait: In 2023, this palace complex in Granada, Andalusia, was the second most visited site in Spain, with 2.6 million visitors.

mosquee-cordoue.fait: This former Roman temple became a Christian basilica, then a mosque from the 8th century, before being consecrated as a cathedral in 1236.

aqueduc-segovie.fait: This 17-kilometer Roman aqueduct remained in service until 1973; its elevated section has 167 arches.

parc-guell.fait: This park in Barcelona, built between 1900 and 1914, is one of the works of the Catalan architect Antoni Gaudí.

teide.fait: This volcano on the island of Tenerife, in the Canaries, is the highest point in Spain at 3,715 m and the highest peak in the Atlantic Ocean.

fallas.fait: All year long, artists make statues out of fabric, papier-mâché or clay; during the festival, in Valencia, all of them are burned except one.

gaspacho.fait: This soup is served cold: blended raw tomatoes and vegetables, olive oil. It is very popular in summer in Andalusia, in southern Spain.

tapas.fait: These hot or cold appetizers are eaten at the table or, more often, standing in bars; a “ración” is a portion of tapa.

hieronymites.fait: This monastery of the Order of Saint Jerome bears witness to the wealth of the Portuguese discoveries; it is an example of the Manueline style, like the Belém Tower.

pont-dom-luis.fait: This bridge over the Douro links Porto to Vila Nova de Gaia; it was built from 1881 to 1886 by Théophile Seyrig, a former partner of Gustave Eiffel.

librairie-lello.fait: This Neo-Gothic and Art Nouveau bookstore, in the historic center of Porto, is considered one of the most beautiful in the world.

santa-justa.fait: This elevator, built in the historic center of Lisbon, links the Pombaline Baixa to Bairro Alto; it is also called Elevador do Carmo.

cabo-da-roca.fait: This cape, with cliffs about 140 meters high, is the westernmost point of mainland Europe; its lighthouse went into service in 1772.

porto-vin.fait: This fortified wine is produced only in the Upper Douro, a hundred kilometers upstream from the city of Porto, from which it takes its name.

ginjinha.fait: This sour cherry liqueur is usually served with the fruit at the bottom of the glass, “com elas” (with them), or plain, “sem elas.”

francesinha.fait: This typical dish originated in the Porto region, in Portugal, and is part of Portuguese cuisine.

tramway-lisbonne.fait: In service since 1873, the Lisbon tram network now has six urban lines, totaling 48 kilometers.

fontaine-trevi.fait: Built between 1732 and 1762 against the Palazzo Poli, it is the largest fountain in Rome; four colossal-order columns give it its structure.

pantheon-rome.fait: This ancient temple in Rome, converted into a church in the 7th century, has a dome 43.30 m in diameter, the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.

pont-rialto.fait: It is the oldest of the four bridges that cross the Grand Canal in Venice, and one of the most visited monuments in the city.

dome-milan.fait: Begun in 1386, this cathedral was not completed until 1932: it took five and a half centuries to finish.

pompei.fait: This ancient city in Campania was buried in the fall of 79 by an eruption of Vesuvius, a volcano located 9 km to the northwest.

cinque-terre.fait: These five villages in Liguria are built in coves and on cliffs; terraces were built there over the centuries for farming.

etna.fait: This volcano in Sicily, 3,403 meters high, is the highest active volcano in Europe; it had nearly 80 eruptions during the 20th century.

carnaval-venise.fait: This festival, which dates back to the Middle Ages, begins ten days before Ash Wednesday and lasts until Mardi Gras; it is known for its masks.

carnaval-ivree.fait: This carnival takes place in Ivrea, in the province of Turin, during the three “fat days” that precede Ash Wednesday.

panettone.fait: This sweet bread with raisins, candied fruit and citrus zest is the traditional cake of Lombardy and Piedmont, eaten at Christmas.

expresso.fait: Its name comes from the Italian “espresso.” This very strong coffee is made by quickly forcing hot water through ground coffee at 9 bars of pressure.

spritz.fait: This long drink combines a sparkling white wine, often prosecco, a bitter and soda water; it is drunk as an aperitif in Veneto and throughout Italy.

mandoline.fait: This short-necked, plucked string instrument descends from the lute and the cittern; it is most widespread in Mediterranean countries and in North America.

verre-murano.fait: Toward the end of the 13th century, the Venetian glass industry moved to the island of Murano, where famous glassworks still have their workshops.

santorin.fait: This island in the Aegean Sea is the remnant of an ancient island partly destroyed by an eruption; its white villages are perched on cliffs.

delphes.fait: At the foot of Mount Parnassus, the Pythia delivered the oracle of Apollo here; the sanctuary also houses the Omphalos, the “navel of the world.”

cnossos.fait: This Bronze Age archaeological site in Crete lies five kilometers southeast of Heraklion; it was one of the main city-states of Crete.

canal-corinthe.fait: This artificial waterway cuts through the isthmus that links the Peloponnese to the rest of Greece, between the Ionian Sea and the Aegean Sea.

mont-olympe.fait: With its summit at 2,918 meters, it is the highest mountain in Greece and, according to tradition, the home of the gods of Greek mythology.

navagio.fait: On this beach on the island of Zakynthos lies the wreck of a ship that left Albania for Piraeus and ran aground in October 1980 in bad weather.

souvlaki.fait: Its name means “skewer”: small pieces of meat, usually pork in Greece, grilled and sometimes served in pita bread.

gyros.fait: Its name comes from the ancient Greek for “ring, circle”; the meat is served in pita bread with tomato, onion and tzatziki sauce.

feta.fait: This brined curd cheese, traditionally made from sheep's milk, owes its name to the Italian “fetta,” which means “slice.”

ouzo.fait: This anise-flavored drink is colorless and turns white when mixed with water; since 1989, it must be produced in Greece to bear this name.

retsina.fait: This dry wine, white or rosé, is flavored with pine resin; it has been a specialty of Greece for nearly two thousand years.

evzone.fait: Their name literally means “well-girdled.” These soldiers of the Presidential Guard guard the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Athens.

buckingham.fait: This official residence of the British sovereigns was originally a large townhouse built in 1703 for the Duke of Buckingham.

chateau-edimbourg.fait: This 12th-century fortress, in Edinburgh, Scotland, has partly become a museum and is a listed historic monument.

mur-hadrien.fait: Built between 122 and 127 across the entire width of what is now northern England, this Roman fortification is about 117.5 km long.

chaussee-geants.fait: This volcanic formation on the coast of Northern Ireland has about 40,000 hexagonal basalt columns, which resemble paving stones.

loch-ness.fait: This freshwater lake in the Highlands of Scotland stretches southwest of the town of Inverness and northeast of Fort Augustus.

cabine-rouge.fait: This world-famous piece of street furniture has become, in popular imagery, a symbol of London, just like Big Ben or the double-decker bus.

routemaster.fait: This double-decker bus, usually open at the rear, ran in London from 1956 to 2005; it survives on a heritage route, the 15.

kilt.fait: This pleated wool wrap skirt is a traditional garment for men in the Highlands; its colorful patterns form a “tartan.”

haggis.fait: This traditional Scottish dish is a sheep's stomach stuffed with minced mutton offal and oats; it was very popular in the 18th century.

yeomen-warders.fait: These ceremonial guards of the Tower of London, 37 in number, are recruited from former military personnel with a total of 22 years of service.

jeux-highlands.fait: At these Scottish competitions, athletes toss a tree trunk 5 to 6.5 meters long, amid parades of bagpipers and participants in kilts.

carnaval-notting-hill.fait: This very popular carnival livens up a London neighborhood in late August, on a Sunday and a Monday; that Monday is a public holiday in the United Kingdom.

newgrange.fait: This mound, 85 meters in diameter, houses a burial chamber reached by a long covered passage; it remained sealed for several millennia.

rock-of-cashel.fait: This site in County Tipperary brings together buildings from a great many periods; it is one of the main sites of Celtic art in Europe.

skellig-michael.fait: This steep island rises 218 meters above the Atlantic; monks probably settled there in the 6th century and stayed until the 13th.

glendalough.fait: Its Irish name means “valley of the two lakes.” Saint Kevin, a hermit priest, founded a monastery there in the 6th century.

kylemore.fait: This Benedictine abbey in Connemara was founded in 1920 on the site of a castle; it has a Neo-Gothic church and Victorian gardens.

football-gaelique.fait: The most popular sport in Ireland, it is entirely amateur, and each player can only ever play for the team of their home county.

currach.fait: This light boat from the west coast of Ireland is made of wooden laths covered with coated canvas; its ancestors are said to have been covered with oxhides.

colcannon.fait: This traditional dish is also served on Halloween: a coin, a thimble, a button or a ring is then hidden in it.

boxty.fait: This kind of pancake combines grated raw potato, mashed potato and buttermilk; it comes from northern Connacht and southern Ulster.

reichstag.fait: This building in Berlin housed the Reichstag from 1894; it has been home to the Bundestag since the institutions returned to Berlin in 1999.

chateau-heidelberg.fait: This 13th-century castle, built on a hillside between two hills, overlooks the city of Heidelberg and controlled the Neckar valley.

zwinger.fait: This Baroque palace in Dresden, once a venue for the festivities of the kings of Saxony, has become a museum; its name refers to the space between two ramparts of a fortress.

lorelei.fait: This rock rises 132 meters above the Rhine. According to legend, a nymph lures sailors there with her songs to their doom.

bastei.fait: Its name means “bastion.” This rock formation in Saxon Switzerland, southeast of Dresden, towers 194 meters above the Elbe.

weisswurst.fait: This white Bavarian sausage made of veal and pork, seasoned with parsley and lemon, is eaten only in the morning, before the stroke of noon.

foret-noire-gateau.fait: Its German name means “Black Forest cherry cake”: a cocoa sponge cake soaked in kirsch, filled with whipped cream and cherries.

stollen.fait: This traditional cake from Germany and Alsace, also called “Christmas roll,” has very old origins.

coucou.fait: Its chime imitates the call of the cuckoo. The concept is said to have been created in 1738 by Franz Ketterer, in a village in the Black Forest.

strandkorb.fait: This “beach basket” is a hooded chair that protects from wind, sun and sand on the beaches of the North Sea and the Baltic.

schultute.fait: This cone filled with candy, toys and school supplies is given by parents to their children when they start primary school.

carnaval-cologne.fait: Its participants consider it the fifth season of the year; the season officially begins on November 11 at 11:11 a.m.

schwebebahn.fait: Opened in 1901, this suspended monorail is the oldest in the world; it runs for 13.3 km, partly twelve meters above a river.

chutes-rhin.fait: At 23 meters high and 150 wide, these falls downstream of Schaffhausen have the most powerful flow in Europe.

jungfraujoch.fait: This pass in the Bernese Alps, at an altitude of 3,463 meters, is often called the “Top of Europe”; it is home to the highest railway station in Europe.

jet-eau.fait: This 140-meter vertical water jet, in Geneva's harbor, has been one of the city's main tourist attractions since 1891.

zytglogge.fait: This clock tower in Bern bears a 16th-century astronomical clock, with a clock jack and a carillon.

tete-de-moine.fait: This cheese made from raw whole cow's milk is unique in the way it is eaten: in rosettes, produced with a “girolle.”

hornuss.fait: In this traditional sport, players use a “whip” to strike a puck whose name means “hornet,” which the opposing team must intercept with wooden boards.

lutte-culotte.fait: This sport, also called Schwingen, is practiced outdoors in rings covered with sawdust; it is described as a national sport.

carnaval-bale.fait: It begins at 4 a.m. on the Monday after Ash Wednesday with a parade of lanterns, and lasts exactly 72 hours.

fete-vignerons.fait: This festival takes place in Vevey only once per generation: the interval between two editions has varied from 14 to 28 years. The most recent was in 2019.

hallstatt.fait: This municipality in Upper Austria lies on the Hallstättersee; “Hall,” an element of probably Celtic origin found in Germanic place names, indicates salt mining.

abbaye-melk.fait: Founded in the 11th century, this Benedictine abbey overlooks the Danube; its Baroque buildings are the work of the architect Jakob Prandtauer.

hohensalzburg.fait: At 250 meters long and 150 wide, this fortress perched atop a mountain in Salzburg is one of the largest medieval castles in Europe.

hofburg.fait: This palace, the largest in Vienna, has more than 2,600 rooms spread over 18 wings; the Habsburgs lived there for more than 600 years.

apfelstrudel.fait: This traditional pastry is a strudel filled with apples (“Apfel” in German), walnuts, almonds, cinnamon and raisins.

kaiserschmarrn.fait: This sweet main dish is made from a pancake batter lightened with beaten egg whites; it owes much of its fame to tourism in Vienna and in ski resorts.

ecole-espagnole.fait: Despite its name, this school is in Vienna; only Lipizzaner stallions are trained there, and they perform in the Winter Riding School.

concert-nouvel-an.fait: Given on the morning of New Year's Day by the Vienna Philharmonic in the Golden Hall of the Musikverein, it is broadcast in 90 countries.

grand-place.fait: Lined by the town hall and the Guildhalls, it was, for Victor Hugo, one of the most beautiful squares in the world.

beffroi-bruges.fait: At 83 meters high, this medieval tower has been leaning slightly for more than four centuries; 366 steps must be climbed to reach the top.

butte-lion.fait: This mound topped by a colossal lion was erected in 1826 on the site of the Battle of Waterloo; the animal faces France.

galeries-saint-hubert.fait: Opened in 1847 in Brussels, these three shopping arcades covered with a wide glass roof form the city's oldest pedestrian area.

waterzooi.fait: This simmered one-pot soup, made with chicken or fish, originates from the city of Ghent; it is spelled “waterzooi” in Dutch.

cuberdon.fait: This cone-shaped candy is made with sugar, gum arabic and gelatin; its flavor is most often raspberry.

lambic.fait: This spontaneously fermented beer, with no fizz or foam, is the base for gueuze and kriek; it is produced near Brussels.

ommegang.fait: Its name means “walking around” in Dutch. Since 1930, this procession has reenacted the entry of Emperor Charles V into Brussels in 1549.

ducasse-mons.fait: It is often called the “Doudou,” after a traditional tune played during the festival, which takes place every year on Trinity weekend.

keukenhof.fait: Covering 32 hectares, it is the largest flower garden in the world; in 2023, it received 1.4 million visitors between mid-March and mid-May.

zaanse-schans.fait: This inhabited neighborhood brings together historic wooden houses and windmills, some of which were moved there to be preserved.

canaux-amsterdam.fait: This network of more than 100 km is crossed by some 1,500 bridges and links about 90 islands; its four main canals date from the 17th century.

giethoorn.fait: This village of 2,765 inhabitants in 2019 attracts several hundred thousand tourists every year with its image of the Dutch countryside.

gouda.fait: This cheese takes its name from a town in South Holland where it was traditionally sold; its best season runs from May to October.

poffertjes.fait: These small, fluffy pancakes made with yeast and buckwheat flour are served with powdered sugar and butter.

stamppot.fait: This dish combines mashed potatoes with vegetables such as kale or sauerkraut; it is usually served with sausages or meat in gravy.

advocaat.fait: This creamy liqueur of Dutch origin is made from egg yolk, sugar and alcohol; its taste is slightly reminiscent of almond.

chateau-vianden.fait: This fortified castle stands in the town of Vianden, in the northeast of the country, and is part of the German-Luxembourg Nature Park.

pont-adolphe.fait: This bridge spans the Pétrusse valley; since its renovation, a footbridge for cyclists and pedestrians has been suspended beneath its deck.

mullerthal.fait: This hilly region is nicknamed “Little Switzerland,” even though its highest point is only 414 meters; visitors climb sandstone rocks there.

procession-echternach.fait: The last of its kind in Europe, this Whit Tuesday procession moves forward by hopping in rows to the basilica that houses the tomb of Saint Willibrord.

schueberfouer.fait: This funfair lasts three weeks, from late August to early September, and attracts an average of nearly 2 million visitors; 2010 saw its 670th edition.

judd-mat-gaardebounen.fait: This dish from the cuisine of Luxembourg consists of smoked pork collar, served with broad beans.

hal-saflieni.fait: Discoveries made in this prehistoric hypogeum have helped define a short phase of the Late Neolithic in the prehistory of Malta.

co-cathedrale-saint-jean.fait: It was built between 1573 and 1577 in Valletta by the Knights of the Order of St. John of Jerusalem, to the plans of a military architect.

mdina.fait: With about 300 inhabitants, it is the least populated locality in Malta, hence its nickname, the “Silent City.”

luzzu.fait: This brightly painted fishing boat bears a pair of eyes on its bow, believed to protect it from the hazards of the sea and to bring good fishing.

pastizzi.fait: This small triangular puff-pastry snack is filled with fresh ricotta; there is also a version filled with mushy peas.

ftira.fait: This bread baked in a wood-fired oven, topped with potatoes, tomatoes, anchovies and olives, was originally the country meal of the shepherds of Gozo.

petra-tou-romiou.fait: According to legend, it is here, near Paphos, that Aphrodite was born; yet the Greek name of the place means “Rock of the Greek.”

kykkos.fait: Founded in the late 11th century by a Byzantine emperor, this monastery has suffered several fires: its buildings date mostly from the 18th century.

choirokoitia.fait: This ancient village built on the slopes of a hill is one of the best-preserved Neolithic sites in the eastern Mediterranean.

halloumi.fait: Known as “hellim” in Turkish, this cheese has had protected designation of origin status at the European level since 2021.

commandaria.fait: This amber-colored sweet wine is made at the foot of the Troodos Mountains from grapes whose bunches are dried in the sun.

zivania.fait: This colorless grape brandy, made from two grape varieties endemic to the island, is generally 45 percent alcohol.

casino-monte-carlo.fait: The current Belle Époque building was designed in 1879 by Charles Garnier; a first casino had opened on this site in 1863.

musee-oceanographique.fait: Built into the cliff face to a height of 85 meters and opened in 1910, it was directed by Commander Cousteau from 1957 to 1988.

palais-princier.fait: Built in 1191 as a fortress of the Republic of Genoa, it has been the residence of the Grimaldi family since the late 13th century.

circuit-monaco.fait: Laid out over 3.34 km of the city's streets, this temporary circuit is the slowest in the Formula 1 World Championship.

barbajuan.fait: This specialty resembles a fried ravioli; there are variations made with artichokes or squash.

festival-cirque.fait: Created in 1974 by Prince Rainier III, this festival takes place every January and awards “Golden Clowns” as well as silver and bronze ones.

casa-de-la-vall.fait: This “House of the Valleys” is the historic seat of the General Council, the country's legislative assembly, which has been housed in a new building since 2011.

madriu.fait: This glacial valley in the Pyrenees is the only site in the Principality of Andorra listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

lac-engolasters.fait: This lake, called “estany d'Engolasters” in Catalan, is in the parish of Encamp, near the capital, Andorra la Vella.

pont-margineda.fait: This single-arch stone bridge, with a span of nine and a half meters, is the largest medieval bridge in the principality; it crosses the Valira.

cesta.fait: This peak of Monte Titano bears one of the three towers that defended the city and that appear in stylized form on the coat of arms of the republic.

montale.fait: It is one of the three summits of Monte Titano, which overlook the capital; each bears a tower that ensured the defense of the city.

palazzo-pubblico-sm.fait: This town hall is also the seat of government: it houses the Captains Regent and the Great and General Council of the Republic.

basilique-saint-pierre.fait: Its construction began in 1506 and was completed in 1626; according to Catholic tradition, the tomb of Saint Peter lies beneath the high altar.

chapelle-sixtine.fait: It is here that the cardinals gathered in conclave elect the new pope, beneath the vault covered with frescoes by Michelangelo between 1508 and 1512.

place-saint-pierre.fait: This Baroque esplanade serves as the forecourt of the basilica; crowds gather there for major celebrations, such as the Urbi et Orbi blessing.

garde-suisse.fait: Created in 1506 by order of Pope Julius II, this army of 135 soldiers recruits only Swiss Catholic citizens at least 174 centimeters tall.

pieta.fait: This marble group, sculpted between 1498 and 1499, shows the Virgin holding the body of Christ on her lap; it is in St. Peter's Basilica.

papamobile.fait: This vehicle allows the pope to be better seen by the faithful; Mercedes-Benz delivered its first car to the Vatican in 1930.

sedia-gestatoria.fait: This portable throne, whose name means “carrying chair,” was used to carry the pope so that the faithful could see him better during ceremonies.

bigos.fait: This cabbage stew, considered the Polish national dish, is usually served the day after Christmas.

zurek.fait: This sour soup made from fermented rye flour is finished with smoked bacon bits or hard-boiled eggs cut in half.

oscypek.fait: This sheep's milk cheese, to which cow's milk is added, has had protected designation of origin status since 2008.

paczki.fait: These round doughnuts filled with strawberry or rose jam are, in Poland, the pastry associated with Fat Thursday.

basilique-sainte-marie.fait: From its tallest tower, a trumpet call, the Hejnał, sounds every hour; national radio has broadcast it since 1928.

smigus-dyngus.fait: On Easter Monday, tradition calls for splashing loved ones with water or symbolically whipping them with willow branches.

saint-guy.fait: Located inside Prague Castle, this Gothic cathedral is the largest and most important church in the country.

place-venceslas.fait: Once called the Horse Market, this square in Prague took its current name in 1848; the equestrian statue of the country's patron saint dominates it.

balaton.fait: This freshwater lake is the largest in Central Europe; it is an important fishing and tourism area, and Siófok is one of the main towns around it.

langos.fait: This flatbread fried in oil is eaten on the street, at fairs and festivals, topped with cheese and sour cream.

halaszle.fait: This soup made from different kinds of fish and seasoned with paprika is a specialty of the south of the country, from the Szeged and Pécs regions.

busojaras.fait: This folk festival in Mohács, whose name means “Busó walking,” takes place in winter, on the Sunday before Ash Wednesday.

brennivin.fait: This potato brandy flavored with caraway is drunk ice-cold; Icelanders nickname it “svarti dauði,” the “black death.”

bunad.fait: This national costume is worn on special occasions: family ceremonies, celebrations and especially the national holiday, on May 17.

rakfisk.fait: This traditional dish from the east of the country consists of trout salted and fermented for two to three months, which is eaten raw.

bateau-oseberg.fait: This burial ship was discovered in a burial mound and excavated in 1904-1905; it is displayed at the Viking Ship Museum in Oslo.

aebleskiver.fait: Their name means “apple slices” in Danish, but these sphere-shaped pancakes usually no longer contain apples.

char-trundholm.fait: This bronze object discovered in 1902, dated to around 1400 BC, is the oldest known depiction of a sun chariot in Europe.

blini.fait: Its name comes from the Russian “blin”: this thick flatbread, a kind of large pancake, is often served at rituals or religious festivals.

pelmeni.fait: This dish from the Ural region generally consists of thin cooked dough filled with minced meat.

chapka.fait: This fur hat, whose flaps cover the ears and the nape of the neck, is actually called an ushanka, from the Russian “ushi,” “ears.”

bolchoi.fait: Its name means “Grand Theater”: this Moscow venue, depicted on the 100-ruble banknote, can hold up to 1,800 spectators.

place-rouge.fait: This square marks the center of Moscow: it is bordered on the west by the Kremlin, and St. Basil's Cathedral stands to the south.

transsiberien.fait: This railway links Moscow to Vladivostok over more than nine thousand kilometers; the journey takes a week on the fastest train.

oeuf-faberge.fait: Alexander III and Nicholas II of Russia gave the most famous of these precious objects to their wives for Easter; of the 54 made, six have been lost.

kokochnik.fait: This tall women's headdress, pointed or rounded, is worn with the sarafan; the front is sometimes decorated with pearls.

valenki.fait: These unstitched felt boots protect the feet from the cold, but also, in industrial settings, from intense heat.

boeuf-stroganov.fait: This recipe from Russian cuisine, created by the French chef André Dupont, is a beef stew served with a sour cream sauce.

gamla-stan.fait: Its name means “old town” in Swedish: it is the historical and geographical heart of Stockholm.

drottningholm.fait: Located on an island in Lake Mälaren, west of Stockholm, this palace has been the residence of King Carl XVI Gustaf and Queen Silvia since 1981.

nyckelharpa.fait: This bowed instrument from the Uppland region is also called a “keyed fiddle”; its earliest depictions date from the 14th century.

kottbullar.fait: These meatballs are usually eaten with mashed potatoes and lingonberry jam; the Ikea chain has popularized them around the world.

smorgasbord.fait: This buffet, whose name means “bread and butter table,” became known internationally at the 1939 New York World's Fair.

bouc-gavle.fait: This giant straw Christmas goat, first erected in 1966, is most often destroyed, usually by fire, before its scheduled dismantling date.

kanelbulle.fait: This cinnamon bun, which appeared in Sweden in the 1920s, has its own holiday, celebrated every year on October 4.

pierre-rok.fait: This stone bears the longest known runic inscription, an enigmatic 9th-century text often considered the first work of Swedish literature.

rouge-falun.fait: The pigment in this paint comes from the slag of the Falun copper mine; it often covers traditional wooden houses.

sauna.fait: People take a dry heat bath there at 70 to 100 °C; the city of Tampere is considered the “sauna capital of the world.”

kantele.fait: This plucked string instrument, traditional in Finland and Karelia, has close relatives such as the Estonian kannel and the Russian gusli.

cathedrale-senat.fait: Before independence in 1917, this Lutheran cathedral in Helsinki was called St. Nicholas' Church; more than 350,000 people visit it every year.

suomenlinna.fait: This sea fortress built on eight islands of Helsinki was begun in 1748 by Sweden to protect itself from the Russian Empire.

village-pere-noel.fait: This tourist destination dedicated to Santa Claus is located on the outskirts of Rovaniemi, capital of Finnish Lapland.

puukko.fait: This small traditional knife, whose blade has a curved cutting edge and a flat back, is made to be worn on the belt.

pesapallo.fait: This sport similar to baseball, invented in the 1920s by Lauri Pihkala, was a demonstration sport at the 1952 Helsinki Olympic Games.

sahti.fait: This fermented drink, whose name comes from the Germanic “saft,” “juice,” is a traditional specialty protected in Europe.

kalakukko.fait: This dish from Savonia and Karelia, made with a loaf of bread that is usually round, is a complete meal in itself.

porter-de-femme.fait: In this sport founded in 1992 in Sonkajärvi, a man carries a woman over an obstacle course; the first regional prize is usually the woman's weight in beer.

karjalanpiirakka.fait: This traditional dish from the Karelia region, also called Karelian pie or pirog, is now found all over Finland.

toompea.fait: According to legend, this limestone hill in the center of Tallinn is a burial mound raised over Kalev's grave by his grieving wife, Linda.

lahemaa.fait: Established in 1971, 70 km east of Tallinn, this park of more than 72,500 hectares is the oldest and largest of the country's six national parks.

kadriorg.fait: This palace in Tallinn was built by Peter the Great starting in the summer of 1718; work on the main building was completed in 1725.

turaida.fait: This brick castle is what makes the village of Turaida famous, along with Gutmanis Cave and the legend of the Rose of Turaida.

baume-noir.fait: This traditional bitter from Riga owes its intense black color to burnt caramel, which the producers make themselves.

jani.fait: This midsummer festival officially falls on June 24; the eve, June 23, is called Līgo or “Herb Day.”

gauja.fait: Established in 1973, this national park is the largest and oldest in the country, and the largest in the Baltic states; it has several castles and ski slopes.

cesis.fait: This fortified castle, the best preserved of the Teutonic Order in Latvia, still looks as it did in the 15th century.

trois-freres.fait: Called “Trīs brāļi” in Latvian, these three buildings in Riga form the oldest residential complex in the city.

sklandrausis.fait: This rye-dough tartlet, filled with mashed potatoes and carrots, is usually eaten cold, with tea or milk.

colline-croix.fait: At this pilgrimage site near Šiauliai, the first crosses were placed in the 14th century; pilgrims have brought many more.

tour-gediminas.fait: The only remaining part of Vilnius Castle, this tower was depicted on the national currency, the litas, until December 31, 2014.

porte-aurore.fait: This gate in the historic center of Vilnius, with its icon of the Virgin, is a Catholic pilgrimage site visited by residents and tourists.

bandoura.fait: This string instrument descends from the kobza, which dates from the 14th century; it should not be confused with the bandurria, a Spanish mandolin.

saint-michel-dome-or.fait: This monastery in Kyiv, a model of Ukrainian Baroque, stands at the edge of a steep rock face, on the west bank of the Dnipro.

bran.fait: Nicknamed “Dracula's Castle,” it is associated with Vlad III the Impaler, who in fact probably never stayed there.

peles.fait: Located near Sinaia, this castle was built in ten years, from 1873 to 1883; the fitting-out continued until 1914.

voronet.fait: This monastery in Bukovina was built in 3 months and 3 weeks, in 1488, by order of Stephen the Great, following a victory over the Ottomans.

calusari.fait: These dancers perform the căluș, the “horse-man dance”; the word comes from the Romanian “cal,” “horse,” derived from the Latin caballus.

alexandre-nevski.fait: This Neo-Byzantine Orthodox cathedral in Sofia has five naves and three altars and can hold nearly 10,000 worshippers.

nessebar.fait: This historic town is perched on a rocky peninsula that juts out into the Black Sea; its ancient Greek name was Messembria.

banitsa.fait: For New Year's, tradition calls for slipping good-luck charms into this savory pastry made of phyllo dough, eggs, yogurt and cheese.

studenica.fait: This 12th-century Orthodox monastery is the largest and richest in the country; its two main churches are built of white marble.

davolja-varos.fait: Its name means “Devil's Town”: this place in southern Serbia is both a region and a natural monument.

pljeskavica.fait: This burger, considered a national dish, combines lamb, beef and grilled onions, served hot in a somun, a thick pita bread.

arenes-pula.fait: This Roman amphitheater, also called the Pula Colosseum, stands in Istria in an exceptional state of preservation.

licitar.fait: These gingerbread cookies from the north of the country are most often heart-shaped; some are used as decorations and are not edible.

klapa.fait: This a cappella singing choir, traditionally male, comes from Dalmatia; its name literally means “group of people.”

lac-bled.fait: This lake of glacial origin, on the edge of the Julian Alps 55 kilometers from Ljubljana, is one of the country's main tourist destinations.

postojna.fait: It was in this karst cave that the first specimens of most groups of cave-dwelling fauna were discovered.

predjama.fait: This 13th-century castle was built into a cliff face, inside a huge cave, 123 meters above a chasm, to make it hard to reach.

triglav.fait: This 2,864-meter peak, whose name means “Three Heads,” appears on the country's flag and on its 50-euro-cent coins.

prekmurska-gibanica.fait: This pastry from the east of the country takes its name from the Prekmurje region and from its structure of stacked layers.

bojnice.fait: This medieval hilltop castle owes its romantic style to the Pálffy family, who owned it from 1643 to 1918.

orava.fait: Many scenes from the 1922 film Nosferatu were shot in this 13th-century castle overlooking the Orava River.

fujara.fait: This instrument, typical of Slovak music, has been part of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity since 2005.

halusky.fait: This national dish combines pieces of boiled potato dough, similar to gnocchi, with bryndza, a soft sheep's milk cheese.

vlkolinec.fait: This village, founded in the 14th century, has kept its typical wooden houses; its name probably comes from the Slovak word “vlk,” meaning “wolf.”

stari-most.fait: Its name means “the Old Bridge”: this 16th-century structure links the two parts of Mostar, from one bank of the Neretva to the other.

bascarsija.fait: Its name comes from Turkish and refers to the main marketplace: this Ottoman quarter of Sarajevo, dating back to the 16th century, housed the shops.

stecak.fait: The country is said to have 60,000 of these monumental medieval tombstones, which appeared in the 12th century; 10,000 more have been found in three neighboring countries.

pocitelj.fait: The urban and historical ensemble of this village of 869 inhabitants is on the country's list of national monuments.

gjirokaster.fait: This city in the south of the country, 142 km from Tirana, has been on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 2005.

butrint.fait: This archaeological site near Sarandë is that of a city once called Bouthroton, “rumor of cattle” in Ancient Greek.

qeleshe.fait: This white felt cap is part of the Albanian folk costume; its height varies from one region to another.

syri-kalter.fait: In this spring in the south of the country, the light blue water can be seen to a depth of more than fifty meters.

xhubleta.fait: This women's costume consists of a wide, wavy, bell-shaped skirt worn with a bodice, an apron, shoulder straps and a scarf.

pont-pierre-skopje.fait: Built in the 15th century by the Ottomans, this pedestrian-only bridge has become the symbol of Skopje and appears on its coat of arms.

tavce-gravce.fait: Its name means “beans in a pan”: this dish, considered the national dish, is served in an earthenware vessel.

kokino.fait: According to archaeologists, this Bronze Age site may have served as a sacred mountain and an astronomical observatory.

stobi.fait: This ancient city held a key position controlling the Vardar valley; it is thought to have been abandoned toward the end of the 6th century.

saint-naum.fait: Founded in the 10th century by Saint Naum on the shore of Lake Ohrid, this monastery lost many of its buildings in a fire in 1875.

sveti-stefan.fait: This village, whose name means “Saint Stephen,” includes a small island now connected to the mainland by a narrow tombolo.

ostrog.fait: This monastery set into a cliff is a place of pilgrimage renowned for miraculous healings; it keeps relics of Saint Basil.

durmitor.fait: This park includes the Tara River gorge, 80 km long and 1,300 meters deep, the second-largest canyon in the world after the Grand Canyon.

milestii-mici.fait: At 18 km from Chișinău, some shafts of an underground mining site serve as cellars for storing the wines that bear the commune's name.

soroca.fait: This late medieval defensive structure stands on the banks of the Nistru, a river better known by its Russian name, Dniester.

nativite-chisinau.fait: This Orthodox cathedral stands in the middle of a park in Chișinău, opposite the National Assembly; it is one of the city's most important monuments.

cricova.fait: This town 15 kilometers north of Chișinău is famous for its wine cellars, which make it a popular attraction for tourists.

mir.fait: Begun in the 1520s in the Gothic style, this castle was bequeathed around 1569 to a Radziwiłł, who decided to complete it in the Renaissance style.

eglise-rouge-minsk.fait: This Catholic church dedicated to Saints Simon and Helena can be seen from all over central Minsk, since it stands on Independence Square.

sophie-polotsk.fait: Built between 1030 and 1060, this cathedral imitated those of Novgorod and Kyiv; the building is now secularized.
