piernik.fait: This pastry made with flour, honey and spices such as cinnamon or ginger has been part of the country's culinary heritage since the Middle Ages.

svickova.fait: Its name means “beef tenderloin” in Czech; the meat is served with a cream and root-vegetable sauce, bread dumplings and cranberries.

thorramatur.fait: This selection of traditional dishes, such as fermented shark or grilled sheep's heads, is eaten mainly in January and February, during the month of Þorri.

huile-argan.fait: Extracted from the kernels of the argan tree, this oil has been protected since 2009 by a European Union geographical indication, at Morocco's request.

erg-chebbi.fait: Better known as the Merzouga dunes, this erg, 22 km long and 5 km wide, has dunes that rise as high as 150 m.

tanjia.fait: This meat dish from Marrakesh, reputedly prepared by men, cooks for four hours in a clay pot placed in the ashes of the neighborhood's wood-fired oven.

gnaoua.fait: Added in 2019 to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list, this music is celebrated in Essaouira, where a festival draws thousands of visitors every year.

notre-dame-afrique.fait: Consecrated in 1872, this basilica overlooks the sea from a 124 m promontory; its apse faces southwest rather than east.

tombeau-chretienne.fait: This ancient funerary monument is a circular structure 60.9 meters in diameter, ringed by sixty Ionic columns; its nickname is a misnomer.

hoggar.fait: This massif in the central Sahara is home to Tahat, the country's highest peak at 2,918 meters; its Tuareg name means “the place where the nobles live.”

chedda.fait: This bridal costume from Tlemcen, which brings together pieces from various periods such as the caftan, has been on the Intangible Cultural Heritage list since 2012.

sebiba.fait: This competitive celebration, which combines dance, song and traditional costumes, is practiced by two communities of the Djanet oasis.

ahellil.fait: This musical and poetic genre of the Zenata of Gourara is performed at collective ceremonies, during religious and secular festivals.

kalb-el-louz.fait: Originally from Constantine, this pastry, one of the most popular in the country, is very widely eaten on Ramadan evenings, with mint tea or coffee.

dougga.fait: UNESCO sees it as the “best-preserved small Roman town in North Africa”; the site covers 75 hectares, in the middle of the countryside.

bardo.fait: Housed since 1888 in a former beylical palace in Tunis, this museum holds one of the largest collections of Roman mosaics in the world.

lablabi.fait: This popular dish made with chickpeas, garlic, cumin or caraway and harissa takes its name from the Turkish leblebi, meaning “roasted chickpeas.”

harissa.fait: This red chili paste originated in Tunisia; the know-how associated with it has been on the Intangible Cultural Heritage list since 2022.

machmoum.fait: This bouquet of flowers is made in Tunisia from jasmine, through several stages of production.

mezoued.fait: This traditional North African wind instrument, widespread mainly in Tunisia, gave its name to a form of Tunisian popular music.

bambalouni.fait: This sweet ring-shaped doughnut, fried in oil, is eaten sprinkled with sugar, ideally in the afternoon around snack time.

poterie-sejnane.fait: Passed down from grandmother to granddaughter, this craft relies on entirely manual shaping, without a wheel, and on natural materials.

karnak.fait: Developed over more than 2,000 years by successive pharaohs, this complex covers more than 2 km²; it is the largest religious complex of antiquity.

temple-louxor.fait: Dedicated to the worship of Amun and built mostly under the 18th and 19th Dynasties, this temple was partly turned into a military camp in Roman times.

pyramide-djeser.fait: Designed by the architect Imhotep at Saqqara, this royal tomb was the first to take the shape of a pyramid.

colosses-memnon.fait: These two monumental statues are the last remains of the temple of Amenhotep III; one of them cracked during an earthquake in 27 BC.

temple-hatchepsout.fait: Built entirely of limestone, this temple at Deir el-Bahari replaces pylons with porticoes at the entrance to each terrace.

canal-suez.fait: Dug between 1859 and 1869 under the direction of Ferdinand de Lesseps, it is 193.3 km long and spares ships from sailing around Africa.

masque-toutankhamon.fait: This gold mask was discovered on October 28, 1925, when the British archaeologist Howard Carter opened the pharaoh's sarcophagus.

papyrus.fait: This writing material made from the stems of a plant is an Egyptian invention about 5,000 years old, used until the 11th century.

vase-canope.fait: In ancient Egypt, these jars, four in number, held the embalmed organs of the deceased and were placed near the sarcophagus.

barque-solaire.fait: Found dismantled in 1954 in a pit at the foot of the pyramid, this twenty-ton boat is made of cedar of Lebanon.

senet.fait: This board game, the most widely played among the ancient Egyptians of the New Kingdom, has existed since the Predynastic period.

leptis-magna.fait: This city was one of the important towns of the Carthaginian Republic before coming under the authority of Rome at the end of the Third Punic War.

sabratha.fait: In antiquity, this city formed, with Oea and Leptis Magna, the trio of cities that gave Tripolitania its name.

cyrene.fait: This city was the oldest and most important of the five Greek colonies of Cyrenaica, a region of which it was the capital.

ghadames.fait: Nicknamed the “Pearl of the Desert,” this oasis is one of the earliest fortified towns of the Sahara; its architecture is designed to withstand the extreme climate.

tadrart-acacus.fait: This massif in the southwest of the country holds a major collection of rock art depicting people, animals, horses and later dromedaries.

waw-an-namus.fait: Its name means “oasis of mosquitoes”: this Saharan caldera contains a volcanic cone and small lakes.

chinguetti.fait: This town in the Adrar is cut in two by a dry wadi: on one side the old town, which is gradually being buried by sand, on the other the new one.

ouadane.fait: This town in the Adrar region, northeast of Chinguetti, has an old town listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

oualata.fait: Like those of Ouadane, Chinguetti and Tichitt, the fortified village of this southeastern town has been a World Heritage Site since 1996.

richat.fait: This circular structure about 50 km in diameter can only be fully seen from space; it is now seen as the remains of a giant collapsed volcano.

banc-arguin.fait: Established in 1976, this 12,000 km² park, shared between the Atlantic Ocean and the Sahara Desert, covers a third of the country's coastline.

mosquee-bleue.fait: Built between 1609 and 1616 in Istanbul, it owes its name to the mainly blue tiles of its interior walls and has six minarets.

topkapi.fait: The residence of the Ottoman sultans from 1465 to 1853, this Istanbul palace bears a name meaning “Cannon Gate Palace.”

grand-bazar.fait: Opened in 1455, this covered market in Istanbul has 65 indoor streets and nearly 4,000 shops.

tour-galata.fait: This cylindrical medieval structure overlooks an Istanbul district north of the Golden Horn and houses a museum.

celsus.fait: Built between 117 and 125 in Ephesus, this Roman public library also served as a mausoleum for the senator whose name it bears.

gobekli-tepe.fait: Occupied from about 9300 to 7500 BC, this prehistoric site is known for its carved T-shaped pillars, which represent stylized humans.

troie.fait: This ancient city, at the center of the stories of the Iliad, is now located on the hill of Hisarlik, at the entrance to the Hellespont.

loukoum.fait: This confection, born in the Ottoman Empire, is a paste of starch and flavored sugar, dusted with powdered sugar and sometimes filled with nuts.

doner.fait: Born in the 19th century in Bursa, this dish takes its name from the Turkish verb dönmek, “to turn”: the meat cooks on a vertical spit that rotates on itself.

raki.fait: This anise-flavored grape brandy is the country's national drink; its name derives from the Arabic araq.

simit.fait: This circular bread with sesame seeds is often sold on the street by vendors who carry it on a cart or on their heads.

dondurma.fait: This beaten ice cream contains salep and mastic; it is said to come from the city of Maraş, whose name it sometimes bears.

karagoz.fait: This shadow theater bears the name of its hero, an illiterate common man whose name means “black eye,” facing the learned Hacivat.

iznik.fait: Produced from the mid-15th century in the town of İznik, ancient Nicaea, this pottery was long called “Rhodes ware.”

persepolis.fait: Founded in 521 BC by order of Darius I, this capital of the Achaemenid Persian Empire was partly destroyed by Alexander the Great.

naghch-e-djahan.fait: Built in the early 17th century by Shah Abbas I in Isfahan, this square measuring 560 by 160 meters is one of the largest in the world.

si-o-se-pol.fait: Its name means “bridge of thirty-three arches”: built around 1608 in Isfahan, this two-level bridge also serves as a dam on the river.

badgir.fait: Its Persian name means “wind catcher”: this element of traditional architecture creates natural ventilation in buildings.

arg-e-bam.fait: This citadel city on the Silk Road is the largest adobe complex in the world; an earthquake almost completely destroyed it in 2003.

palais-golestan.fait: This former royal palace of the Qajar dynasty is in Tehran; its Persian name means “palace of the flower garden.”

tchelo-kabab.fait: Considered the national dish, it combines steamed rice with a kebab; it was probably created under the Qajar dynasty.

faloodeh.fait: This frozen dessert made with rice vermicelli, lemon juice and rosewater was originally prepared in the Shiraz region.

gabbeh.fait: This small rug with a very thick pile is hand-knotted, almost exclusively by women of nomadic tribes; its Persian name means “raw.”

ziggourat-ur.fait: Built at the beginning of the 21st century BC, it is one of the best-preserved ziggurats in Mesopotamia; its remains were excavated in the 1920s and 1930s.

babylone.fait: This ancient city on the banks of the Euphrates reached its peak in the 6th century BC; its ziggurat may have inspired the myth of the Tower of Babel.

samarra.fait: This spiral minaret belongs to a 9th-century mosque that was for centuries the largest in Islamic civilization.

hatra.fait: The capital of a kingdom allied with the Parthian Empire, this city flourished mainly in the 2nd century and withstood several sieges by the armies of the Roman Empire.

citadelle-erbil.fait: The oldest traces of occupation of this tell date back at least to the 5th millennium BC; it rises 25 to 32 meters above the plain.

mudhif.fait: This large ceremonial reed house is built by the Marsh Arabs in the south of the country; a local sheikh pays for it and maintains it for his guests.

samoon.fait: This yeast bread baked in traditional stone ovens is one of the most popular in the country; yogurt with live cultures often serves as its starter.

baalbek.fait: The Romans left three giant temples there, including that of Bacchus, one of the best preserved in the Greco-Roman world.

jeita.fait: This system of two caves can be visited by boat in its lower part; the largest chamber reaches 120 meters in height.

byblos.fait: The Greeks gave it this name because papyrus, búblos in Ancient Greek, was imported into Greece from this city, which is said to have been founded around 5000 BC.

cedres-dieu.fait: This forest is one of the last remnants of the ancient cedar forest of Mount Lebanon; it has been a World Heritage Site since 1998.

raouche.fait: These two limestone islets washed by the Mediterranean rise off the Corniche of Beirut; the site is also called the Pigeons' Grotto.

palmyre.fait: This ancient city stood near a desert oasis, 210 km northeast of Damascus; the site has been a World Heritage Site since 1980.

krak-chevaliers.fait: The Knights Hospitaller held this castle from 1142 to 1271, when it was conquered by Sultan Baybars after 129 years of invincibility.

omeyyades.fait: This great mosque was built in Damascus between 706 and 715 by the Umayyad caliph Al-Walid I.

citadelle-alep.fait: This fortified medieval palace, built on a tell overlooking the city center, is recognizable by its imposing fortified entrance.

savon-alep.fait: This soap is made from olive oil and contains laurel berry oil; it bears the name of its city of origin.

piment-alep.fait: Its pods turn burgundy as they ripen, then are semi-dried, seeded and crushed; it owes its name to a city on the Silk Road.

hegra.fait: Nicknamed the second Petra for its rock-cut tombs, this Nabataean site became in 2008 the country's first World Heritage Site.

kaaba.fait: Its Arabic name means “the cube”: this building covered with black silk cloth is the holiest site in Islam.

masjid-nabawi.fait: The original mosque, built by Muhammad in Medina, was only a small part of the present building, enlarged by the caliphs and then by the kingdom.

kabsa.fait: This dish of rice and mutton or chicken is seasoned with a blend of spices: cumin, coriander, cinnamon, cardamom, cloves and dried lime.

socotra.fait: This island in the Arabian Sea, 133 kilometers long, is home to some 700 species found nowhere else in the world.

dar-al-hajar.fait: Built in the 1920s on a 50 m high rock, this palace near Sanaa was the summer residence of Imam Yahya.

janbiya.fait: This dagger with a short, curved blade is worn on the belt with traditional clothing; it tends to be more a symbol than a weapon.

zabid.fait: One of the oldest cities in the country, it was its capital between the 13th and 15th centuries; its university was then prestigious.

saltah.fait: This meat stew topped with fenugreek froth is often eaten with flatbread, which serves as a spoon to scoop up the food.

massada.fait: These ancient palaces and fortifications, built by Herod the Great, are perched on top of an isolated mountain in the Judaean Desert.

ville-blanche.fait: This ensemble forms the center of the new city of Tel Aviv; UNESCO added it to the World Heritage List in 2003.

makhtesh-ramon.fait: This erosion cirque in the Negev Desert is 40 km long and 500 m deep; its Hebrew name means “the Ramon crater.”

cesaree.fait: This ancient city on the Mediterranean coast preserves the ruins of Herod the Great's royal capital and many Roman and medieval monuments.

garni.fait: The only surviving Hellenistic Greek temple in the country, it collapsed in the earthquake of 1679 and was rebuilt between 1969 and 1975.

khatchkar.fait: Its name means “cross stone”: this stele carved with one or more crosses is generally 1.5 to 2 m high.

lac-sevan.fait: The country's largest lake, this “true inland sea” covers 1,400 km², two and a half times the size of Lake Geneva.

tatev.fait: This monastery in the Goris region, 316 km from Yerevan, is the most important monument in the south of the country.

khor-virap.fait: This monastery is in the Ararat region, not far from the capital Yerevan; it is overlooked by Mount Ararat.

vardavar.fait: During this traditional festival, also called Vartavar, people of all ages drench one another with water.

khorovats.fait: This barbecued meat skewer, made with lamb, pork, beef or chicken, is usually reserved for festive occasions.

chirvanchahs.fait: Built in Baku in the 15th century, this palace of the rulers of Shirvan includes a mosque from 1441, baths and a mausoleum.

gobustan.fait: About 65 km from Baku, this reserve holds some 6,000 rock drawings 5,000 to 20,000 years old, as well as mud volcanoes.

ateshgah.fait: This temple of fire worshippers, now an open-air museum, is located on the Absheron Peninsula, 30 km from the center of Baku.

palais-chaki.fait: Built in 1797 by Muhammad Hasan Khan, this palace was the summer residence of the khans of Shaki.

mugham.fait: This classical musical genre gives a leading role to improvisation; it combines singing with the tar, an 11-string lute, and the kamancheh, a bowed fiddle.

chekerboura.fait: This sweet pastry, popular in the country, is eaten in Baku in particular during the Novruz holiday.

khinkali.fait: This dumpling, most often filled with meat, contains broth: you hold it in your hands, bite into the dough and suck out the broth.

tchourtchkhela.fait: This traditional confection consists mainly of grape juice, nuts and flour; it is listed as part of the country's intangible cultural heritage.

vardzia.fait: This 12th-century cave monastery complex was surrounded by a network of fortresses, to serve as a stronghold in case of attack from the south.

ouplistsikhe.fait: This rock-hewn town near Gori brings together structures ranging from the Iron Age to the late Middle Ages, where pagan and Christian architecture stand side by side.

supra.fait: This meal is also a ritual of community gathering; there are two types, one to celebrate a festive occasion, the other to mark a time of mourning.

panduri.fait: This three-stringed instrument, once reserved for nobles, symbolizes joy; it may not be played when someone has died.

katskhi.fait: This limestone monolith about forty meters high has a 9th- or 10th-century hermitage on its summit; researchers did not climb it until 1944.

tkemali.fait: This name refers both to a variety of plum from the country and to the plum sauce of which it is the main ingredient.

tchonguri.fait: This four-stringed instrument is played in the west of the country, in the regions of Mingrelia, Guria and Adjara.

gour-emir.fait: This mausoleum in Samarkand is the burial place of Tamerlane, also called Timur the Lame, and of his descendants.

bibi-khanym.fait: Built from 1399 to 1404 in Samarkand, it is said, according to the chronicles, to have required five hundred workers and ninety-five Indian elephants.

samanides.fait: Built around 900 in Bukhara, this mausoleum made entirely of brick bears decoration that imitates the weave of basketry.

tchor-minor.fait: Its Persian name means “four minarets”; this Bukhara building was constructed in 1807 with funds from a wealthy Turkmen merchant.

minaret-jam.fait: Standing 65 meters tall, this slender minaret dates from the late 12th or early 13th century and rises along the Hari Rud river.

band-e-amir.fait: Their name means “dam of the emir” in Dari: these six lakes lie in the heart of the Hindu Kush mountains.

bouzkachi.fait: This collective equestrian activity, whose Persian name means “goat-grabbing game,” is the national sport in Afghanistan.

citadelle-herat.fait: Also called the Citadel of Alexander, this fortress founded by Alexander the Great has been destroyed and rebuilt many times.

jardins-babur.fait: Located southeast of Kabul, this historic park is one of the oldest Mughal gardens to have survived to the present day.

kabuli-palaw.fait: This pilaf combines steamed rice, carrots, caramelized raisins and marinated lamb; it is traditionally garnished with almonds and pistachios.

braai.fait: This Afrikaner barbecue is above all a social custom; “braai vleis” means “grilled meat” in Afrikaans.

bobotie.fait: This dish made with ground meat, chutney, raisins and spices has a topping of egg and milk-soaked bread; it is browned in the oven.

rooibos.fait: Its Afrikaans name means “reddish bush”; its oxidized leaves make a caffeine-free infusion, traditionally served with milk.

cap-bonne-esperance.fait: This rocky headland is not the southernmost point of Africa: that title goes to Cape Agulhas, 149 km to the east-southeast.

parc-kruger.fait: The largest wildlife reserve in South Africa, this park covers nearly 20,000 km², a size comparable to that of Slovenia.

yassa.fait: In this dish, meat or fish is marinated in lemon juice and spices, then fried and simmered in an onion sauce.

pont-faidherbe.fait: This bridge is the only crossing to the historic island of Saint-Louis; it is named after General Louis Faidherbe.

djoudj.fait: This national park, located about sixty kilometers north of Saint-Louis, is a paradise for migratory birds.

cafe-touba.fait: This coffee is flavored with Guinea pepper, a spice ground and mixed with the coffee, then prepared using the classic drip coffee method.

djingareyber.fait: Built between 1325 and 1327 in Timbuktu, it takes its name from Songhay: “jingaray,” mosque, and “beer,” great.

ciwara.fait: This ritual crest mask from Bambara culture has the shape of a roan antelope; its name means “head of the wild beast of farming.”

sanke-mon.fait: This collective fishing rite takes place in a pond in the town of San, on the second Thursday of the seventh lunar month, to commemorate its founding.

mosquee-mopti.fait: Often called the Komoguel Mosque, it is the main place of worship in the town of Mopti, in Mali.

kakum.fait: In this tropical rainforest national park, walkways cross the canopy at a height of about forty meters.

homowo.fait: The name of this festival of the Ga people means “to mock hunger”: it recalls a famine that occurred in precolonial times.

lucy.fait: This 3.18-million-year-old australopithecine fossil, 40% complete, was discovered in 1974 at the Hadar site.

lac-nakuru.fait: This soda lake in the Great Rift Valley is protected by a national park and designated a Ramsar site for the importance of its wetland.

nyama-choma.fait: This grilled goat meat is considered the national dish of Kenya; its name means “barbecue meat” in Kiswahili.

matatu.fait: The name of these minibuses, often painted with graffiti, comes from “tatu,” “three” in Swahili, in reference to the former fare.

lac-natron.fait: This soda lake takes its name from natron, a mineral one of whose components is dissolved in its waters; they attract a large community of lesser flamingos.

olduvai.fait: This gorge has yielded stone tools and fossils aged from 1.8 million to 400,000 years; it gave its name to the Oldowan.

kilwa-kisiwani.fait: This island very close to the coast had more than 10,000 inhabitants at its peak in the Middle Ages; today it is home to fewer than 1,000.

ravitoto.fait: The name of this recipe means “pounded cassava leaves”: they are cooked with garlic and served with pork or zebu and rice.

rova.fait: This fortified royal enclosure overlooks the capital from the hill of Analamanga; the word “rova” means a royal fortress.

nosy-be.fait: Its name means “big island” in Malagasy; located in the Mozambique Channel, it has become a major tourist destination.

fanorona.fait: This abstract strategy board game exists in three categories; Malagasy people play it everywhere, in towns as well as in the countryside.

zuma-rock.fait: This granite monolith rises 300 meters above the surrounding terrain; it is pictured on the 100-naira note.

osun-oshogbo.fait: This 75-hectare “sacred forest” is also an archaeological site, added to the World Heritage List in 2005.

eyo.fait: This Yoruba masquerade unique to Lagos, also called the Adamu Orisa Play, is traditionally celebrated on Lagos Island.

adire.fait: This indigo-dyed cloth is made by Yoruba women in the southwest of the country; its name means “tie and dye.”

udu.fait: The name of this percussion instrument means “jar” in the Igbo language, after its shape; it is a cousin of the ghatam of India.

attieke.fait: This fermented, steamed cassava semolina has a slightly sour taste; it is eaten with fish, meat and vegetables.

alloco.fait: This is the Ivorian name for a plantain-based dish, called “dodo” in Benin or “loco” in Senegal.

koutoukou.fait: This spirit, also called gbêlê, is made by distilling the sap of palm trees such as the oil palm, the raffia palm or the palmyra palm.

grand-bassam.fait: This town was the first capital of Côte d'Ivoire, from 1893 to 1900; its historic heart, the Quartier France, is a World Heritage Site.

mosquee-kong.fait: Destroyed by Samory Touré around 1897, this great mosque in northern Côte d'Ivoire was rebuilt at the dawn of the 20th century.

zaouli.fait: This name refers at once to a mask, a costume and a dance of the Guro people; the best dancers have been timed at more than 200 steps per minute.

palais-abomey.fait: This group of royal palaces houses a history museum; the 47-hectare site has been a World Heritage Site since 1985.

ganvie.fait: This lake village on Lake Nokoué, north of the Cotonou metropolitan area, is nicknamed the Venice of Africa.

temple-pythons.fait: This voodoo sanctuary in Ouidah houses live sacred pythons; a snake cult has been attested there since the late 17th century.

zangbeto.fait: The name of this masked society means “night hunter”: it hunts sorcerers and evil spirits. Its stronghold is in Porto-Novo.

zemidjan.fait: The name of this motorcycle taxi means “take me quickly” in the Fon language; it is widespread throughout West Africa.

evala.fait: These initiation rites of Kabye country, marked mainly by wrestling, take young people aged 18 to 20 into adulthood.

mont-agou.fait: The highest peak in Togo at 986 meters, this mountain covered with dense forests is home to many small Ewe villages.

cathedrale-lome.fait: This cathedral was erected in just over a year, from April 1901 to September 1902, by the German colonial authorities.

ayimolou.fait: This dish of rice and beans cooked together, often sold on the street, is eaten for breakfast as well as for lunch or dinner.

loropeni.fait: These ruins in the South-West Region of Burkina Faso have been on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 2009.

tiebele.fait: This traditional architectural complex, more than 500 years old, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since July 2024.

dan-fani.fait: The full name of this hand-spun and hand-woven cotton textile, Faso Dan Fani, comes from Dyula and means “woven wrapper of the homeland.”

chapeau-sapone.fait: This traditional braided straw hat, decorated with leather, is called “Sapon pougla” in Mooré; it comes from the rural commune of Saponé.

mosquee-agadez.fait: Built in 1515 with the clay known as “banco” and restored in 1844, it has a 27-meter minaret, the tallest structure in the town.

arbre-tenere.fait: This solitary acacia, once considered the most isolated tree on Earth, served as a landmark for caravans; a truck knocked it down in 1973.

guerewol.fait: During this courtship ritual of the Wodaabe, young men put on makeup, dance and sing to attract the attention of young women.

croix-agadez.fait: This Tuareg pendant, formed of a lozenge topped by a circle, is said to have been created in the Aïr; it is the most famous piece of Tuareg jewelry.

dabous.fait: These rock engravings dated to the Neolithic are found on the western side of the Aïr Mountains, in central Niger.

ndole.fait: This dish bears the Cameroonian name of a leaf vegetable, Vernonia, whose leaves are eaten fresh or, more rarely, dried.

poulet-dg.fait: In this sauté of chicken and plantains, “DG” stands for “directeur général,” managing director: the dish was originally reserved for important people.

chutes-lobe.fait: Seven kilometers south of Kribi, these falls have a rare feature: the Lobé River flows directly into the Atlantic Ocean.

nguon.fait: This cultural event of the Bamum kingdom, made up of rituals and festivities, was established by Nchare Yen one year after the founding of the kingdom, in 1394.

toghu.fait: This royal garment with colorful patterns of the Grassfields peoples was chosen as the traditional outfit at the 2012 London Olympic Games.

virunga.fait: Created in 1925 to protect mountain gorillas, it is the oldest national park in Africa; it was originally called Albert Park.

nyiragongo.fait: This 3,470-meter stratovolcano holds an almost permanent lava lake; its lava flows are considered the fastest in the world.

velours-kasai.fait: This traditional raffia cloth is made by the Kuba in the Kasai region, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

lola-ya-bonobo.fait: Its name means “paradise of the bonobos”: this sanctuary south of Kinshasa takes in baby bonobos that are victims of poaching.

parc-volcans.fait: This national park is in northwestern Rwanda, near the town of Ruhengeri, 120 kilometers north of Kigali.

nyungwe.fait: This forest massif in southwestern Rwanda, protected by a national park, covers an area of about 970 km².

akagera.fait: Created in 1934 to protect the animals of the savanna, mountains and swamps, this park takes its name from the Kagera River, which flows through it.

imigongo.fait: The relief of these panels painted with geometric patterns is created with calf dung; this art is traditionally practiced by women.

sossusvlei.fait: This salt and clay pan, surrounded by high red sand dunes, is the most visited tourist site in Namibia.

fish-river-canyon.fait: At 160 km long, this canyon is the largest in Africa and one of the largest in the world; it reaches a depth of 550 meters.

etosha.fait: Created in 1907 as a game reserve, this protected area is home to 114 species of mammals; the public has access to only about a third of the park.

kolmanskop.fait: Once a thriving diamond-mining site, this ghost town near Lüderitz is being invaded by sand from the Namib Desert.

hoba.fait: At 60 metric tons in a single piece, it is the largest known meteorite and the largest known natural block of iron on the Earth's surface.

otjize.fait: This cosmetic paste of the OvaHimba, made of red ocher mixed with fat or clarified butter, gives the skin and hair a red tint.

okavango.fait: It is the second-largest inland delta in the world: with no outlet to the sea, its waters coming from Angola spill into the Kalahari Desert.

chobe.fait: The first national park in Botswana, it is known for its lions that hunt African elephants, often young ones but sometimes adults.

tsodilo.fait: With nearly 4,500 rock paintings over about 10 km² in the Kalahari Desert, this site is sometimes nicknamed the “Louvre of the Desert.”

seswaa.fait: This dish of boiled then pounded meat, most often beef, is traditionally prepared by men for major celebrations.

mokoro.fait: This dugout canoe about 6 meters long is maneuvered standing at the stern, pushing with a long pole in the shallow waters of the delta.

kgotla.fait: In this traditional public assembly, usually in the center of the village, everyone has the right to speak without being interrupted, and discussions must reach a consensus.

cachupa.fait: Considered a national dish, this stew has corn and dried beans as its basic ingredients.

grogue.fait: This sugarcane spirit, with an alcohol content of around 40%, is related to rhum agricole; it is the national drink of Cape Verde.

pico-do-fogo.fait: The highest point in the country at 2,829 meters, this active volcano is also the highest peak in West Africa.

cidade-velha.fait: The first colonial town built by Europeans in the tropics, it was once the capital of Cape Verde; it was originally called Ribeira Grande.

carnaval-mindelo.fait: This annual festival takes place on an island of Cape Verde, of which it is a symbol of identity, as Cesária Évora says in a song.

morne-brabant.fait: This mountain in the southwest of the island was a refuge for runaway slaves; today it is a place of remembrance of the colonial period.

sept-couleurs.fait: This geological formation, now a tourist attraction, is located in Chamarel, in the Black River district.

aapravasi-ghat.fait: It was here, in the Port Louis district, that Indian indentured laborers arriving on the island landed, from November 1834 to 1910.

pamplemousses.fait: Created by Pierre Poivre, it is the first tropical botanical garden in the world; it succeeded a garden founded in 1735 to supply ships.

coco-de-mer.fait: This palm produces the largest seed in the world, nicknamed “cocofesse,” which can weigh around twenty kilograms.

vallee-de-mai.fait: On the island of Praslin, this reserve, listed as a World Heritage Site in 1983, is home to one of the largest forests of coco de mer palms.

anse-source-argent.fait: This 2-km beach on the island of La Digue is famous for its white sand, its clusters of granite boulders and its shallow turquoise waters.

aldabra.fait: It is the largest raised atoll in the world; it is home to the largest population of giant tortoises in Seychelles.

la-digue.fait: The fourth-largest island in the archipelago, it lives off tourism thanks to its fine white sand beaches, including the famous Anse Source d'Argent.

moutya.fait: This traditional dance is performed around a fire to the sound of a drum; once practiced by slaves, it has been inscribed by UNESCO since 2021.

ounianga.fait: These lakes in the middle of the Sahara Desert are a relic of the Chadian floodplain; they have been a World Heritage Site since 2012.

guelta-archei.fait: In a remote part of this guelta on the Ennedi Plateau survives a completely isolated population of desert crocodiles.

zakouma.fait: Created in 1963 in southeastern Chad, this national park is managed by the NGO African Parks, which combines tourism and wildlife conservation there.

toumai.fait: This fossil skull about 7 million years old, discovered in 2001 in the Djurab Desert, bears a nickname meaning “hope of life.”

mont-fuji.fait: This 3,776-meter stratovolcano, the highest point in the archipelago, is still considered active: its last certain eruption dates from late 1707.

fushimi-inari.fait: Located in Kyoto, in the Fushimi-ku district, it is the head shrine of the goddess Inari.

kinkaku-ji.fait: This Kyōto temple is actually called Rokuon-ji, “imperial temple of the deer garden”; Kinkaku-ji is only its common name.

itsukushima.fait: This Shinto shrine in Hiroshima Prefecture is largely lacquered in vermilion red; several of its buildings are National Treasures.

todai-ji.fait: This Buddhist temple in Nara houses the largest wooden building in the world still standing, which shelters a colossal bronze Great Buddha.

kiyomizu-dera.fait: Its name means “temple of pure water”; located in eastern Kyoto, it is one of the most famous places in the city.

ramen.fait: This noodle soup was imported from China in the late 19th century; its name comes from the Mandarin lāmiàn, “pulled noodles.”

takoyaki.fait: Its name means “grilled octopus”: these batter balls filled with octopus, cooked in a mold, are a specialty of Osaka.

okonomiyaki.fait: Its name combines “what you like” and “grilled”: a batter coats highly variable ingredients, all cooked on a hot plate.

mochi.fait: This particularly sticky paste is made by kneading cooked glutinous rice; shaped into balls, it is called dango.

bento.fait: This complete individual meal is presented in a compartmentalized box, from simple disposable packaging to a lacquered wooden case.

sashimi.fait: Its name means “cut body”: these are slices of fresh fish eaten raw, not to be confused with sushi, which is made with vinegared rice.

yakitori.fait: Its name means “grilled bird”: these skewers cooked on a grill, with bite-sized pieces, are traditionally made with chicken.

udon.fait: These soft wheat flour noodles are, along with soba and ramen, among the most widely eaten noodles in Japan.

wagashi.fait: These traditional confections, made with cane sugar and azuki beans, are often enjoyed with green tea, notably at the tea ceremony.

sake.fait: This rice alcohol produced by fermentation contains 11 to 20% alcohol; to be precise, the Japanese tend to call it nihonshu, “Japanese alcohol.”

matcha.fait: This very fine powder of green tea, ground between two stone millstones, is used in the Japanese tea ceremony; the tradition comes from China.

chanoyu.fait: Its name, chanoyu, means “hot water for tea”; matcha is prepared in a codified manner and a full service lasts about four hours.

kimono.fait: Its name means “thing to wear”: this garment is made of folded and sewn rectangles of fabric, held in place by a wide sash called an obi.

katana.fait: A symbol of the samurai caste, this curved, single-edged sword is worn slipped through the belt, with the edge facing upward.

origami.fait: Its name comes from the Japanese oru, “to fold,” and kami, “paper”; the Japanese tradition of this art strongly influenced its history in the West.

bonsai.fait: This art of growing a miniature tree in a pot descends from Chinese penjing, introduced to Japan around the year 700 and then codified by the Japanese.

ikebana.fait: This traditional art of flower arrangement is also called kadō, “the way of flowers” or “the art of giving life to flowers.”

sumo.fait: Two simple rules: do not leave the ring, and do not touch the ground with anything but the soles of the feet. The name means “to strike one another.”

kabuki.fait: This epic form of traditional theater stands out for the actors' elaborate makeup; its name is written with the characters for song, dance and skill.

theatre-no.fait: This theater of spare, codified acting uses 138 different masks; actors pass down the secrets of their art from father to son.

bunraku.fait: In this theater dating from the 17th century, each large puppet is manipulated in full view by three people, while a narrator sings all the roles.

taiko.fait: This word simply means “drum” in Japanese; these percussion instruments are heard especially at popular festivals, the matsuri.

shakuhachi.fait: This five-hole, end-blown bamboo flute of Chinese origin is based on a pentatonic scale and is used mainly in traditional music.

maneki-neko.fait: Its name means “inviting cat”: this figurine with a raised paw, a good-luck charm linked to business prosperity, adorns many shops.

daruma.fait: This papier-mâché wishing doll has the shape of a Buddhist monk: daruma is the Japanese name for Bodhidharma.

onsen.fait: This hot spring bath is fed by volcanic springs; nudity is required, and the word also refers to the resort built around it.

gion-matsuri.fait: This Kyōto festival was established in 869 as a rite against plague and disasters; it is one of the three great festivals of Japan.

geisha.fait: The word can be interpreted as “person of the arts”: these artists devote their lives to traditional arts such as music, dance and conversation.

tanabata.fait: This Star Festival celebrates the meeting of two celestial lovers, Vega and Altair, whom the Milky Way separates for the rest of the year.

tatami.fait: The dimensions of this padded mat are so standardized that its area has become, in Japan, the unit for measuring floor space.

pachinko.fait: This machine is a cross between a pinball machine and a slot machine; there are more than five million of them in Japan.

chateau-matsumoto.fait: This castle is nicknamed “the crow” because of its black color; it is one of the last twelve original castles in Japan.

nikko-tosho-gu.fait: This Shinto shrine in Tochigi Prefecture is located in Nikkō National Park; visitors can see the wise monkeys there.

ryoan-ji.fait: The name of this Zen temple in northwestern Kyōto means “Temple of the Resting Dragon”; its site originally belonged to the Fujiwara clan.

kotoku-in.fait: This monumental bronze statue of Amitābha stands at Kōtoku-in temple in Kamakura; the site attracted about two million visitors in 2016.

senso-ji.fait: The oldest temple in Tokyo, dedicated to the goddess Kannon, it is known for its giant red lanterns and receives 30 million visitors a year.

kendo.fait: Its name means “the way of the sword”: it is the modern version of the sword fencing once practiced by the samurai.

temple-ciel.fait: Through its layout, this Beijing monument symbolizes the Chinese belief that the Earth is square and Heaven is round.

palais-ete.fait: Its Chinese name means “Gardens of Preserved Harmony”; this Beijing palace was built by Empress Cixi starting in 1886.

bouddha-leshan.fait: Carved into a cliff in Sichuan between about 713 and 803, this 71-meter statue was, according to legend, meant to protect sailors.

grottes-longmen.fait: These Buddhist grottoes were carved into the limestone after 494; they stretch for about one kilometer along a gorge in Henan.

grottes-mogao.fait: These 492 Buddhist chapels decorated with paintings and sculptures were dug by monks from the 4th century onward, on the edge of the Gobi Desert.

grottes-yungang.fait: Near Datong, 53 caves hold about 50,000 statues; work began around 460, and five caves were made under the direction of the monk Tan Yao.

huang-shan.fait: These granite peaks surrounded by clouds inspire traditional Chinese painting; 4,000 steps lead to the summit of Lotus Peak.

jiuzhaigou.fait: According to Tibetan tradition, a goddess dropped a mirror there that shattered into 118 pieces, forming as many lakes.

pingyao.fait: Little changed since the Ming dynasty, this town in Shanxi has preserved all of its high historic ramparts.

lijiang.fait: Its name means “beautiful river,” in reference to the Yangtze; this old quarter of Yunnan is at the heart of the region of the Naxi minority.

shaolin.fait: Founded in the 5th century on Mount Song, this Chan Buddhist temple is famous for its association with martial arts, including Shaolin kung fu.

tombeaux-ming.fait: These are the tombs of the dynasty that ruled China between 1368 and 1644; they were listed as World Heritage Sites in 2000 and 2003.

pagode-oie.fait: Built in 652 in Xi'an under the Tang dynasty, it housed the sutras brought back from India by the traveler and translator Xuanzang.

mont-tai.fait: The most revered of the five sacred mountains of China, it has attracted pilgrims for 3,000 years; its highest point reaches 1,545 m.

dim-sum.fait: Its name translates literally as “touch the heart”: these small portions of Cantonese cuisine accompany the drinking of tea.

jiaozi.fait: This turnover-shaped dumpling, boiled, steamed or fried, wraps a varied filling in a soft wheat flour dough.

baozi.fait: This filled, steamed bun varies by region: the dough contains sugar in the south, while it is salted or plain in the north.

zongzi.fait: Originating in central China, this kind of parcel wrapped in leaves is similar to Mesoamerican tamales.

gateau-lune.fait: This pastry is eaten at the Mid-Autumn Festival; it often contains a salted egg yolk, which recalls the full moon once the cake is cut in half.

tanghulu.fait: Its name means “sugar gourd”: these skewers of fruit coated in a thin, crunchy sugar shell are a winter specialty of Beijing.

pu-erh.fait: This dark tea from Yunnan was compressed to travel by caravan to Tibet; it can improve with age, like wine.

baijiu.fait: Its name means “white alcohol”: this spirit is made by distilling a grain wine, most often from sorghum.

danse-lion.fait: Two dancers share each lion costume; performed most often for Chinese New Year, this dance is believed to bring good luck.

danse-dragon.fait: A team of dancers brings a long, flexible figure to life using poles; the dragon is a Chinese symbol of happiness and prosperity.

opera-pekin.fait: Born in the late 18th century, this performance combines music, acrobatic dance, theater and flamboyant costumes to tell of the past and of folklore.

tai-chi.fait: Often reduced to a health exercise, it is a so-called “internal” martial art whose name means “boxing of the supreme ultimate.”

mah-jong.fait: This game is played by four people with tiles: you must assemble four groups of three or four identical or consecutive tiles, plus a pair.

hutong.fait: These narrow alleys of Beijing serve siheyuan, dwellings grouped around a courtyard; a single name designates a whole set of alleys.

gyeongbokgung.fait: Its name means “palace of Shining Happiness”; built in 1394 in Seoul, it is the main one of the five grand palaces of the Joseon dynasty.

changdeokgung.fait: Often called the East Palace, it blends into the natural topography of the site instead of imposing itself on it; many Joseon kings preferred it.

bulguksa.fait: This temple houses seven national treasures, including two bronze statues of the Buddha; it is regarded as a masterpiece of the Buddhist art of the Silla kingdom.

seokguram.fait: This hermitage of the Bulguksa temple complex stands at an altitude of 750 m on Mount Toham, in Gyeongju, four kilometers east of the temple.

hwaseong.fait: This fortress in Suwon was built between 1794 and 1796 on the orders of King Jeongjo, to honor and house the remains of his father, Prince Sado.

dol-hareubang.fait: Their name means “stone grandfathers”: these statues from Jeju Island represented deities protecting the inhabitants from demons.

taekwondo.fait: Its name, proposed in 1955, can be translated as “the way of the feet and fists”; it has been on the Summer Olympics program since 2000.

soju.fait: This clear spirit, traditionally made from rice, is most often 20% alcohol; most modern brands come from South Korea.

tteokbokki.fait: These short, thick rice cakes, spiced up with gochujang, a chili sauce, are often sold on the street by pojangmacha.

gimbap.fait: White rice, sesame oil and other ingredients are rolled in dried seaweed, then served cold in bite-sized slices.

bingsu.fait: This dessert consists of finely shaved ice topped with a mixture of boiled red beans; it is very popular in South Korea.

pansori.fait: This art of sung storytelling, accompanied by a double-headed drum, takes its name from the “song of the public place,” the village square or marketplace.

haegeum.fait: This two-stringed instrument with silk strings, which resembles a violin, is held upright on the knee and played with a bow.

tripitaka-koreana.fait: This Buddhist canon, known as the Tripitaka Koreana, is carved in reverse on 81,258 wooden blocks, kept since 1398 at Haeinsa Temple.

namdaemun.fait: Its name means “Great South Gate”: built in 1398, it was the main entrance gate to Seoul, whose city wall had eight gates.

jongmyo.fait: According to UNESCO, it is the oldest Confucian royal shrine; the ceremonies still held there carry on a tradition from the 14th century.

erdene-zuu.fait: This Buddhist monastery was built in 1585, partly with stones from the ruins of Karakorum; its wall is made up of 108 stupas.

ovoo.fait: Its name means “stone mound”: this cairn is used in Mongolian shamanic culture, notably for sacrifices to mountain deities.

bokh.fait: This wrestling has no weight classes: you just have to force your opponent to touch the ground with a knee, the back or the buttocks.

tsagaan-sar.fait: This New Year, whose name means “white month,” begins with the new waxing moon; families gather for ritual offerings.

shagai.fait: These sheep or goat anklebones are used in very popular games during the Naadam festival; Mongolians exchange them as a sign of friendship.

massaman.fait: This rather mild curry, of Muslim tradition and Persian origin, was introduced to Thailand during the reign of Rama II.

muay-thai.fait: This nickname for Muay Thai refers to the eight parts of the arms and legs that are used; it is the most popular form of boxing in Southeast Asia.

wat-pho.fait: Also called the Temple of the Reclining Buddha, it is one of the largest and oldest Buddhist temples in Bangkok.

doi-suthep.fait: In local Thai, doi means “mountain” and Suthep is the name of the one that bears this temple, thirteen kilometers north of Chiang Mai.

iles-phi-phi.fait: This small archipelago in Krabi Province has two main islands; its name is pronounced “pee-pee,” not “fee-fee.”

baie-phang-nga.fait: This 400 km² bay has 42 small islands and islets; its nail-shaped rock, Ko Tapu, appears in the film The Man with the Golden Gun (1974).

bouddha-emeraude.fait: Standing 76.2 cm tall, this statue is made of jadeite; venerated in Bangkok in the royal chapel of the Grand Palace, it is usually dressed in gold.

hoi-an.fait: Called Faifo in colonial times, this city preserves an old town, an exceptionally well-preserved example of a Far Eastern port.

cite-imperiale-hue.fait: It lies within the Huế Citadel, together with the Purple Forbidden City; the whole has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1993.

my-son.fait: Its ruins include some seventy temples and annex buildings in red brick; the site was long the religious and political capital of Champa.

temple-litterature.fait: This Confucian temple in Hanoi is divided into five courtyards; in the days of French Indochina, the colonists called it “the Pagoda of the Crows.”

lac-hoan-kiem.fait: This lake in Hanoi is also called the Lake of the Returned Sword; it gave its name to the district that surrounds it.

phong-nha.fait: This park has a network of 300 caverns and caves; in April 2009, British explorers discovered the largest cave in the world there.

delta-mekong.fait: Its Vietnamese name means “Nine Dragons delta”; this region in the south of the country covers about 39,000 km² and has twelve provinces.

sa-pa.fait: At an altitude of 1,500 meters, Sa Pa overlooks the Mường Hoa valley; it was once an isolated place, with terraced fields.

fete-tet.fait: This Lunar New Year festival, the most important of the year, falls between January 21 and February 20, on the day of the first new moon.

bun-bo-hue.fait: Its name combines bò, “beef,” bún, “rice vermicelli,” and Huế, the region where this spicy soup is a specialty.

trang-an.fait: Nicknamed the “Hạ Long Bay on land,” this landscape of karst peaks crisscrossed by valleys borders the Red River delta.

notre-dame-saigon.fait: This cathedral in the center of Ho Chi Minh City was built by the French from 1877 to 1880; it stands on Paris Commune Square.

ballet-royal-khmer.fait: This sacred art has accompanied royal ceremonies for more than a thousand years; its repertoire features the woman, the man, the giant and the monkey.

banteay-srei.fait: Its name means “the citadel of women,” or “of fortune”; this temple lies 20 km northeast of Angkor, on the site of the ancient city of Iśvarapura.

angkor-thom.fait: Its name means “great city”: this royal city was built by the Buddhist king Jayavarman VII in the late 12th and early 13th centuries.

preah-khan.fait: This Buddhist temple was built around 1191 by the Khmer king Jayavarman VII, north of the city of Angkor Thom.

koh-ker.fait: This former Khmer capital, from 928 to 944, owes its name to the Old Khmer for “the grove of koki trees”; its ruins lie 80 km northeast of Angkor.

palais-royal-phnom-penh.fait: The king's residence, this complex was built in stages on the remains of an old citadel, on the western bank of the Tonlé Sap and the Mekong.

sambor-prei-kuk.fait: Its name means “the temple in the lush forest”; this pre-Angkorian site is identified with Ishanapura, the former capital of the Chenla kingdom.

prahok.fait: This paste of salted, fermented fish owes the nickname “Cambodian cheese” to its strong smell; it was originally used to preserve fish.

terrasse-elephants.fait: Built in the late 12th century under Jayavarman VII, it stands in front of the ruins of the Royal Palace, near the center of Angkor Thom.

norry.fait: This motorized handcar is a simple bamboo platform of about 2.5 by 4 meters, which runs on the railroad track near Battambang.

poivre-kampot.fait: It is the first Cambodian agricultural product to have obtained a protected geographical indication, granted on April 2, 2010.

kawah-ijen.fait: Its name means “green crater” in Javanese; its crater holds a lake reputed to be the most acidic on the planet and produces “blue flames” seen at night.

lac-toba.fait: 100 km long and 35 wide, this lake on Sumatra is the largest volcanic lake in the world; its maximum confirmed depth is 505 m.

raja-ampat.fait: The name of this archipelago means “the four kings”; it lies near the northwest coast of New Guinea.

ulun-danu-bratan.fait: This Hindu temple in Bali stands on the shores of Lake Bratan; downstream, many smaller water temples are linked to irrigation associations.

batik.fait: This technique, born in Java, consists of drawing on fabric with wax: the wax resists the dyes, then it is removed with boiling water.

nasi-goreng.fait: Its name literally means “fried rice”: the rice is seasoned with sweet soy sauce, shallot, garlic and tamarind.

gado-gado.fait: This salad of crunchy vegetables coated in a peanut sauce was promoted in 2018 as one of the country's six national dishes.

tempeh.fait: This cake of whole soybeans, bound together by a fungus during fermentation, is a staple source of protein in Java.

kopi-luwak.fait: This coffee is collected from the droppings of a civet, the luwak, which digests the pulp of the coffee cherries but not their pits.

nyepi.fait: For this Balinese New Year, silence is observed for 24 hours: no work or travel, and even Bali's airport closes.

tumpeng.fait: This cone of rice colored yellow with turmeric, accompanied by vegetables and meats, is presented at a ceremonial meal, the selamatan.

bakso.fait: These meatballs of ground beef and tapioca flour, served in a clear broth, are one of the country's most popular street foods.

rinjani.fait: This volcano on the island of Lombok rises to 3,726 meters: by altitude, it is the second-highest volcano in Indonesia after Kerinci.

lac-inle.fait: The second-largest lake in the country, at an altitude of 884 m, it has an average depth of only 2.10 m in the dry season and is home to many endemic species.

thingyan.fait: This New Year water festival lasts four or five days in mid-April; splashing water in all its forms is an essential part of it.

lahpet.fait: This fermented or pickled tea is eaten: Burma is one of the few countries where tea is also a delicacy, served to guests.

pagode-kuthodaw.fait: It houses the world's largest book by size: the Pali Buddhist canon, carved on 729 marble slabs, each under a small stupa.

grottes-batu.fait: These caves in a limestone hill, 10 kilometers north of Kuala Lumpur, form the largest Hindu shrine outside India.

mont-kinabalu.fait: The highest point on the island of Borneo at 4,095 meters, this mountain is home to several carnivorous plants and many orchids.

taman-negara.fait: Its name means “national park” in Malay; its rainforest, one of the oldest in the world, is thought to have existed for 130 million years.

sipadan.fait: This island was formed from living corals that grew over thousands of years on top of an extinct volcano.

roti-canai.fait: This kind of flatbread, very popular in the morning as well as at dinner, is served with a small bowl of sauce, usually curry.

iles-perhentian.fait: This archipelago in the South China Sea is part of a marine park: fishing, collecting coral and throwing litter are forbidden there.

mayon.fait: This active volcano rises on the island of Luzon, in the province of Albay, between the cities of Legazpi, Tabaco and Ligao.

taal.fait: Its caldera holds a lake with an island, itself hollowed by a lake from which a rocky peak juts out: an island in a lake on an island in a lake on an island.

barong-tagalog.fait: In its finest version, this traditional tunic is made of pineapple-leaf fiber fabric; today it is considered the country's national garment.

intramuros.fait: This district, the oldest in Manila, was built by the Spanish in the 16th century; its name then referred to the city itself.

el-nido.fait: Its name means “the nest” in Spanish; this municipality, which is also a protected area, is located in the province of Palawan.

boracay.fait: This small island in the Visayas archipelago lies less than a kilometer from the northern tip of Panay Island, about 300 kilometers south of Manila.

fort-santiago.fait: This citadel was originally built by the Spanish conquistador Miguel López de Legazpi; it forms the tip of the old district of Intramuros, in Manila.

pinatubo.fait: Considered extinct, this volcano awoke in June 1991 after 500 years of dormancy; its eruption cooled the climate by about half a degree.

that-luang.fait: Believed to contain a hair of the Buddha, this stupa in Vientiane is the most sacred monument in the country and appears on its coat of arms and banknotes.

luang-prabang.fait: Every morning, hundreds of monks walk the streets of this former royal capital to receive alms from the inhabitants.

plaine-jarres.fait: This region in the north of the country is dotted with imposing ancient stone jars, whose origin and meaning have not been fully explained.

vat-phou.fait: Its name means “mountain temple”; this complex of Khmer art predates the construction of the Angkor Wat complex.

khene.fait: This polyphonic mouth organ, of a type that dates back to the Bronze Age, is now associated with the Lao people of Laos and northeastern Thailand.

larb.fait: This minced dish, usually very spicy, is eaten with sticky rice; there are versions with fish, cooked meat, raw meat and even blood.

si-phan-don.nom: Si Phan Don (the Four Thousand Islands)
si-phan-don.fait: Despite its name, this archipelago in the Mekong actually has only a few hundred islands, most of them small and uninhabited.

vang-vieng.fait: This town on the Nam Song River is surrounded by karst peaks, caves and lagoons, a natural setting it seeks to showcase.

hotel-raffles.fait: Opened in 1887, this colonial-style hotel is named after the Briton Thomas Stamford Raffles, founder of the city.

sentosa.fait: Its name means “peaceful” in Malay. This island of Singapore, a tourist resort, receives about 5 million visitors a year and has a 2 km beach.

pulau-ubin.fait: In Malay, “pulau” means “island”: this small island lies northeast of Pulau Ujong, the largest island of Singapore.

orchard-road.fait: This major thoroughfare lined with shopping malls and department stores is Singapore's main shopping street.

fort-rouge.fait: Every August 15, the Indian Prime Minister addresses the nation from this Mughal fortress in Delhi, a former imperial residence.

qutb-minar.fait: This minaret in Delhi, the tallest in India, was begun in 1192 by the first sultan of Delhi; its fifth and final story dates from 1368.

hawa-mahal.fait: This “palace of the winds” in red and pink sandstone was built in the late 18th century in Jaipur, the capital of Rajasthan.

temple-or.fait: The holiest building of the Sikhs, this temple in Amritsar, in Punjab, owes its nickname to its gilded covering.

ellora.fait: These 34 caves dug into a vertical rock face are shared among three religions: 12 are Buddhist, 17 Hindu and 5 Jain.

ajanta.fait: These 29 Buddhist caves in Maharashtra, three of them unfinished, were carved into hard basalt and decorated with paintings and sculptures.

khajuraho.fait: This village in Madhya Pradesh, once one of the capitals of the Chandela dynasty, preserves 22 large temples from the 10th and 11th centuries adorned with sculptures.

hampi.fait: This village in Karnataka lies within the walls of the ruined city of Vijayanagara, former capital of the kingdom of the same name.

konarak.fait: Nicknamed the “Black Pagoda,” this 13th-century temple originally stood on the shore; the silting of the coast has moved it away from the sea.

fort-amber.fait: This fort in Rajasthan, 11 km from Jaipur, is connected to the neighboring Jaigarh Fort by an underground passage intended for the royal family in case of threat.

benares.fait: On the left bank of the Ganges, this city, the holiest in Hinduism, is considered one of the oldest continuously inhabited places in the world.

poulet-tandoori.fait: This chicken is marinated in a mixture of yogurt and spices, then traditionally roasted in an Indian oven called a tandoor.

dosa.fait: This South Indian crepe, made from black lentil, chickpea or rice flour, is traditionally eaten for breakfast or dinner.

idli.fait: These savory cakes 5 to 7 cm across, enjoyed throughout South India, are steamed from a fermented batter of black lentils and rice.

thali.fait: This meal brings together an assortment of dishes served in small metal bowls on a round tray; its name means “plate” or “tray.”

gulab-jamun.fait: These balls of dough fried in oil are served with a thick syrup; “gulab” refers to this rosewater-scented syrup.

paneer.fait: This cheese, originally made from buffalo milk, is an important source of protein in a country where part of the population is vegetarian.

panipuri.fait: This roadside snack is a hollow, fried puri eaten with “flavored water,” tamarind chutney and chickpeas.

rasgulla.fait: This dessert from Bengal and Odisha consists of balls of curdled milk boiled in a light sugar syrup until they are soaked through.

poulet-beurre.fait: This chicken marinated in a butter sauce, probably originating in New Delhi, is usually served with naan bread and rice.

pav-bhaji.fait: This fast-food dish from Maharashtra combines a thick vegetable curry cooked in butter, the bhaji, with a soft bread roll, the pav.

dhokla.fait: Originating in Gujarat, this vegetarian dish is made from a fermented batter of rice and split chickpeas.

laddu.fait: These balls of flour coated in sugar syrup are often made for festivals and weddings; their ingredients vary by region.

lassi.fait: This traditional drink made from fermented milk is a staple in the Punjab region.

masala-chai.fait: This very sweet black tea is mixed with spices and brewed in boiling milk; “chai” is the Hindi word for tea.

the-darjeeling.fait: This black tea from West Bengal was developed by the British Empire to compete with Chinese tea; today it is mostly exported.

kumbh-mela.fait: This Hindu pilgrimage, whose name means “festival of the pitcher,” brings together several million people: it is probably the largest in the world.

durga-puja.fait: Celebrated in eastern India in honor of the goddess Durga, this Hindu festival is prepared several weeks in advance.

ganesh-chaturthi.fait: This festival honors Ganesh, son of Shiva and Parvati; its Sanskrit name means “the fourth of Ganesh.”

onam.fait: This harvest festival in Kerala lasts ten days, with floral decorations, feasts and boat races; it commemorates the coming of the legendary king Maveli.

pongal.fait: The name of this harvest festival means “boiling over” in Tamil; it is mainly celebrated in Tamil Nadu and Puducherry.

ratha-yatra.fait: During this annual festival, painted and decorated chariots carrying Hindu deities are pulled through the streets by the faithful; the most famous takes place in Puri.

kalarippayatt.fait: This martial art from Kerala is said to be one of the oldest known fighting techniques; its masters are both warriors and healers.

yoga.fait: This discipline combines meditation, asceticism and physical exercises; in 2014, the UN made June 21 its international day.

kathak.fait: In this classical dance of northern India, the performer strings together rapid footwork, accentuated by ankle bells, and spins.

odissi.fait: This classical dance from the state of Odisha stands out for its fluid movements and a pose in which the head, shoulders and hips form a broken line.

mallakhamb.fait: This traditional sport resembles acrobatic gymnastics: the figures are performed using a central pole.

dabbawala.fait: This Mumbai meal deliveryman takes his name from “dabba,” the box, and “wallah,” the one who does; the system's logistics are complex and precise.

rangoli.fait: Every morning in the villages, women draw these geometric designs on the ground with white powder; the patterns are passed down from mother to daughter.

kolam.fait: Before dawn, millions of women in Tamil Nadu draw these geometric patterns on the ground with rice powder, as an offering at daybreak.

tabla.fait: This North Indian percussion instrument combines two drums: the dayan, the right-hand drum with high-pitched sounds, and the bayan, which provides the bass.

bansuri.fait: This large transverse flute is probably the oldest musical instrument of North India; it is strongly associated with the god Krishna.

shehnai.fait: This rustic double-reed instrument, like the oboe, is highly prized in India because it is considered auspicious.

sari.fait: This strip of fabric about 1.20 m wide and 5 to 6 m long is draped in different ways depending on the region, caste or activity.

dhoti.fait: This men's garment is a piece of fine cotton about 5 m by 1.20 m, knotted at the waist, with one end passed between the legs.

train-darjeeling.fait: Nicknamed the “Toy Train,” this railway line built from 1879 to 1881 is narrow gauge, with a track gauge of 61 centimeters.

pashupatinath.fait: On the banks of the Bagmati River in Kathmandu, this Hindu temple is dedicated to Pashupati, a form of Shiva as “lord of animals.”

bhaktapur.fait: Its name combines “bhakta,” devotee, and “pura,” city: this town lies 13 kilometers east of Kathmandu, at an altitude of 1,401 meters.

lumbini.fait: This village near the Indian border is considered the birthplace of the Buddha; it is one of the four holy sites of Buddhism.

annapurna.fait: This Himalayan massif has six main peaks; the highest rises to 8,091 meters, making it the tenth-highest mountain in the world.

chitwan.fait: Established in 1973, this park is the oldest national park in Nepal; it is home to the Indian rhinoceros, the Bengal tiger and the Ganges gharial.

sagarmatha.fait: This park bears the Nepali name of Everest and rises from an altitude of 2,845 meters to the summit, at 8,849 meters.

dal-bhat.fait: This dish of white rice and lentil soup is often eaten twice a day, with the right hand and without cutlery.

tongba.fait: This fermented millet drink, served hot or warm and sipped through a straw, is the traditional beverage of the Limbu people in eastern Nepal.

yomari.fait: This dessert of the Newar community is a steamed rice-flour dumpling filled with sesame; “yoh” means “to like” in Newar.

polonnaruwa.fait: This city in north-central Sri Lanka is one of the island's ancient capitals and one of the sites of its “Cultural Triangle.”

anuradhapura.fait: Capital of a kingdom from the 4th century BC to the 10th century, it is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world.

dambulla.fait: A large granite rock contains this complex of Buddhist caves, which has 157 statues and 2,100 m² of murals.

pic-adam.fait: This 2,243 m conical peak is a holy place for Hindus, Buddhists and Muslims; its Sinhalese name means “noble foot.”

yala.fait: This 979 km² national park, the most visited in Sri Lanka, is home to 44 species of mammals and one of the highest densities of leopards in the world.

gal-vihara.fait: This Buddhist temple in Polonnaruwa was created in the 12th century by Parakramabahu I; it was originally called Uttararama.

sinharaja.fait: Its name combines “sinha,” lion, and “raja,” king. This mountainous virgin forest was saved from logging by its inaccessibility.

danse-kandy.fait: These sacred dances are called “up-country dances” in Sinhalese; Kandy has kept its role as the religious capital of Sri Lanka.

badshahi.fait: This mosque in Lahore can hold 10,000 worshippers in its main prayer hall and 100,000 in its arcades and courtyard, the largest mosque courtyard in the world.

fort-lahore.fait: Earthen fortifications existed here as early as the 12th century; the Mughal emperor Akbar rebuilt the fort in brick in 1566.

shalimar.fait: These royal gardens in Lahore were created in 1641 by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, then at the height of his reign.

mohenjo-daro.fait: This city of the Indus civilization, built in the 3rd millennium BC, is thought to have been abandoned because of a change in the river's course.

taxila.fait: West of Islamabad, this archaeological site of ancient Gandhara holds the remains of three successive ancient cities and many monasteries.

rohtas.fait: Built by the Afghan king Sher Shah Suri, this garrison fort is, in the Indian subcontinent, the first successful blend of Hindu, Afghan and Persian architecture.

harappa.fait: This fortified Bronze Age city is thought to have had up to 40,000 inhabitants; it gave its name to the Harappan civilization.

khewra.fait: Discovered by the troops of Alexander the Great, this mine in Punjab produces on average more than 350,000 tons of rock salt a year.

sel-himalaya.fait: This raw, unrefined rock salt is extracted from a mine in Pakistan; its pink hues come from the presence of iron oxides.

bagerhat.fait: Despite its name, this mosque in Bagerhat, one of the oldest in Bangladesh, has 81 domes, 77 of which form the roof.

paharpur.fait: These remains, in Naogaon, are those of the largest Buddhist monastery in South Asia; they have been a World Heritage Site since 1985.

lalbagh.fait: This 17th-century Mughal fort, which was never completed, stands in the old town of Dhaka, along the Buriganga River.

cox-bazar.fait: This 120 km long beach borders a fishing port in the far southeast of Bangladesh, the country's most visited tourist attraction.

mahasthangarh.fait: It is the oldest urban archaeological site discovered in Bangladesh: an inscription found in 1931 dates it to the 3rd century BC at the latest.

jamdani.fait: This cotton fabric is used in particular to make saris; the know-how of its weavers has been inscribed as intangible cultural heritage since 2013.

mangal-shobhajatra.fait: This mass procession takes place at dawn on Bengali New Year; it is organized by the teachers and students of the Faculty of Fine Arts at the University of Dhaka.

taktshang.fait: This monastery clings to a cliff at an altitude of 3,120 meters; according to legend, Padmasambhava arrived there flying on the back of a tiger.

punakha.fait: Built in 1637-1638, this “palace of great happiness” was the seat of the government of Bhutan until 1955, before the capital was moved to Thimphu.

tashichho.fait: This “fortress of the glorious religion,” in Thimphu, houses the throne room and the offices of the King of Bhutan.

rinpung.fait: Often called Paro Dzong, this fortress-temple houses both the monastic body of the Paro district and the offices of its administration.

ema-datshi.fait: The national dish of Bhutan, it combines chili and cheese: “ema” means chili and “datshi” cheese in Dzongkha, the official language.

kira.fait: This women's garment is a long rectangular cloth wrapped around the body, held at the shoulders by brooches and at the waist by a belt.

tsechu.fait: These annual religious festivals take place in every district of Bhutan; they come with large markets and bring together remote villages.

douze-apotres.fait: These limestone stacks rise from the sea along the Great Ocean Road, in Port Campbell National Park, in the state of Victoria.

great-ocean-road.fait: This 243 km coastal road was built between 1919 and 1932 by soldiers returning from the First World War.

kata-tjuta.fait: This group of rock domes, also called the Olgas, rises 365 km southwest of Alice Springs, in Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park.

kakadu.fait: This park in the Northern Territory is renowned for its many animal species and for the ancient Aboriginal paintings it contains.

bondi-beach.fait: Seven kilometers from central Sydney, this beach is known for its fine sand and for its rolling waves, which make it a surfing spot.

kgari.fait: Near the eastern coast of Queensland, it is the largest sand island in the world: 1,840 km², 123 km long and a highest point of 260 m.

wave-rock.fait: This ocher granite formation, shaped by erosion, owes its name to its shape, that of a large wave about to break.

lac-hillier.fait: The very salty waters of this Western Australian lagoon are bright pink; it is one of the country's seven “pink lakes.”

coober-pedy.fait: In this opal-mining village, most residents live in cave homes because of the scorching daytime heat.

lamington.fait: This cake is made of cubes of sponge cake coated in cocoa icing and then rolled in desiccated coconut.

damper.fait: This rustic bread was made by the first European settlers; it rises without yeast, thanks to baking powder or baking soda.

fairy-bread.fait: This “fairy bread,” buttered white bread covered with sprinkles, is served at children's parties; it was first mentioned in the 1920s.

melbourne-cup.fait: This horse race, the most important in Australia, is run on the first Tuesday of November; it was first held in 1861.

the-ghan.fait: This train links Adelaide and Darwin in 53 hours 15 minutes over 2,979 kilometers; its name comes from the Afghan cameleers who crisscrossed the Outback.

barriere-dingos.fait: At 5,320 kilometers long, it is the longest fence in the world; it protects sheep farms in the southeast of the country from dingoes.

wharenui.fait: This Māori communal house, whose name means “big house,” is often decorated with wood carvings depicting the tribe's ancestors.

wai-o-tapu.fait: This active geothermal area lies in the region of the Taupo volcano, in the center of New Zealand's North Island.

waitomo.fait: Their Māori name can be translated as “water passing through a hole”; the most famous of these caves are known for their bioluminescence.

mont-cook.fait: The highest point in New Zealand, at 3,724 m, this peak of the Southern Alps was first climbed in 1894.

tongariro.fait: The first national park created in New Zealand and the fourth in the world, it includes the volcanoes Ruapehu, Ngauruhoe and Tongariro and many sites sacred to the Māori.

moeraki.fait: These unusually large spherical boulders lie on Koekohe Beach, on the South Island of New Zealand.

franz-josef.fait: At 12 km long, this glacier descends from the Southern Alps to less than 300 m above sea level; its Western name honors Franz Joseph I of Austria.

waka.fait: These Māori vessels range from small, unadorned fishing canoes to large decorated war canoes up to 40 meters long.

hongi.fait: This Māori greeting consists of pressing one's nose and forehead against another person's; the Māori believe it exchanges the “ha,” the breath of life.

pounamu.fait: This term refers to hard stones found in the south of New Zealand; carvings made from them play a central role in Māori culture.

kapa-haka.fait: In Māori, “kapa” means “rank”: the groups that perform these songs and dances usually stand in rows.

koru.fait: This motif depicts the unfurling young frond of a fern; common in Māori carving and tattooing, it symbolizes rebirth and growth.

koauau.fait: This Māori flute, 10 to 20 centimeters long, has three to six holes; its players were believed to have the power to win women's affection.

levuka.fait: Located on the east coast of Ovalau Island, this town was the capital of Fiji from 1874 to 1882.

taveuni.fait: Nicknamed the “Garden Island of Fiji” for its abundant flora, this island is crossed by the 180th meridian.

meke.fait: These traditional dances and songs bring together two groups: one dances, the other provides the music and singing, to the sound of mainly wooden percussion.

cibi.fait: This war dance once celebrated the return from victorious wars; Fiji's national rugby union team performs it before every match.

camakau.fait: This outrigger canoe with a triangular sail is the most common traditional sailing boat in Fiji; it is smaller than the drua.

totokia.fait: This war club is nicknamed the “pineapple club” for the shape of its head, although its model was probably the pandanus.

haus-tambaran.fait: This traditional religious building of East Sepik inspired the facade of the National Parliament, in the suburbs of Port Moresby.

piste-kokoda.fait: This 96-kilometer trail crosses jungle and mountains; hikers take five to twelve days to walk it, local people three.

mont-wilhelm.fait: Rising to 4,509 m in the Bismarck Range, it is the country's highest mountain; its summit lies where three provinces meet.

tavurvur.fait: This volcanic cone rises on the rim of the Rabaul caldera, on New Britain, whose natural harbor shelters the town of Rabaul.

kundu.fait: This hourglass-shaped drum, covered with snakeskin, appears on the country's coat of arms; for Papuans, the sound it makes is the voice of the ancestors.

haamonga.fait: This trilithon in the north of Tongatapu Island bears a name meaning “Māui's burden”; it is one of the most famous monuments in Tonga.

palais-nukualofa.fait: This wooden building, built in 1867, is the official residence of the King of Tonga and his family, in the capital Nuku'alofa.

langi.fait: These burial complexes, built from the 11th century onward, are stone tombs on earth mounds, reached by paved steps.

vavau.fait: This group consists of one main island and forty smaller ones; according to legend, Maui pulled it up to the surface while fishing.

lakalaka.fait: This national dance of Tonga is performed at major ceremonies, such as the coronation of the king or the anniversary of the constitution.

taovala.fait: This mat, wrapped around the waist and held in place by a kafa made of coconut fiber, is worn by men and women on formal occasions.

nakamal.fait: This meeting place for the men of the village can be a community house or a clearing under a banyan tree; kava is drunk there.

roi-mata.fait: This domain brings together three sites on the islands of Efate, Lelepa and Artok, associated with the life and death, around 1600, of the last chief Roi Mata.

tanna.fait: This volcanic island in the Coral Sea, the second most populous in Vanuatu, is best known for its active volcano, Yasur.

ambrym.fait: This volcanic island of the Vanuatu archipelago, in the Coral Sea, has two craters named Marum and Benbow.

saut-gol.fait: On Pentecost Island, men leap from a wooden tower with a vine tied to their ankles; this rite inspired a pioneer of bungee jumping.

dessins-sable.fait: This tradition is practiced mainly in central and northern Vanuatu, where it is a notable part of the national culture.

laplap.fait: This traditional dish of Vanuatu is made from yam or taro, with coconut milk and sometimes meat.

nan-madol.fait: These artificial islets off Pohnpei Island were the capital of a dynasty until around 1500; this canal-laced site is nicknamed the “Venice of the Pacific.”

lelu.fait: This coral and basalt city on Lelu Island is the remnant of a civilization that peaked around the 14th and 15th centuries; the king lived there behind high walls.

pohnpei.fait: This island in the Carolines is home both to Kolonia, the capital of its state, and to Palikir, the country's federal capital.

kosrae.fait: The easternmost island of the Carolines, it forms the country's smallest and least populated state; it was formerly called Kusaie.

ulithi.fait: This atoll in the Carolines had 847 inhabitants in 2010; together with its associated islands, it comprises about forty islands and islets, four of them inhabited.

pierres-rai.fait: These calcite disks, 4 to 350 cm wide, were quarried in Palau and then transported by boat or raft to the Yap Islands.

chelbacheb.fait: This uninhabited archipelago stretches south of Koror, the country's largest town, across the states of Koror and Peleliu.

lac-meduses.fait: This brackish lake is home to 10 million jellyfish, which multiplied in the absence of predators; they arrived through a tunnel that is now blocked.

babeldaob.fait: It is the country's largest island: it is divided among ten of the sixteen states and is home to the capital, Melekeok.

tet-el-bad.fait: This giant sarcophagus lies near the village of Ollei, in the north of Ngarchelong State; it has been on the World Heritage Tentative List since 2004.

hamburger.fait: This sandwich of German origin has been, since the 1950s, one of the symbols of American culture and cuisine.

hot-dog.fait: This sandwich comes from German and New York cuisine; originally, its name referred only to the sausage, before being extended to the whole.

donut.fait: Its name comes from “doughnut,” literally “nut of dough”; this sweet fried pastry from North America is usually ring-shaped.

jambalaya.fait: This specialty of Louisiana Cajun cuisine is made with rice, meat, seafood and spices.

bourbon.fait: This American whiskey must contain at least 51% corn and is aged in new oak barrels, blackened by charring.
