root-beer.fait: This sweet carbonated drink is flavored with sassafras and sarsaparilla; in Quebec, it is called “racinette.”

jour-marmotte.fait: On February 2, people watch for a groundhog coming out of its burrow: according to tradition, if it sees its shadow, winter will last six more weeks.

fete-4-juillet.fait: This national holiday commemorates the Declaration of Independence of 1776; it is celebrated with fireworks, parades and barbecues.

mardi-gras-nola.fait: This Louisiana carnival begins on January 6 and ends at midnight on the night of Mardi Gras: depending on the year, it lasts between 28 and 63 days.

rodeo.fait: Its events come from the work of cowboys on ranches; the show opens with a parade on horseback with flags, followed by the national anthem.

baseball.fait: The origins of this sport are disputed, but its first modern rules were codified in the United States in 1845.

cheerleading.fait: Originating in the United States, this activity had 3.47 million participants there in 2021, compared with about 100,000 in the rest of the world.

hula.fait: This dance, developed in the Hawaiian Islands, is accompanied by a chant called “mele,” which it enacts or comments on; it includes many hand gestures.

cable-cars.fait: These cable-hauled streetcars still run on three lines in San Francisco, where they are used mostly by tourists.

liberty-bell.fait: Ordered from London in 1752, this Philadelphia bell cracked the first time it was used; it symbolizes American independence.

hollywood-sign.fait: This monumental sign in capital letters stands on Mount Lee, a hill overlooking the neighborhood of the same name, in Los Angeles.

empire-state.fait: Opened in 1931, this 102-story Art Deco skyscraper is 381 meters tall and was for decades the tallest building in the world.

maison-blanche.fait: Built between 1792 and 1800 of sandstone painted white, this residence has housed every American president since John Adams.

capitole-us.fait: The seat of Congress, this neoclassical building has its own subway, opened in 1909: three lines and six stations connect its various halls.

lincoln-memorial.fait: Its 36 white marble columns recall the 36 states the country had when Lincoln died; Martin Luther King delivered “I Have a Dream” there.

pont-brooklyn.fait: Opened in 1883 after 14 years of construction, this 1,825-meter suspension bridge crosses the East River to connect Manhattan and Brooklyn.

alcatraz.fait: Named in 1775 after the pelicans that took refuge there, this island in San Francisco Bay housed a federal prison from 1934 to 1963.

barrage-hoover.fait: Built from 1931 to 1936 on the Colorado River, between Arizona and Nevada, this structure required nearly 7 million tons of concrete.

times-square.fait: Nicknamed the “Crossroads of the World,” this Manhattan neighborhood sees about 365,000 people pass through every day.

route-66.fait: Nicknamed “The Mother Road,” it linked Chicago to Santa Monica, California, over nearly 3,670 km, between 1926 and 1985.

walk-of-fame.fait: This Los Angeles sidewalk is embedded with stars bearing the names of entertainers: there were 2,741 of them in December 2022.

las-vegas-strip.fait: This 6.7 km stretch of boulevard is home to many of the world's largest hotels and casinos; 5.6 km of it actually lies in Paradise, outside the city.

central-park.fait: Completed in 1873 after sixteen years of work, this 341-hectare park is the most visited in the country, with 37.5 million visitors a year.

yellowstone.fait: Established in 1872, it is the oldest national park in the world; its caldera contains two-thirds of the planet's geysers.

yosemite.fait: Designated a national park in 1890, this site in the Sierra Nevada, in California, attracts hikers and climbers with its waterfalls and granite domes.

monument-valley.fait: The Navajo call this landscape of mesas and buttes “the valley of the rocks”; it lies on the border between Arizona and Utah.

antelope-canyon.fait: Its Navajo name means “the place where water runs through the rocks”; it is one of the most photographed slot canyons in the American Southwest.

devils-tower.fait: This Wyoming monolith rises 386 meters above the surrounding land; in 1906, it became the country's first national monument.

vallee-mort.fait: It contains the lowest point in the United States, 85.5 meters below sea level, and a temperature of 56.7 °C was recorded there on July 10, 1913.

colline-parlement.fait: It is on this hill in Ottawa that the country's Parliament is built; a parliamentary protective service is responsible for it.

vieux-quebec.fait: Samuel de Champlain built his Habitation here in 1608; this historic heart is divided between the Upper Town, on Cap Diamant, and the Lower Town, at its foot.

basilique-nd-montreal.fait: The mother church of Montreal, this basilica houses religious ornaments whose richness is unmatched in the city.

chute-montmorency.fait: At 83 meters high, this Quebec waterfall is thirty meters taller than Niagara Falls; staircases of 487 steps allow visitors to view it.

rocher-perce.fait: This rocky islet with steep cliffs and a natural arch rises in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, at the far eastern tip of the Gaspé Peninsula.

hockey-glace.fait: Originating in Canada, this sport developed in the late 19th century is often described as “the fastest team sport in the world.”

canot-glace.fait: In winter, this canoe was once used to link the shores and islands of the St. Lawrence, in Quebec; today it is a leisure activity and a competitive event.

cabane-sucre.fait: Maple sap harvested in spring is boiled there to make syrup; some also serve meals, popular with tourists and locals alike.

tourtiere.fait: This meat pie, filled with pork, veal or beef and potatoes, is part of Christmas Eve and New Year's Eve feasts in Quebec.

pate-chinois.fait: Ground beef, corn, mashed potatoes: this dish was informally crowned “Quebec's national dish” after a public consultation conducted by Le Devoir.

ceinture-flechee.fait: Finger-woven from wool, this sash can easily exceed two meters in length; it is associated with the fur trade.

teotihuacan.fait: At its height, this metropolis was the largest city in pre-Columbian America and may have had more than 200,000 inhabitants.

palenque.fait: It is estimated that less than 10% of this Maya city in Chiapas has been explored: more than a thousand structures remain covered by forest.

tulum.fait: This ancient Maya city, also called Zama, borders the Caribbean Sea on the Yucatán Peninsula; the site has been part of a national park since 1981.

uxmal.fait: The name of this Maya city is said to mean “built three times”; it reached its peak over some hundred and fifty years, from about 800 to 950.

monte-alban.fait: This city was built on the leveled summit of a mountain that rises 400 meters above the valley; it reached its peak during the Zapotec period.

pierre-soleil.fait: Wrongly called the “Aztec calendar,” this lava disk, 3.6 m in diameter, weighs 24.6 tons; it was rediscovered by chance in 1790 in Mexico City.

popocatepetl.fait: At 5,426 meters high, this volcano located 70 km from Mexico City is the country's second-highest mountain; it has been active since January 2005.

tetes-olmeques.fait: There are 17 known basalt heads of this kind, believed to be portraits of Olmec rulers; the smallest weighs 6 tons.

sombrero.fait: In Spanish, this word refers to any hat; in French, it generally refers to a type of hat originating in Mexico.

pinata.fait: This hollow, brightly colored figure, often made of papier-mâché, is filled with treats: it is broken open blindfolded to get at its contents.

alebrije.fait: These brightly colored fantastic creatures were born from a dream of Pedro Linares, who fell ill in the 1930s and recreated them in papier-mâché.

catrina.fait: This female skeleton dressed in rich clothes and wearing a hat is generally attributed to the cartoonist José Guadalupe Posada, around 1912.

papel-picado.fait: These colorful perforated sheets, hung as garlands, decorate altars dedicated to the dead in Mexico during the Day of the Dead.

tequila.fait: This spirit is made from a single plant, Agave tequilana; to bear this name, it must come from Jalisco or a few municipalities in four other states.

mezcal.fait: Its name comes from Nahuatl and means “oven-cooked agave”: this spirit is made from agave, also called “maguey.”

pulque.fait: This drink of 6 to 8 percent alcohol comes from the fermentation of agave sap; in pre-Hispanic times, it held an essential place in ritual life.

guacamole.fait: In this preparation of Mexican origin, the avocado is mashed rather than puréed; its distinctive feature is that it contains no spices.

mole.fait: This sauce of pre-Hispanic origin combines chili pepper, cocoa, sesame and peanuts; some recipes have more than a hundred ingredients.

burrito.fait: Its tortilla, usually made of wheat flour, is rolled into a cylinder and not fried: otherwise, the dish would become a “chimichanga.”

quesadilla.fait: Its name comes from the Spanish “queso,” cheese: this snack, or “antojito,” is found in Mexico and throughout Central America.

pain-des-morts.fait: This sugar-dusted sweet bun is made only for the Day of the Dead; its most basic shape evokes a skull, and the marks on top suggest shinbones.

voladores.fait: Four dancers tied by their legs let go from the top of a 30-meter pole and descend while spinning, as a fifth plays music at the top.

charreria.fait: Similar to rodeo, this sporting event is based on the work of charros; it includes nine events for men and one for women.

daiquiri.fait: Originating in Cuba, this cocktail is based on three main ingredients: white rum, lime juice and sugar.

malecon.fait: This seafront promenade runs along Havana for 8 kilometers; its name means “the jetty,” but it is officially called “Maceo Avenue.”

vieille-havane.fait: This historic center is a World Heritage Site for its Baroque and neoclassical monuments and its houses with arcades, balconies and wrought-iron grilles.

cha-cha-cha.fait: This musical genre was born in Cuba; the titles of songs and dance pieces very often use its shortened name, “cha-cha.”

conga.fait: This single-headed drum, played with the hands, appeared in Cuba in the 18th century and spread throughout Latin music.

varadero.fait: On the north coast of the island, this beach resort, one of the largest in the Caribbean, is mainly frequented by Canadian and European tourists.

tikal.fait: The capital of one of the most powerful Maya kingdoms, this city reached its peak between 200 and 900, before being abandoned at the end of the 10th century.

antigua-gt.fait: This former capital is known for its Baroque colonial architecture and for its ruins, caused by the two earthquakes of 1773.

quirigua.fait: This Maya archaeological site lies in the Motagua Valley, along a railway line; it has been a World Heritage Site since 1981.

rabinal-achi.fait: This 15th-century Maya musical drama is danced with masks every January 25, the feast of Saint Paul, in the town of Rabinal.

grand-trou-bleu.fait: This underwater cenote opens off the coast, in Lighthouse Reef; it is protected as part of the Belize Barrier Reef.

xunantunich.fait: Its name means “stone maiden” in Maya; this hilltop site is famous for its well-preserved stucco frescoes.

altun-ha.fait: The largest temple of this ancient Maya city, 16 meters high, appears on the logo of the country's main beer brand, Belikin.

lamanai.fait: The name of this Maya archaeological site, of pre-Columbian origin, means “submerged crocodile”; it is located in the north of the country.

copan.fait: This Maya city reached its peak in the 7th century before being abandoned around the 10th; it lies deep in the jungle, 12 km from the Guatemalan border.

roatan.fait: On this Caribbean island, about 60 kilometers long and less than 8 wide, most people still speak a dialect form of English.

rio-platano.fait: This region of tropical forests, where 2,000 Indigenous people still live, has been a World Heritage Site since 1982 and listed as in danger since 2011.

yojoa.fait: This lake straddles three departments, 184 km from the capital, Tegucigalpa; it was designated a Ramsar site on May 5, 2005.

cayos-cochinos.fait: This archipelago consists of two small islands and 13 smaller coral cays, 30 km northeast of La Ceiba.

guanaja.fait: Most of its 10,000 inhabitants live in Bonacca, a main town built not on the island itself but on a pair of coral reefs.

pupusa.fait: This thick corn or rice flatbread, stuffed with cheese or beans, has been declared the national dish; it even has a day dedicated to it.

joya-ceren.fait: This archaeological site, 25 km from San Salvador in the department of La Libertad, is nicknamed the “Pompeii of the Americas.”

tazumal.fait: The metal objects found in this Maya complex date from the 8th century and are among the oldest reported in Mesoamerica.

volcan-santa-ana.fait: At 2,381 meters, it is the country's highest volcano; its last eruption, in 2005, hurled ash and rocks over more than a kilometer.

coatepeque.fait: This lake fills a caldera and is part of the Apaneca-Ilamatepec Biosphere Reserve, recognized by UNESCO in 2007.

granada-ni.fait: Its Andalusian-style buildings earned it the nickname “Great Sultana”; this city stretches along Lake Nicaragua, overlooked by the Mombacho volcano.

cathedrale-leon-ni.nom: Cathedral of the Assumption of León
cathedrale-leon-ni.fait: Built from 1747 to 1814, this Baroque cathedral has withstood earthquakes and volcanic eruptions thanks to the sturdiness of its walls.

volcan-masaya.fait: It is one of the few volcanoes in the world where you can drive right up to the edge of the crater; it is only 25 km from Managua.

gueguense.fait: This satirical theatrical tradition combines masked street theater, music and folk ballet; it is also spelled “Güegüence.”

iles-mais.fait: These two islands in the Caribbean Sea, Big and Little, lie about 75 km off the coast; they are most often called the Corn Islands.

arenal.fait: The youngest volcano in the country, this almost symmetrical cone remained in eruption from July 29, 1968, to December 2010.

spheres-diquis.fait: Several hundred of these stone balls have been discovered in the south of the country; they are commonly attributed to the ancient Diquís culture.

corcovado-cr.fait: Established in 1975 on the Osa Peninsula, this park was described by National Geographic as the most intense place in the world in terms of biodiversity.

ile-cocos.fait: Lying 491 km off the coast, this volcanic island in the Pacific is known for having hosted pirates who hid their treasures there.

monteverde.fait: This reserve protects about 10,500 hectares of tropical cloud forest on the foothills of the Cordillera de Tilarán.

manuel-antonio.fait: Established in 1972 on the Pacific coast, this park covers 1,983 hectares of land and 55,000 of sea; in 2011, Forbes ranked it among the 12 most beautiful in the world.

canal-panama.nom: Canal linking the Atlantic and the Pacific
canal-panama.fait: At 80 km long, it opened on August 15, 1914: from New York to San Francisco, it cuts the journey from 22,500 to 9,500 kilometers.

san-blas.fait: This coastal archipelago in the Caribbean Sea, sometimes called the Mulatas Archipelago, is administratively part of the comarca of Guna Yala.

mola.fait: Kuna women sew together several layers of fabric in different colors, then cut them with scissors to reveal designs.

fort-san-lorenzo.fait: This ruined fort overlooks the mouth of the Chagres River; it was part of the Spanish Crown's defense system for transatlantic trade.

bocas-del-toro.fait: The main town of this Caribbean archipelago is Bocas del Toro, on Colón Island; all its islands can be reached by water taxi.

citadelle-ferriere.fait: Built in the early 19th century by Henri Christophe, it is the largest fortress in the Americas; it could hold up to 5,000 men.

sans-souci.fait: This palace in Milot, in the north of the country, was the main residence of Henri Christophe; it lies about twenty kilometers from Cap-Haïtien.

tap-tap.fait: These shared taxis are the country's main means of transportation, including in its capital, Port-au-Prince.

soupe-joumou.fait: This pumpkin soup has been on the list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity since December 16, 2021.

rara.fait: This musical form originating in Haiti is played during street parades, usually during Easter week.

compas.fait: Created in the mid-1950s by saxophonist Nemours Jean-Baptiste, this genre borrows elements from jazz and Cuban music.

carnaval-jacmel.fait: Celebrated since 1991 on the Sunday before the national carnival, it showcases local culture, including giant papier-mâché masks.

marche-fer.fait: Also called the Hyppolite Market or the Vallières Market, it is the best known of the public markets in Port-au-Prince, the capital.

pikliz.fait: This condiment combines shredded carrots and white cabbage, onions and chili peppers, seasoned with lime juice or vinegar; it is served with pressed fried plantains.

bachata.fait: Initially scorned because it came from the lower social classes, this guitar music began to gain popularity in the 1980s.

zone-coloniale-sd.fait: This historic heart of the capital, called “Zona Colonial” in Spanish, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cathedrale-primatiale.fait: Built in the early 16th century by the Spanish in Santo Domingo, it is the first cathedral constructed on the American continent.

punta-cana.fait: At the country's eastern tip, this town of about 50,000 inhabitants is its main beach resort.

forteresse-ozama.fait: Built between 1502 and 1505, it is one of the first European military structures in the Americas; it served as a prison until the 1960s.

larimar.fait: This gemstone, a variety of pectolite, is found in the Dominican Republic; its color ranges from white to dark blue.

trou-bleu-dean.fait: At 202 meters deep, this blue hole was the deepest in the world before the discovery of the Dragon Hole in the South China Sea.

exumas.fait: This archipelago of more than 360 islands or islets stretches over more than 200 kilometers; the Tropic of Cancer runs through George Town, on the island of Great Exuma.

bimini-road.fait: Some have seen it as a remnant of Atlantis; to geologists, these underwater stones are beach deposits hardened by natural processes.

eleuthera.fait: Very elongated, this island is 180 km long and barely 2 km wide; its name comes from a Greek word meaning “free.”

pig-beach.fait: This uninhabited island in the Exumas is home to many released pigs, which root around the beaches at low tide and even go into the water.

steel-drum.fait: This melodic percussion instrument is played in orchestras called “steelbands”; their rehearsal space is known as a “panyard.”

calypso.fait: Also called “kaiso,” this musical genre closely tied to carnival has spread to the rest of the Caribbean and to Venezuela.

carnaval-tt.fait: This festival takes place on the Monday and Tuesday before Ash Wednesday; since the '70s, soca has been the music most played in the streets.

lac-brea.fait: This natural asphalt lake, one of the largest in the world, covers about 40 hectares and reaches 75 meters at its deepest point.

pitons.fait: These volcanic spires are the emblem of Saint Lucia; they appear, in stylized form, on the national flag.

qualibou.fait: Also called Soufrière, this volcano in Saint Lucia consists of a caldera partly submerged by the Caribbean Sea.

mont-gimie.fait: The highest mountain in Saint Lucia at 950 m, this peak of volcanic origin can only be climbed with an accredited local guide.

cathedrale-castries.nom: Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception, Castries
cathedrale-castries.fait: This large Catholic building in Castries, Saint Lucia, is both a basilica and a cathedral; it is the seat of the Archdiocese of Castries.

pain-de-sucre.fait: This 396-meter granite monolith rises at the mouth of Guanabara Bay in Rio de Janeiro; it is reached by cable car.

copacabana.fait: Stretching 4.5 km, this Rio de Janeiro beach is nicknamed the “Princess of the Sea” and is considered one of the most famous in the world.

ouro-preto.fait: Born from the discovery of gold in the rivers of Minas Gerais, this town founded in 1711 had more inhabitants around 1750 than Rio de Janeiro or New York.

rencontre-eaux.fait: Near Manaus, the ocher waters of the Solimões River and the black waters of the Rio Negro flow side by side without mixing for dozens of kilometers.

brigadeiro.fait: This Brazilian chocolate confection has uncertain origins: depending on the source, it dates back to the 1940s or to the 19th century.

pao-de-queijo.fait: This “cheese bread” is typical of the Brazilian states of Minas Gerais and Goiás; it is also found in Paraguay under the name chipa.

acaraje.fait: These small balls of black-eyed pea dough, onion and salt are fried in palm oil; they are an Afro-Brazilian culinary specialty.

moqueca.fait: This fish stew with tomatoes, onions, peppers and cilantro simmers slowly in a clay pot; it is typical of Bahia, Pará and Espírito Santo.

coxinha.fait: Its name means “little chicken thigh”: chopped or shredded chicken, covered in dough, shaped like a teardrop, then breaded and fried.

caipirinha.fait: This Brazilian cocktail combines cachaça, sugar and lime; it is said to have been created by peasants, hence its name, which means “little country girl.”

cachaca.fait: This Brazilian spirit is made from fresh sugarcane juice, fermented and then distilled; it is older than rum.

pandeiro.fait: A Brazilian version of the tambourine, this percussion instrument was brought to Brazil by the first Portuguese colonizers.

tamborim.fait: This Brazilian percussion instrument is a modern small frame drum; it is very different from the pandeiro.

samba.fait: This genre of music and dance was born in the early 20th century in the Afro-Brazilian communities of Rio de Janeiro; its dancers are called sambistas.

frevo.fait: This word refers to both a carnival music and a dance from Recife, capital of the state of Pernambuco, in northeastern Brazil.

maracatu.fait: This carnival procession from Pernambuco, Brazil, is rooted in the history of enslaved people and in ceremonies crowning Kongo kings and queens.

ecole-samba.fait: Originating in Rio de Janeiro, these groups parade in costume around a theme, with several hundred or even a few thousand people.

bumba-meu-boi.fait: This Brazilian folk dance brings together human characters and fantastic animals around the death and resurrection of an ox.

festival-parintins.fait: This popular festival is held every year on the last weekend of June in Parintins, in the Amazon region of Brazil.

cirio-nazare.fait: This Catholic festival in northern Brazil draws more than two million people every year to the city of Belém, in the state of Pará.

jangada.fait: This Portuguese word refers both to a wooden raft drifting down a river and to a traditional boat used by fishermen along the Brazilian coast.

aconcagua.fait: At 6,962 meters, this peak located thirteen kilometers from the Chilean border is the highest mountain outside Asia.

humahuaca.fait: This deep canyon in Jujuy Province, in northwestern Argentina, is home to villages rich in pre-Columbian and colonial remains.

ushuaia.fait: This capital of Tierra del Fuego Province is considered the southernmost city in the world; its port is one of the closest to Antarctica.

casa-rosada.fait: This seat of Argentina's executive branch, in central Buenos Aires, owes its name to the pink color of its facades; the president has an office there.

theatre-colon.fait: This Buenos Aires opera house is considered one of the best in the world for its size, its acoustics and its history.

ischigualasto.fait: Also called Valle de la Luna, this 63,000-hectare provincial park lies in the far northeast of San Juan Province, Argentina.

san-ignacio-mini.fait: These ruins in Misiones Province are those of a Jesuit mission founded in the early 17th century to evangelize the Guarani.

cafe-tortoni.fait: Opened in 1858 in Buenos Aires by a French Basque immigrant, this café is named after a Parisian establishment on the Boulevard des Italiens.

chimichurri.fait: This chili-based condiment, originally from Argentina, is a variant of green sauce, although a red version also exists.

choripan.fait: This sandwich combines a sausage and a bread roll, sometimes seasoned with chimichurri; in Argentina, it is eaten at an asado or as fast food.

pato.fait: This equestrian sport born among the gauchos was originally played with a dead bird, usually a duck, inside a leather bag; it is Argentina's national sport.

chacarera.fait: This couple dance from northern Argentina is characterized by its triple rhythm and the use of string instruments and the bombo legüero.

malambo.fait: This Argentine folk dance is performed solo; created in the 17th century in the Pampas, it is accompanied by a drum called a bombo and by guitars.

fileteado.fait: Born in Buenos Aires toward the end of the 19th century, this style of decorative painting originally adorned animal-drawn freight carts.

eglises-chiloe.fait: These wooden churches from the 17th and 18th centuries blend European Jesuit culture with the traditions and techniques of the archipelago's local peoples.

cap-horn.fait: Located in the Chilean part of Tierra del Fuego, this cape with strong and frequent storms has a reputation as a graveyard of ships.

la-moneda.fait: Its name means “Palace of the Mint”; located in Santiago, this building is the seat of the presidency of Chile.

humberstone.nom: Humberstone and Santa Laura Saltpeter Works
humberstone.fait: These two former sites in the Tarapacá Region, in northern Chile, were used to process potassium nitrate.

detroit-magellan.fait: At 611 kilometers long, this natural passage between the Atlantic and the Pacific is named after the first European to cross it, in 1520.

curanto.fait: This dish from the Chiloé archipelago is traditionally prepared in a hole about a meter and a half deep, on red-hot stones.

completo.fait: This Chilean version of the hot dog, bigger than the American one, is topped, depending on the variant, with avocado, tomato, mayonnaise or sauerkraut.

mote-huesillo.fait: This nonalcoholic drink made with cooked wheat and dried peach inspired the expression “more Chilean than mote con huesillo.”

chorrillana.fait: This dish of Chilean cuisine is a plate of French fries topped with various meats, eggs or fried onions.

rodeo-huaso.fait: The second most popular sport in Chile after soccer, it is practiced by pairs of huasos on horseback who must stop a bull.

rongo-rongo.fait: These signs carved in wood, discovered on Easter Island, have resisted every attempt at decipherment; they may constitute a script.

sacsayhuaman.fait: This Inca fortress at 3,700 m above sea level, two kilometers from Cusco, is shaped like the head of a puma, a sacred animal in Inca tradition.

ollantaytambo.fait: The name of this Inca fortress means “Ollantay's inn,” after a warrior; Manco Inca took refuge there after the fall of Cusco.

moray.fait: These Inca terraces in concentric circles create some twenty microclimates; they may have been an ancient agricultural research center.

chan-chan.fait: Capital of the Chimor empire from 900 to 1470, this site near Trujillo was the largest city of the pre-Columbian era in South America.

kuelap.fait: This fortress was built in the 10th century by the Chachapoyas on a ridge overlooking the Utcubamba Valley, in northern Peru.

colca.fait: At 3,270 m deep, this canyon was once thought to be the deepest in the world; from a natural lookout, condors can be seen soaring.

caral.fait: This archaeological site, in the desert 23 km from the coast of Peru, is the remnant of the oldest known city in the Americas to date.

santa-catalina.fait: This convent in Arequipa, which covers 2 hectares, is home to a community of Dominican nuns; it is presented as the largest in the world.

huacachina.fait: This village near Ica is built around a small lake; according to legend, a princess turned mermaid still swims in its waters.

lomo-saltado.fait: This sliced beef stir-fry appeared around the mid-19th century under the influence of Cantonese Chinese immigrants; it is cooked in a wok with soy sauce.

aji-gallina.fait: Its name means “hen with chili pepper”; this dish from Lima, with Spanish and French influences, is widespread throughout Peru.

anticucho.fait: In Peru, these skewers are notably made with pieces of beef heart, marinated and then grilled; they are also eaten in Bolivia and Chile.

pachamanca.fait: This Peruvian specialty is cooked underground with hot stones; it is usually prepared for gatherings.

picarones.fait: These fritters made from squash and sweet potato, originally from Lima, are covered in chancaca, a kind of solid molasses.

chicha-morada.fait: This nonalcoholic drink is made from purple corn, a Peruvian variety; depending on the season, it is drunk hot or well chilled.

inti-raymi.fait: This “festival of the sun” of Inca origin honors the winter solstice; it is held on June 24 at the fortress of Sacsayhuamán, near Cusco.

qoyllur-riti.fait: This pilgrimage brings together about 90,000 people from the Cusco region every year; its high point is a night walk to the top of a glacier.

quipu.fait: Lacking writing, the Inca administration recorded numbers with knots on cords of various colors attached to a main rope.

tumi.fait: This knife with a semicircular blade was used for sacrifices before the Spanish conquest; in Peru, hanging one on the wall is believed to bring good luck.

ciudad-perdida.fait: This ancient city in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta is believed to have been founded around 800 AD, 650 years earlier than Machu Picchu.

san-agustin.fait: This park in the Andes has 300 monumental sculptures, left by a culture that reached its peak during the first eight centuries of the Common Era.

las-lajas.fait: This Catholic sanctuary in the canyon of the Guáitara River, 7 km from Ipiales, has been a major pilgrimage center since the 18th century.

penon-guatape.fait: This 220-meter-high monolith, also called Piedra del Peñol, rises in Guatapé, in the department of Antioquia, Colombia.

monserrate.fait: This hill bordering Bogotá to the east was called “cerro de las Nieves,” the Hill of the Snows, until the mid-17th century.

villa-de-leyva.fait: This small colonial town in the department of Boyacá is known for its huge cobblestone main square; a kite festival is held there in mid-August.

san-felipe-barajas.fait: This fort in Cartagena de Indias is the largest fortress built by the Spanish during their colonial period; the first fort dates from 1536.

tayrona.fait: This protected area in the Caribbean region, 34 km from Santa Marta, includes 150 km² of land and 30 km² of marine area.

bandeja-paisa.fait: This typical dish of Antioquian cuisine stands out for its abundance and variety; served in full, it comes only on a platter.

lechona.fait: This typical dish of the Tolima region consists of pieces of suckling pig and peas; it is served with insulso, a corn-based dough.

tejo.fait: This traditional sport, also called turmequé, originated with the Chibcha Indigenous people in west-central Colombia.

sombrero-vueltiao.fait: This hat made of arrow cane has its origins in the Indigenous Zenú culture; in 2004, the Colombian Congress declared it a cultural symbol of the nation.

carnaval-barranquilla.fait: This 19th-century tradition begins on the Saturday before Ash Wednesday and ends on Mardi Gras; thousands of people take part.

noirs-et-blancs.fait: This carnival in San Juan de Pasto takes place from December 28 to January 7, outside the usual calendar of carnivals around Mardi Gras.

velitas.fait: On the night of December 7, Colombians light lanterns and candles in the streets to celebrate the Immaculate Conception.

poporo.fait: Among certain ethnic groups such as the Kogi, this gourd is given to a young boy to mark his passage from child to adult of marrying age.

salar-uyuni.fait: This salt desert stretches across the high plateaus of southwestern Bolivia; it takes its name from the nearby town of Uyuni.

laguna-colorada.fait: This salt lake on the Bolivian Altiplano, at an altitude of 4,278 m, covers 60 km² with an average depth of 35 centimeters.

isla-del-sol.fait: The largest island in Lake Titicaca, it was originally called Isla Titikaka: it is the island that gave the great lake its name.

cerro-rico.fait: Mined for its mineral resources since the 16th century, this 4,782 m peak towers over Potosí; its profile appears on the coat of arms of Bolivia.

route-yungas.fait: Very narrow, without guardrails and often shrouded in fog, this road from 1930 linking La Paz to Coroico was nicknamed the “Road of Death.”

marche-sorcieres.fait: In downtown La Paz, this market sells ritual objects from Aymara culture; magic rites are also performed there.

chiquitos.fait: These settlements founded by the Jesuits in the 17th and 18th centuries are located in the north of the department of Santa Cruz, Bolivia.

carnaval-oruro.fait: The largest annual cultural event in Bolivia, this carnival is part of the Ito festival, celebrated in honor of the Uru people.

ekeko.fait: This Aymara god of abundance, fertility and happiness remains present in Bolivia in the form of a figurine called an equeco.

alasitas.fait: Starting on January 24 in La Paz, people buy a miniature of a dream they wish to fulfill there, then offer it to Ekeko, the Aymara god of abundance.

saltena.fait: This baked empanada contains broth, meat, hard-boiled egg and spices; in Bolivia, it is eaten mostly in the morning.

api.fait: This drink from the Andean Altiplano owes its purple color to purple corn; its Quechua name refers to a preparation made from corn flour.

pique-macho.fait: This dish of beef, French fries, onions and hard-boiled eggs is said to have been born in the 1970s at the El Prado restaurant in Cochabamba.

silpancho.fait: Its Quechua name means “flat and thin”: a round piece of breaded, fried beef covers the plate in this dish from Cochabamba.

galapagos.fait: This archipelago of some forty volcanic islands has been a province of Ecuador since 1832; the easternmost one is 929 km from the mainland.

cotopaxi.fait: The highest active volcano in Ecuador at 5,897 meters, this perfect cone destroyed several towns during its 1877 eruption.

chimborazo.fait: The highest summit in the Ecuadorian Andes at 6,263 m, this volcano is nicknamed Taita Chimborazo, meaning “Papa Chimborazo.”

quilotoa.fait: The volcano in Ecuador that bears this name rises to 3,914 m, about thirty kilometers west of Latacunga, in the south of the Cordillera Occidental.

ingapirca.fait: The name of this archaeological complex in Cañar Province, Ecuador, means “Inca wall” in the Kichwa language.

compania-quito.fait: This 17th-century Jesuit church, in the historic center of Quito, is considered one of the seven wonders of Ecuador.

basilique-voeu.fait: Dedicated to the Sacred Heart, this basilica is the largest neo-Gothic building in Latin America; its towers are the tallest structures in Quito.

panama-chapeau.fait: Despite its name, this hat is of Ecuadorian origin; it is handmade from the leaves of a plant, Carludovica palmata.

encebollado.fait: This fish dish from Ecuador's Pacific coast is cooked with yuca, red onions and lime in a tomato broth.

fanesca.fait: This soup is prepared the week before Easter with twelve grains from the Ecuadorian Andes, each representing a disciple of Jesus.

llapingacho.fait: These mashed potato patties with melted cheese are a popular and very inexpensive dish in Ecuador, served as a side.

colada-morada.fait: This thick purple drink is made in Ecuador with fruits typical of the country, spices and corn flour.

rondador.fait: This set of reed panpipes produces two sounds at once; it is considered the national instrument of Ecuador.

salto-angel.fait: At 807 m, this waterfall has the highest drop in the world; it is named after Jimmy Angel, an American aviator who flew over the site in 1933.

canaima.fait: Created on June 12, 1962 on the Guiana Shield, in the state of Bolívar, this park has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1994.

auyan-tepuy.fait: Its Arekuna name means “devil's mountain”; this plateau of nearly 700 km² towers nearly 1,000 meters above the forest of the Gran Sabana.

los-roques.fait: This archipelago of about 350 islands, cays or islets lies about 130 km off the coast of Venezuela and has 1,500 inhabitants.

catatumbo.fait: This storm occurs 140 to 160 nights a year above the mouth of the Catatumbo River, with a frequency of 280 lightning strikes per hour.

hallaca.fait: This Venezuelan Christmas dish is a corn dough usually filled with meat, olives and raisins, boiled in a banana leaf.

cachapa.fait: This thick pancake of fresh yellow corn, worked with milk and sugar, comes from Venezuela; it is often served with fresh cheese.

tequeno.fait: According to popular belief, these sticks of hard white cheese wrapped in a strip of dough and then fried owe their name to the town of Los Teques, their place of origin.

diables-yare.fait: On the ninth Thursday after Holy Thursday, dancers in red costumes and demon masks represent the triumph of good over evil.

liqui-liqui.fait: This outfit from the Llanos region is a Creole adaptation of clothing from the Philippines; it has been the national costume of Venezuela since 2017.

colonia-sacramento.fait: Capital of the department of Colonia, in southwestern Uruguay, this town is also the oldest in the country.

stade-centenario.fait: Located in the Parque Batlle neighborhood of Montevideo, this stadium, used mainly for soccer, commemorates the centenary of Uruguay's independence.

theatre-solis.fait: Opened in 1856 in the Old Town of Montevideo, this theater is considered the oldest in South America.

cabo-polonio.fait: This hamlet in the department of Rocha, Uruguay, is both a beach resort and a national and natural park.

punta-del-este.fait: This beach resort on Maldonado Bay stands out for its two large beaches, Playa Mansa and Playa Brava, which contribute greatly to its reputation.

palais-legislatif-uy.fait: This palace is the seat of the General Assembly of Uruguay, a parliament made up of the Chamber of Representatives and the Senate.

candombe.fait: This musical genre emerged in Uruguay; according to some musicologists, it has its origins in the rhythms of Bantu Africa.

chivito.fait: This meat sandwich, typical of Uruguay, is usually served with mayonnaise, French fries and Olivier salad.

palacio-lopez.fait: This neoclassical palace, on the bank of the Paraguay River in central Asunción, houses the seat of the presidency of the Republic.

tavarangue.fait: These ruins in the department of Itapúa are those of one of the thirty reductions founded by the Jesuits for the Guarani people.

terere.fait: Similar to mate but drunk cold, with lots of ice and often medicinal herbs, this beverage originated in Paraguay.

chipa.fait: This food, traditionally made from cassava starch and cheese, comes in about 70 varieties in Paraguay, where a national day is dedicated to it on August 9.

fort-zeelandia.fait: This pentagon-shaped fort, built by the Dutch in Paramaribo to protect a trading post, has become a museum.

jodensavanne.fait: This name referred to a Jewish settlement on the banks of the Suriname River, about 50 km south of Paramaribo, that grew sugarcane.

palais-presidentiel-sr.fait: Facing Independence Square, this palace is one of the best-maintained examples of Dutch colonial architecture in Suriname.

neve-shalom.fait: Completed in 1842, it is the only synagogue in Suriname; in Paramaribo, it stands next to the city's main mosque.

keti-koti.fait: Every July 1, this holiday celebrates the abolition of slavery; its name, in Sranan Tongo, literally means “broken chains.”

caacupe.fait: This church in Caacupé, Paraguay, is at once a cathedral, a minor basilica and a national shrine for the Catholic Church.

port-envalira.fait: This pass, the only road link between France and Andorra, separates the waters flowing toward the Atlantic from those heading to the Mediterranean.

statue-liberte-palais-public.fait: This marble warrior wears a three-towered crown representing the fortified city; a countess from Berlin gave it to the Republic.

chambres-raphael.fait: These four reception rooms in the papal apartments are famous for their frescoes, painted by Raphael and his pupils.

obelisque-saint-pierre.fait: This Egyptian obelisk of Aswan granite was brought to Rome by Caligula to adorn his circus, before being erected in St. Peter's Square.

cour-belvedere.fait: Designed by Bramante for Pope Julius II, this terraced courtyard was cut into three by a building; part of it is now used as a parking lot.

notre-dame-immaculee.fait: This Romanesque-Byzantine cathedral hosts the pontifical services of the major religious holidays, of Saint Devota's Day and of Monaco's National Day.

jardin-exotique-mc.fait: This botanical garden run by Monaco's city hall lies at the foot of a cliff, in a district that bears its name.

salle-garnier.fait: This opera house adjoining the Monte Carlo Casino was designed by Charles Garnier and inaugurated with a performance by Sarah Bernhardt.

port-hercule.fait: This historic marina in the La Condamine district offers nearly 700 berths on the Riviera.

hotel-de-paris.fait: This Belle Époque luxury hotel in Monte Carlo was founded in 1864 by Prince Charles III's Société des Bains de Mer.

ggantija.fait: Its name means “giants' tower”: these two prehistoric temples on the island of Gozo gave their name to an entire phase of the megalithic temples.

rotonde-mosta.fait: Inspired by the Pantheon in Rome, this church has one of the largest domes in the world, supported by walls more than 9 meters thick.

fort-saint-ange.fait: Once called Castrum Maris, this fort in Birgu is positioned to watch over the entrance to the Grand Harbour and the approaches to the neighboring inlets.

gozo.fait: Called Gaulos in antiquity, this secondary island of the Maltese archipelago has its own minister, who sits in its main town, Rabat.

comino.fait: This island owes its name to cumin, one of the few plants that grow in its arid soil; it has only a handful of permanent residents.

gbejna.fait: This small cheese is made from sheep's milk on Gozo, from goat's milk elsewhere in the archipelago, and increasingly from cow's milk in industrial production.

kusksu.fait: This fava bean soup takes its name from its small pasta beads, similar to couscous but thicker, which give it its creamy texture.

hala-sultan-tekke.fait: This Muslim shrine on the shore of the Salt Lake, near Larnaca, is also called the Mosque of Umm Haram, the wet nurse of the Prophet Muhammad.

cap-greco.fait: At the island's southeastern tip, this cape with cliffs riddled with sea caves has housed the transmitters of Radio Monte Carlo Doualiya since 1972.

eglises-troodos.fait: These ten painted Byzantine churches in the Troodos region form a group inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List.

afelia.fait: This Cypriot stew is made with pork first marinated in red wine, then seasoned with coriander seeds.

palais-grand-ducal.fait: This Renaissance palace is the town residence of the Grand Duke, the head of state; a ceremonial changing of the guard takes place there once a month.

abbaye-echternach.fait: The tomb of Saint Willibrord, its founder, lies in the crypt of this abbey, which became a pilgrimage center that gave rise to a dancing procession.

beaufort-lu.fait: This site in Beaufort brings together the ruins of a medieval fortress and, right next to it, a 17th-century residence.

couteau-suisse.fait: The blade and tools all fold into the handle, so this knife stays pocket-sized despite its many functions.

glacier-express.fait: It is said to be the slowest express train in the world: it is not fast, but you make the whole journey without changing seats and it skips local stops.

eiger.fait: This peak's name does not mean “ogre” but probably “great spear”; the confusion comes from the climbers who died on its north face.

viaduc-landwasser.fait: Barely out of a tunnel, trains come straight onto this viaduct spanning the gorge; about 60 cross it every day.

abbaye-saint-gall.fait: Founded in the 8th century, this abbey, with its library, was for several centuries one of the most important Benedictine monasteries in Europe.

chateau-gruyeres.fait: This castle in the canton of Fribourg is the second most visited in Switzerland, after Chillon, and also hosts temporary exhibitions.

lackerli.fait: Their name means “sweet treat”: these small glazed squares from Basel, similar to gingerbread, combine honey, candied fruit and almonds.

schnitzel.fait: This thin slice of breaded and fried meat is a traditional dish from Vienna, called escalope viennoise in French.

opera-etat.fait: This name refers both to a public opera and ballet company in Vienna and to the building, inaugurated in 1869, that houses it.

stephansdom.fait: The great bell of this Gothic cathedral, named “Die Pummerin,” weighs 20 tons; its glazed tile roof forms diagonal patterns.

grossglockner.fait: The highest point in Austria, this peak sees about 5,000 ascents a year and played an important role in the rise of mountaineering.

eisriesenwelt.fait: Its name means “world of the ice giants”: this cave near Werfen is the largest natural ice cave in the world.

abbaye-admont.fait: This Benedictine monastery houses the largest monastic library in the world, completed in 1776, as well as a modern museum.

hochosterwitz.fait: Perched on a dolomite crag, this medieval castle is one of the symbols of Carinthia and one of its most visited monuments.

linzer-torte.fait: This lattice-topped tart is usually filled with red currant jam in Austria and Switzerland, and with raspberry jam in Germany and Alsace.

chateau-mirabell.fait: This Baroque palace stands in the old town of Salzburg; the building is part of UNESCO's World Heritage.

couque-dinant.fait: This honey cookie is so hard that many people cannot bite into it; on the other hand, it keeps indefinitely.

kattenstoet.fait: Until 1817, real cats were thrown from the top of the tower of the Cloth Hall in Ypres; this parade now replaces them with stuffed toys.

grottes-han.fait: These caves at Han-sur-Lesse, in the municipality of Rochefort in Wallonia, form a system linked to the Lesse River, in the geological region of the Calestienne.

beguinages-flamands.fait: These enclaves built by communities of beguines have outlived their residents: there are no longer any beguine communities in Belgium today.

tram-cote.fait: This tram serves the Belgian coast from De Panne, near the French border, to Knokke, near the Dutch border.

edam.fait: This cheese is traditionally sold as a pale yellow ball, coated in a thick layer of yellow or red paraffin wax.

hareng-nouveau.fait: In the Netherlands, this name refers to the first herring of the season ready to be eaten, also called maatje.

kibbeling.fait: These pieces of fried cod bear a name that, in the 19th century, referred to the salted cheeks of codfish, a popular food.

jeune-fille-perle.fait: Nicknamed the “Mona Lisa of the North,” this Vermeer painting remained forgotten for more than two hundred years before being rediscovered by a collector.

afsluitdijk.fait: Despite its name, meaning “closing dike,” this structure is, strictly speaking, a dam, since the water level differs on each side.

chateau-haar.fait: This castle was rebuilt by Pierre Cuypers, the architect who also designed the Rijksmuseum and Amsterdam Central Station.

magere-brug.fait: Its name means “skinny bridge”: the first bridge, built in 1670, was so narrow that two people could barely pass each other on it.

bourtange.fait: This fortified village in the province of Groningen, very close to the German border, was built during the Eighty Years' War.

barmbrack.fait: This Halloween raisin bread hides an object, often a ring: whoever finds it in their slice is considered lucky.

anneau-kerry.fait: This tourist route in County Kerry, in southwestern Ireland, loops around the Iveragh Peninsula.

iles-aran.fait: Geologically, this archipelago lying at the mouth of Galway Bay is an extension of the Burren karst landscape in County Clare.

pierre-blarney.fait: According to legend, kissing this stone in the battlements of Blarney Castle while upside down grants the gift of eloquence.

chateau-kilkenny.fait: Long owned by the Butler family, this castle was handed over to the people of Kilkenny for just 50 Irish pounds.

poulnabrone.fait: This dolmen is now just a “stone skeleton”: it was once covered with earth, and human remains have been found buried beneath it.

hapenny-bridge.fait: This cast-iron footbridge in Dublin is officially called the Liffey Bridge, a name that hardly anyone really uses anymore.

croix-brigitte.fait: Usually made of rushes, this cross protects the home from fire according to tradition; on St. Brigid's Day, the old one was burned.

guitarra.fait: The main instrument of fado soloists, this guitar comes in two main models: the Lisbon one has a scroll-shaped head, the Coimbra one a shield called a “tear.”

rabelo.fait: This flat-bottomed, keelless boat, fitted with a square sail, was used from the 13th century onward to carry wine on the Douro.

batalha.fait: This monastery was built to commemorate the victory of the Portuguese over the Castilians at the Battle of Aljubarrota, in 1385.

bibliotheque-joanina.fait: This Baroque library of the University of Coimbra owes its decorations to the riches the Portuguese brought back from Brazil.

chateau-maures.fait: Perched on a summit of the Sintra Mountains, this castle offers from its walls a view that stretches all the way to the Atlantic Ocean.

salade-horiatiki.fait: Its name means “peasant salad”: it combines tomato, cucumber, feta, olives, onion, green pepper, capers, oregano and olive oil.

mykonos.fait: This island in the northern Cyclades has Chóra and Áno Merá as its main towns; its inhabitants are called Mykoniates or Mykonians.

erechtheion.fait: This temple housed a saltwater well, the mythical gift of Poseidon, and the sacred olive tree, the mythical gift of Athena during her dispute with Poseidon.

porte-lionnes.fait: This gate of Mycenae, topped by two carved lionesses, is the only known example of monumental sculpture from the Mycenaean civilization.

cap-sounion.fait: This cape owes its fame mainly to the ruins of a temple of Poseidon; the Odyssey already called it “the holy cape of Athens.”

spanakopita.fait: Its name combines the Greek words for “spinach” and “pastry”: this savory pastry is, literally, a spinach pie.

tsipouro.fait: This pomace brandy is called tsikoudiá or rakí in Crete, where, unlike other varieties, it is never flavored with anise.

frappe.fait: This coffee, created in 1957, is made in a shaker: instant coffee, cold water, sugar and ice cubes are shaken until they form a foam.

avgolemono.fait: This Greek soup of Jewish origin is thickened with a mixture of egg and lemon, heated in the broth.

tortilla-patatas.fait: This thick potato omelet is cooked on both sides; in some bars, it is also served in slices on bread or as a sandwich.

patatas-bravas.fait: These diced potatoes, fried in olive oil, come from Madrid cuisine and are topped with a spicy paprika sauce.

casa-batllo.fait: For the facade of this Barcelona building, Gaudí combined stone, wrought iron, shards of glass and ceramics of every color.

giralda.fait: This former mosque minaret became the bell tower of Seville Cathedral; an unwritten rule forbids buildings in the center from reaching its height.

xeres.fait: These white wines from Jerez de la Frontera are fortified with brandy; in Great Britain, they are known by the name sherry.

manchego.fait: This cheese from Castilla–La Mancha is made with milk from Manchega sheep; its best season for eating runs from September to January.

porron.fait: This traditional glass wine pitcher comes from Aragon and Catalonia, but it is also known throughout Spain.

botafumeiro.fait: This censer in the Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela is swung by human strength, thanks to a phenomenon called parametric excitation.

calcotada.fait: At this gathering of family and friends, people eat calçots, leek-like onions that originated in Valls and are grown only in southern Catalonia.

casas-colgadas.fait: These two- or three-story houses cling to a cliff, above the void; the best known are in Cuenca.

lasagnes.fait: This word refers both to sheets of pasta and to the baked dish that layers them with Parmesan, Bolognese sauce and béchamel.

risotto.fait: In Italy, this rice cooked in broth is normally served before the main course, but the Milanese version often accompanies ossobuco.

mozzarella.fait: This stretched-curd cheese is made from cow's or buffalo milk; the one from Campania, made from buffalo milk, has a protected designation.

ponte-vecchio.fait: This bridge in Florence is both a pedestrian street and a shopping arcade, a center of jewelry and luxury goldsmithing.

palais-doges.fait: This Gothic and Renaissance palace on St. Mark's Square housed the doges and the main institutions of the Republic of Venice.

cannoli.fait: In the singular, it is called a cannolo, or cannolu in Sicilian: this pastry comes from Sicily and is also widely made in Naples.

dolomites.fait: This mountain range, once called the “Pale Mountains,” takes its current name from dolomite, a sedimentary rock that abounds there.

bocca-verita.fait: This marble disk probably served as a drain cover; according to legend, it cut off the hand of those who did not tell the truth.

launeddas.fait: This three-pipe Sardinian clarinet works a bit like a bagpipe whose air reservoir is the musician's lungs.

notre-dame-paris.fait: This cathedral saw the coronation of Napoleon I and inspired Victor Hugo to write a novel that, in turn, partly influenced its history.

sacre-coeur.fait: This basilica, built after the war of 1870, belongs to the city of Paris; perched on the hill of Montmartre, it can be seen from far away.

ratatouille.fait: This stew of vegetables simmered in olive oil takes its name from the Occitan ratatolha; it is a specialty of Niçoise and Provençal cuisine.

boeuf-bourguignon.fait: This braised beef simmers in red wine with pearl onions, carrots, mushrooms and lardons; it is one of the most popular dishes in the country.

beaujolais-nouveau.fait: This wine, made mostly from Gamay, can be sold as soon as vinification is complete; it is released worldwide on the third Thursday of November.

bouillabaisse.fait: This fish soup from Marseille is served with garlic-rubbed croutons spread with rouille, pieces of fish and potatoes.

bouquinistes.fait: These booksellers sell old and secondhand books from nearly 900 boxes set up along the quays of the Seine, in Paris.

chenonceau.fait: This château, whose two-story gallery overlooks the Cher, is nicknamed the “Ladies' Château”: women built and transformed it.

gorges-verdon.fait: This canyon, also called the Grand Canyon, was carved by the Verdon and separates two ranges of the Pre-Alps; cliff-edge roads run along it.

fest-noz.fait: This Breton dance recreates the peasant festivities that followed collective work; noz means “night,” and in the daytime it is called a fest-deiz.

lebkuchen.fait: This gingerbread from Nuremberg is said to have been invented by Franconian monks; it is found at holiday-season markets, and all year round in Nuremberg.

speicherstadt.fait: Literally “warehouse city,” the name says exactly what this Hamburg district is: an entire area devoted to warehouses.

schweinshaxe.fait: This roast pork knuckle is a “poor man's food”: this cheap cut is usually marinated for days, then roasted for a long time at low temperature.

maultaschen.fait: These rectangular dumplings from Swabia, in Baden-Württemberg, are filled with a wide variety of stuffings, homemade or factory-made.

kolsch.fait: This beer from Cologne is governed by an agreement among brewers; one million liters of it are brewed every day.

casse-noisette-bois.fait: This figurine from the Ore Mountains is not just a Christmas decoration: a lever opens and closes its jaw to crack nuts.

pyramide-noel.fait: This carousel, usually made of wood, is turned by its candles: the hot air they give off drives a propeller, which moves the figurines.

sanssouci.fait: This palace in Potsdam was the summer residence of Frederick the Great, King of Prussia, built in a style called Frederician Rococo.

holstentor.fait: This Gothic gate is one of only two remaining gates of the medieval fortifications of Lübeck, of which it is the symbol.

porta-nigra.fait: This Roman gate in Trier, made of sandstone blocks laid without mortar, owes its name “Black Gate” to the patina of the centuries.

cathedrale-aix.fait: Built during the reign of Charlemagne, who is buried there, this cathedral saw the coronation of thirty-one German kings.

konigssee.fait: This Alpine lake in Bavaria, surrounded by high mountains, looks like a fjord: it was shaped by the glaciers of the last ice age.

tour-de-londres.fait: This fortress has been a prison, a royal palace, an armory, a treasury and even a menagerie; it houses the Crown Jewels.

christmas-pudding.fait: It has been called “the most English of dishes” made with “the least English ingredients”: spices, raisins and sugar are imported.

yorkshire-pudding.fait: Unlike most British puddings, this one is not a dessert: it accompanies the main course, for example roast beef.

shortbread.fait: This Scottish cookie usually contains twice as much butter as sugar; rice flour is sometimes added to change its texture.

viaduc-glenfinnan.fait: This Scottish railway viaduct, completed in 1901, carries the West Highland Line at the northern end of Loch Shiel.

falaises-douvres.fait: These chalk cliffs facing the continent were, before air travel, travelers' first or last view of the country.

morris-dance.fait: In this English folk dance, dancers wave large handkerchiefs; its name is thought to come from a corruption of moorish, meaning “Moorish.”

eisteddfod.fait: This Welsh festival holds poetry, music and theater competitions in the Welsh language; its tradition dates back at least to the 12th century.

eilean-donan.fait: Left in ruins after a battle, this Scottish castle, linked to the mainland by a stone bridge, was rebuilt by the Clan MacRae.

ballokume.fait: This cookie from Elbasan is considered the symbol of Summer Day, a pagan festival held on March 14; it is also called “summer cake.”

apollonia-illyrie.fait: This ancient Greek city is not in Greece: it stood in Illyria, on the bank of the Vjosa, near the Albanian village of Pojani.

chateau-rozafa.fait: Perched on Tepe Hill, near Shkodër, this castle is surrounded by two rivers, the Buna and the Drin.

mosquee-ethem-bey.fait: Near Skanderbeg Square, in the heart of Tirana, this Ottoman-style mosque is open to visitors outside prayer times.

palais-roujany.fait: These ruins are those of the residence of the noble Sapieha family, who lived there for more than two centuries, in the village of Ruzhany.

vieux-chateau-hrodna.fait: After the old wooden castle burned down in 1398, Grand Duke Vytautas had it rebuilt in brick, in the Gothic style, to prevent another fire.

chateau-navahroudak.fait: This ruined fortress was taken by the Teutonic Order in 1314, before being strengthened with stone towers by Vytautas the Great.

mosquee-gazi-husrev-bey.fait: Built in 1531 in Sarajevo, this mosque is now on the list of national monuments of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

pont-des-chevres.fait: Built in the 16th century near Sarajevo, this bridge has a curious name: Kozija ćuprija, the “goats' bridge.”

mosquee-karadjoz-bey.fait: Built in 1557 and 1558 in Mostar, this mosque is listed as a national monument, as is the neighborhood around it.

parc-national-una.fait: This park owes its name to the Una River, which flows through it: it was created to keep the river intact, along with its tributaries the Krka and the Unac.

bosanski-lonac.fait: This stew of chunks of meat and vegetables varies with each family and each region; it has been described as a national dish of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

gadoulka.fait: This Bulgarian bowed string instrument is a variant of the family of fiddles widespread in the Byzantine and Ottoman world.

perperikon.fait: This ancient city of Thrace, built into the rock of the Rhodopes, was already mentioned by Herodotus.

paski-sir.fait: This hard sheep's milk cheese comes from the island of Pag; it has been protected by a European designation of origin since 2019.

soparnik.fait: This Swiss chard pie is baked on the stone of an open hearth, under the embers and ashes, then covered with garlic and olive oil.

alka-sinj.fait: This equestrian tournament is held every first Sunday of August in Sinj to commemorate a victory against the Ottoman Empire in 1715.

cathedrale-sibenik.fait: Built by three different architects, this cathedral bears witness to the transition from Gothic to Renaissance and to the exchanges between Dalmatia and Tuscany.

zlatni-rat.fait: This spit of white pebbles juts out into a channel with strong currents; its very distinctive shape appears in many travel brochures.

parc-national-krka.fait: For two-thirds of its course, the Krka makes its way through deep canyons before reaching the Adriatic; its waterfalls are the park's main attraction.

mons-klint.fait: These chalk cliffs rise at the eastern tip of the island of Møn; their Danish name simply means “the cliffs of Møn.”

pierres-jelling.fait: The large runestone, raised by Harald Bluetooth, tells of his conquest of Denmark and Norway and of the conversion of the Danes to Christianity.

flaeskesteg.fait: This roast pork is always prepared with its rind; Danes like to serve it at Christmas dinner, on the evening of December 24.

sepik.fait: This whole-grain bread is traditionally served at New Year, on Vastlapäev or on St. Martin's Day; its ancestor is a barley bread, karask.

cratere-kaali.fait: Its origin was sought in volcanism before it was proven that this crater on Saaremaa was created by the impact of a meteorite, more than 4,000 years ago.

leipajuusto.fait: This Finnish cheese is not made with ordinary milk: it is produced from cow's colostrum.

jouhikko.fait: This bowed lyre came to Finland by way of Norway; it is close to the crwth, a Welsh instrument.

olavinlinna.fait: Built by the Swedes between two lakes, this castle is the northernmost of the medieval castles still standing in the world.

gare-centrale-helsinki.fait: This station, on Rautatientori Square in central Helsinki, is the busiest in all of Finland.

bains-gellert.fait: These baths, at the foot of Gellért Hill in Budapest, adjoin a hotel famous for its Secession-style decor.

basilique-esztergom.fait: For the consecration of this basilica in 1856, Franz Liszt composed and performed a mass, known as the “Esztergom Mass.”

arany-galuska.fait: Its name evokes golden balls: this dessert brings together balls of yeast dough rolled in butter, sugar and walnuts, then baked until golden.

teliszalami.fait: This “winter salami” is made from woolly Mangalitsa pork, smoked very slowly at a very low temperature; a coating then forms around it.

lecso.fait: According to most recipes, this stew of peppers, tomatoes and onions with paprika is made with the mildest Hungarian pepper, in season from August to October.

tarhonya.fait: This dried pasta, shaped by pinching the dough with the fingertips or with a grater, came from Persia by way of the Turks.

szaloncukor.fait: This chocolate-coated fondant is a Christmas treat in Hungary; its Hungarian name is borrowed from the German Salonzuckerl.

gullfoss.fait: Its name means “the golden falls”: here the Hvítá River plunges in two steps into a narrow gorge, very close to the Geysir site.

skogafoss.fait: Legend has it that a Viking hid a chest behind this waterfall; a child supposedly got only its handle, which is kept at the Skógar museum.

hangikjot.fait: This lamb or mutton, whose name means “hung meat,” is smoked over birch wood or dried sheep dung.

vinarterta.fait: This layer cake filled with plum jam was born in Iceland, but its name, “Viennese cake,” suggests Austrian roots.

palais-rundale.fait: This Baroque palace was not built in one go: its construction took place in two campaigns, more than twenty years apart.

rupjmaize.fait: This bread of coarse rye flour, with malt and caraway, is baked in a wood-fired oven; in 2014, the European Commission recognized it as a traditional specialty guaranteed.

kugelis.fait: This potato cake, a Lithuanian national dish, is eaten with applesauce, lingonberry jam or sour cream.

cathedrale-vilnius.fait: Dedicated to Saint Stanislaus and Saint Ladislaus, this cathedral is the main Catholic church in all of Lithuania.

kernave.fait: This tourist village was the first known capital of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania; King Mindaugas was crowned there in 1253.

vieux-bazar-skopje.fait: The largest bazaar in the Balkans outside Istanbul, it is the only old district of Skopje to have largely survived the 1963 earthquake.

forteresse-kale-skopje.fait: Its name, Kale, comes from Turkish and means “fortress”; it overlooks the old town and appears on Skopje's coat of arms.

bryggen.fait: This district of Bergen is aptly named: it is built on a wharf, and “brygge” means wharf or pier in Norwegian.

cap-nord.fait: Its cliff is often presented as the northernmost point of Europe, but Knivskjellodden actually lies 1,611 meters farther north.

kjeragbolten.fait: This boulder got wedged in a crevice in the mountain, suspended above the Lysefjord; it attracts many hikers.

lefse.fait: This traditional Norwegian bread is made of potatoes, milk or cream and flour, all cooked on a griddle.

rosemaling.fait: This art of painting floral motifs, born in the Norwegian countryside, lives on across the Atlantic among Americans of Norwegian descent.

palais-royal-varsovie.fait: The former official residence of the kings of Poland, this palace in the old town was destroyed in 1944, then rebuilt.

desert-bledow.fait: This “desert” is an area of sand in Poland, between Błędów, part of the town of Dąbrowa Górnicza in Upper Silesia, and the village of Klucze.

morskie-oko.fait: This lake, the largest of glacial origin in the High Tatras, was ranked by the Wall Street Journal among the five most beautiful lakes in the world.

kabanos.fait: This long, very thin dry sausage often serves as a hiking provision, as it keeps without spoiling much.

nalewka.fait: This traditional Polish liquor can reach 75% alcohol, although most versions are considerably weaker.

oplatek.fait: On Christmas Eve, everyone breaks this wafer of unleavened bread and shares it with their loved ones while offering them good wishes.

obwarzanek.fait: This braided ring of bread is boiled before being baked; in Kraków, it is traditionally bought on the street, from stalls.

bar-mleczny.fait: In the communist era, this “milk bar” served cheap meals, most often based on dairy products.

mine-sel-turda.fait: This former salt mine in Transylvania has been converted into a leisure and health center, located underground.

sighisoara.fait: This town in Transylvania has several names: Schäßburg in German, Segesvár in Hungarian and even Castrum Saxorum in Latin.

chateau-corvin.fait: Also called Hunedoara Castle, this castle in Transylvania is the largest in all of Romania.

eglise-fortifiee-biertan.fait: This fortified church was built by the Saxons, a German community in Transylvania; at first Catholic, it became Lutheran with the Reformation.

kremlin-kazan.fait: This kremlin was built on the orders of Ivan IV, on the site of the ruins of the former castle of the khans of Kazan.

cathedrale-saint-isaac.fait: Inspired by St. Paul's Cathedral in London, this Orthodox cathedral was designed to hold 14,000 worshippers.

pogost-kiji.fait: According to a legend, its Church of the Transfiguration, built without nails, was made with a single ax, which the craftsman then threw into the lake.

troika.fait: In this three-horse team, the middle horse trots while the side horses gallop: it is the only known team with different gaits.

koulibiak.fait: This pie hides layers of fish or meat, rice and eggs, steamed beneath its puff pastry, and is then served in slices.

bayan.fait: This chromatic accordion owes its name to Bayan, a legendary old singer and storyteller said to have performed before several princes.

stroganina.fait: This dish of the peoples of Arctic Siberia consists of long, thin slices of raw fish; its name means “shavings.”

forteresse-golubac.fait: Its foundations are now underwater: the level of the Danube rose markedly after the construction of the Iron Gates dam.

lepenski-vir.fait: This site on the bank of the Danube, whose name means “Linden Whirlpool,” seems linked to the settlement of the first European farmers.

monastere-sopocani.fait: This Orthodox monastery stands near the source of the Raška, not far from Stari Ras, which was the center of the medieval Serbian state of Rascia.

forteresse-petrovaradin.fait: This fortress near Novi Sad hides 16 km of underground galleries; the cornerstone of its southern part was laid in 1692 by the Prince of Croÿ.

monastere-zica.fait: This Orthodox monastery, located at the entrance to the Ibar Gorge near Kraljevo, is also the seat of the eparchy that bears its name.

banska-stiavnica.fait: Once known for metal mining, especially silver, this mining town has a fully preserved medieval town, added to the UNESCO list in 1993.

cicmany.fait: This village in the Žilina Region, in Slovakia, is famous for its typical folk architecture.

chateau-bratislava.fait: Its four corner towers are considered the symbol of the city; the castle appears on the Slovak 10, 20 and 50 euro cent coins.

parenica.fait: This Slovak stretched-curd cheese, made from sheep's milk, is protected by a European Union geographical indication.

grottes-skocjan.fait: These limestone caves of the Karst, extensively studied for karst phenomena, form the largest underground wetland in the world.

lac-bohinj.fait: It is the largest permanent lake in Slovenia; it lies in the northwest of the country, within Triglav National Park.

prinsesstarta.fait: This “princess cake” hides sponge cake, raspberry jam and cream under a thin layer of marzipan, usually green.

lussekatt.fait: These small buns owe their bright yellow color to saffron; they are associated with Saint Lucy's Day celebrations.

kroppkaka.fait: This boiled potato dumpling hides at its heart a filling of onions and pork or bacon.

spettekaka.fait: This cake, baked on a spit turning over a fire, is very dry: large ones are cut with a hacksaw, otherwise they crumble.

smorgastarta.fait: This “cake” is actually a sandwich: layers of white bread with fillings, covered with mayonnaise and crème fraîche, then decorated.

kraftskiva.fait: Every year at the end of summer, Swedes gather for this popular festivity where crayfish are eaten.

janssons-frestelse.fait: This dish of potatoes, onions and sprats is normally part of the Swedish Christmas buffet, but is also served on other occasions.

hasselbackspotatis.fait: These potatoes are cut into thin slices only halfway down, then baked with butter, breadcrumbs and almonds.

ostkaka.fait: This “cheese cake” should not be confused with cheesecake: it is eaten warm, typically with cloudberry, cherry or strawberry jam.

ales-stenar.fait: According to Scanian folklore, these megaliths in southern Sweden are the tomb of King Ale, who gave them their name.

hotel-ville-stockholm.fait: This building, seat of the Stockholm city council, stands at the eastern tip of the island of Kungsholmen, on the shore of Lake Mälaren.

chateau-prague.fait: Guinness World Records lists it as the largest ancient castle in the world; the Bohemian Crown Jewels are kept there.

chateau-karlstejn.fait: Founded by Emperor Charles IV, this castle served as a treasury for the Imperial Crown Jewels and for various relics.

pravcicka-brana.fait: It is the largest natural sandstone arch in Europe; it is located in “Czech Switzerland” and can only be reached on foot.

olomoucke-syrecky.fait: This Moravian cheese is recognizable by its strong smell and pungent taste; yet it contains only 0.6% fat.

pampushka.fait: These small yeast buns or doughnuts from Ukrainian cuisine are made both savory and sweet.

sainte-sophie-kiev.fait: Named after Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, it houses the tomb of its founder Yaroslav the Wise, the only one to have survived.

chateau-olesko.fait: This castle is considered the oldest stronghold in western Ukraine, in the historical region of Galicia.

soupe-miso.fait: This broth of fermented soybean paste and dashi is, together with rice, one of the staple dishes of traditional Japanese meals.

wasabi.fait: This condiment is the stem, ground into a paste, of a semi-aquatic plant of the same family as mustard and horseradish.

teriyaki.fait: This glazed meat or fish is grilled in a mixture of sake, mirin and soy sauce, the three pillars of Japanese cuisine.

sukiyaki.fait: Its name comes from suki, “spade,” and yaki, “to grill”: this sweet-and-savory hot pot simmers beef and vegetables in a broth.

shabu-shabu.fait: The name of this Japanese hot pot, saltier than sukiyaki, imitates the sound of meat dipped into the hot broth.

tonkatsu.fait: Japanese students customarily eat this breaded pork before an exam: katsu also evokes the verb “to win” or “to succeed.”

onigiri.fait: These rice balls, often filled with a very salty dried plum, are not seen as a meal in Japan but as a snack.

soba.fait: These Japanese noodles are made from buckwheat flour, and soba is also the name the Japanese give to this plant.

natto.fait: These fermented soybeans, sticky and smelling of ammonia, are eaten on plain rice, often at breakfast.

dorayaki.fait: This pastry, two sponge-cake pancakes filled with red bean paste, is said to take its name from dora, “gong” in Japanese.

taiyaki.fait: This fish-shaped cake, whose name means “baked sea bream,” is most often filled with sweet red bean paste.

umeshu.fait: This liqueur is flavored by steeping Japanese apricots in it; not to be confused with umezu, a plum vinegar.

karate.fait: This so-called Japanese martial art was born in Okinawa, in the former independent Ryūkyū Kingdom, deriving from a Chinese style of boxing.

judo.fait: Its name means “the gentle way”: its founder removed the dangerous techniques of the old schools to make it a form of education for young people.

aikido.fait: This martial art does not seek to defeat the opponent but to reduce their aggression to nothing; almost everywhere, it does without competition.

shuriken.fait: This ninja throwing weapon is not very effective in direct combat: it is used rather to distract the opponent or in ambushes.

shinkansen.fait: Put into service in 1964, this train made Japan the pioneer of high-speed rail; its name also refers to its lines.

grande-vague.fait: This Hokusai print blends Japanese tradition with Western perspective; in Europe, it inspired the Impressionists.

ukiyo-e.fait: Its name means “pictures of the floating world”: these inexpensive prints, considered vulgar in Japan, won over the West.

yukata.fait: This light summer kimono, worn by men and women alike, was traditionally indigo and white; modern ones are machine-washable.

koinobori.fait: These koi carp-shaped windsocks are flown for Children's Day, celebrated every May 5 in Japan.

hina-matsuri.fait: For this girls' festival, dolls representing the imperial court are displayed on tiered stands; the rest of the year, they sleep in a box.

kendama.fait: This wooden skill toy resembles a cup-and-ball, but its handle also has two small cups on which the ball is maneuvered.

koto.fait: Brought from China around the 8th century, this plucked string instrument was first played at the imperial court before spreading to the wider public.

furoshiki.fait: This technique of folding and knotting a cloth is used to wrap gifts, but also to carry a bento or even a watermelon.

ginkaku-ji.fait: This Buddhist temple in Kyoto, called Ginkaku-ji in Japanese, “Temple of the Silver Pavilion,” dates from the late 15th century.

byodo-in.fait: Before becoming a Buddhist temple, this estate in Uji served as a country residence; its most famous building is the Phoenix Hall.

horyu-ji.fait: The oldest buildings of this temple in Nara Prefecture, including the five-story pagoda, are considered the oldest wooden structures in the world.

meiji-jingu.fait: This Shinto shrine lies right in the heart of Tokyo, in the Shibuya ward, on the edge of the Harajuku district.

sanctuaire-ise.fait: This shrine is the most important one in Shinto in Japan: it is considered the most sacred place of this religion.

chateau-kumamoto.fait: This heavily fortified castle is considered one of the three most beautiful in Japan, along with those of Himeji and Matsumoto.

shirakawa-go.fait: The very steep thatched roofs of these houses, called “hands joined in prayer,” allow them to bear heavy snowfall.

sakurajima.fait: This volcano was an island until the 1914 eruption, when lava filled the strait that separated it from Kyūshū.

mapo-doufu.fait: Its name means “grandma’s spicy tofu”: this Sichuan dish consists of fresh tofu cooked in a sauce of chili and Sichuan pepper.

poulet-kung-pao.fait: Its Chinese name means “diced chicken in the style of the palace guardian”: this Sichuan stir-fry combines chicken, peanuts and chilies.

xiaolongbao.fait: The broth inside these Shanghai dumplings comes from a meat jelly added to the filling, which melts as they steam.

chow-mein.fait: Its name means “stir-fried noodles”: this Cantonese dish usually brings together wheat noodles, vegetables, meat or seafood with soy sauce.

roujiamo.fait: Its name means “meat stuffed in bread”: in China, the döner kebab is sometimes nicknamed the “Turkish rou jia mo.”

tangyuan.fait: These glutinous rice balls, served in a sweet soup or a broth, are traditionally eaten at the Lantern Festival.

wonton.fait: The Cantonese name of these dumplings, “swallowing clouds,” is a homophone of the original Chinese term hundun, which refers to the primordial chaos of the cosmos.

lapsang-souchong.fait: This smoked black tea, originally from Fujian province, is considered one of the teas with the strongest flavor.

long-jing.fait: Its name means “dragon well tea”: it is a green tea from Hangzhou, in Zhejiang province.

fete-printemps.fait: It opens fifteen days of festivities, and its date changes every year because it follows the Chinese lunisolar calendar.

fete-lanternes.fait: During this festival, which closes the New Year, people try to solve riddles written on the lanterns to win a gift.

festival-glace-neige.nom: Harbin Ice and Snow Sculpture Festival
festival-glace-neige.fait: In Harbin, where January averages −16.8 °C, residents have developed a culture of ice and snow that this festival celebrates.

kung-fu.fait: This popular name covers hundreds of Chinese fighting styles, armed or unarmed, developed over the centuries.

acupuncture.fait: These needles inserted at precise points on the skin come from the Chinese medical tradition, but their effect does not go beyond that of a placebo.
