wok.fait: Its long-handled utensils protect the cook from the heat, and the art of wok cooking has a Cantonese name: wok hei, “breath of the wok.”

hanfu.fait: This clothing of the Han people predates the Qing dynasty; the qipao dress, often seen as typically Chinese, is of Manchu origin.

xiangqi.fait: In this Chinese chess, a river divides the board in two and limits the movement of certain pieces, which are placed on the intersections.

suanpan.fait: The name of this Chinese abacus means “calculating plate”; the traditional method of calculation that uses it is called zhusuan.

bianzhong.fait: These bronze bells hung from a wooden frame play melodies; Korea, which imported them, still uses them for its court music.

enveloppe-rouge.fait: The amount slipped into this envelope is often a lucky number, for example one rich in eights, a digit whose name sounds almost like “prosperity” in Chinese.

papier-decoupe.fait: These paper silhouettes mainly decorate doors and windows, hence their other name, “window flowers.”

jardin-yuyuan.fait: This 16th-century garden, in the heart of Shanghai’s old town, has a name that means “garden of hesitation.”

jardin-modeste-administrateur.fait: It is the largest of the classical gardens of Suzhou; it is also called the “Garden of the Politics of Simple People.”

lac-ouest-hangzhou.fait: This lake in the historic center of Hangzhou is the one shown on the back of the Chinese one-yuan note.

riviere-li.fait: Along this river, between Guilin and Yangshuo, the landscape bristles with karst limestone peaks.

wulingyuan.fait: This area of Hunan, bristling with about 3,100 sandstone pillars, inspired the settings of James Cameron’s film Avatar.

mont-emei.fait: Located in Sichuan province, this mountain is one of the four sacred mountains of Buddhism in China.

mont-hua.fait: Also called the “Western Mountain,” it is one of the five sacred mountains of China, in Shaanxi province.

pont-zhaozhou.fait: Completed around the year 605, this masonry segmental arch bridge is the oldest bridge in China still standing.

tulou.fait: These large communal buildings of Fujian, inhabited by the Hakka, serve both as collective housing and as fortresses.

dazu.fait: Near Chongqing, these religious sculptures carved into the rock form an exceptional series, created over several centuries.

temple-lamas.fait: Its first building was constructed to house eunuchs; this Beijing temple is now devoted to Tibetan Buddhism.

yangtse.fait: Also called the Blue River, it is the largest river in the world to flow entirely within a single country.

fleuve-jaune.fait: Chinese civilization was born on the banks of this river, whose violent floods shaped and fertilized the great North Plain.

foret-pierres-shilin.fait: Its large vertical limestone blades rise from the ground like stone trees, hence its name, “stone forest.”

rizieres-hani.fait: These rice terraces in Yunnan province, linked to the Hani people, have a history spanning nearly 1,200 years.

diaolou.fait: These fortified towers of Kaiping offered protection from bandits; emigrants from the diaspora added details of foreign architecture to them.

bulgogi.fait: Its name means “fire meat”: this marinated and then grilled meat is nicknamed “Korean barbecue.”

galbi.fait: These grilled cuts of beef or pork marinated in Korean soy sauce are a culinary specialty of the city of Suwon.

samgyeopsal.fait: Its name means “three-layer meat”: these slices of pork belly are grilled at the table by the diners themselves.

japchae.fait: This dish of sweet potato vermicelli and vegetables was once intended for the king; today it is served at festivities.

samgyetang.fait: For this ginseng soup, a young chicken is stuffed with glutinous rice before being cooked with jujubes, garlic and ginger.

hotteok.fait: This filled pancake, eaten as a snack, is a popular street food specialty in South Korea.

gochujang.fait: This spicy condiment traditionally ferments in large jars; it is one of the three basic condiments of Korean cuisine.

doenjang.fait: This fermented soybean paste, traditional in Korean cuisine, has a name that simply means “thick paste.”

banchan.fait: These side dishes, served in small containers, are placed in the center of the table, usually at least four or five different ones at a time.

tteok.fait: In Korea, a soup of these glutinous rice cakes is traditionally eaten at New Year, and sweet versions at weddings.

songpyeon.fait: These glutinous rice dumplings of the Mid-Autumn Festival are steamed on pine needles, hence their name: song means “pine.”

pajeon.fait: This green onion pancake, often topped with squid or seafood, is one of the small Korean side dishes.

the-yuja.fait: This tea is made with a citrus marmalade, peel included, a spoonful of which is diluted in hot water, notably to fight colds.

daegeum.fait: This large bamboo flute has a hole covered with a thin plant membrane, whose sound can be kept or cut off by moving a piece of metal.

geomungo.fait: According to the Samguk sagi, this plucked string instrument, which appeared in the Koguryo period, was created by Wang San-ak.

jjimjilbang.fait: These public bathhouses stay open day and night: with their floor-heated rooms where people can sleep, they also serve as cheap lodging.

seollal.fait: For this New Year, children in hanbok bow before their elders, who give them money as a reward for this greeting.

chuseok.fait: For this harvest festival, every family returns to its home region to honor its ancestors, which causes huge traffic jams in South Korea.

hanji.fait: This paper, handmade from paper mulberry, is also used as fabric for bags or clothing, and to restore works of art.

jangseung.fait: These wooden posts carved into crude human figures, set up at the entrance to villages, are meant to protect against evil spirits.

onggi.fait: These earthenware pots serve both as tableware and as containers for storing food; their current form dates from the Joseon era.

gat-chapeau.fait: This horsehair and bamboo hat, partly transparent, was reserved for nobles until the end of the 19th century and showed their social rank.

bojagi.fait: This piece of fabric, often square, sometimes embroidered or made of pieces sewn together, is used to wrap gifts, notably for weddings.

yunnori.fait: This board game, of Chinese origin, is played in Korea notably during Seollal, the New Year festival.

jultagi.fait: This tightrope-walking performance has been staged in Korea since the Goryeo period, and UNESCO has inscribed it as intangible heritage.

hallasan.fait: This volcano, the highest point in South Korea, towers over Jeju Island; it has produced many very long lava tubes.

seongsan-ilchulbong.fait: This “Sunrise Peak” is a volcanic cone formed by eruptions under a shallow sea, about 5,000 years ago, on Jeju Island.

deoksugung.fait: In front of the main gate of this Seoul palace, the changing of the royal guard is reenacted every day as under the Joseon dynasty.

haeinsa.fait: On the slopes of Mount Gayasan, this Buddhist temple oversees about 150 affiliated temples; one of its buildings is a World Heritage Site.

bongeunsa.fait: This Buddhist temple, founded in 794 by a monk, now stands in Seoul, directly across from the COEX shopping mall.

seoraksan.fait: This mountain, the highest in the Taebaek Mountains, overlooks the port of Sokcho; Koreans admire its wild appearance.

cheomseongdae.fait: This tower, whose name means “where the stars are observed,” is the oldest astronomical observatory in East Asia.

namhansanseong.fait: This mountain fortress, built by Buddhist warrior monks, served as an “emergency capital” during the Joseon period.

ulleungdo.fait: This volcanic island lives from tourism and fishing; it is famous for its squid, which can be seen drying in the sun.

hanok.fait: This traditional house follows an architectural style handed down from the Three Kingdoms period to the Joseon dynasty.

jogyesa.fait: This temple in central Seoul, headquarters of the Jogye Order of Korean Buddhism, has a 500-year-old pine tree on its grounds.

hahoe.fait: This traditional village is laid out according to the principles of geomancy, hence its plan in the shape of a lotus flower.

lac-khovsgol.fait: Many streams flow into this lake, which is considered sacred, but only one river flows out of it, the Egiin Gol.

gandan.fait: This Buddhist monastery in Ulaanbaatar escaped the destruction of the 1930s; it houses a giant statue of the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara.

amarbayasgalant.fait: This monastery was built in the 18th century to house the remains of Zanabazar, the first Bogd Gegeen.

palais-bogd-khan.nom: Winter Palace of the Bogd Khan
palais-bogd-khan.fait: The only one of the Khan’s four palaces not to have been destroyed, this museum even displays the jeweled ornaments of his pet elephant.

temple-choijin-lama.fait: This Buddhist monastery in Ulaanbaatar owes its official name, “Temple of Compassion Perfection,” to the Guangxu Emperor.

vallee-orkhon.fait: This valley, through which the Orkhon River flows, holds archaeological remains left by Turco-Mongol and Mongol peoples.

gorkhi-terelj.fait: The name of this national park near the capital, Ulaanbaatar, means “stream – rhododendron” in Mongolian.

gobi-gurvansaikhan.fait: This park on the edge of the Gobi Desert is home to “singing sands” and a valley where a strip of ice persists almost all year round.

monts-khangai.fait: Many rivers rise in this range, including the Orkhon and one of the sources of the Selenga; it borders the Gobi Desert to the east.

burkhan-khaldun.fait: Genghis Khan declared this mountain sacred; according to the most likely hypothesis, it is also his burial place.

khuushuur.fait: This fried turnover is filled with meat and fat, most often mutton; each family has its own filling recipe.

khorkhog.fait: For this dish, pieces of meat are cooked in a container holding water and very hot stones.

suutei-tsai.fait: This milk tea is drunk salted; the milk can come from a mare, a yak, a camel, a ewe or a cow.

fuvahmulah.fait: Nearly half of this island in the Maldives is taken up by its lagoon; it is also home to a biosphere reserve recognized by UNESCO.

atoll-ari.fait: In addition to its inhabited islands, this atoll has 26 resort islands; its land covers only 8.3 km² out of more than 2,270 km², lagoon included.

atoll-addu.fait: It is the southernmost atoll of the Maldives: together with the island of Fuvahmulah, it is the only place in the country located in the Southern Hemisphere.

sling-raffles.fait: This cocktail was created in 1915 at the bar of the Raffles Hotel: it allowed women, who were forbidden to drink alcohol in public, to keep up appearances.

sungei-buloh.fait: This mangrove in northwestern Singapore is of global importance: it is a stopover point for migratory birds.

thian-hock-keng.fait: This Singapore temple is dedicated to Mazu, the Chinese goddess of the sea, but hides at the back a Buddhist shrine dedicated to Guanyin.

lau-pa-sat.fait: This former fish market in Singapore, one of the first buildings in Asia made of prefabricated cast iron, now houses food stalls.

hotel-fullerton.fait: This Singapore building, originally known as the “General Post Office Building,” was designed as an office building before becoming a luxury hotel.

nasi-lemak.fait: Its name means “rice in cream”: the rice is boiled in coconut milk, and it is taken away folded into a pyramid in a banana leaf.

teh-tarik.fait: This milk tea is called “pulled tea” because it is poured, or “pulled,” during its preparation; Malaysia has made it its national drink.

nasi-kandar.fait: This rice dish served with several curries comes from the state of Penang, where it was introduced by Indian Muslim merchants.

tengkolok.fait: This men’s headdress is made of a long piece of songket cloth folded and tied in a particular way; it is worn mainly at ceremonies.

langkawi.fait: This archipelago has 99 islands, plus a few others that only emerge at low tide; UNESCO has designated it a Global Geopark.

gunung-mulu.fait: This park in Sarawak, on the island of Borneo, is protected for its caves, its karst landscapes eroded into cones and its tropical wildlife.

grottes-niah.fait: These caves in Sarawak, on the island of Borneo, have yielded a Homo sapiens skull about 38,000 years old.

sultan-abdul-samad.fait: Its architect, who had lived in Africa, drew on the Moorish style for this Kuala Lumpur building topped with a copper dome.

gare-neo-mauresque.fait: This station in Kuala Lumpur, the capital, stands out for an architecture that blends Eastern and Western styles.

ile-tioman.fait: This island in the South China Sea, which belongs to the state of Pahang, is said to be of volcanic origin.

lac-kaptai.fait: There is nothing natural about this lake: it was created by a hydroelectric dam on the Karnaphuli River, and it is the largest artificial lake in the country.

eglise-sainte-resurrection.nom: Church of the Holy Resurrection, Dhaka
eglise-sainte-resurrection.fait: This Armenian church in Old Dhaka recalls a community that has now left: services there have become rare.

drametse-ngacham.fait: This ritual dance is performed in a monastery: the dancers are masked and an orchestra that includes drums accompanies them.

dzong-simtokha.fait: The first dzong built in Bhutan, this fortified monastery now houses one of the main institutes for learning Dzongkha.

mohinga.fait: This fish soup with rice vermicelli, often seen as the national dish, is traditionally eaten for breakfast.

cloche-mingun.fait: Several times in history, this bell on the banks of the Irrawaddy has been the heaviest working bell in the world.

chinthe.fait: This lion-like creature guards pagodas, almost always in pairs; before coins, some bronze weights had its shape.

saung.fait: According to temple carvings, this harp dates back to the 8th century; music was later composed for it to accompany the Ramayana.

chinlone.fait: This sport is played with the feet and a woven rattan ball; its name means “round basket” in Burmese.

rocher-dor.fait: This huge rock, about 6 meters in diameter, also called the Kyaiktiyo Pagoda, balances in Mon State.

mrauk-u.fait: This city in Arakan was the capital of a kingdom of the same name until it was taken by the Burmese in 1785.

mont-popa.fait: On this volcano, a refuge of the nat spirits, people avoid wearing black or red and bringing meat, so as not to offend them.

temple-ananda.fait: Its name comes from a confusion: dedicated to the “infinite wisdom” of the Buddha, this temple in Bagan took the name of Ananda, the Buddha’s cousin.

pagode-shwezigon.fait: This stupa is said to have been built to house a jawbone and a tooth of the Buddha; it served as a model for many other Burmese stupas.

ava-inwa.fait: This former royal capital of Myanmar was also called Ratanapura, which means “city of gems.”

vat-xieng-thong.fait: In 1887, looters spared this temple in Luang Prabang, because their leader had been a monk there in his youth.

chutes-kuang-si.fait: Near Luang Prabang, these falls cascade down three levels before plunging over a final drop.

grottes-pak-ou.fait: These caves above the Mekong house hundreds of small wooden Buddha statues, lined up on shelves along the walls.

vat-si-saket.fait: The oldest temple in Vientiane, it was the only building spared by the Siamese during the sack of the city, probably thanks to its Thai style.

ho-phra-keo.fait: This royal temple in Vientiane once housed the Emerald Buddha, carried off by the Siamese to Bangkok; rebuilt, it has become a museum.

plateau-bolovens.fait: This plateau in southern Laos, which extends over the provinces of Champasak and Salavan, takes its name from the majority ethnic group: the Laven.

haw-kham.fait: This palace in Luang Prabang was placed on the bank of the Mekong so that official visitors arriving by river would land at its foot.

adobo.fait: Meat, seafood or vegetables are simmered in their own marinade of vinegar, soy sauce and garlic.

sinigang.fait: In this sour broth, often flavored with tamarind, meat or fish and vegetables are cooked; it is eaten with rice in almost the entire archipelago.

pancit.fait: These noodles, which came with Chinese immigrants, are often served with calamansi; some versions even replace the noodles with coconut.

bibingka.fait: This rice cake is generally eaten for breakfast, especially at Christmas; it is traditionally baked in clay pots lined with leaves.

sinulog.fait: This festival in Cebu honors the Child Jesus; its ritual dance takes two steps forward and then one step back, to the sound of drums.

rizieres-banaue.fait: These terraces are thought to have been built almost by hand, with few tools, by the ancestors of the Batad people; rice is still grown there.

chocolate-hills.fait: These cone-shaped hills on the island of Bohol owe their name to their shape and to their grass, which turns brown at the end of the dry season.

riviere-souterraine.fait: This park on the island of Palawan, in the Saint Paul Mountains, is both a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a Ramsar site.

recif-tubbataha.fait: Its name means “a long reef exposed at low tide” in the Sama language; coast guards are permanently stationed there to protect it from poachers.

eglise-paoay.fait: This Baroque church, completed in 1710, is known for its huge buttresses, on the sides and at the back of the building.

basilique-santo-nino.nom: Basilica of the Santo Niño de Cebu
basilique-santo-nino.fait: This basilica in Cebu was built where Spaniards found a statue of the Child Jesus, once given by Magellan to the queen of Cebu.

mosquee-wazir-khan.fait: This mosque in Lahore, built by a governor of Punjab, is famous for its mosaics that combine floral motifs and calligraphy.

mausolee-jahangir.fait: This Mughal tomb in Lahore, in Punjab, was built in 1637 for the emperor Jahangir.

fort-derawar.fait: The forty bastions of this fort can be seen for kilometers in the Cholistan Desert; it still belongs to the Abbasi family.

fort-ranikot.fait: Nicknamed the “Great Wall of Sindh,” this fort is, according to Hanif Raza, the largest in the world.

takht-i-bahi.fait: Its name means “throne of the spring”: this Buddhist monastery, originally Zoroastrian, stands on a hill near a stream.

lac-saiful-muluk.fait: This mountain lake at the end of the Kaghan Valley owes its name to a poem by Mian Muhammad Bakhsh.

ruwanwelisaya.fait: This hemispherical stupa in Anuradhapura, sacred to many Buddhists, is believed to contain relics of the Buddha.

horton-plains.fait: Three major rivers of Sri Lanka rise on this plateau, where a precipice is called World’s End.

uda-walawe.fait: The elephants of this park come to drink at the large reservoir that gave it its name, built on the Walawe River.

jardin-peradeniya.fait: This botanical garden near Kandy, nestled in a bend of the Mahaweli River, is renowned for its orchid collection.

gai-jatra.fait: This “festival of cows” is in fact a festival of the dead, in memory of people who died during the past year.

changu-narayan.fait: This Hindu temple dedicated to Vishnu stands on a mountain called Changu or Dolagiri, in Bhaktapur District.

temple-muktinath.fait: This temple is sacred both to Hindus, who worship Vishnu there, and to Tibetan Buddhists, who call it Chumig Gyatsa, “Hundred Waters.”

lac-phewa.fait: This lake bordering Pokhara is the second largest in Nepal, but its average depth is less than ten meters.

lo-manthang.fait: This walled city in Mustang District, at an altitude of 3,840 meters, is the former capital of the Kingdom of Mustang, also called the Kingdom of Lo.

machapuchare.fait: Its name means “fish tail,” because of its double summit; considered highly sacred, this mountain is off-limits to climbers.

curry-vert.fait: Its Thai name means “sweet green curry”: this variety of curry comes from central Thailand.

curry-panang.fait: This thick red curry, both salty and sweet, has a peanut flavor; its oldest known mention appears in a book from 1890.

phat-kaphrao.fait: This dish with Thai holy basil, made with meat or seafood, is served with steamed rice and a fried egg on top.

krabi-krabong.fait: This martial art was invented by idle warriors who wanted to practice fighting and stay ready for war.

grand-palais-royal.fait: The king no longer lives there, but this palace built by Rama I houses the Temple of the Emerald Buddha and still hosts official ceremonies.

ko-samui.fait: In 2005, most of this island’s inhabitants still lived from growing coconut palms; by 2018, tourism had become their main activity.

beng-mealea.fait: This Hindu temple, which nevertheless bears a few Buddhist motifs, is said to have served as a model for the construction of Angkor Wat.

phnom-kulen.fait: The Khmer name of this national park in Siem Reap province simply means “the mountain of lychees.”

phsar-thmei.fait: Cambodians call this yellow Art Deco market Phsar Thmey, “new market,” even though it was built in the 1930s.

nems.fait: It is called chả giò in the south of Vietnam and nem in the north: this savory fritter, stuffed and fried, is wrapped in rice paper.

ca-phe-sua-da.fait: This coffee drips slowly from a metal filter set on a cup of sweetened condensed milk, before being poured over ice.

ca-phe-trung.fait: According to its inventor’s family, this coffee topped with beaten egg yolk was born when milk was scarce: the egg replaced the dairy product.

banh-xeo.fait: This rice flour and turmeric pancake, folded in half, is eaten with mustard or lettuce leaves and nước mắm.

bun-cha.fait: A Hanoi restaurant serving this dish of grilled pork and noodles became famous after Barack Obama dined there with chef Anthony Bourdain.

banh-chung.fait: Its name means “steamed cake,” but this square of glutinous rice wrapped in leaves is not cooked that way; it is eaten at Tết.

banh-cuon.fait: Its Vietnamese name means “rolled steamed cake”; it is also called “wet steamed cake.”

dan-bau.fait: This instrument has only one string, half plucked, half bowed; a flexible rod held in the left hand varies its pitch.

dan-tranh.fait: This plucked table zither is close to the Chinese guzheng, the Japanese koto, the Korean gayageum and the Mongolian yatga.

ca-tru.fait: This sung poetry from the north of the country, practiced since the 11th century, is endangered: most of its musicians are elderly.

quan-ho.fait: These songs from Bắc Ninh province come from old love songs between young men and young women.

rendang.fait: This meat simmers for hours in spiced coconut milk until the liquid evaporates; once dry, it keeps for three to four months.

soto.fait: In Indonesia, traditional soups are called soto, while those of foreign influence are called sop.

kecak.fait: This performance has no instruments: about a hundred men sitting in a circle chant “chak-a-chak” nonstop to set the rhythm of the story.

barong.fait: In this dance, Barong, a lion-like creature and lord of the forest, fights the demon queen Rangda: it is the struggle between good and evil.

danse-saman.fait: Nicknamed the “dance of a thousand hands,” it is danced in a line, often kneeling, and creates its rhythm by slapping hands, thighs and the floor.

danse-topeng.fait: The word topeng means “mask”; this masked dance is said to be linked to ancestor worship, which made the dancers interpreters of the gods.

subak.fait: In Bali, irrigating rice fields is not just watering: this cooperative system, developed in the 9th century, is organized around water temples.

pinisi.fait: This traditional sailing ship from Sulawesi still carries goods from island to island, but an engine has often replaced one of its masts.

prambanan.fait: This Javanese complex of 240 Shaivite temples, built in the 9th century near Yogyakarta, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

tanah-lot.fait: This Hindu temple is built on an islet near Bali; it is both a place of pilgrimage and a favorite spot for photographers.

komodo.fait: This park was first created in 1980 to protect the Komodo dragon and cetaceans, before extending its protection to the region’s flora and fauna.

krakatoa.fait: The explosion of this volcano in 1883 was so violent that its suspended ash disturbed the sky as far away as Europe for several years.

bromo.fait: This still-active volcano in eastern Java, also called Brama, rises in the Tengger caldera and peaks at 2,329 meters.

bharata-natyam.fait: This dance was banned under British rule, but it remained permitted in the French trading posts of Pondicherry.

kuchipudi.fait: This dance is named after the village it comes from; the dancers portray characters through mime and facial expressions.

garba.fait: This dance is often performed in a circle around a lamp during the nine nights of the Navaratri festival; its name evokes the “womb.”

theyyam.fait: During this ritual in Kerala, “possessed” individuals embody spirits or deities, combining trance, makeup and costumes.

kettuvallam.fait: Its name means “tied boat”: its wood is tied with coconut fiber, and it mainly serves as a floating house for tourists.

foire-pushkar.fait: Every year, the town of Pushkar, on the edge of the Thar Desert, hosts the largest camel market in India.

vindaloo.fait: Its name comes from the Portuguese for “garlic wine”: a legacy of Goa, this dish replaces coconut milk or curd with vinegar or wine.

temple-minakshi.fait: This temple in Madurai honors Meenakshi, “the fish-eyed one,” one of the few Hindu goddesses to have a major temple of her own.

chiles-en-nogada.fait: These mild chilies, stuffed with pork and covered in a walnut sauce, are eaten at the end of summer or the beginning of fall, walnut season.

pozole.fait: The corn kernels in this stew are first boiled with lime, which removes the fibrous membrane that covers them.

cochinita-pibil.fait: This pork marinated in annatto is cooked, wrapped in a banana leaf, in an underground oven. The Maya first cooked pheasant, peccary or deer in it.

nachos.fait: These cheese-topped corn chips were created by Ignacio Anaya, nicknamed El Nacho: his recipe combined melted cheddar and jalapeño peppers.

carnitas.fait: This pork is braised for a long time in oil or lard to make it tender; its Spanish name simply means “little meats.”

michelada.fait: This drink starts with a beer, spiced up with lime, salt and a sauce; topped up with tomato juice, it resembles a Bloody Mary in which beer replaces vodka.

paloma.fait: Its name means “dove”: in Mexico, this mix of tequila and grapefruit soda is more popular than the margarita.

cafe-de-olla.fait: This coffee with cinnamon and piloncillo takes its name from the olla, the small ceramic pot in which it is prepared.

molcajete.fait: In this traditional mortar, spices and vegetables for sauces are crushed with a stone cylinder called a tejolote.

chac-mool.fait: This fanciful name, “great red jaguar” in Maya, was invented in 1875 by an explorer; archaeologists have kept it simply out of habit.

jarabe-tapatio.fait: This folk music and its dance alternate a fast zapateado rhythm with waltz passages, then polka passages.

palacio-bellas-artes.fait: This opera house is so heavy that it is gradually sinking; Diego Rivera repainted there a mural destroyed in New York because of a portrait of Lenin.

templo-mayor.fait: Razed after the conquest, this Aztec temple was forgotten until the excavations: buildings in Mexico City had to be demolished to uncover it.

pyramide-cholula.fait: Its Nahuatl name means “artificial mountain”: by volume, it is the largest monument ever built, and a church crowns its summit.

el-tajin.fait: After the city’s fall, no European seems to have known of it until an inspector stumbled upon its Pyramid of the Niches.

arbre-de-tule.fait: This colossal, ancient cypress, an ahuehuete in Nahuatl, stands in front of the church of Santa María del Tule, near Oaxaca.

hierve-el-agua.fait: These two white waterfalls are petrified: mineral-laden springs formed them like stalactites, and one has been fitted out for swimming.

gumbo.fait: This Louisiana stew is thickened with okra from Africa, powdered sassafras leaves inherited from the Choctaw, or a French-style roux.

corn-dog.fait: This smoked sausage coated in batter and stuck on a stick appeared in the United States in the 1920s.

key-lime-pie.fait: This lime pie is made with condensed milk, because fresh milk was scarce in South Florida before refrigerators.

mint-julep.fait: Associated with the cuisine of the Southern United States, this bourbon and mint cocktail is the one that inspired the mojito.

juke-box.fait: This coin-operated machine played records in American bars and diners; it has become a collector’s item.

musique-country.fait: This music blends the African banjo, the Italian mandolin and the Hawaiian lap steel; its yodel comes from a Swiss German community in Appalachia.

milk-shake.fait: In Canada it is called lait frappé, in French-speaking Switzerland simply frappé: this cold drink blends milk, ice cream and syrups.

banana-split.fait: This dessert owes its name to its banana split in two lengthwise, topped with three scoops of ice cream, hot chocolate sauce and whipped cream.

club-sandwich.fait: This sandwich with two layers of filling is cut into quarters, set upright with the point facing up and held together with toothpicks.

cupcake.fait: In England, this small cake is called a fairy cake; it is baked in a paper cup and is usually covered with frosting.

deep-dish-pizza.fait: This pizza was born in 1943 in a Chicago pizzeria, Pizzeria Uno: it is in fact also called Chicago pizza.

poke.fait: Its Hawaiian name means “cut into pieces”: this dish of diced marinated raw fish, often tuna or octopus, comes from Hawaiian cuisine.

washington-monument.fait: This obelisk erected in honor of George Washington was the tallest monument in the world until the Eiffel Tower was built.

flatiron.fait: Its name means “clothes iron”: this building is pointed because Broadway, the only avenue in New York outside the grid, crosses 5th Avenue there.

everglades.fait: These marshes form a slow-moving system of rivers that flows southwest; Florida panthers, American crocodiles and manatees can be seen there.

parc-arches.fait: This park in Utah is home to a large concentration of natural rock arches, amid cliffs and buttes sculpted by erosion.

caesar-cocktail.fait: This cocktail invented in Calgary differs from the Bloody Mary in one unexpected ingredient: clam broth mixed with tomato juice.

ballon-balai.fait: This sport is played like hockey, but with a broom with a triangular head and spongy shoes instead of skates.

canal-rideau.fait: Completed in 1832, this canal between Ottawa and Kingston is the oldest canal system in North America to have operated continuously since its opening.

parc-stanley.fait: This urban park in Vancouver is named after Frederick Stanley, Governor General of Canada at the time of its opening.

anse-aux-meadows.fait: The remains of a Viking village, one of the first Norse settlements in America, were discovered here, on the island of Newfoundland.

parc-jasper.fait: The largest of the Canadian national parks in the Rockies, it is home to the Columbia Icefield, elk, moose, grizzly bears and caribou.

bongo.fait: These two joined drums, one larger than the other, come from Cuba; the person who plays them is called a bongocero.

danzon.fait: Born in Matanzas in 1879, this musical genre falls chronologically between the contradanza and the Cuban son, which would later give rise to salsa.

mambo.fait: Invented by the Cuban Arsenio Rodríguez, this genre set off a “mambomania” on dance floors around the world, before giving way to the cha-cha-chá.

rumba-cubaine.fait: In Spanish, its name means “party”; this dance developed in the Afro-Cuban communities of Havana and Matanzas.

cayo-coco.fait: This cay in the Jardines del Rey archipelago, also called the Sabana-Camagüey archipelago, north of Cuba, is one of the country’s tourist hubs.

san-pedro-roca.nom: San Pedro de la Roca Castle
san-pedro-roca.fait: It is colloquially called the Castillo del Morro: this fortress overlooks the bay of Santiago de Cuba.

gran-teatro-havane.fait: This famous neo-Baroque theater and opera house, called Grand Théâtre de La Havane in French, stands in the old town.

mento.fait: The first popular music of Jamaica, born in the countryside at the end of the 19th century, it is one of the ancestors of reggae.

griot.fait: This pork shoulder marinated in citrus is first braised, then fried; it is commonly served at celebrations.

ile-tortue.fait: Christopher Columbus named it this because of its shape; in the 17th century, it served as a stronghold for freebooters and buccaneers.

pic-duarte.fait: This peak is the highest in the country, and also in the entire Caribbean; it honors Juan Pablo Duarte, one of the Founding Fathers of the nation.

ile-saona.fait: This tropical island, popular with tourists who arrive by catamaran, has seen its beaches used as a desert island setting for films and commercials.

los-haitises.fait: In the language of the Taíno, the island’s first inhabitants, “Haiti” means “mountainous area”; their caves are preserved there.

san-salvador-bs.fait: Christopher Columbus very probably made landfall here in 1492: it is thought to be his first shore in the Americas.

cahal-pech.fait: This Maya site perched on a hill above the Macal River has two ball courts and perhaps even a steam bath.

ambergris-caye.fait: It is the largest island in Belize: a cay in the Caribbean Sea that is called Ambergris Caye in English.

glovers-reef.fait: This partly submerged atoll is one of the three atolls of the Belize Barrier Reef, whose southern limit it marks.

yaxha.fait: Its name means “green water” in Maya and, unusually, it has not changed since the Classic period: its glyph already reads “Yaxha.”

takalik-abaj.fait: This site blends Olmec and Maya features; it preserves a royal tomb and some of the oldest Maya hieroglyphic inscriptions.

lac-peten-itza.fait: The town of Flores, capital of the Petén department, is built on an island near the southern shore of this lake in northern Guatemala.

utila.fait: This Honduran island in the Caribbean lies at the southern end of the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef, the second largest in the world.

ometepe.fait: Its name comes from the Nahuatl for “two mountains”: set in Lake Nicaragua, the island is formed by two volcanoes, once two separate islands.

momotombo.fait: This volcano with Strombolian eruptions, rising on the shore of Lake Managua near León, is relatively young: it is thought to be about 4,500 years old.

laguna-apoyo.fait: This lake fills the caldera of a volcano: it is wrongly called a “lagoon,” through a literal translation of the Spanish word laguna.

leon-viejo.fait: Damaged by the Momotombo volcano and then ruined by an earthquake in 1610, this colonial town was abandoned: its inhabitants founded present-day León.

poas.fait: The crater of this very active volcano gives off toxic fumes and holds an acid lake that can disappear depending on its activity.

irazu.fait: This volcano and Turrialba are sometimes called twins because they rest on the same base; the acid lake in its crater evaporated in April 2013.

tortuguero.fait: This northeastern park is the third most visited in Costa Rica, even though it can only be reached by plane or by boat.

chirripo.fait: The surroundings of Costa Rica's highest point bear traces of ancient glaciers, and its fauna and flora are partly related to those of the Andes.

basilique-cartago.nom: Basilica of Our Lady of the Angels
basilique-cartago.fait: According to tradition, a woman found a stone statue of the Virgin here in 1635; it is now the main pilgrimage site in Costa Rica.

volcan-baru.fait: This dormant volcano in the west of the country is Panama's highest point, and its rich vegetation is protected to the north by a national park.

archipel-perles.fait: This archipelago in the Gulf of Panama has more than two hundred islands and islets; the largest is called King's Island.

casco-viejo.fait: This district was born when Panama City, destroyed, was moved and rebuilt in 1673 on a small peninsula surrounded by reefs.

ilopango.fait: The largest lake in El Salvador, this body of water is also a volcano, made up of a caldera and a few lava domes.

pigeon-island.fait: Once surrounded by water, this peninsula is linked by a road; it holds the ruins of Fort Rodney, fought over by the French and the English.

peninsule-valdes.fait: This almost rectangular peninsula is joined to the mainland only by an isthmus; old maps called it the “San José Peninsula.”

la-bombonera.fait: Its nickname, “the candy box,” comes from its shape: three slightly curved stands and a straight building unconnected to the rest.

el-ateneo.fait: Here, people buy their books in a former neo-Baroque theater in Buenos Aires, turned into a bookstore in 2000.

train-des-nuages.fait: This former section of the Belgrano railway, now a tourist line, leaves from Salta and crosses the Andes to a pass on the Chilean border.

train-bout-du-monde.fait: Its official name means “Southern Fuegian Railway”: this line in Tierra del Fuego links Ushuaia to Tierra del Fuego National Park.

bombo-leguero.fait: The deep sound of this drum can carry several kilometers in the mountains, hence its name: “it can be heard for leagues around.”

maracana.fait: When it opened, this Rio stadium offered more than 200,000 places, a world record at the time; its capacity has since been reduced.

ipanema.fait: The name of this upscale Rio neighborhood, bordered by the Atlantic Ocean, comes from a Guarani word meaning “bad waters.”

pelourinho.fait: This neighborhood of Salvador, at the heart of colonial Brazil's first capital, is often wrongly confused with the whole historic center.

lambada.fait: This Brazilian dance became popular worldwide thanks to a French summer hit of 1989, which was in fact a plagiarism.

acai-na-tigela.fait: In northern Brazil, the original recipe for this açaí bowl is usually savory: it contains shrimp or fried fish.

picanha.fait: This cut of beef, popular in Brazilian cuisine, consists of the biceps femoris muscle and its cap of fat.

surdo.fait: This drum, the largest in the samba rhythm section, is now mostly made of metal; some shells are even made of Plexiglas.

pamonha.fait: This delicate dish, common in Brazil's Northeast and in Goiás, probably comes from Indigenous cuisine.

tucupi.fait: This yellow sauce comes from cassava juice, which is toxic when raw: it must be boiled for several hours to remove the poison.

quindim.fait: This dessert from northeastern Brazil requires only three ingredients: egg yolk, sugar and grated coconut.

maculele.fait: This combat dance linked to capoeira is performed with a stick in each hand, sometimes replaced by knives.

litterature-cordel.fait: In Brazil, this form of self-publishing spreads popular poetry in booklets called folhetos.

ile-robinson-crusoe.fait: This Chilean island in the Pacific is the largest in the Juan Fernández archipelago, and the only one that is inhabited.

chuquicamata.fait: The largest open-pit copper mine in the world, this chasm in the Atacama Desert alone holds 13% of global reserves.

tangata-manu.fait: To choose the “birdman” of Easter Island, each clan sent a swimmer to an islet to fetch the first tern egg of the season.

barros-luco.fait: This hot beef and cheese sandwich is named after a Chilean president who used to order it at the Congress restaurant.

vallee-sacree.fait: The Incas valued this valley for its fertility; even today, cornfields and vegetable gardens thrive there.

coricancha.fait: Its Quechua name means “golden enclosure”: this temple in Cusco was the most sacred place in the Inca Empire.

choquequirao.fait: This ruined Inca city is nicknamed the “sister” of Machu Picchu, but it is more isolated and far less visited.

iles-ballestas.fait: The guano piled up on these islands made Peru rich in the 19th century: it was exported as fertilizer to Europe and North America.

papa-huancaina.fait: These “Huancayo-style” potatoes are served cold, covered with a creamy sauce of cheese and yellow chili pepper.

carapulcra.fait: Its Aymara name means “dish of hot stones”; it is one of the oldest dishes recorded since the conquest of Peru.

seigneur-miracles.fait: Every October since 1687, this image of the crucified Christ has drawn millions of faithful in a procession through Lima.

desert-tatacoa.fait: Despite its desert appearance, it is actually a tropical dry forest, rich in fossils millions of years old.

tierradentro.fait: At this site, listed by UNESCO in 1995 and a witness to pre-Columbian culture, hypogea and monumental statues of human figures have been found.

ile-margarita.fait: Nicknamed “the Pearl of the Caribbean,” this island forms, with Coche and Cubagua, Venezuela's only island state.

pic-bolivar.fait: This summit of the Sierra Nevada de Mérida, the highest point in Venezuela, was named in honor of Simón Bolívar.

colonia-tovar.fait: This town, at an altitude of 1,800 meters, is a former colony founded in 1843 by a group of German families.

grotte-guacharo.fait: This park was created around a remarkable cave, named after the guácharo, a bird that lives there; this Spanish word derives from Quechua.

henri-pittier.fait: Venezuela's first national park, it honors a Swiss biologist who pioneered nature conservation in the country.

cuicocha.fait: This lake fills the caldera of a volcano that is only “dormant”; its two islets, the tops of volcanic domes, are off-limits.

tungurahua.fait: This 5,023-meter stratovolcano, straddling two provinces, has been erupting since 1999 and entered a new explosive phase in 2011.

samaipata.fait: Despite being called a “fort,” this site was probably religious: a huge rock carved with basins and channels, decorated with two felines.

ile-de-lobos.fait: This rocky islet with its lighthouse, off Punta del Este, is the southernmost point of Uruguay above water.

place-independance-uy.fait: In this Montevideo square stands the equestrian statue of Artigas, Uruguay's national hero, with his mausoleum beneath it.

trinidad-parana.fait: This former Guarani Jesuit reduction, founded in 1706, is one of the largest and best preserved in Paraguay.

reserve-suriname-central.fait: This vast tropical primary forest is home to jaguars, tapirs and giant armadillos, as well as more than 5,000 plant species.

ile-kangourou.fait: Located to the south of South Australia, it is the country's third largest island, after Tasmania and Melville Island.

bungle-bungle.fait: The black and orange stripes of these massifs come from alternating dark lichen and bare silica.

gare-flinders-street.fait: In Melbourne, “meet me under the clocks” refers to the row of clocks above the entrance of this station, which show the departures.

baie-shark.fait: Its English name means “bay of sharks”; in French, it was once called the baie des Chiens-Marins.

art-aborigene.fait: For Aboriginal people, this art is first of all spirituality: it is always linked to a territory, such as a water hole, a cave or a route.

footy.fait: Close to rugby, this sport is nevertheless played mostly with the feet, because players must cover a much larger oval field.

lac-tekapo.fait: Its turquoise color comes from the glacial silt that tints the snowmelt coming down from the Southern Alps.

mont-taranaki.fait: This dormant volcano is known for its conical shape with regular slopes, considered one of the most symmetrical in the world.

tane-mahuta.fait: It is not a monument, but a tree: a giant kauri in the Waipoua Forest, in the Northland region.

poi.fait: These small weights on the end of a string, inherited from the Māori, are now used for juggling and fire arts.

iles-yasawa.fait: Isolated from the rest of Fiji until the 1940s, these volcanic islands have become a major tourist destination.

beqa.fait: This island is known for its firewalking ritual, the vilavilairevo, which has become a show for tourists throughout the country.

kadavu.fait: The fourth largest island in Fiji, it is almost cut in two at an isthmus, where there are an airport, a high school and a hospital.

eua.fait: Unlike many islands in the region, this one, of volcanic origin, has a pronounced relief.

haapai.fait: Most of these islands are uninhabited atolls, but two volcanic islands, Tofua and Kao, have volcanoes that are still active.

lac-letas.fait: The largest lake in Vanuatu, it fills the caldera of Gaua Island, at the foot of Mount Gharat, which gives it its crescent shape.

tikopia.fait: Although it lies in Melanesia, this small island, a former volcano, is inhabited by Polynesians who speak Tikopia.

rennell-est.fait: This former lagoon, the largest in the Pacific, is dotted with limestone islands and is home to endemic animal and plant species.

ontong-java.fait: This roughly boot-shaped atoll has 122 islets; yet the nearest island, geographically and culturally, belongs to Papua New Guinea.

iles-santa-cruz.fait: These islands belong to the Solomons, but geographically they form a small separate archipelago, far to the southeast of the rest of the country.

tarawa.fait: Its pass, through which the largest ships easily enter the lagoon, earned this atoll the role of capital of the British colony of the Gilbert and Ellice Islands.

kiritimati.fait: This Pacific atoll has two names: Christmas Island, its English name, and Kiritimati in Gilbertese.

abemama.fait: Toward the end of the 19th century, this atoll was the capital of a kingdom ruled by King Tembinok'; Robert Louis Stevenson lived there.

butaritari.fait: In Gilbertese, the name of this atoll means “smell of the sea,” and not in a pleasant sense: it refers to an unpleasant odor.

fort-al-fahidi.fait: This fort, the oldest building still standing in Dubai, now houses the city's main museum.

abra.fait: These traditional wooden boats carry passengers across the Dubai inlet, leaving every few minutes, for one dirham paid to the driver.

palm-jumeirah.fait: This artificial archipelago forms a palm tree: a trunk and sixteen fronds, surrounded by a crescent that encloses a lagoon.

khor-dubai.fait: Its Arabic name literally means “Dubai river,” yet it is not a river but an inlet of the sea.

lac-yssyk-koul.fait: Although perched in the mountains in a harsh climate, this lake rarely freezes thanks to its slight salinity, hence its Kyrgyz name of “warm lake.”

tour-burana.fait: This minaret is part of the remains of Balasagun, a vanished city founded by the Karakhanids at the end of the 9th century.

sulaiman-too.fait: This mountain overlooking the Fergana Valley long served as a landmark on the Silk Road, and many ancient places of worship are found there.

tchatyr-koul.fait: Its Kyrgyz name means “celestial lake,” literally “roof lake”; it lies at the low point of a depression near the Chinese border.

arslanbob.fait: This mountain village is surrounded by a vast stand of walnut trees, said to be the oldest and largest walnut forest in the world.

sarazm.fait: This proto-urban site from the 4th millennium BCE has a name that means “the beginning of the land.”

pic-ismail-samani.fait: This summit was called Stalin Peak and then Communism Peak; it is the highest point in Tajikistan and in the former Soviet Union.

parc-national-du-pamir.fait: With its nature reserve, this protected area is the largest in Central Asia; it includes Ismoil Somoni Peak and the Fedchenko Glacier.

lac-iskanderkoul.fait: Its name means “Alexander's lake,” in memory of Alexander the Great, who went there during his expedition to India.

darvaza.fait: This crater, nicknamed the “Gate to Hell,” lies near Darvaza, a village in the Karakum Desert whose name means “gate.”

merv.fait: A former stop on the Silk Road, this city was the satrapy of Margiana; its remains lie near the present-day city of Mary.

kunya-urgench.fait: This former capital of the Khwarazm-Shahs probably gave its name to organdy, a stiffened muslin fabric.

tapis-a-guls.fait: These rugs of the Turkmen tribes do not only cover the floor: they also serve as door hangings, tent rugs or bags.

akhal-teke.fait: This horse with a metallic-sheen coat nearly disappeared in the Soviet era; it has become the emblem of Turkmenistan.

pyramides-de-meroe.fait: These steep-sided pyramids form the necropolises of Meroë, capital of the Kingdom of Kush during the last period of its history.

gebel-barkal.fait: The Egyptians called this rocky promontory the “Pure Mountain” and believed that the god Amun lived there.

naqa.fait: A stop on the road to the East, this city of the Kingdom of Meroë preserves two temples, one dedicated to Amun, the other to Apedemak.

temple-de-soleb.fait: Built under Amenhotep III and dedicated to Amun, this temple was rededicated to Aten after Akhenaten came to power.

suakin.fait: This former Red Sea port town was built mainly of coral, and Rimbaud even worked there.

kerma.fait: Digging through a very thin layer, archaeologists found up to ten superimposed towns there; its main temple is the Deffufa.

fort-masmak.fait: This fort of clay and mud brick played an important role in 1902, when Abdulaziz Al Saud and his men retook Riyadh.

dumat-al-jandal.fait: The name of this ancient city means “Duma of the stone,” after Duma, one of the twelve sons of Ishmael.

alardah.fait: This ceremony combines sung poetry, dance and percussion; it marks the beginning or the end of important occasions.

avdat.fait: This Nabataean caravan stop owes its name to King Obodas, revered as a divine presence; it was deserted after an earthquake.

megiddo.fait: This site also bears the Greek name Armageddon, linked to the biblical narrative; its oldest layers date back to 7000 BCE.

parc-de-timna.fait: This horseshoe-shaped valley in the Negev is crossed by the Israel National Trail, which runs from one end of the country to the other.

sepphoris.fait: Excavations of this Galilean city shed light on life in the time of Jesus, so much so that a pilgrimage route, the Jesus Trail, passes through it.

qasr-kharana.fait: It is called a castle, but its layout and decoration suggest no military use: its purpose is still unclear.

kerak-de-moab.fait: Also called the Krak of the Moabites, this fortress was built in the 12th century, at the time of the Crusades, in what is now the city of Al-Karak.

carte-de-madaba.fait: This church mosaic is the oldest surviving map of the Holy Land and Jerusalem.

palais-de-beiteddine.fait: This palace, the former seat of the Emirate of Mount Lebanon, now serves as the summer residence of the President of the Lebanese Republic.

gouffre-de-baatara.fait: When the snow melts, a tall waterfall forms in this chasm in Tannourine, also called the Chasm of the Three Bridges.

anjar.fait: This town in the Beqaa, inhabited mostly by people of Armenian descent, lies roughly halfway along the road from Beirut to Damascus.

chateau-de-la-mer.fait: This fortress, built on a peninsula in Sidon, present-day Saida, was called Sagette or Sayette by the Crusaders.

koumbi-saleh.fait: Capital of the Kingdom of Ghana, this city served as a depot for salt and gold; yet its ruins lie in present-day Mauritania.

kedia-d-idjil.fait: This massif owes its blue-gray color to iron oxides; its deposits even disturb the Earth's magnetic field.

ai-khanoum.fait: Founded by the Greeks in the wake of Alexander the Great, this ancient city was nicknamed Alexandria on the Oxus by Ptolemy.

surkh-kotal.fait: The inscriptions in Greek letters at this Kushan site revealed a previously unknown language: Bactrian.

tour-de-la-vierge.fait: Built on a cliff and protected by a rampart, this fortified tower is part of the seafront of Baku's old town.

lac-goygol.fait: Its name means “the blue lake”: it is a natural dammed lake on the foothills of the Murovdag range, near Ganja.

khinalyg.fait: Perched at 2,350 meters in the Caucasus, this village, called Kətş in the Khinalug language, is the highest settlement in Azerbaijan.

arc-de-marc-aurele.fait: This Roman triumphal arch stands in the ancient city of Oea, which has become present-day Tripoli.

germa.fait: This town in the southwest of the country, ancient Garama, was the capital of the Garamantes, a Saharan Berber people.

ptolemais.fait: This Greek port colony was one of the ancient capitals of Cyrenaica; its remains lie near present-day Tolmeita.

norias-de-hama.fait: Only seventeen of them remain on the Orontes, and they are no longer used: they are preserved for their beauty and their history.

saint-simeon-le-stylite.fait: This ruined 5th-century monastery was built around the column on which Saint Simeon Stylites lived.

forteresse-de-saladin.fait: In use since Antiquity, this fortress is also called the Castle of Saône, a distortion of its Arabic name.

zvartnots.fait: This archaeological site, one of the most important in the country, lies in a suburb of Yerevan partly occupied by the international airport of the same name.

noravank.fait: Its name means “new monastery”; it served as a mausoleum for the Orbelians and was famous for its scriptorium.

zorats-karer.fait: This megalithic site in the Syunik region is also called Karahunj, which means “voice of the stones.”

ghapama.fait: This stew is cooked in a hollowed-out pumpkin stuffed with rice and dried fruit, often during the holiday season.

matnakash.fait: Its name means “pulled with the fingers”; in the Soviet era, the authorities replaced the grooves drawn on this bread with a crisscross pattern.

arc-de-ctesiphon.fait: This ruined Sasanian monument is the only visible remnant of ancient Ctesiphon, called Al-Mada'in by the Arabs.

etendard-d-ur.fait: Found in the Royal Cemetery of Ur, this Sumerian object is on display in London, and no one knows what it was used for.

vase-d-uruk.fait: This alabaster vase bears one of the oldest depictions of scenes of life in human history.

dame-de-warka.fait: This Sumerian piece in the National Museum of Iraq, in Baghdad, is sometimes nicknamed locally the “Mona Lisa of Uruk.”

kalta-minor.fait: Its name means “short minaret”; it stands in Itchan Kala, the walled quarter of Khiva.

medersa-mir-i-arab.fait: This madrasa in the Po-i-Kalan complex, in Bukhara, is still in use, but it remains closed to visitors.

tchoga-zanbil.fait: Its Elamite ziggurat is one of the only ones preserved outside Mesopotamia, and probably the best preserved of all.

kandovan.fait: This village in East Azerbaijan province, near Tabriz, has the distinctive feature of being troglodytic.

ghormeh-sabzi.fait: This stew is based on sautéed herbs, parsley, leek, spinach and fenugreek, simmered with beans, dried limes and lamb.

sangak.fait: This whole-wheat sourdough flatbread is not round: it is shaped into a rectangle or a triangle.

sohan.fait: This confection of wheat, sugar, saffron and cardamom is mainly produced in the cities of Qom and Isfahan.

tahtchine.fait: This saffron and yogurt rice dish comes with a golden rice crust, the tahdig, and is often served with pistachios and zereshk berries.

mirza-ghassemi.fait: These grilled eggplants, bound with eggs, come from Gilan, on the shores of the Caspian; made with zucchini, the dish becomes kadoo ghassemi.

khatam-kari.fait: This star-patterned marquetry was so prized at the Safavid court that some princes learned the technique, like music or calligraphy.

tapis-de-tabriz.fait: The first rugs made for export came out of the Tabriz workshops, woven to the sizes and colors ordered by European merchants.

tapis-de-kachan.fait: After the Afghan invasion, weaving stopped in Kashan until the end of the 19th century; it resumed with higher-quality wool.

tombak.fait: The name of this drum is said to imitate its two strokes: “tom,” deep, in the center of the skin, and “bak,” high-pitched, on the edge.

mehregan.fait: The counterpart of Nowruz at the autumn equinox, this festival of Mithra was so popular that the Talmud mentions it.

sadeh.fait: For this fire festival, the Persians lit fires on the hills or on rooftops and prayed for the return of the warm season.

tirgan.fait: For this summer solstice festival, children tie a rainbow ribbon around their wrist, then throw it into a stream about ten days later.

slata-mechouia.fait: This grilled vegetable salad owes its tomatoes and chili peppers to the Andalusian Arabs, who arrived at Cap Bon after the fall of Granada with these New World plants.

assidat-zgougou.fait: Its name means “pine cream”: this Tunisian dessert is prepared for the Mouled festival.

fes-el-bali.fait: The oldest quarter of Fez, with some 10,000 very narrow alleys, is probably the largest contiguous car-free area in the world.

briouate.fait: This pastry of Ottoman origin bears this name only in Morocco; its sweet version, with almonds and orange blossom, is coated in honey.

tadelakt.fait: Its name comes from an Arabic word meaning “to rub, to polish”: this plaster of lime and black soap is used to waterproof cisterns, hammams and pools.

ahidous.fait: In this Berber dance, men and women form undulating circles elbow to elbow; in summer, after the harvest, it is danced almost every evening.

monastere-de-djvari.fait: This 6th-century Orthodox monastery near Mtskheta has a name that literally means “Monastery of the Cross.”

satsivi.fait: Its name means “cold dish”: this poultry in a walnut and garlic sauce is served mainly at the New Year meal, not at Christmas.

khartcho.fait: This beef soup from Mingrelia contains cherry plums, in the form of tkemali sauce, with rice and walnuts.

lobiani.fait: This bread is filled with beans, hence its name, from lobio, “bean” in Georgian; its most popular version resembles a bean khachapuri.

chakhokhbili.fait: This chicken stewed with tomatoes and fresh herbs nevertheless owes its name to the Georgian word khokhobi, which means “pheasant.”

sulguni.fait: This brined cheese from Mingrelia and Svaneti, nicknamed “pickle cheese,” is often served fried, which masks its smell.

gozinaki.fait: This treat is traditionally eaten only at New Year; since the 20th century, it is sometimes eaten at Christmas as well.

ankh.fait: This hieroglyph means “life”: for the Egyptians, it symbolized both existence on Earth and eternal life after death.

nemes.fait: This pharaoh's headdress is the one worn by Tutankhamun's gold funerary mask and by the head of the Sphinx of Giza.

pschent.fait: This double crown fits the white crown of the South together with the red crown of the North: with it, the pharaoh proclaims the union of the Two Lands.

uraeus.fait: This rearing female cobra on the pharaoh's forehead served to protect him against his enemies.

palette-de-narmer.fait: This cosmetic palette bears some of the oldest known hieroglyphs, which evoke the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt.

tahtib.fait: Practiced mainly in Upper Egypt, this form of fighting is not just combat: it is also a form of martial dance.

hawawshi.fait: This bread stuffed with spiced minced meat is baked in the oven; in Alexandria, the filling is enclosed between two discs of dough.

nemrut-dagi.fait: Its summit bears the tomb of King Antiochus I of Commagene, a tumulus surrounded by places of worship and monumental statues.

iskender-kebap.fait: This dish stands out for the hot butter poured over the meat, served on sliced pita bread with tomato sauce and yogurt.

kumpir.fait: This large baked potato is cut in half, its flesh mixed with butter and cheese, then topped with corn, olives or red cabbage.

gozleme.fait: This flatbread of yufka dough is filled with a choice of minced meat, spinach, potatoes, cheese or egg.

karniyarik.fait: Its name means “split belly”: these eggplants are stuffed with minced meat; without meat and served cold, the dish is called imam bayıldı.

cilbir.fait: Ottoman sultans were already eating these poached eggs on yogurt in the 15th century; today they are topped with melted butter and Aleppo pepper.

tantuni.fait: This julienned and sautéed beef, lightly spiced, is a specialty of the city of Mersin, in Turkey.

tavuk-gogsu.fait: This sweet milk pudding, flavored with cinnamon, contains chicken: the cooked meat is shredded into fine threads, then blended with the rice.

kazandibi.fait: Its name means “bottom of the kazan”: this Turkish dessert can be likened to a caramelized milk pudding.

boyoz.fait: This small bun is a specialty of Izmir; in the rest of the country, one is more likely to find a similar bread called açma.

salgam.fait: This fermented “turnip juice” is often drunk after a kebab, or alongside rakı in a separate glass, because their flavors complement each other.

dolmus.fait: This public transport minibus follows a fixed route, but without set schedules or stops, both in the city and in the outskirts.

okey.fait: This tabletop game, with rules close to those of rummy and Rummikub, is played in cafés, like tavla, or online.

mehter.fait: Made up mostly of Janissaries, this company ran the band, but was originally responsible for pitching the sultan's tent on campaign or looking after the horses.

cirit.fait: In this equestrian team sport, points are scored by throwing a wooden javelin at the opposing riders.

pico-cao-grande.fait: The Portuguese name of this peak on São Tomé Island literally means “great dog peak.”

ilheu-rolas.fait: The equator crosses the north of this islet: a monument marks its passage with a marker and a mosaic map of the world.

cathedrale-sao-tome.fait: Seat of the country's Catholic diocese, this cathedral stands on the People's Square, very close to the presidential palace.

parc-obo.fait: This park on São Tomé Island has a twin: the Obô Natural Park of Príncipe, created the same year on Príncipe Island.

pic-basile.fait: This shield volcano on Bioko Island carries the city of Malabo on its northern slope; its last known eruption dates from 1923.

bioko.fait: The country's capital was not on the mainland: Malabo, the political capital until 2026, is on this island in the Gulf of Guinea.

annobon.fait: The country's only island in the Southern Hemisphere, it is home mostly to women, children and elders: lacking prospects, many men leave to live elsewhere.

corisco.fait: The name of this island comes from the Portuguese word for lightning; it is also called Mandji Benga.

monte-alen.fait: This park, the largest in Equatorial Guinea, stretches across the center of the country over the Niefang mountain range.

elobey-chico.fait: This small uninhabited island of 19 hectares, in the estuary of the Muni River, is administered by the municipality of Corisco.

karthala.fait: The lava flows of this active volcano on Grande Comore sometimes reach the sea, and a lava lake can appear in a crater.

parc-moheli.fait: This marine park protects the southern coast of Mohéli Island, where sea turtles have many nesting sites.

ile-moheli.fait: Called Mwali in Comorian, it is the smallest of the three islands of the Union of the Comoros, but also the most touristic.

anjouan.fait: This volcanic island, called Ndzuwani in Comorian, is the most densely populated in the entire Comoros archipelago.

lac-assal.fait: This salt lake, in the center of Djibouti, lies below sea level: it is the lowest point in all of Africa.

ghoubbet.fait: Its Arabic name means “the Chasm of Demons,” and two volcanic islands set in its middle are called the Devil's Islands.

ile-moucha.fait: This small semi-desert island lies at the entrance to the Gulf of Tadjoura, off the city of Djibouti.

mosquee-hamoudi.fait: Founded in 1897 by Haji Hamoudi, this mosque in downtown Djibouti has remained faithful to traditional Islamic architecture.

sept-freres.fait: Despite their name, there are only six of these islands: the “seventh brother” is Ras Siyan, a peninsula that forms the link with the coast.

fiat-tagliero.fait: This former gas station in Asmara, completed in 1938, was designed as a reinforced-concrete “airplane.”

dahlak.fait: This Eritrean archipelago in the Red Sea is made up of more than a hundred islands, islets and reefs, including two main islands.

cinema-impero.fait: This Art Deco cinema in Asmara owes its name to the “Italian Empire” proclaimed by Mussolini after the conquest of Ethiopia.

mosquee-asmara.fait: This great mosque of Asmara was built in 1938 on Mussolini's initiative, to impress the city's Muslim population.

bijagos.fait: Only about ten of the islands and islets of this archipelago, located opposite Bissau, are permanently inhabited.

bolama.fait: This town was the capital of Portuguese Guinea until 1941: a shortage of fresh water then forced the move to Bissau.

canhabaque.fait: A queen governs this island with a council of women elected for life; the king is only her spokesman and is not her husband.

cathedrale-bissau.fait: This cathedral also serves as a lighthouse: its north tower houses a light that guides ships through the Geba estuary to the port of Bissau.

parc-iona.fait: This park in Namibe province is both the largest and the oldest in Angola: it has been protected since 1937.

capulana.fait: This simple piece of fabric serves in turn as a wrap skirt, a dress or a baby carrier worn on the back.

ile-ibo.fait: A former trading port fortified by the Portuguese, this island in the Quirimbas is known today for its silversmiths.

matoke.fait: This banana is eaten green and is never sweet; in Kampala, its name has even become synonymous with food.

chutes-ngonye.fait: These falls on the Zambezi, several hundred kilometers upstream from Victoria Falls, remain less known than the latter because of their isolation.

kasanka.fait: Every season, this park, one of the smallest in the country, hosts gatherings of more than ten million Eidolon helvum.

khami.fait: These ruins are those of the former capital of the Torwa dynasty, which ruled the kingdom of Butua for more than two centuries.

matobo.fait: This park, formerly called Rhodes Matopos National Park, lies in the heart of the Matobo Hills, famous for their rock paintings.

kahuzi-biega.fait: Two extinct volcanoes, Kahuzi and Biega, dominate this park covered in tropical forest, home to gorillas and elephants.

achu.fait: This dish for special occasions combines pounded taro and plantains with a spicy yellow soup, seasoned with rock salt.

eru.fait: A specialty of the Banyang people, this dish of leafy vegetables, palm oil and meats is eaten with fufu or garri.

suya.fait: These skewers of meat marinated in spices and ground peanuts are bought on the street, often wrapped in newspaper.

nok.fait: They are named after the village of Nok, where they were discovered; they are considered the oldest large terracotta sculptures in Africa.

tetes-ife.fait: The realism and refinement of this sculpture went against the idea that Westerners had of African art.

bunny-chow.fait: This sandwich is a hollowed-out loaf of white bread filled with curry; it was born among South Africans of Indian origin in Durban.

koeksister.fait: This braided doughnut dough is fried and then dipped in cold cane syrup; it is eaten cold, very sticky and sweet.

boerewors.fait: Its name means “farmer's sausage” in Afrikaans, and regulations require it to contain at least 90% meat or fat.

pinotage.fait: This grape variety is a cross between Pinot Noir and Cinsault, once called Hermitage: hence its name, a contraction of “Pinot” and “Hermitage.”

potjiekos.fait: This stew simmers outdoors in the potjie, a three-legged cast-iron pot brought by the Dutch.

gumboot.fait: This percussive dance is performed in rubber boots, sometimes adorned with small bells that jingle when the dancer stamps on the ground.

melktert.fait: Its name means “milk tart” in Afrikaans: its custard has more milk relative to eggs than a Portuguese tart, giving it a lighter texture.

chakalaka.fait: This vegetable relish, usually very spicy, goes as well with bread as with pap, samp, stews or curries.

meskel.fait: This feast of the True Cross commemorates its discovery by Empress Helena; Ethiopia has celebrated it for more than 1,600 years.

begena.fait: According to tradition, this large lyre was brought from Israel by Menelik I; David is said to have used it to soothe King Saul.

romazava.fait: This Malagasy dish, also found in the Comoros, combines meat, shrimp and fish with leafy greens, notably mafana greens.

kabosy.fait: This plucked string instrument from Madagascar resembles a small guitar or a mandolin.

kedjenou.fait: This stew of farm workers and hunters is slow-cooked in a sealed canari, a terracotta pot set over a wood fire.

chateau-vaduz.fait: This castle overlooking the capital is the residence of the princely family: it is not open to visitors, and the prince receives his official guests there.

saint-florin-vaduz.fait: Originally a simple parish church, it only became a cathedral in 1997; it houses the burial vault of the princely family.

chateau-gutenberg.fait: Unlike Vaduz Castle, this castle in Balzers is not home to the princely family: it is open to the general public as a museum.

curta.fait: This hand-cranked mechanical calculator looks like a pepper mill, but it performs all four arithmetic operations and, with practice, square roots.

basilique-saint-marin.fait: It is dedicated to Saint Marinus, a deacon who in the 4th century founded the community that gave rise to the Republic of San Marino.

rocher-monaco.fait: This district, the oldest in the principality, is home to the Prince's Palace, the parliament and even the country's only prison, clinging to the Rock.

creation-adam.fait: In this Sistine Chapel fresco, God's index finger reaches toward Adam's without touching it: it is the gesture that gives life to Man.

ecole-athenes.fait: This fresco by Raphael brings together the great figures of ancient thought; it is the most famous work of the painter from Urbino.

jugement-dernier.fait: More than 300 figures appear in it, almost all originally painted nude; many were later partly covered with painted drapery.

transfiguration-raphael.fait: It is the last painting by Raphael: he was still working on it when he died, and the work was left unfinished by his hand.

chateau-berg.fait: This castle in Colmar-Berg is the main residence of the grand ducal family, near the confluence of the Alzette and the Attert.

fort-thungen.fait: All that remains of this fort are three round towers nicknamed “the three acorns”; today the site houses the Mudam modern art museum.

lac-haute-sure.fait: This artificial lake, created by a dam on the Sûre, supplies about a third of the country's drinking water while also serving as a recreation area.

saint-michel-lux.fait: It is the oldest religious site in the city: a castle chapel was built here in 987, and the current church blends Romanesque and Baroque.

chateau-schengen.fait: This castle stands very close to the French and German borders; almost entirely rebuilt in the 19th century, it retains a medieval tower.

passerelle-lux.fait: Luxembourgers call it “Al Bréck,” the old bridge: it crosses the Pétrusse valley to link the Upper Town to the station district.

chateau-clervaux.fait: This 12th-century fortified castle overlooks the village of Clervaux, in the midst of the Ardennes landscape.

villa-louvigny.fait: For 64 years, this villa in the municipal park housed the studios of Radio Luxembourg, the station that became the RTL Group.

kition.fait: This ancient city remains little known because Larnaca was built right on top of its site; the Bible already mentions it under the name “Kittim.”

amathonte.fait: Near Limassol, this ancient city was the seat of one of the kingdoms of Cyprus and had a sanctuary dedicated to Aphrodite.

saint-lazare-larnaca.fait: It stands over the tomb of Lazarus: according to one tradition, he is said to have come to Cyprus after his resurrection and to have been a bishop there.

fort-paphos.fait: Built by the Byzantines on the edge of the harbor, this fort later served the various occupiers who fought over the island of Cyprus.

chateau-larnaca.fait: Built to defend the island's south coast, this fortress later served as an artillery post, a prison, and then a museum.

idole-pomos.fait: This small cross-shaped prehistoric sculpture appears on Cyprus's euro coins; it can also be glimpsed in the film “Troy.”

chateau-limassol.fait: This castle in the old port was rebuilt around 1590, during Ottoman rule over the island, and now serves as a museum.

olympe-troodos.fait: This peak, the highest in Cyprus, has the country's only ski slope; it made it possible to train a national ski team.

tarxien.fait: These four megalithic temples date from the Neolithic; in the Bronze Age, a cemetery was set up in the middle of their ruins.

grotte-bleue-malte.fait: This sea cave owes its fame to its blue and turquoise water, so clear that the seabed, its fauna and its flora can be seen perfectly.

fort-saint-elme.fait: At the tip of the Xiberras peninsula, this fort built in 1552 by the Order of Saint John of Jerusalem commands the entrance to the Grand Harbour.

citadelle-gozo.fait: Until the early 17th century, these fortifications were the only refuge for the inhabitants of Gozo against Barbary and Ottoman raids.

palais-magistral.fait: This palace in Valletta, simply called “the Palace” (Il-Palazz), is the official residence of the President of Malta.

cathedrale-mdina.fait: It is built on the spot where the governor Publius, the first Maltese bishop and a future saint, is believed to have met Saint Paul.

auberge-castille.fait: Built to house knights of the Order of Saint John of Jerusalem, this auberge is now home to the Prime Minister's office.

grand-harbour.fait: This natural harbor at the foot of Valletta was home to a vast shipyard and a naval base; today it mainly receives oil tankers and cargo ships.

ghar-dalam.fait: Its Maltese name means “the dark cave”: this cavern in the southeast of Malta, near Birżebbuġa, is also a prehistoric site.

fungus-rock.fait: On this islet grows a rare plant mistaken for a fungus; the Knights of Malta used it as a remedy and forbade access to it.

mitraillette.fait: Half a baguette filled with meat, fries and sauce: this sandwich from Belgian friteries is called “routier” in the province of Liège.

cathedrale-anvers.fait: Its construction stretched over more than a century and a half; its bell tower is one of the belfries of Belgium and France protected by UNESCO.

gare-anvers.fait: Long a terminal station, this station, counted among the most beautiful in the world, now has a tunnel running through it toward the Netherlands.

gravensteen.fait: This medieval castle in Ghent contains weapons and armor, a torture chamber, a crypt, a keep and oubliettes.

koekelberg.fait: Designed as a national monument, this Art Deco basilica, straddling two Brussels municipalities, was only consecrated in 1951.

hotel-tassel.fait: Victor Horta built this Brussels house for his friend Émile Tassel, a professor at the Free University of Brussels.

hotel-ville-louvain.fait: This building is considered a masterpiece of civil Gothic architecture in Belgium, in the style known as Brabantine Gothic.

serra-estrela.fait: This sheep's milk cheese curdles thanks to an infusion of thistle flower, not rennet; when young, it flows “like butter.”

galao.fait: This milky coffee is served in a tall glass: the espresso is poured over the milk foam, which is prepared first and makes up by far the largest part.

cataplana.fait: This vessel from the Algarve is used both to cook and to serve, and it gives its name to the many Portuguese recipes prepared in it.

regaleira.fait: The palace and gardens abound in references to alchemy, Freemasonry and the Templars; it is nicknamed the palace of “Monteiro of the Millions.”

universite-coimbra.fait: Founded in 1290 by King Denis, it is the oldest university in the country and one of the oldest still operating in Europe.

couvent-christ.fait: This former Templar fortress passed to the knights of the Order of Christ, who supported the Portuguese maritime discoveries.

alfama.fait: Its name comes from the Arabic “alf maa,” “a thousand springs”; it is the oldest district of Lisbon, known for its fado bars.

sintra-palais.fait: Its two tall white conical chimneys give it a distinctive silhouette, which has become the symbol of the town of Sintra.

mozartkugel.fait: Invented in 1880 by confectioner Rudolf Baumann, this pistachio, marzipan and dark chocolate praline is still made in Salzburg.

heuriger.fait: These taverns originally served the year's wine: Austrian winegrowers have long had the right to serve their own wine without a license.

festival-salzbourg.fait: This summer festival of opera, theater and music attracts nearly 240,000 visitors every year, most of them from abroad.

karlskirche.fait: This domed church in Vienna, dedicated to Saint Charles Borromeo, is considered one of the finest examples of Baroque in Central Europe.

musikverein.fait: This hall, renowned for its acoustics, hosts the Vienna New Year's Concert every year and is the home of the Philharmonic Orchestra.

petit-toit-or.fait: This Gothic balcony owes its name to its copper shingles gilded with fine gold; Emperor Maximilian showed himself to the people from it.

chutes-krimml.fait: These are the highest waterfalls in Austria; formed by the Krimmler Ache, they are located in Hohe Tauern National Park.

wachau.fait: In this Danube valley, at Dürnstein, King Richard the Lionheart of England was held prisoner by Duke Leopold V.

gruyere.fait: Contrary to popular belief, this cheese has no holes: the confusion comes from Emmental exporters who borrowed its name.

muesli.fait: Born in German-speaking Switzerland, this mix of flakes, seeds and dried fruit is called “bircher” in French-speaking Switzerland, where it is also eaten in the evening.

lion-lucerne.fait: This sculpture honors the Swiss Guards who died in 1792 in the service of Louis XVI, when revolutionaries stormed the Tuileries.

palais-federal.fait: This building in Bern houses both the Swiss government, the Federal Council, and the parliament, the Federal Assembly.

lavaux.fait: In this wine region of the canton of Vaud, the vineyards descend in terraces to the shore of Lake Geneva.

oeschinensee.fait: This mountain lake was formed by several landslides that came down from the slopes of the Fründenhorn and the Doldenhorn.

valere.fait: This fortified church in Sion houses the oldest playable organ in the world, which can be heard during an annual festival.

hagelslag.fait: These chocolate sprinkles are scattered on buttered slices of bread; their Dutch name means “hailstorm.”

rookworst.fait: Its name simply means “smoked sausage”: this ring-shaped sausage, similar to cervelat, is also exported to the United Kingdom.

kapsalon.fait: This dish, very popular in Rotterdam snack bars, has a surprising name: in Dutch, it means “hair salon.”

klompen.fait: These willow or poplar clogs are still worn by festivalgoers who don't want their feet stepped on at concerts.

mauritshuis.fait: This museum in The Hague occupies the former residence of John Maurice of Nassau-Siegen, hence its name, “Maurice House.”

binnenhof.fait: Parliament sits in this complex in The Hague, which grew out of a castle of the Counts of Holland; the Prime Minister also has an office there.

rietveld-schroder.fait: Built for a pharmacist from the De Stijl movement, this house in Utrecht is one of the first symbols of modern architecture.

irish-coffee.fait: This traditional Irish cocktail is drunk hot: it combines coffee with brown sugar, Irish whiskey and cream.
