coddle.fait: This Dublin stew of sausages, bacon and potatoes takes its name from an English verb meaning “to cook in simmering water.”

claddagh.fait: According to the most widespread legend, an Irishman made it while enslaved in Algeria, hoping to see his beloved again.

shillelagh.fait: The large knob of this blackthorn stick was sometimes filled with lead; those sold today are more often carved from hawthorn.

trinity-college.fait: Founded by Queen Elizabeth I, this Dublin university keeps in its library the Book of Kells, an 8th-century manuscript.

colline-tara.fait: In Celtic mythology, this site in County Meath was the mythical capital of Ireland, the “hill of kings.”

temple-bar.fait: This Dublin district known for its nightlife owes its name to William Temple, a provost of Trinity College.

churros.fait: In Seville, these long fritters were called calentitos, in Granada tejeringos: the word churro eventually replaced all these names.

creme-catalane.fait: Flavored with lemon, anise and cinnamon, this custard is served under a layer of burnt sugar that makes it similar to crème brûlée.

pintxo.fait: A Basque variant of tapas, these small topped slices of bread are served as appetizers, held in place by a wooden skewer.

salmorejo.fait: This cold cream from Córdoba is made of bread, tomato, garlic and olive oil; it is also served as a sauce.

castagnettes.fait: Their Spanish name, castañuelas, means “little chestnuts”: an image for this percussion instrument of Spanish folklore.

mantille.fait: This lace scarf draped over the head was traditionally worn by Spanish Catholic women to go to Mass.

san-fermin.fait: During this festival in Pamplona, residents dress all in white, with a red scarf and sash.

sardane.fait: In this Catalan dance, the dancers form a circle holding hands, to the sound of an instrumental ensemble called a cobla.

escurial.fait: At once a monastery, palace, museum and library, this vast complex was the heart of the Spanish Empire under Philip II.

alcazar-segovie.fait: This castle shaped like a ship's prow has served in turn as a royal palace, a state prison and then a military academy.

tzatziki.fait: This yogurt and cucumber meze is pronounced “dzadzíki” in Greek; in Turkish, it is called caciki.

pastitsio.fait: This baked dish of pasta, ground meat and béchamel is a variant of an Italian dish, whose name it keeps: pasticcio.

bougatsa.fait: This phyllo pastry is eaten mainly at breakfast, especially in Thessaloniki, filled with semolina custard.

melomakarono.fait: These olive oil Christmas cookies are soaked in a hot honey syrup, then covered with ground walnuts.

olive-kalamata.fait: Outside Messenia, this large purple olive is not entitled to the name Kalamata: it is then sold under the name “Kalamón.”

mont-athos.fait: Nicknamed the “Holy Mountain,” it is home to a monastic community and remains a major center of Orthodox Christianity.

olympie.fait: This is where the Olympic flame is still lit, a few months before the opening ceremony of the modern Games.

tour-blanche.fait: A former prison from the Ottoman period on the Thessaloniki waterfront, this tower has become the symbol of the city and a museum.

monemvasia.fait: This fortified town in the southern Peloponnese, on the coast of Laconia, is also known as Malvasia.

pasty.fait: This Cornish turnover is shaped without a mold: the dough is folded over the meat and vegetable filling, then baked in the oven.

scotch-egg.fait: This “Scottish-style egg” hides a hard- or soft-boiled egg in a ball of breaded and fried sausage meat; it is taken along on picnics.

stilton.fait: This English cheese comes in a blue and a white version; it is best enjoyed between October and March.

sporran.fait: This pouch worn on the belt replaces the pockets the kilt lacks; its name means “pouch” in Scottish Gaelic.

westminster.fait: Almost all English monarchs have been crowned here, and its Poets' Corner pays tribute to the kingdom's writers.

ile-skye.fait: This island off the west coast of Scotland is the largest and northernmost of the Inner Hebrides archipelago.

pesto.fait: Its name comes from the Italian pestare, “to pound”: this Ligurian basil sauce is prepared cold, without any cooking.

parmigiano.fait: The European courts ruled that its translation “parmesan” was also protected by this cheese's designation of origin.

panna-cotta.fait: Its name means “cooked cream”: this dessert born in Piedmont combines cream, milk, sugar and gelatin.

arancini.fait: These breaded and fried rice balls, a specialty of Sicily, are often filled with meat ragù and peas.

osso-buco.fait: Its name means “bone with a hole”: in this braised Milanese veal shank, the marrow is cooked and served in its bone.

prosecco.fait: This sparkling white wine, made mainly from the Glera grape, is produced in provinces of Veneto and Friuli-Venezia Giulia.

calcio-florentin.fait: Almost without rules, this Renaissance ball game pits two teams of 27 players against each other every June in Piazza Santa Croce.

trullo.fait: These dry-stone houses in Apulia served as seasonal shelters in the fields or as permanent homes for small farmers.

vesuve.fait: This volcano, which buried Pompeii, is the only one in mainland Europe to have erupted in the last hundred years.

pumpernickel.fait: This very dense, very dark rye bread is said to have fed the city of Osnabrück during a famine in the 15th century.

marche-noel-nuremberg.fait: The oldest record of this Christmas market is found on the bottom of a wooden box, which mentions it in 1628.

frauenkirche-dresde.fait: Rebuilt exactly as it was, this church mixes its old stones, darkened by time, with new light-colored stones.

hohenzollern.fait: Built as a family memorial, this castle was not lived in by any Hohenzollern before 1945.

cathedrale-berlin.fait: Despite its name, this Protestant church is not really a cathedral: it has never been the seat of a bishop.

rothenburg.fait: This small town in Bavaria has not been altered since the Thirty Years' War and has kept its entire fortified wall.

zollverein.fait: Thanks to its Bauhaus-style shaft, this mining site in Essen has a reputation as “the most beautiful coal mine in the world.”

croque-monsieur.fait: This hot sandwich was once cooked over a wood fire or in the fireplace, using a cast-iron press with long handles.

tarte-tatin.fait: This apple tart is baked with the pastry placed on top, then turned over onto a plate to be served warm.

roquefort.fait: This sheep's milk cheese ripens in caves crossed by fleurines, fissures in the rock that create a continuous draft.

coq-au-vin.fait: This marinated, then braised rooster can be cooked in red or white wine; it belongs to the cuisines from Auvergne to Alsace.

aligot.fait: This purée made with fresh tomme, born on the Aubrac plateau, spread all the way to Paris with the rural exodus of the bougnats.

kouign-amann.fait: In Breton, kouign means “cake” and amann “butter”: this laminated pastry is made with lightly salted butter and caramelized sugar.

canele.fait: This small Bordeaux cake flavored with rum and vanilla owes its thin caramelized crust to its mold, originally made of copper.

cognac.fait: This wine brandy has three authorized names: cognac, eau-de-vie de Cognac or eau-de-vie des Charentes.

savon-marseille.fait: This name is not a designation of origin but a manufacturing process: China and Turkey are now its largest producers.

carnaval-nice.fait: Every February, this festival takes over Nice for three weekends and attracts several hundred thousand participants.

louvre.fait: This royal palace became a museum during the Revolution, opening in August 1793 on the anniversary of the fall of the monarchy.

windsor.fait: Begun shortly after the conquest by William the Conqueror, this castle is the oldest continuously inhabited palace in Europe.

lascaux.fait: Damaged notably by fungi, this decorated cave has been closed to the public since 1963: visitors discover life-size replicas.

gorgonzola.fait: This blue-veined cow's milk cheese comes from Lombardy and Piedmont; it is best enjoyed from April to November.

casa-mila.fait: Ironically nicknamed “La Pedrera,” the stone quarry, this Gaudí house in Barcelona was at first the target of mockery from residents.

palais-vatican.fait: With about 1,400 rooms, it is the largest fully inhabited palace in the world; yet Pope Francis chose to live elsewhere.

iles-saint-paul.fait: According to tradition, Saint Paul may have been shipwrecked here; at low tide, the channel separating these two small islands can disappear.

olympieion.fait: Begun in the 6th century BC, this vast Corinthian temple in Athens was not completed until the reign of Hadrian.

place-dam.fait: It is known for short as “the Dam”: it is the main square of Amsterdam, at the heart of its historic center.

linderhof.fait: Built under Ludwig II of Bavaria near Oberammergau and Ettal Abbey, this royal palace is also described as a “royal villa.”

cathedrale-porto.fait: This 12th-century Romanesque cathedral is a fortress church; it is among the oldest monuments in Porto.

char-siu.fait: This glazed pork from Cantonese cuisine, roasted or barbecued, has a name that literally means “fork-roast.”

youtiao.fait: This long fried dough stick, whose name means “long fried piece,” is eaten at breakfast, dipped in soy milk or with congee.

mantou.fait: This steamed bun stays perfectly white because it has no crust; in China, bread holds a smaller place than in the West.

sauce-hoisin.fait: Its Cantonese name means “seafood,” but this sauce generally contains none: it was first used to accompany such dishes.

lamian.fait: These fresh wheat noodles are not cut: the cook stretches them by hand, hence their name, which means “pulled noodles.”

porc-dongpo.fait: This pork belly dish is named after the poet Su Dongpo; when well prepared, after about three hours of cooking, it melts in the mouth.

zhajiangmian.fait: These wheat noodles owe their name to a fermented black soybean sauce; the dish was exported to Korea and Japan under other names.

niangao.fait: This rice cake is eaten at New Year: its name sounds like the word “high,” and it expresses the wish to rise higher year after year.

the-jasmin.fait: This green or white tea, to which jasmine flowers are added, is the most popular scented tea in China and is exported in large quantities.

da-hong-pao.fait: According to legend, a Ming emperor had the bushes whose tea had cured his mother dressed in great red robes, hence the name “Big Red Robe.”

mi-automne.fait: This festival, also called the “Moon Festival” or the “Night of the Fifteenth,” is above all a day of reunion when the whole family gathers.

gongfu-cha.fait: This method of preparing tea is not a ceremony but a convivial art, with little in common with the Japanese tea ceremony.

qi-gong.fait: This form of exercise combines slow movements, breathing and concentration; its name literally means “mastery of the breath.”

kunqu.fait: Also called “Kunshan opera,” it is the oldest form of Chinese opera still performed on stage today.

suona.fait: This double-reed instrument, very common in Chinese folk music, has also reached Cuba, where it is called the “Chinese trumpet.”

yangqin.fait: This dulcimer, whose strings are struck with bamboo hammers, may have arrived via the Silk Road, or by sea with missionaries.

hulusi.fait: This wind instrument of the Dai minority combines a gourd and bamboo pipes; its sound is reminiscent of a clarinet.

ruan-luth.fait: This long-necked Chinese lute is also nicknamed the “moon guitar” and is found, under other names, throughout Southeast Asia.

gaiwan.fait: This Chinese lidded cup is used both to steep tea and to drink it; it is also called zhong.

dougong.fait: These interlocking wooden brackets were used to fix roofs onto columns, before also becoming an ornament of Chinese architecture.

sancai.fait: The name of this ceramic means “three colors,” those of the glazes of its decoration, even though it sometimes has more.

paifang.fait: This gateway of classical Chinese architecture, also called pailou, has also found its place in Korea, Japan and Vietnam.

yaodong.fait: These “cave dwellings” of the Loess Plateau, in northern China, are sometimes dug directly into the loess, under a semicircular vault.

mont-putuo.fait: Located on an island, this mountain is the Chinese center of the cult of Guanyin and takes its name from Mount Potala, the mythical residence of this bodhisattva.

mont-lu.fait: Between the Yangtze and Poyang Lake, this mountain has mattered as much for Buddhism as for Chinese painting and poetry.

monts-wudang.fait: These mountains with their many Taoist monasteries are considered one of the cradles of the internal martial arts, such as taijiquan.

mont-song.fait: In Taoism, this mountain symbolizes the Earth, hence its status as the Central Mountain; it is also home to the Shaolin Monastery.

mont-sanqing.fait: This Taoist mountain in Jiangxi owes its name, “mountains of the three purities,” to the three heavens of the Taoist religion.

mont-jiuhua.fait: This mountain with 99 peaks, a sacred mountain of Chinese Buddhism, is dedicated to the bodhisattva Ksitigarbha and renowned for its ancient temples.

mont-qingcheng.fait: According to Taoist mythology, it was on this mountain that the Yellow Emperor received the teachings of Ning Fengzhi.

temple-cheval-blanc.fait: According to tradition, this monastery stands on the spot where the horse carrying the first Buddhist sutras from present-day Afghanistan came to a halt.

huanglong.fait: Calcite deposits give its pools exceptional colors, hence their nickname of “five-colored ponds.”

saut-du-tigre.fait: According to legend, a tiger fleeing a hunter leaped across this canyon at its narrowest point, hence its name.

lac-qinghai.fait: This lake, the largest in China, gave its name to Qinghai Province; the name literally means “blue sea.”

taklamakan.fait: Nicknamed the “sea of death,” this desert bears a name of uncertain origin, said to mean “place of ruins” or “abandoned place.”

zhouzhuang.fait: With its many canals, this town between Shanghai and Suzhou is one of those nicknamed the “Venice of the Far East.”

wuzhen.fait: Built entirely around canals, this small town lives mainly from crafts: weaving, wood carving and rice liquor distilling.

jardins-suzhou.fait: Laid out over several centuries in the historic city of Suzhou, these gardens are masterpieces of the Chinese art of garden design.

chengde.fait: The Qing emperors came here to escape the heat of Beijing: it is three degrees cooler than in the city of Chengde itself.

foret-steles.fait: This museum in Xi'an owes its name “forest of steles” to the very large number of steles it gathers, in a former Confucian temple.

remparts-xian.fait: Built in the 14th century, these ramparts are among the oldest and best-preserved city walls in China.

gulangyu.fait: This small island is nicknamed “piano island,” because many pianos are placed in its gardens and parks to be played in public.

dujiangyan.fait: Its irrigation system, designed in the 3rd century BC against flooding, has operated without interruption since it was built.

parc-beihai.fait: This imperial garden in Beijing, more than 1,000 years old, is laid out around a lake whose island bears a white stupa.

parc-jingshan.fait: Its hill is artificial: it was created along with the Forbidden City so that, according to feng shui, the city would lie south of a mountain.

temple-confucius-qufu.fait: In the city of Qufu, this temple is the first and most important of all the temples dedicated to Confucius.

qianmen.fait: This gate in Beijing's old city wall, the tallest in the city, is one of the few not destroyed in the 1950s.

sanxingdui.fait: The objects from this site have a style completely different from Chinese art of the same period, and their culture disappeared suddenly, for unknown reasons.

karaage.fait: This fried dish, most often chicken, is made with pieces first marinated in soy sauce, garlic and ginger.

tamagoyaki.fait: This sweet and savory omelet is cooked in a rectangular pan, rolled layer by layer, then cut into slices.

nikujaga.fait: Its name means “meat-potato”: this dish simmered in a sweet soy broth was invented in the late 19th century.

katsudon.fait: Japanese students eat it the night before an exam, because “katsu” also evokes the verb meaning “to win” or “to succeed.”

gyudon.fait: Its name simply means “beef bowl”: hot rice topped with strips of beef, onion and sometimes egg.

oyakodon.fait: Its name means “parent and child,” because this rice bowl brings together chicken, the “parent,” and eggs, its “children.”

tsukemono.fait: These foods steeped in brine or vinegar accompany rice, are nibbled with a drink and even appear on the menu of the tea ceremony.

umeboshi.fait: These very sour salted plums are naturally orange-brown: their raspberry red often comes from shiso leaves.

kaiseki.fait: This meal of small dishes served together also refers to the simple meal the host offers guests before the tea ceremony.

yakisoba.fait: These noodles stir-fried in yakisoba sauce are a variant of ramen; in Cantonese, this type of dish is called chow mein.

dango.fait: These glutinous rice dough dumplings are often eaten on a skewer with green tea, and change in flavor and shape with the seasons.

daifuku.fait: Its name means “great luck”: this soft ball of glutinous rice hides a sweet filling, often red bean paste.

yokan.fait: This red bean paste set with agar-agar resembles a fruit jelly; its water-based version is eaten cold in summer.

senbei.fait: These glutinous rice crackers, usually savory and coated in soy sauce, are often offered to guests with green tea.

kakigori.fait: This dessert is shaved ice drizzled with green tea, fruit or sesame syrup, sometimes with condensed milk or azuki beans.

anpan.fait: The name of this sweet roll comes from anko, the sweet azuki bean paste that fills it, as the diminutive “anko-pan” indicates.

omurice.fait: Its name combines “omelette” and “rice”: this omelet filled with ketchup fried rice was born from adapting Western recipes.

miso.fait: This paste of soybeans, rice or barley and salt can ferment from a few weeks to three years, depending on the variety.

genmaicha.fait: The name of this popular green tea means “brown rice tea”: it is mixed with roasted rice grains.

sencha.fait: The most common tea in Japan, this green tea, whose name means “infused tea,” can also be drunk cold in summer.

obon.fait: During this festival of the ancestors that came from China, city dwellers return to their hometowns to tend the family graves.

shichigosan.fait: Its name, “Seven-Five-Three,” refers to the ages of the children this rite of passage celebrates every year in November.

setsubun.fait: Also called the “bean-throwing festival,” this festival celebrates the arrival of spring according to the old lunar calendar.

yuki-matsuri.fait: Every year in early February, Sapporo displays snow sculptures; one of the festival sites is even a Self-Defense Forces base.

hadaka-matsuri.fait: In this “naked festival,” people are almost never naked: participants wear a simple loincloth, the fundoshi, and remain dressed inside the shrines.

kyudo.fait: In this form of archery, hitting the target is merely the result of a balanced body and mind; the target itself is a sheet of paper.

iaido.fait: This martial art rests on a single gesture: drawing the sword and striking in the same movement, before the opponent can act.

jujutsu.fait: These combat techniques from the Edo period taught samurai to defend themselves when they found themselves unarmed, in a duel or on the battlefield.

buto.fait: This “dance of the dark body” is often performed with the body almost naked, painted white, the head shaved, with extremely slow movements.

rakugo.fait: The name of this comic performance means “story with a punchline”; the genre was born at the beginning of the Edo period.

karaoke.fait: This entertainment, whose name comes from the Japanese カラオケ, consists of singing along to lyrics displayed on a screen.

kamishibai.fait: This traveling “paper theater” told stories by showing a succession of illustrations; the superhero Ōgon Bat was born there.

sento.fait: Some Japanese people visit these public baths for a social reason: in their view, physical intimacy allows emotional intimacy.

hotel-capsule.fait: In these hotels, the room is reduced to a simple bed pod: everything is designed to take up as little space as possible.

izakaya.fait: These pubs can sometimes be recognized by the red paper lanterns hanging at the entrance, hence their nickname akachōchin, “red lantern.”

kaiten-zushi.fait: In these restaurants, sushi passes by on a conveyor belt, and the bill is calculated according to the number and type of plates stacked up.

netsuke.fait: This clothing accessory was used to secure sagemono, “hanging objects”; its name combines the words “root” and “attach.”

shogi.fait: In this cousin of chess, captured pieces can be put back into play: their side is therefore shown by their orientation, not their color.

hanafuda.fait: These flower cards, inspired by those of Portuguese missionaries, were created to get around the ban on foreign games and gambling.

omikuji.fait: At shrines and temples, people draw these paper strips bearing a prediction at random, hence their name, “sacred lottery.”

ema-plaquette.fait: Worshippers write a wish on these wooden plaques, then hang them near the shrine so that the kami, the gods, can read it.

teru-teru-bozu.fait: This white doll is hung in the window to drive away the rain; in a forgotten verse of the nursery rhyme, it is threatened with losing its head.

shoji.fait: These translucent paper panels slide instead of swinging, which saves the space a hinged door would require.

kotatsu.fait: This low table covered with a futon and heated from below was the most common form of heating in Japan before reversible air conditioners.

futon.fait: This Japanese bed was supposedly not born in Japan: it is said to have come from India, then China, before being imported to the archipelago.

tabi.fait: These socks separate the big toe from the others so they can be worn with geta or zōri; their thick sole also lets them serve as slippers.

hakama.fait: These wide pants with seven pleats were worn by nobles and samurai; today, both men and women wear them.

haniwa.fait: These terracotta figures, whose name means “terracotta cylinders,” have been found on many mound tombs of the Kofun period.

dogu.fait: These terracotta figurines sometimes have “coffee bean” or “snow goggle” eyes; their exact use remains unknown.

washi.fait: This handmade paper is made from long interwoven fibers of paper mulberry bark, which makes it light, flexible and strong at the same time.

chateau-osaka.fait: This castle was at the heart of one of the last great revolts against the Tokugawa, crushed during the sieges of Osaka in the early 17th century.

chateau-nijo.fait: Tokugawa Ieyasu had this Kyoto castle built in 1603; its palaces and gardens are protected by concentric rings of fortifications.

kasuga-taisha.fait: More than a thousand stone lanterns line the path to this shrine in Nara, which crosses a park where tame deer roam freely.

mont-koya.fait: This mountainous area southeast of Osaka gave its name to an entire complex of 117 Buddhist temples.

chateau-shuri.fait: This castle in Naha was the residence of the kings of Ryukyu; a fire destroyed a very large part of it in 2019.

mont-aso.fait: This volcano, the largest in Japan, is also one of the most active; its caldera is among the largest in the world.

akihabara.fait: This Tokyo district, famous for its electronics shops and manga, is known around the world as “Electric Town.”

kyoto-gosho.fait: The emperors lived in this Kyoto palace until 1868, when Tokyo became the capital; it is now only a secondary residence.

kofuku-ji.fait: This temple in Nara belonged to the Fujiwara family; with Enryaku-ji, it formed the pair of the most powerful temples of the Heian era.

enryaku-ji.fait: This monastery on Mount Hiei is the seat of Tendai Buddhism, a school that gave rise to Pure Land, Zen and Nichiren Buddhism.

izumo-taisha.fait: According to legend, the kami Ōkuninushi gave up his land in exchange for this shrine, a palace as vast as that of the heavenly gods.

sundubu.fait: This soft tofu stew cooks directly in its thick porcelain or stone dish and arrives boiling, sometimes topped with a raw egg.

kimchi-jjigae.fait: This kimchi-based stew, with pork or seafood and diced tofu, is one of the most common in Korean cuisine.

jajangmyeon.fait: These noodles in black soybean sauce were invented in Incheon by Chinese immigrants; they are often eaten to celebrate a graduation.

yakgwa.fait: This flower-shaped cookie, made with honey, sesame oil and wheat flour, has gone from being a dessert to a confection.

haejangguk.fait: The name of these soups means “soup to chase away a hangover”; one of their variants contains slices of beef blood.

hangwa.fait: These traditional confections were served at ancestral rites and weddings; today they can be found in cafés and tea rooms.

ssam.fait: The name of this dish means “wrapped”: meat, often pork, is wrapped in a leaf of lettuce, cabbage or perilla.

yukhoe.fait: This raw chopped beef, the Korean version of steak tartare, is seasoned with soy sauce, sesame oil and julienned Korean pear.

beondegi.fait: This popular snack consists of boiled or steamed silkworm pupae; it can even be found canned in grocery stores.

daeboreum.fait: The name of this festival means “great full moon”: it celebrates the first full moon of the new year in the lunar calendar.

yeondeunghoe.fait: In South Korea, this lantern festival, Yeondeunghoe, is held to celebrate the Buddha's birthday.

talchum.fait: In this traditional dance, each dancer wears a mask; it has its origins in Korean shamanism.

pungmul.fait: This tradition of drumming, dance and song is rooted in shamanism and is linked to nongak, the “farmers' music.”

buchaechum.fait: In this dance, women handle fans painted with peonies to depict birds, flowers, butterflies and waves.

pc-bang.fait: These networked video game rooms are unique to South Korea; they took off with the release of the game StarCraft.

janggi.fait: This cousin of Chinese chess is played without the river that divides the board; professional games often exceed 150 moves.

piri.fait: This double-reed instrument with a cylindrical bore is played in court music as well as in religious and folk music.

danso.fait: This short bamboo flute is to South Korea what the recorder is to Europe: the instrument used to learn music at school.

geobukseon.fait: This warship fought the Japanese during the Imjin War; forgotten, it was rediscovered and improved by Admiral Yi Sun-sin.

myeongdong.fait: The name of this Seoul district means “bright neighborhood”; it is mainly a shopping and tourist area, with its cathedral.

insadong.fait: This Seoul district was once the largest market for antiques and artworks in Korea; its alleys lead to galleries and tea rooms.

haedong-yonggungsa.fait: This Buddhist temple in Busan, South Korea, has one distinctive feature: it stands by the sea.

hwaeomsa.fait: Among the national treasures of this Jirisan temple is an ancient stone pagoda supported by four stone lions.

beopjusa.fait: This temple, one of the main temples of the Jogye Order, has authority over twenty-seven smaller temples; it lies at the heart of Mount Soknisan.

jirisan.fait: This mountain is home to seven major Buddhist temples, including Hwaeomsa, the largest, which holds many national treasures.

gyeonghuigung.fait: This royal palace in Seoul was largely destroyed during the Japanese occupation to make way for a school, then rebuilt from 1987 onward.

seowon.fait: These private academies of the Joseon era were part Confucian temple and part school, and carried weight even in court struggles.

gwanghwamun.fait: This gate is the main entrance to Gyeongbokgung Palace, in the heart of Seoul, in the Jongno-gu district.

heunginjimun.fait: This great East Gate of Seoul, known as Dongdaemun, gave its name to a market, a subway station and a district in which it does not stand.

odaesan.fait: The name of this mountain means “mountain of the five plains,” after the high plateaus lying between its peaks.

yatga.fait: This plucked zither of Mongolian music is close to the Chinese guzheng, the Korean gayageum and the Japanese koto.

orkhon-inscriptions.fait: Standing in Mongolia, these steles carved in Old Turkic and Chinese tell of the legendary origins of the Turks and the golden age of their history.

otgontenger.fait: This peak is the only one in the Khangai Mountains to bear a glacier, and its south face is the largest granite cliff in Mongolia.

dak-galbi.fait: This chicken stir-fried in gochujang was born in the 1960s as a cheap side dish to go with drinks in the taverns of Chuncheon.

sundae-boudin.fait: This sausage of pig intestines stuffed with noodles, blood and glutinous rice is a popular street food; in Seoul, a whole neighborhood is devoted to it.

mandu.fait: These dumplings long belonged to royal court cuisine; today they can be found even in snack bars and supermarkets.

jeon-galette.fait: Meat, seafood, vegetables or mushrooms are coated in pancake batter and then cooked in oil, to be served as a side dish.

tteokguk.fait: This soup is eaten at New Year: it is said to bring luck all year long and to add a year of life expectancy to whoever eats it.

miyeok-guk.fait: This seaweed soup is eaten at birthday breakfasts, in honor of the mother, and for several months after giving birth.

patjuk.fait: This red bean porridge is eaten at the winter solstice: its red color was believed to drive away evil spirits.

hoe-poisson-cru.fait: Meat, fish or seafood are eaten raw here, or barely blanched; a Korean encyclopedia already mentioned it in 1614.

doljanchi.fait: This celebration marks a child's first birthday; the child wears a hanbok and a traditional hat that differs for girls and boys.

cheoyongmu.fait: This dance was once performed at court; today it is staged in theaters, with a name and costumes of symbolic origins.

buncheong.fait: This stoneware ceramic was a Korean tradition for only about two centuries, from the mid-14th to the mid-16th century.

jarre-de-lune.fait: This pottery was used to store rice, soy sauce or alcohol; its asymmetry was seen as the mark of nature, which man must not hinder.

hwacha.fait: This ancestor of the multiple rocket launcher, mounted on a cart, allowed a single man to carry about 100 rockets into battle.

dolmens-gochang.fait: Korea has nearly 40% of the world's dolmens, and most of them are grouped at these three burial sites.

village-folklorique-yongin.fait: This typical Joseon-era village did not grow up on the spot: it was created by moving and restoring about 270 houses.

mireuksa.fait: This temple dedicated to the Buddha of the future was the largest in the kingdom of Baekje; only two pagodas remain, one of which is a reconstruction.

deel.fait: This traditional garment changes cut and colors according to ethnic group or tribe, and is worn with a hat and a belt of silk or leather.

lac-khar-us.fait: Its Mongolian name means “black water lake”; it lies in western Mongolia, near Jargalant Khairkhan.

tuul.fait: This river, considered sacred in Mongolia, flows down from the Khentii Mountains and crosses the capital, Ulaanbaatar.

cuanza.fait: This Angolan river, which flows into the Atlantic, also gave its name to the country's national currency, the kwanza.

quicama.fait: It is the only national park in Angola that still functions: all the others suffered heavy damage during the civil war.

arly.fait: Often called a national park, this protected area is in fact a total wildlife reserve, recognized as a World Heritage Site and a biosphere reserve.

karfiguela.fait: Also called the Banfora Falls, these waterfalls are staggered along the Comoé River, in southwestern Burkina Faso.

lac-bam.fait: Considered the country's largest natural reservoir of surface water, this lake is home to Nile crocodiles, but it is gradually drying up.

mare-oursi.fait: This Sahelian wetland in northern Burkina Faso is listed among the Ramsar sites of international importance for its biodiversity.

cathedrale-ouaga.fait: This Ouagadougou cathedral blends European Romanesque architecture with the traditional buildings of West Africa.

karera.fait: These waterfalls do not form a single fall: they split into six branches that descend over several tiers.

ruvubu.fait: This national park straddles four provinces of Burundi: Karuzi, Muyinga, Ruyigi and Cankuzo.

pendjari.fait: It is described as the most beautiful and most important wildlife park in West Africa; it borders Burkina Faso.

moremi.fait: This protected area is a “game reserve” and not a national park, because members of the BaSarwa and Bushman tribes were living there when it was created.

nxai.fait: This park includes fossil salt pans that turn into grassland in the rainy season, as well as the Baines' Baobabs site.

boyoma.fait: On the last cataract, Wagenia fishermen hang large conical traps from wooden scaffolds anchored in the rock.

maiko.fait: This isolated forest is home to three animals found only in the country: the okapi, the Congo peafowl and the eastern lowland gorilla.

okapis.fait: This reserve in the Ituri Forest is home to about 5,000 okapis; nomadic Mbuti Pygmies and Efe hunters also live there.

salonga.fait: This park, the largest in the DRC, can only be reached by water; it was created mainly to save the bonobo and the forest elephant.

inga.fait: These two hydroelectric dams were built on the Congo River itself, near the city of Matadi.

banco.fait: This primary tropical forest grows right in the heart of Abidjan; its name comes from the Ebrié word “Gbancô,” “source of refreshing water.”

tai.fait: This park in western Ivory Coast contains one of the last primary forests in Africa, home in particular to pygmy hippopotamuses.

korup.fait: This park in southwestern Cameroon shares a border with Cross River National Park, located on the other side, in Nigeria.

waza.fait: Near Lake Chad, this park was first a hunting reserve, called Zina-Waza, before being granted national park status.

bikutsi.fait: This traditional music and dance, sometimes called tipi, are specific to the Beti ethnic group and were born in the Centre provinces.

boa-vista.fait: The name of this island means “beautiful view” in Portuguese; it is the third largest island in the Cape Verde archipelago.

brava.fait: This island, the smallest inhabited one in Cape Verde, was first called São João, because it was discovered on June 24, Saint John's Day.

ile-sal.fait: The name of this island in the Cape Verde archipelago means “salt” in Portuguese, because of the Pedra de Lume mines.

santo-antao.fait: A mountain range long considered impassable cuts this island in two: a green north farmed in terraces, and a stony, desert-like south.

sao-vicente.fait: This island is the homeland of the singer Cesária Évora, after whom the island's international airport is now named.

foret-day.fait: This forest is home to the Djibouti francolin, a critically endangered bird and the only one endemic to the country.

tella.fait: This traditional beer, most often made from teff or barley, is flavored with gesho leaves, a kind of local hops.

erta-ale.fait: The name of this volcano means “smoking mountain” in Afar, and it is one of three in the world to hold a permanent lava lake.

lac-tana.fait: This lake, the largest in Ethiopia, dates back to the Tertiary period and the uplift of the Arabian-Ethiopian Shield.

nil-bleu.fait: In Amharic, these waterfalls on the Blue Nile are called Tis Abay, which means “great smoke.”

obelisque-aksoum.fait: These 4th-century steles are wrongly called “obelisks”: they are Aksumite steles, next to a necropolis.

mitmita.fait: This reddish-orange spice blend, based on pili-pili chili, is used to season ketfo, a dish of raw beef.

ivindo.fait: This park, crossed by the equator, contains Langoué Bai, a clearing where the highest concentration of gorillas in Gabon was found.

loango-np.fait: This coastal park includes the Iguéla Lagoon, one of the only lagoons in Central Africa located entirely within a protected area.

lope.fait: This park is listed both for its forest and for the remains of past cultures it preserves: it is a “mixed” World Heritage Site.

akosombo.fait: This dam created Lake Volta, the largest artificial lake in the world; it was first meant to power the aluminum industry.

batiments-ashanti.fait: These huts of wood, thatch and earth, inherited from the height of the Ashanti in the 18th century, are slowly deteriorating because of the climate.

chateau-osu.fait: This fort in Accra, also called Christiansborg, was built in 1652 on behalf of the Swedes, on Ga territory.

tabouret-or.fait: According to legend, this throne came down from the sky onto the knees of the first Ashanti king; it is said to hold the spirit of the whole people.

dame-mali.fait: This mountain in Guinea is where the highest point of the entire Fouta Djallon massif is found.

cathedrale-malabo.fait: The country's largest Christian church took nearly twenty years to rise from the ground, funded by parishioners, merchants and Spain.

baringo.fait: This Great Rift Valley lake, the northernmost after Lake Turkana, is expanding rapidly and is threatened by global warming.

bogoria.fait: This saline soda lake regularly hosts one of the largest colonies of lesser flamingos in the world.

hells-gate.fait: This park owes its name to a narrow break in the cliffs, named this way by the explorers Fisher and Thomson in 1883.

kaya.fait: These forests hide ancient fortified villages, abandoned in the 20th century and revered today as the dwellings of the Mijikenda ancestors.

nairobi-np.fait: Right next to the capital, this park is fenced on three sides: the south remains open to let migrating wildlife through.

naivasha.fait: The name of this freshwater lake in the Great Rift comes from the Maa Nai'posha, which means “rough water.”

tsavo-est.fait: Opened in 1948, this park is one of the oldest in Kenya; a road and a railway cut it into two sections, east and west.

gedi.fait: Abandoned in the early 17th century, this Swahili town has yielded imported pottery, beads and coins, proof of its commercial prosperity.

andasibe.fait: These primary forests of eastern Madagascar, once called the Périnet reserve, are home to large populations of lemurs, including the indri.

ankarana.fait: In Malagasy, “tsingy” means “to walk on tiptoe,” so sharp are these rocks; Antakarana tombs occupy the caves.

isalo.fait: Erosion has carved this sandstone massif into canyons and peaks; it is the national park in Madagascar most visited by foreign tourists.

masoala.fait: According to a botanist filmed by Yann Arthus-Bertrand, this rainforest is so dense that 90% of the light never reaches the ground.

montagne-ambre.fait: During colonization, this park was private property: its owners planted Chilean araucarias and lemon-scented eucalyptus there.

nosy-boraha.fait: Formerly named Nosy-Ibrahim, this island is known for the humpback whales that gather there and for its romantic history.

tritriva.fait: This lake of volcanic origin occupies the very summit of Mount Tritriva; its opaque green waters give off a strange impression.

ambohimanga.fait: One of the twelve sacred hills of Imerina, this fortified village contains tombs of Merina kings and still welcomes pilgrims.

moraingy.fait: This bare-knuckle Malagasy boxing allows kicks, knee strikes, elbow strikes and sometimes headbutts, as well as grappling.

hombori.fait: This rocky massif, which extends the Bandiagara Escarpment, bears Hombori Tondo, the highest peak in Mali.

sankore.fait: Built of banco in 1325, this Timbuktu mosque is also a university that has trained generations of Muslim scholars.

kanaga.fait: This Dogon mask is worn during the dama, the ceremonies that end the mourning period in the cult of the dead, by members of the Awa society.

grand-bassin.fait: This lake nestled in an old crater is the most sacred Hindu site in Mauritius; temples dedicated to Shiva, Hanuman or Ganesh line its shores.

le-pouce.fait: This mountain owes its name to its thumb-shaped silhouette; from its summit, the view opens onto the north of Mauritius and its islets.

trou-aux-cerfs.fait: This volcanic crater is not out in the wild: it lies within the limits of a town in Mauritius, Curepipe.

chongoni.fait: These 127 sites painted on granite combine works by Batwa hunter-gatherers with more recent ones by Chewa farmers.

kasungu.fait: The second largest park in Malawi, it runs along the Zambian border and usually closes in March, during the rainy season.

lac-malombe.fait: This small Great Rift lake receives the river flowing out of Lake Malawi, then its waters join the Zambezi and end up in the Indian Ocean.

liwonde.fait: An electric fence surrounds this park, managed by the organization African Parks, to limit conflicts between people and wildlife.

bazaruto.fait: This archipelago is home to the last population of dugongs on the African coast, and crocodiles live in the lakes of its two large islands.

ponta-ouro.fait: This seaside resort owes its name, “the golden point,” to a cape whose beaches made its reputation; dolphins can be seen there.

quirimbas.fait: This archipelago has 32 islands, often uninhabited and surrounded by mangroves; a national park protects most of them.

cahora-bassa.fait: Commissioned shortly after independence, this dam on the Zambezi feeds one of the most powerful hydroelectric plants in Africa.

cote-squelettes.fait: Its name is sometimes used for the whole coast of the Namib Desert, but it only covers the north of the Namibian coastline, up to Angola.

deadvlei.fait: This white clay pan lies in the Namib Desert, very close to the famous Sossusvlei salt pan.

spitzkoppe.fait: Nicknamed the “Matterhorn of Namibia,” this group of granite peaks towers over perfectly flat terrain; Bushman paintings adorn its rocks.

twyfelfontein.fait: This name means “the spring of doubt”; more than 2,500 rock engravings were created there to perform shamanic rituals.

waterberg.fait: This high, hard-to-reach plateau towers over the plains of the Kalahari, in central Namibia; a national park protects it.

alte-feste.fait: Its German name means “old fortress”: this fort in central Windhoek, the Namibian capital, now houses a museum.

tintenpalast.fait: Its German name means “ink palace”; built in the days of the German colony, it now houses both chambers of Parliament.

air.fait: This vast Saharan plateau is mostly made up of flat expanses, dotted with granite peaks sometimes topped by volcanic structures.

air-tenere.fait: These reserves bring together the Aïr Mountains, part of the Ténéré Desert and the addax sanctuary, a separate protected area.

djado.fait: The cave paintings of this plateau often show large mammals long gone from the region; forts lie abandoned there.

sukur.fait: The chief's palace, the terraced fields and the village of this landscape have remained unchanged for centuries; access is nearly impassable.

yankari.fait: Caves and old iron-smelting furnaces show that this park, without a permanent village for more than a century, was once inhabited.

afang.fait: This vegetable soup comes from the Ibibio people of southern Nigeria, who share it with their neighbors, the Efik people of Calabar.

lac-burera.fait: This lake drains into its twin, Lake Ruhondo, through a short torrent with such a steep drop that a hydroelectric plant was built on it.

ile-denis.fait: This private island, equipped with an airstrip, has received Seychelles fodies and warblers brought from other islands to protect them.

mahe.fait: This island is the main one of the Inner Islands of the Seychelles archipelago; it is home to the country's capital, Victoria.

silhouette.fait: Younger than its granite neighbors, this island is made of volcanic rock; it is named after Étienne de Silhouette, the king's commissioner.

carabane.fait: On this island in Casamance, the Jola live by the rhythm of rice more than of fishing; it was the first French colonial trading post in the region.

delta-saloum.fait: This delta, where the Saloum flows into the Atlantic, also preserves shell middens, heaps of shells that form a historic site.

niokolo-koba.fait: This national park in southeastern Senegal, near the Guinean border, is served by a simple dirt airstrip.

bom-bom.fait: This islet, one of the smallest in the São Tomé and Príncipe archipelago, lies north of the island of Príncipe, in the Gulf of Guinea.

emi-koussi.fait: This extinct volcano in the Tibesti Mountains is the highest point in Chad, and also in the entire Sahara.

lac-fitri.fait: This lake in the Sahelian zone, one of the main bodies of water in Chad, matters as much to waterbirds as to the people living on its shores.

fazao.fait: It is the largest of Togo's three national parks; it adjoins Kyabobo National Park, located in Ghana.

keran.fait: Listed as a Ramsar site, this park forms, together with the Oti-Mandouri reserve, a biosphere reserve recognized by UNESCO.

gombe.fait: Also called Gombe Stream National Park, this park stretches along the Tanzanian shore of Lake Tanganyika, in East Africa.

jozani.fait: The only national park in Zanzibar, this reserve is home to a large population of red colobus, a monkey that has become the emblem of its protection.

mafia.fait: This island, the main one of the Mafia archipelago in the Indian Ocean, forms one of the six districts of the Pwani Region.

mont-meru.fait: This horseshoe-shaped volcano, still considered active, bears an almost forgotten official name, “Socialist Peak,” inherited from the socialist period.

ol-doinyo.fait: The only active volcano in Tanzania, this “Mountain of God” in the Maa language is the sacred mountain of the Maasai.

pemba.fait: Its Arabic name means “the green island”; it is one of the three islands of the Zanzibar archipelago, off the Tanzanian coast.

ruaha.fait: The second largest park in Tanzania after the Serengeti, it is named after the Ruaha River, which flows through it.

selous.fait: Only a small northern part of this reserve is open to photo safaris: all the rest is reserved for hunting by specialized companies.

tarangire.fait: This park, one of the most important in northern Tanzania, is named after the Tarangire River, which flows through it.

kazinga.fait: This natural waterway links Lake Edward to Lake George and is home to one of the largest concentrations of hippos, along with many Nile crocodiles.

lac-kyoga.fait: The Victoria Nile flows through this shallow lake between Lake Victoria and Lake Albert; yet it is not itself counted among the Great Lakes.

mgahinga.fait: This park in southwestern Uganda, near Kisoro, bears in its official name the animals it notably protects: mountain gorillas.

queen-elizabeth.fait: This park, one of the largest in Uganda, is not only a national park: UNESCO has also recognized it as a biosphere reserve.

ssese.fait: This lake archipelago in Lake Victoria has more than 80 islands, divided into two groups: that of Bugala, the largest, and that of Koome.

boulders-beach.fait: On this beach near Cape Town, you can swim next to a colony of penguins, which boardwalks let you watch from above.

kirstenbosch.fait: This botanical garden in the suburbs of Cape Town owes its worldwide fame as much to its collections as to its exceptional setting.

union-buildings.fait: Their name recalls the Union of South Africa, but was also meant to symbolize the union of a once-divided people; the president has his offices there.

gatsby-sandwich.fait: This sandwich born in Cape Town is a bread roll filled with fries and sauces, usually so big that it is shared among several people.

malva-pudding.fait: A cream sauce is poured over this apricot dessert while it is still hot, and it is then often served with cold custard.

sosatie.fait: The name of these lamb skewers comes from two Cape Malay words: sate, “skewered meat,” and saus, “spicy sauce.”

umngqusho.fait: This Xhosa dish of corn and beans, adopted throughout the country, was apparently one of Nelson Mandela's favorite dishes.

vetkoek.fait: This fried dough bread, called igwinya in Xhosa and Zulu, resembles both the Antillean bokit and the Dutch oliebol.

gonarezhou.fait: The name of this park comes from Shona and translates as “the place of elephants”; it is Zimbabwe's second game reserve.

inyangani.fait: This summit, the highest in Zimbabwe, is the source of several rivers, including the Pungue, in the heart of Nyanga National Park.

grand-zimbabwe.fait: The country takes its name from this ruined city: in Shona, “Zimbabwe” means “the great house made of stones.”

grand-central.fait: This Manhattan station no longer sees long-distance trains: it serves local trains and remains a major subway station.

rockefeller-center.fait: This New York commercial complex, built by the family whose name it bears, comprises nineteen buildings.

jefferson-memorial.fait: This Washington monument dedicated to Thomas Jefferson adopts the neoclassical style, with a white dome and portico.

mont-st-helens.fait: During its 1980 eruption, a huge landslide carried away its summit, which was replaced by a horseshoe-shaped crater.

bryce-canyon.fait: Despite its name, it is not a canyon but a natural amphitheater, bristling with hoodoos sculpted by erosion.

horseshoe-bend.fait: This meander of the Colorado, little known before the 2010s, became so popular thanks to Instagram that it had to be developed for tourists.

waikiki.fait: Its name means “spouting fresh water” in Hawaiian; on the beach, the statue of the surfer Duke Kahanamoku is always covered in flowers.

graceland.fait: Elvis Presley's former residence in Memphis, this house now serves as both a museum and a mausoleum.

calakmul.fait: This Maya city, seat of the “Kingdom of the Snake,” was inhabited for more than a millennium before being swallowed up by the jungle.

paricutin.fait: This volcano was born in 1943; the bell tower of the old village of San Juan Parangaricutiro still rises from its lava flows.

naica-2.fait: This cave hides giant selenite crystals, a variety of gypsum; it connects to a mine that also extracts silver.

oratoire-st-joseph.fait: Its cross is the highest point in Montreal; it is the largest church in Canada and the most important place of pilgrimage dedicated to Saint Joseph.

citadelle-quebec.fait: This fort is an official residence of the King of Canada; along with Campeche, Quebec City is the only city in North America to have kept its entire city wall.

baie-fundy.fait: In the days of Acadia and New France, this arm of the sea between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia was called the Baie Française.

head-smashed-in.fait: Its English name literally means “smashed head”; this site in Alberta is an open-air museum of Native American culture.

mont-royal.fait: This hill overlooking Montreal is one of the ten Monteregian Hills in the southwest of the province of Quebec.

cathedrale-havane.fait: This 18th-century Baroque cathedral, in the old town of Havana, is one of the oldest cathedrals in the Americas.

pic-turquino.fait: At the summit of Cuba's highest point, a bust of the national hero José Martí, erected in 1953, draws a kind of pilgrimage.

ile-a-vache.fait: This island in the Caribbean Sea, off the town of Les Cayes, forms a commune of Haiti in the Sud department.

ile-gonave.fait: Formerly called Gonaïve Island, this Caribbean island belonging to Haiti lies in the gulf that bears the same name.

cayemites.fait: These two islands form a commune of Haiti; a species of amphisbaenian, Amphisbaena caudalis, lives on Grande Cayemite.

samana.fait: When Europeans discovered it in the 15th century, this peninsula was still an island that could be sailed around by boat to the west.

ile-beata.fait: This island, near Cape Beata, the southernmost point of Hispaniola, is part of Jaragua National Park.

palais-national-do.fait: This building in Santo Domingo houses the offices of the executive branch: the presidency and vice presidency of the Dominican Republic.

blue-mountains-jm.fait: This range covers the eastern third of Jamaica and serves as the island's main water tower, covered with very rich montane forests.

chutes-dunn.fait: These waterfalls flow directly into the Caribbean Sea, and visitors climb up them on foot, sometimes forming human chains.

musee-marley.fait: This colonial house in Kingston was Bob Marley's residence and recording studio before becoming a museum in 1985.

chacachacare.fait: This island, the largest of the Bocas Islands, has remained uninhabited since its leper colony was abandoned in 1984.

el-tucuche.fait: This mountain, on the border between two regions of the country, is the second highest peak in Trinidad and Tobago, after Cerro del Aripo.

andros-bs.fait: This archipelago is bordered by the fifth longest barrier reef in the world, dotted with many “blue holes.”

half-moon-caye.fait: This caye lies on the edge of Lighthouse Reef, the farthest of Belize's three atolls, on the barrier reef.

nim-li-punit.fait: Its Maya name means “the big hat”; a stele there shows King Lajun Caan performing an act of self-sacrifice.

pacaya.fait: This volcano near Antigua, dormant for nearly a century, awoke violently in 1961; its activity has remained fairly constant since then.

el-mirador.fait: It was in this city of the Petén forest that the Maya began building massive pyramids, around 600 BC.

iximche.fait: This capital of the Kaqchikel kingdom hosted the first Spanish town in the country, before being burned and abandoned after a revolt.

cerro-las-minas.fait: This mountain is the highest point in Honduras; the whole area around it is included in Celaque National Park.

ile-tigre.fait: This small island is the southernmost volcano in Honduras; thanks to a deep natural channel, its port of Amapala serves the country on the Pacific.

el-imposible.fait: Its name, “the Impossible,” recalls how hard it was for the farmers and mule drivers carrying coffee to cross this massif.

lac-managua.fait: Also called Lake Managua, it is the second largest lake in Nicaragua, after Lake Nicaragua, and the second largest in Central America.

mombacho.fait: This dormant volcano near Granada is home to one of the last rainforests in Nicaragua, with unique flora and fauna.

cerro-negro-2.fait: Born in 1850, this volcano owes its name, “Black Hill,” to its cinder cone, which contrasts sharply with the green hills around it.

rincon-vieja.fait: The name of this volcano in the Guanacaste mountain range, in the northwest of the country, literally means “the old woman's nook.”

turrialba-2.fait: The summit of this volcano is truncated by a caldera that contains three craters, including an active one under close watch.

guayabo.fait: This site holds the oldest pre-Hispanic heritage in Costa Rica; an American engineering society has honored it for its engineering.

panama-viejo.nom: Ruins of the city founded in 1519
panama-viejo.fait: These ruins are all that remains of the old city of Panama, now located in the outskirts of the modern capital.

lac-gatun.fait: This artificial lake, which forms an important part of the Panama Canal, was the largest artificial lake in the world when it was created.

barro-colorado.fait: This island was born from the rising waters of Gatun Lake: it was once the top of a hill, in the middle of the forest.

rocksteady.fait: This genre slowed down the tempo of ska and paved the way for reggae, but its heyday lasted only about two years.

aloo-pie.fait: This fried turnover from Indo-Caribbean street food is filled with spiced potatoes: aloo means potato in Hindi.

nueva-trova.fait: This musical genre was born in Havana in the 1960s, at the first cultural congress held after the Cuban Revolution.

chilaquiles.fait: This dish of tortillas topped with green or red sauce comes with cream, fresh cheese, chicken or onions.

tlayuda.fait: This large, firm and crispy corn tortilla keeps for a long time thanks to the way it is cooked; it is listed as part of Oaxaca's heritage.

esquites.fait: Its name comes from the Nahuatl ízquitl, “toasted corn”; it is also served in a cup, hence its other name, elote en vaso.

sope.fait: This fried corn base with pinched edges looks like a very thick tortilla; it is topped with refried beans, crumbled cheese and cream.

pico-de-gallo.fait: Its name means “rooster's beak” in Spanish, yet it is a simple mix of diced tomatoes, onions and jalapeño peppers.

chapulines.fait: This dish consists of fried grasshoppers: they are eaten in Mexico, especially in the city of Oaxaca, where they are very popular.

champurrado.fait: This drink made with milk, chocolate and panela, sometimes flavored with cinnamon, is traditionally drunk in the morning with churros.

sarape.fait: This multicolored cloth, originally made of wool, is worn like a shawl or a cape; it long made the reputation of the city of Saltillo.

frijoles-refritos.fait: These beans are first cooked and mashed, then fried in a pan in oil or lard; they are used to fill tacos and tostadas.

huevos-rancheros.fait: These fried eggs served on a tortilla, with salsa, avocado and chili peppers, probably come from 16th-century Mexico.

crosse.fait: This sport of Indigenous origin, played with a stick fitted with a net, is the official national summer sport of Canada, where it was created.

barre-nanaimo.fait: This no-bake dessert, with three layers (cookie, cream, chocolate), comes from the Nanaimo area, in British Columbia.

crokinole.fait: In this table game, players flick small wooden discs toward the center of a round board to knock out their opponent's discs.

buffalo-wings.fait: These chicken wings coated in a spicy sauce are named after the city of Buffalo, in the United States, where they originated.

pecan-pie.fait: This nut pie, bound with eggs, butter and often corn syrup, is a Southern specialty served at festive meals.

sloppy-joe.fait: This sandwich filled with ground beef cooked with onions and tomato sauce or ketchup is sometimes served with coleslaw.

cheesesteak.fait: This steak sandwich is such a specialty of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, that its full name is “Philly cheesesteak.”

grits.fait: This porridge of ground corn, of Indigenous origin, is very often eaten for breakfast in the South; in Louisiana, it is called gru.

po-boy.fait: Its name comes from “poor boy” pronounced with a Southern accent: this inexpensive sandwich was born in Louisiana.

cobb-salad.fait: Its ingredients are remembered thanks to the English mnemonic “EAT COBB”: egg, avocado, tomato, chicken, onion, bacon, blue cheese.

waldorf-salad.fait: This salad of apple, celery, walnuts and grapes in mayonnaise was created around 1893 at the Waldorf Hotel in New York.

loco-moco.fait: This Hawaiian dish layers white rice, a hamburger patty, a fried egg and gravy; some people add Spam.

sazerac.fait: This cocktail, one of the oldest known, remains popular in some parts of the United States, especially in New Orleans.

hip-hop.fait: Born in New York's South Bronx, this movement is not limited to rap: it also includes DJing, breakdancing, graffiti and beatboxing.

chemise-hawaienne.fait: This short-sleeved shirt with a spread collar, also called the Aloha shirt, was born in the Hawaiian Islands and had its heyday after the war.

burning-man.fait: Its organizers insist: it is not a festival. For the duration of the gathering, its temporary desert city becomes one of the most populous in Nevada.

bluegrass.fait: This style of country music takes its name from Bill Monroe's band, the Blue Grass Boys, itself inspired by Kentucky's nickname, “the Bluegrass State.”

taxi-jaune.fait: Their yellow bodywork sets them apart at first glance: these taxis have become a widely recognized symbol of New York City.

basketball.fait: This sport was invented in Massachusetts by a Canadian teacher, James Naismith, to keep his students fit during the winter.

chopper.fait: This typically American motorcycle starts from an original frame that is cut and then modified; choppers are built among friends and insiders.

rock-n-roll.fait: In the first records of this genre, the piano or the saxophone took the lead, before being supplemented or replaced by the guitar.

skateboard.fait: It is said to have started as a children's game: a surfer is said to have given his son his surfboard fitted with wooden wheels.

dixieland.fait: This early jazz born in New Orleans made tunes like When the Saints Go Marching In famous, even among people who are not jazz fans.

red-velvet.fait: Its red color once came from treated cocoa; today, beet juice or food coloring is often used.

musique-cadienne.fait: This music of Louisiana's French speakers draws on the ballads of the Acadians who came from Canada, and it has influenced country music.

zydeco.fait: Born in Louisiana, this genre close to Cajun music, nourished by the blues, is played by both white Cajuns and Black Creoles.

fortune-cookie.fait: Despite its reputation as a Chinese cookie, this treat that hides a prediction on a slip of paper was invented in San Francisco.

shirley-temple.fait: This nonalcoholic cocktail, created in a hotel in Waikiki, Hawaii, pays tribute to Shirley Temple, who was then too young to drink alcohol.

angel-food.fait: Its whiteness and lightness earned it its name of food of the angels, the opposite of the heavy chocolate cake known as “devil's” cake.

cornbread.fait: This corn bread belongs both to the Indigenous cuisine of North America and to the cuisine of the Southern United States.

claquettes.fait: This dance was born in the United States from the meeting of the slaves' African percussive dances and the settlers' Irish jigs.

lindy-hop.fait: This swing dance was born in Harlem in the 1920s and flourished at the Savoy Ballroom, a club that refused segregation.

amphitheatre-durres.fait: This Roman amphitheater could hold up to 20,000 people, and a large part of its structure has still not been uncovered.

chateau-kruje.fait: It was in this castle that Skanderbeg led his rebellion against the Ottoman Empire; today it houses the Skanderbeg National Museum and a Turkish bath.

ksamil.fait: This coastal village was only built in 1966, under the communist regime, on the road leading to Butrint, south of Sarandë.

valbona.fait: This national park in northern Albania, on the border with Montenegro, protects very remote areas whose ecosystem has remained almost intact.

nouveau-chateau-hrodna.fait: It was in this palace that the Sejm ratified the Second Partition of Poland in 1793; it owes its name to the old castle built just opposite.

sutjeska.fait: This park, the oldest in the country, also contains the highest peak in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mount Maglić, on the border with Montenegro.

vallee-des-roses.fait: Damask roses are grown here in the open air to produce rose oil, and the end of the harvest, in late June, kicks off many village festivals.

monastere-batchkovo.fait: Set on the wooded edge of the Rhodopes, this monastery is the second largest in Bulgaria, right after Rila.

pirin.fait: This park covers most of the Pirin Mountains and is home to Bayuvi Dupki–Dzhindzhiritsa, one of the oldest nature reserves in the country.

trogir.fait: This old Dalmatian town is built on a small island, squeezed between the mainland and the island of Čiovo, west of Split.

kornati.fait: This national park brings together 89 islands, but it is the sea that takes up most of its area.

motovun.fait: This Istrian municipality is bilingual, Croatian and Italian, and hosts a film festival: the Motovun Film Festival.

chaudron-gundestrup.fait: Found in 1891 in a Jutland peat bog, this “cauldron” is actually a basin: it never had handles or fittings.

cornes-gallehus.fait: These horns made of double sheets of gold, covered with figures and inscriptions, date back to the 5th century AD.

eglise-saint-olaf-tallinn.fait: This Tallinn church now belongs to the Baptists: it is affiliated with the Union of Free Evangelical and Baptist Churches of Estonia.

chateau-narva.fait: This medieval fortress stands on the banks of the Narva River, right on the border between Estonia and Russia.

saaremaa.fait: This island, the largest in Estonia, has other names among its neighbors: Ösel in Swedish, Øsel in Danish, Saarenmaa in Finnish.

soomaa.fait: The name of this park means “land of bogs,” and it has a “fifth season”: the floods, between winter and spring.

tarte-runeberg.fait: This almond pastry, soaked in rum, usually hides raspberry jam in its center, surrounded by a layer of sugar.

chateau-buda.fait: This palace was the historic castle of the kings of Hungary; in fact, it was once simply called the “Royal Palace.”

strokkur.fait: Its name means “churn” in Icelandic: this geyser shoots hot water into the air several times an hour.

vatnajokull.fait: This ice cap, the largest in Iceland, is also the second-largest glacier by volume in Europe.

palais-jelgava.fait: This palace of the Dukes of Courland, in their former capital then called Mitau, is the work of Rastrelli, like their summer palace at Rundāle.

hotel-ville-kaunas.fait: Nicknamed the “White Swan” for its large white shape, this town hall now serves only as a “wedding palace.”

pazaislis.fait: This Kaunas monastery is the most important monastic complex in Lithuania and one of the finest examples of the Baroque in Eastern Europe.

ohrid.fait: Saint Clement founded a large monastery here in the 9th century and helped establish the Cyrillic alphabet.

mavrovo.fait: The largest national park in the country, it brings together the Šar Mountains, Mount Korab and picturesque villages such as Galičnik.

mosquee-peinte-tetovo.fait: More than 30,000 eggs were used to bind the paint of the panels covering its facades, hence the name of this mosque.

budva.fait: At 2,500 years old, this town is one of the oldest settlements on the coast of the Adriatic Sea.

monastere-moraca.fait: This Orthodox monastery was founded in 1252 by Stefan, grandson of Stefan Nemanja, the founding father of the medieval Serbian state.

monastere-piva.fait: This monastery was moved to a new site in 1982, following the construction of the Mratinje Dam; it is renowned for its frescoes.

fram.fait: This schooner was designed to let itself be trapped in the pack ice and thus drift over the North Pole, on Nansen's expedition.

zapiekanka.fait: This half-baguette, toasted with mushrooms and cheese, is sold on the street and is often eaten with ketchup and chives.

vieille-ville-varsovie.fait: It is the oldest district of Warsaw; its market square, lined with restaurants, cafés and shops, is its heart.

eglises-maramures.fait: These tall, narrow churches, built of wood, have at their western end a bell tower fitted with a semantron, sometimes a bell or a clock.

athenee-roumain.fait: This Bucharest concert hall, inaugurated in 1889, is home to the George Enescu Philharmonic Orchestra and part of the Enescu Festival.

chtchi.fait: This cabbage soup, often made with sauerkraut, has been the traditional first course of Russian meals for more than a thousand years.

okrochka.fait: This soup is eaten cold; its name may come from the Russian verb “kroshit,” which means “to crumble.”

peterhof.fait: Nicknamed the “Russian Versailles,” this town is known for its palaces and gardens built on the orders of Peter the Great.

tsar-kolokol.fait: This bronze bell broke during a fire as it fell into its casting pit, and was only dug out a century later.

tsar-pouchka.fait: This giant cannon has never been used, and the cannonballs on display are too big for it: a Saint Petersburg joke, according to legend.

lapti.fait: These shoes are made from strips of linden, birch or elm bark; they were worn in Russia until the 1930s.

sarafane.fait: This straight sleeveless dress was worn in villages until the early 20th century; the upper classes had abandoned it under Peter the Great.

felix-romuliana.fait: Emperor Galerius had a fortified palace built here, as well as a memorial with mausoleums for himself and his mother Romula.

smederevo.fait: This medieval fortified town served for a time as the country's capital, and only suffered serious damage during World War II.

huit-sargan.fait: This narrow-gauge tourist railway runs through the mountainous Zlatibor District, between Mokra Gora and Šargan Vitasi.

bardejov.fait: This town is a World Heritage Site as a very well-preserved example of the medieval merchant towns of Central Europe.

dobsina.fait: This natural icehouse is the largest ice-filled cave in the country; its average annual temperature is −1 °C.

chateau-devin.fait: Perched above the confluence of the Morava and the Danube, this ruined fortress now hosts costume festivals and historical reenactments.

eglise-bleue.fait: Nicknamed the “Blue Church,” this Bratislava church belongs to the Hungarian Secession style and is dedicated to Elizabeth of Hungary.

piran.fait: This Istrian municipality, on the Adriatic, is officially bilingual: its languages are Slovene and Italian.

lac-cerknica.fait: This intermittent lake, the largest in Europe, is not always there: in summer, the largest lake in the country is once again Lake Bohinj.

chateau-bled.fait: Built on a cliff above Lake Bled, this medieval castle is the oldest in the country.

triple-pont.fait: To the 1842 stone bridge, architect Jože Plečnik added pedestrian footbridges on either side, so that it would stop being a bottleneck.

kubb.fait: Nicknamed “Viking chess,” this game consists of knocking over the opponent's wooden blocks with sticks, then toppling the king last.

iso-polyphonie.fait: Inherited from Byzantine sacred music, this elaborate form of choral singing is mostly performed by men.

byllis.fait: This ancient city was the largest in southern Illyria; perched on a plateau that is hard to reach, it remains little visited.

berezinsky.fait: Here you can come across the three great European predators, the wolf, the brown bear and the lynx, as well as the European bison and the moose.

zmijanje.fait: This traditional embroidery serves as a marker of identity for displaced populations; UNESCO has inscribed it on its intangible heritage list.

pont-arslanagic.fait: This 16th-century bridge is no longer in its original location: it was moved and rebuilt identically because of a hydroelectric dam.

tombe-sveshtari.fait: This tomb buried beneath a mound is decorated with polychrome caryatids, half-human and half-plant, considered unique in Thrace.

rochers-belogradtchik.fait: These strangely shaped sandstone, limestone and conglomerate rocks take on colors ranging from ocher to yellow.

pobiti-kamani.fait: Its Bulgarian name means “stones planted in the ground”: natural rock columns here reach six meters in height.

tablette-baska.fait: Dated to the year 1100, this stone is one of the earliest monuments of the Croatian language; it is also called the Baška stele.

basilique-euphrasienne.fait: Dating from the 6th century, this basilica in Poreč is part of an episcopal complex with a baptistery, a bell tower and the bishop's palace.

risalamande.fait: Its name comes from the French “riz à l'amande”: this rice pudding with whipped cream and almonds is a Christmas dessert in Denmark.

rugbrod.fait: Most Danes eat this dense rye bread every day; in the past, some prisoners were punished with a diet of water and rugbrød.

fete-chant-estonie.fait: Every five years, this Tallinn festival, one of the world's largest amateur choral events, is held at the same time as the dance festival.

toomkirik.fait: The oldest church in Tallinn, this cathedral was the only building on Toompea Hill to survive the great fire of 1684.

cathedrale-tartu.fait: This cathedral perched on a hill above Tartu is in ruins; a restored part houses the university museum.

molkky.fait: Invented in 1996 by a Finnish company, this outdoor skill game requires no strength: people of all ages can play it.

lohikeitto.fait: This soup combines salmon, potatoes and cream; in Finnish, its name simply means “salmon soup.”

dobos-torta.fait: This Hungarian pastry alternates layers of sponge cake and chocolate cream, and is finished with a caramel top.

crepe-gundel.fait: This crêpe-based dessert, one of Hungary's national dishes, remains popular in the countries of the former Austria-Hungary.

esterhazy-torta.fait: This cake is named after a Prince Esterházy; in Hungary, the almonds of the original recipe have been entirely replaced by walnuts.

fete-chant-lettonie.fait: Every five years, this festival brings together amateur choirs and dance groups for several days, for concerts broadcast on television.

eglise-saint-pierre-riga.nom: St. Peter's Church and its spire
eglise-saint-pierre-riga.fait: This Lutheran church, one of the best-known symbols of Riga, is already mentioned in documents from 1209.

cathedrale-riga.fait: Considered the largest medieval church in the Baltic states, this cathedral houses an organ with 6,768 pipes.

eglise-pierre-paul-vilnius.nom: Church of St. Peter and St. Paul in Antakalnis
eglise-pierre-paul-vilnius.fait: Built in 1688, this church, a gem of Lithuanian Baroque art, holds Masses in Lithuanian and in Polish.

nida.fait: This seaside resort on the Curonian Spit, between the Baltic and the lagoon, lives mainly from tourism and has a famous nudist beach.

aukstaitija.fait: Created in 1974, it is the oldest national park in Lithuania; its name refers to Upper Lithuania, the region where it lies.

aqueduc-skopje.fait: No one knows when this aqueduct was built: it was thought to be Roman or Byzantine, but it probably dates only from the 16th century.

canyon-matka.fait: This canyon near Skopje, filled by an artificial lake, is home to monasteries and to a cave with one of the deepest siphons in the world.

monastere-bigorski.fait: According to legend, this monastery's icon of Saint John the Baptist, which shows him with three hands, came back on its own after it disappeared.

nerezi.fait: Built under the Komnenos dynasty on a slope overlooking Skopje, this Byzantine church is best known for its colorful and expressive frescoes.

bobotov-kuk.fait: This peak was long thought to be the highest point in Montenegro, until the ascent of Zla Kolata, on the Albanian border.

rommegrot.fait: The melted fat removed at the start of cooking is poured over this cream porridge, which is then eaten with sugar and cinnamon.

raspeball.fait: These grated potato dumplings change name depending on the region of Norway: komle, kumle, klubb or kumpe.

gamalost.fait: Its name literally means “old cheese”: this Norwegian cheese has a grainy texture and a strong taste.

langeleik.fait: This drone zither dates back to the 16th century; it is rarely played today, and it is a cousin of the épinette des Vosges.

gokstad.fait: This Viking ship from the late 9th century was discovered in a large burial mound near a farm in Vestfold.

lajkonik.fait: This bearded rider from Kraków folklore wears a Turco-Tatar costume, with a kind of flared robe that represents his horse.

vierge-noire.fait: Attributed by legend to Saint Luke, this icon shows Mary and the Child Jesus with a particularly dark complexion.

transfagarasan.fait: This road across the Făgăraș Mountains is usually blocked by snow from mid-October to mid-June.

palekh.fait: These lacquered miniatures, painted in tempera on papier-mâché, decorate boxes, caskets, brooches or powder compacts.

kossovorotka.fait: This shirt does not button down the middle: according to a Russian academician, this was so that the cross worn on the chest would not fall out during work.

bania.fait: These public baths existed before homes had bathrooms, and Russians are still very fond of them.

slava.fait: Every Serbian family has its patron saint, which it celebrates at the slava; the word could be translated as “glory” or “praise.”

fruska-gora.fait: This massif is an “island mountain” rising south of the Pannonian Plain, and it is home to many Orthodox monasteries.

vintgar.fait: Discovered in 1891 by a mayor and his photographer friend, this gorge can be visited thanks to wooden bridges clinging to its rock walls.

vasterbotten.fait: According to legend, this cheese was born when a dairymaid, interrupted in her work, alternately heated and stirred the curd.

couteau-mora.fait: This small straight knife serves as an all-purpose tool; it is very widespread in Scandinavia, from the army to building sites and hiking.

pils.fait: This pale lager owes its name to the city of Pilsen; it is drunk cool but not ice-cold, to bring out its aromas.

chevauchee-rois.fait: This spring festival takes place at Pentecost in the southeast of the Czech Republic; UNESCO has inscribed it on its intangible heritage list.

salo.fait: Salted, this pork fat keeps for a long time without refrigeration: very high in energy, it was an important part of the diet in the past.

khotyn.fait: This Moldavian fortress overlooked one of the main fords of the Dniester; Poles, Ottomans and Russians often fought over it.

pidhirtsi.fait: This Renaissance residence of a Polish general is considered the most precious palace-and-garden ensemble in Eastern Europe.

telnyashka.fait: The stripes of this military shirt alternate white with a color that varies by unit, most often blue.

medovik.fait: According to Russian tradition, this layered honey cake was created in the 19th century by a young chef for the wife of Alexander I.

rassolnik.fait: This hot soup takes its name from rassol, a liquid made from pickled cucumber juice; it has been known since the 15th century.

dymkovo.fait: These painted clay figurines, which sometimes take the form of a whistle, are traditionally made by women.

gjel.fait: This ceramic ware takes its name from a village where, as early as 1752, a chemist had recognized the excellent quality of the material.

vertep.fait: This traditional Ukrainian puppet theater also exists in Belarus, where it is known as batleika.

arkan.fait: The name of this Hutsul dance means “lasso”; the men dance it around a bonfire, with their arms on each other's shoulders.

szopka-cracovie.fait: In these Kraków cribs, the Nativity is not set in front of a stable, but in front of a well-known building in the city.

vanocka.fait: According to custom, you should think of all your loved ones while making this braided Christmas bread, and avoid touching it with metal.

gomboc.fait: Placed on a flat surface, this object always returns to the same position; its name comes from the Hungarian gömb, “sphere.”

falukorv.fait: This sausage is so common in Sweden that it can be found in hypermarkets as well as in the smallest convenience store.

broderie-hardanger.fait: Born in the Norwegian region of Hardanger, this openwork embroidery is sometimes made by several people together, to compose a large fresco like a patchwork.

paskha.fait: This Easter dessert shaped like a truncated pyramid, a symbol of Christ's tomb, combines eggs and dairy products, which are forbidden during Great Lent.

halling.fait: This folk dance from rural Norway is traditionally performed by young men at weddings and celebrations.

telemea.fait: This Romanian curd cheese is kept in brine or salted whey and bears the imprint of the cheesecloth in which it was drained.
