loubok.fait: Sold at markets from the 17th century until the 1950s, this Russian popular print is reminiscent of the French images d'Épinal.

le-cri.fait: This work by Munch exists in five versions, including a pastel and a lithograph; the landscape in the background is the Oslofjord, seen from Ekeberg.

neuvieme-vague.fait: This seascape, one of Ivan Aivazovsky's most famous paintings, is on display at the Russian Museum in Saint Petersburg.

couronne-venceslas.fait: This crown was placed on the king's head only on the day of his coronation; it is kept with the skull of Saint Wenceslas.

couronne-monomaque.fait: This “cap” was the crown of all the grand princes of Moscow and of the tsars, from Dmitry Donskoy to Peter the Great.

venus-dolni.fait: This ceramic female figurine dates back to the Paleolithic: it is more than 24,000 years old.

the-world.fait: These artificial islands off Dubai form a map of the world; construction was slowed down by the financial crisis of 2007.

bolani.fait: This stuffed and fried flatbread is prepared for celebrations, such as birthdays or engagements, and is sold in the streets of Kabul.

erebouni.fait: This fortress built by the kings of Urartu probably gave its name to Yerevan, whose outskirts it now occupies.

etchmiadzin.fait: The oldest Armenian Christian building houses three relics, including the Holy Lance and wood from Noah's Ark.

geghard.fait: This monastery founded in the 13th century near Yerevan has an underground section, where the priests practice their liturgy.

vishap.fait: These fish-shaped megaliths stand near rivers; their name also refers to the dragons of Armenian paganism.

chigirtma.fait: The name of this egg dish means “scream”: it is thought to evoke the sound of food cooking in hot oil.

festival-grenade.fait: Every year, usually in October, the town of Göyçay celebrates its pomegranates with a parade, traditional dances and music.

momine-khatoun.fait: This 12th-century funerary building in Nakhchivan is the work of Ajami Nakhchivani, a great architect of the local school.

yanar-dag.fait: On this hill near Baku, on the shore of the Caspian Sea, a fire fed by natural gas burns continuously.

arbre-de-vie-bahrein.fait: This lone tree in the middle of the desert is about 400 years old, and no one knows where it gets its water.

qalat-al-bahrein.fait: This tell, inhabited from the Bronze Age until the 17th century, was very probably the capital of the ancient Dilmun civilization.

temple-de-barbar.fait: This temple was dedicated to Enki, god of fresh underground waters; it does indeed contain a natural spring.

tombes-de-dilmun.fait: These burial mounds were raised in the early Bronze Age, when the island was part of a land called Dilmun.

djurdjura.fait: This lens-shaped massif in Kabylia is separated from the Mediterranean by the Sebaou valley; it is home to a national park.

ketchaoua.fait: Converted into a cathedral during the colonial period, this mosque in the Casbah of Algiers became a mosque again in 1962.

mansourah-tlemcen.fait: These remains are those of a town built by the Marinids while they were besieging Tlemcen; its name means “victorious.”

buste-de-nefertiti.fait: This painted limestone bust is considered the most famous depiction of a woman's face in the world after the Mona Lisa.

dukkah.fait: This blend of seeds, nuts and spices is eaten by dipping fresh bread first in olive oil, then in the powder.

edfou.fait: Dedicated to the falcon god Horus, this Ptolemaic temple is one of the best preserved in Egypt and the most important sanctuary in the country after Karnak.

foul-medames.fait: This inexpensive fava bean dish, which Egyptians consider a “gift from God,” is the country's national dish.

grand-sphinx-de-tanis.fait: Carved from pink granite during the Old Kingdom, this sphinx is one of the largest preserved outside Egypt.

livre-des-morts.fait: These scrolls of spells placed near the mummy had another title at the time: “Book of Coming Forth by Day.”

massue-de-narmer.fait: This ceremonial macehead bears the engraved name of King Narmer; it was found in a deposit at the temple of Horus in Hierakonpolis.

oiseau-de-saqqarah.fait: This bird carved from sycamore wood was discovered in the Saqqara necropolis; it dates from the Ptolemaic period.

ouchebti.fait: These funerary figurines replaced the sacrifice of servants; their name means “the one who answers.”

pierre-de-rosette.fait: Before helping to decipher hieroglyphs, this stele had been used as building material for a fort in the town of Rosetta.

pyramide-de-khephren.fait: Smaller than that of Khufu, it nevertheless looks taller, because it stands on a rocky rise and has a steeper slope.

scarabee.fait: The ball that the dung beetle rolls to its burrow reminded the Egyptians of the course of the sun: hence this symbol of rebirth.

scribe-accroupi.fait: This scribe sitting cross-legged, found at Saqqara, combines painted limestone, alabaster, rock crystal and copper; it is in the Louvre.

stele-de-merenptah.fait: This victory stele of Pharaoh Merneptah is also called the “Israel Stele”; the original is in Cairo, a copy in his temple.

stele-de-metternich.fait: This stele, both magical and medical, of the “Horus on the crocodiles” type, dates from the reign of Nectanebo II; it is in New York.

trompettes-toutankhamon.fait: Found in the pharaoh's burial chamber, they are considered the oldest trumpets in the world that can still be played.

zodiaque-de-denderah.fait: This relief of the sky adorned the ceiling of a chapel on the roof of the Dendera temple; taken to France, it has been replaced by a copy.

badridjani.fait: These grilled eggplants are stuffed with a spiced walnut paste, then often garnished with pomegranate seeds.

bagrati.fait: Bombarded by Ottoman troops, this Kutaisi cathedral lost its dome and roof, and remained in ruins until the 2010s.

croix-de-sainte-nino.fait: The arms of this cross droop slightly downward; according to tradition, Saint Nino brought it at the time of the kingdom's conversion.

ghelati.fait: This monastery, where King David IV is buried, housed an academy of scholars; it was nicknamed “the new Athens.”

kubdari.fait: This sourdough bread, filled with pieces of meat, spices and onions, is notably a national dish of the Svans.

lobio.fait: This dish of beans seasoned with cilantro, walnuts, garlic and onions is eaten both hot and cold.

narikala.fait: This fortress overlooking Tbilisi owes its name to the Mongols, who had renamed it Narin Qala, “little fortress.”

poulet-tabaka.fait: To fry properly, this chicken is flattened in a traditional pan called a tapa and pressed under a weight.

svetitskhoveli.fait: The name of this cathedral means “Living Pillar”; it stands in Mtskheta, the ancient capital of the Kingdom of Iberia.

tchatcha.fait: This grape brandy, similar to marc, can reach 65% alcohol when it is homemade.

ein-gedi.fait: This oasis on the shore of the Dead Sea marks the edge of the Judaean Desert, very close to the fortress of Masada and to Qumran.

mont-carmel.fait: Its name means “the vineyard of God”; the Bible places the stay of the prophets Elijah and Elisha here.

tel-dan.fait: Only a tiny part of this tell in the north of the country has been excavated, but a stele of great archaeological importance was discovered there.

assur.fait: In this Assyrian capital, the god Assur was regarded as the true sovereign: the kings presented themselves as his delegates on earth.

carte-babylonienne.fait: This clay fragment bears the oldest known map of the world: Babylon appears on it slightly north of the center.

lentille-de-nimrud.fait: This object is probably the oldest optical instrument ever discovered, but it is not certain that it was used as a lens.

ninive.fait: King Sennacherib made it the capital of his empire; its ruins now lie in the outskirts of Mosul.

obelisque-noir.fait: This black limestone monolith, sculpted and engraved on all four sides, was found at Nimrud, the former capital of Assyria.

plimpton-322.fait: This Babylonian clay tablet sets out a table of numbers that can be linked to Pythagorean triples.

porte-d-ishtar.fait: This gate of Babylon dedicated to the goddess Ishtar was partly reconstructed at the Pergamon Museum in Berlin after the excavations.

statue-de-bassetki.fait: Only the lower part of this copper statue remains: a seated naked man, whose base mentions a palace of King Naram-Sin.

gender-instrument.fait: Each bar of this gamelan metallophone is tuned to a different note and suspended over a bamboo or metal resonator.

saron.fait: This metallophone with seven bronze bars is played sitting on the floor and carries the basic melody in Javanese gamelan.

kacapi.fait: This plucked zither from the Sunda region also exists in Central Java, where it is called siter.

gangsa.fait: The musician strikes the bars of this metallophone with one hand and, with the fingers of the other, dampens them to control the length of the sound.

tambora.fait: Its 1815 eruption, the most violent in recorded history, made the following year “the Year Without a Summer” in the Northern Hemisphere.

mont-agung.fait: For Balinese Hindus, this volcano is the son of Semeru on Java, itself the son of Mount Meru in Hinduism.

puncak-jaya.fait: This peak in New Guinea is one of the few places in the world with glaciers at equatorial latitudes.

pungi.fait: This clarinet is the one used by snake charmers; it is a cousin of the hulusi played by the Dai minority of Yunnan, in China.

thavil.fait: This ancient drum from southern India, which resembles the dhol, is a rare instrument in Carnatic music.

jal-tarang.fait: This instrument is played on porcelain bowls filled with water: to change the note, you simply add or remove water.

esraj.fait: This fiddle was designed in the 19th century for sitar players, at a time when sarangi players were becoming scarce.

mizhavu.fait: This drum from Kerala is played by the Nambiar community and probably descends from the medieval mulavu of Tamil Nadu.

swarmandal.fait: This plucked Indian zither has a very specific use: only singers play it, to accompany themselves.

surbahar.fait: This instrument from northern India, rarely played in Hindustani music, is a kind of bass sitar.

ghunghuru.fait: These bronze bells, strung by the dozen around the ankles of classical dancers, form an instrument that rings to the rhythm of the steps.

chhau.fait: This martial, acrobatic dance enacts Hindu epics; traditionally, only men perform it, sometimes masked.

gotipua.fait: This dance from Odisha is performed by young boys dressed as women, until their androgynous appearance changes.

karakattam.fait: The dancers balance a pot on their heads to honor Mariamman, the rain goddess, so that she will send rain.

mohiniattam.fait: This “dance of the enchantress” from Kerala tells how Vishnu takes the form of a charming woman to bewitch demons.

yakshagana.fait: This theater, both musical and danced, is popular in Karnataka, in the Malenadu region and on the Kanara coast.

mudiyettu.fait: This danced and musical theater from Kerala enacts the battle of the goddess Kali against the demon Darika.

manipuri.fait: The dancers wear a cylindrical dress decorated with small mirrors, and their faces remain still to a slow rhythm.

navratri.fait: Its name means “nine nights”: this Hindu festival honors Shakti, the divine feminine energy, in various forms.

vishu.fait: This festival celebrates the astronomical New Year in Kerala, and it is also observed in Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry.

ramlila.fait: This folk play recounts the deeds of Rāma and his duel with the demon Ravana; its most famous version is performed in Ramnagar.

ramman.fait: This ritual of religious theater exists only in one village in Uttarakhand, where it is offered to the local deity, Bhumiyal Devta.

bihu.fait: This festival in Assam takes place in three stages over the year, linked to the farming seasons; one of them marks the new year.

hanimaadhoo.fait: This island is home to one of the few airports in the Maldives: it handles only domestic flights, notably from Malé, and serves the north of the country.

atoll-makunudhoo.fait: This atoll in the Maldives is made up of four islands, but its inhabitants all live on just one of them.

fort-frederick.fait: This Portuguese fort passed to the Dutch, the English and the French; Suffren made Trincomalee, with its well-sheltered harbor, his main base.

viharamahadevi-park.fait: Formerly “Victoria Park,” this park in Colombo is named after Viharamahadevi, mother of King Dutugamunu, who extended his rule over the whole island.

galle-face.fait: This park in Colombo on the shore of the Indian Ocean first served as a racecourse and golf course, then hosted cricket, polo and rugby.

banbhore.fait: This ruined fortified city in Sindh is home to one of the oldest mosques, the Great Mosque of Bhanbhore, dated to the year 727.

fraser-s-hill.fait: This hill station in the Titiwangsa Mountains is named after Louis James Fraser, a British adventurer, mule driver and tin trader.

grottes-gomantong.fait: The largest cave system in Sabah, this site shelters gigantic colonies of bats and swiftlets in its main cave.

pasar-seni.fait: This covered market in Kuala Lumpur, built in 1888, is also known as Pasar Budaya and Central Market.

nat-hlaung-kyaung.fait: The last Hindu temple at the Bagan site, this shrine to Vishnu is thought to have been built for Indians living in Burma, merchants and Brahmins.

temple-shitthaung.fait: Its name means “shrine of the 80,000 Buddha statues”; built like a fortress, this temple is said to have served as a refuge in times of war.

banteay-samre.fait: This Hindu temple at Angkor is called “the citadel of the Samré,” after the people who lived between the Tonlé Sap and Phnom Kulēn.

lacs-gokyo.fait: These lakes in Sagarmatha National Park are described as the highest in the world; the largest of the six main lakes is Thonak Cho.

pattachitra.fait: In Sanskrit, “patta” means cloth and “chitra” means picture: this painting from Orissa mainly tells stories of Hindu deities.

karva-chauth.fait: This Hindu festival is celebrated by women in northern and western India, in October or November, during the lunar month of Kartika.

sambar.fait: According to legend, a king of Tanjore created this dish while cooking for his guest, the Maratha emperor Sambhaji, and named it in his honor.

rasam.fait: This South Indian soup is made with tamarind or tomato juice, seasoned with pepper and other spices.

mysore-pak.fait: Lacking any idea for a name, the Mysore palace chef who invented this sweet simply called it “Mysore sweet.”

palak-paneer.fait: This vegetarian dish from Punjab is a thick purée of spinach and paneer, served hot with roti, naan or rice.

rajma.fait: This vegetarian dish of red kidney beans in a very spicy sauce is usually served with rice, especially in northern India.

chicken-65.fait: Born in a restaurant in Madras, this spicy fried chicken has inspired vegetarian versions made with paneer or cauliflower; its origin is still debated.

thandai.fait: This sweet drink made with milk, almonds and poppy seeds is drunk mainly at Holi, and is sometimes prepared with bhang.

balisong.fait: This folding knife was invented by a soldier-armorer during Spanish colonization; it is also called “veintinueve,” meaning “29” in Spanish.

siopao.fait: This steamed bun is the Filipino version of a Cantonese bun; its Chinese name means “little hot bun.”

ogoh-ogoh.fait: These giant papier-mâché monsters parade noisily on the eve of the Balinese New Year, and are then, in principle, burned.

modak.fait: This dumpling made of rice or wheat flour dough hides a sweet filling of grated coconut and jaggery, an unrefined sugar.

pesarattu.fait: This crepe resembles dosa, but its batter is made from mung beans, without urad dal; it is eaten for breakfast.

bisi-bele-bath.fait: It is said that this rice and lentil dish, born in the Mysore palace, took centuries to spread throughout Karnataka.

east-coast-park.fait: This seaside park, where people go roller-skating, cycling and running, is built entirely on land reclaimed from the sea.

fort-bala-hissar.fait: This fort in Peshawar served as the winter capital of the Durrani Empire, whose summer capital was Kabul.

himalchuli.fait: This Himalayan peak, a neighbor of Manaslu, is presented as the eighteenth-highest mountain in the world.

puerto-madero.fait: This neighborhood, the youngest in Buenos Aires, is named after Eduardo Madero, a merchant who submitted three port projects for the city.

place-de-mai.fait: This central square in Buenos Aires was formed by joining two neighboring squares, after the building that separated them was demolished in 1884.

congres-nation-ar.fait: Inaugurated in 1906, this parliament building was at the time the tallest building in Argentina, thanks to its high dome.

talampaya.fait: This park in La Rioja Province protects important archaeological and paleontological deposits, which give the landscape its particular beauty.

nahuel-huapi.fait: Its name, of Mapuche origin, means “island of the jaguars”: this glacial lake lies in the Andes.

blue-mountains-park.fait: This park in the Blue Mountains, west of Sydney, welcomes nearly 570,000 visitors each year.

whitsunday.fait: Off Queensland, in the turquoise waters of the Coral Sea, this much-visited archipelago is also home to more than 150 bird species.

daintree.fait: This tropical rainforest has existed without interruption for more than 130 million years: it is probably the oldest in the world.

royal-exhibition.fait: This palace hosted the opening session of the Australian Parliament: it was the only building in Melbourne large enough for its 14,000 guests.

kosciuszko.fait: This peak owes its name to the Polish explorer Strzelecki, who reached it in 1840 and named it in honor of his compatriot Kościuszko.

lord-howe.fait: About 300 people live permanently on this crescent-shaped volcanic island, whose isolation has preserved several endemic species.

frog-cake.fait: This cake shaped like a frog's head, at first sold only in green, is listed as part of South Australia's cultural heritage.

mcg.fait: This stadium in Melbourne, centerpiece of the 1956 Olympic Games, holds the world record for the tallest stadium light tower.

porte-soleil.fait: Called Inti Punku in Quechua, this stone gate stands at the archaeological site of Tiwanaku, in Bolivia.

huayna-potosi.fait: The ice cap of this peak near La Paz loses two meters of thickness every year: it is probably doomed to disappear.

sajama.fait: This volcano covered with perpetual snow is the highest point in Bolivia; Austrians were the first to climb it, in 1939.

madidi.fait: From the foothills of the Andes to the Amazon forests, this park brings together some of the most diverse fauna and flora in the world.

teleferique-la-paz.fait: This cable car network links La Paz to El Alto like an aerial subway: it is the largest urban cable car network in the world.

noel-kempff.fait: This park is named after a Bolivian naturalist, Noel Kempff Mercado, who was murdered inside the park itself in 1986.

aqueduc-carioca.fait: Built in the 18th century to bring water from the Carioca River to Rio de Janeiro, this aqueduct now carries a tram line.

feijoada.fait: This stew of beans and pork, often served on Saturdays in restaurants, brings together family and friends and appeals to all social classes.

farofa.fait: This Brazilian side dish is made with cassava flour or even stale bread toasted in the oven, fried in butter or oil.

vatapa.fait: This creamy paste made with coconut milk, shrimp and dendê oil is an essential part of the famous acarajé of Bahia.

pacoca.fait: Its Tupi name first referred to a dish of dried meat pounded with cassava flour; today it is a peanut candy.

carnaval-salvador.fait: This street carnival is said to have broken the record for the largest in the world, but the Guinness Book of Records still gives first place to Rio.

orongo.fait: This stone village, near the Rano Kau volcano, was a ceremonial center of Easter Island before the arrival of Europeans.

valle-luna-cl.fait: In this valley near San Pedro de Atacama, with no moisture or plants, the only animal present is a species of lizard, Liolaemus.

laguna-san-rafael.fait: This park in the Aysén Region encompasses the Northern Patagonian Ice Field and reaches its highest point at Monte San Valentín.

osorno.fait: Charles Darwin saw this volcano erupt from afar in January 1835, during his voyage aboard HMS Beagle.

villarrica.fait: This volcano, one of the most active in Chile, rises above Lake Villarrica and the nearby town of Pucón.

lauca.fait: This park in the far north of Chile is named after the Lauca River, whose source it contains, and is part of a biosphere reserve.

chungara.fait: Despite the cold nights, flamingos live on this lake of the Chilean altiplano, overlooked by the Parinacota volcano.

nevado-ruiz.fait: Its eruptions mix ash and glacial meltwater into devastating mudflows, lahars: the one in 1985 wiped out the town of Armero.

cajas.fait: Its many lakes make this Andean park a vast complex of high-altitude wetlands, managed by the city of Cuenca.

sangay.fait: This snow-capped volcano, one of the most active in the Andes, remained in constant eruption for decades, until 2011.

el-panecillo.fait: Its name means “little bread”: on top of this hill in Quito stands the statue of the Virgin of Quito.

danse-ciseaux.fait: A satire of the king's vassals, but above all an act of loyalty to the Andean gods, this ritual dance is a form of cultural resistance.

huaconada.fait: This ritual dance from the village of Mito, which originated before the arrival of the Spanish, now blends Spanish and Inca elements.

huascaran.fait: This highest point of Peru actually has two summits, Huascarán Sur and Huascarán Norte, separated by the Garganta pass.

cathedrale-lima.fait: Begun as soon as Lima was founded and often damaged by earthquakes, this cathedral did not have its towers completed until 1797.

chavin.fait: Located on a route between the Pacific coast and the Amazon, this site is considered the most important pilgrimage center of the Andean world.

pisac.fait: In this village in the Vilcanota Valley, you can attend a Mass in Quechua alongside the varayocs, the local chiefs.

paracas.fait: In this desert reserve, very cold ocean currents produce an abundance of plankton that feeds fish, crustaceans and mollusks.

cordillera-blanca.fait: It owes its name “white” to the snow, but also to the color of its rock, made notably of quartz and feldspar.

gorriti.fait: This small island facing the beach of Punta del Este extends the Cuchilla Grande out to sea, just like its neighbor, Lobos Island.

pan-azucar-uy.fait: This granite hill is only the third-highest peak in Uruguay, behind Cerro Catedral and Cerro de las Ánimas.

lac-maracaibo.fait: This “lake” is actually a brackish bay open to the Caribbean Sea, polluted by the oil extracted beneath its waters.

teleferique-merida.fait: This cable car, which climbs from Mérida to Pico Espejo, near the highest point in Venezuela, is the highest in the world.

champagne-pool.fait: This hot pool owes its name to its abundant carbon dioxide bubbles, which recall those in a glass of champagne.

abel-tasman.fait: This park, the smallest in the country, is named after the first European to have seen New Zealand, in 1642.

cap-reinga.fait: Its Maori name means “the Underworld”: according to the Maori, the souls of the dead go to this cape to reach the afterlife.

huka.fait: The Waikato River rushes here into a narrow canyon carved into the lakebed sediments of Lake Taupo, left by an ancient eruption.

ruapehu.fait: This active volcano, the highest point of the North Island, has the only glaciers and the largest ski areas on that island.

stewart.fait: South of the South Island, this large island has only 387 inhabitants, all living in its only village, Oban.

vanua-levu.fait: It is the second-largest island in the Fiji archipelago, with about 160,000 inhabitants.

rotuma.fait: Its inhabitants, the Rotumans, speak Rotuman and form a people distinct from other Fijians, recognized as a minority.

lau.fait: A Tongan chief, Enele Maʻafu, proclaimed himself king here in 1869; his title of Tui Lau was later held by high Fijian chiefs.

ovalau.fait: Its only inland village, Lovoni, nestles in an ancient crater; Levuka, on the coast, was for a time the capital of Fiji.

niuafo-ou.fait: Nicknamed “Tin Can Mail Island,” this volcanic island was evacuated after its volcano erupted in 1946.

niuatoputapu.fait: Dutch navigators nicknamed it “Traitors' Island”; Captain Samuel Wallis later named it “Keppel Island.”

efate.fait: It is the most populous island in Vanuatu: most of its inhabitants live in Port Vila, the country's capital.

anatom.fait: This volcanic island is the southernmost in Vanuatu, if you exclude the Matthew and Hunter Islands, which the country claims.

gaua.fait: Formerly called Santa Maria, this volcanic island is part of the Banks Islands, in northern Vanuatu.

guadalcanal.fait: This jungle-covered island, home to the capital Honiara, was the scene of a major battle of World War II.

tulagi.fait: Chosen by the British because it was isolated and healthier than the large islands, this small island was the capital of the protectorate until 1942.

choiseul.fait: It is named after Choiseul, Secretary of State for the Navy under Louis XV; its inhabitants created a funerary currency, the zaru mbavara.

savo.fait: Savosavo, a Papuan language, is spoken here; its bay, Ironbottom Sound, attracts divers who come to explore the wrecks.

kavachi.fait: This very active underwater volcano has emerged many times, each time forming a small island quickly erased by the waves.

tabuaeran.fait: This atoll in the Line Islands, which belongs to the Republic of Kiribati, is also known as Fanning Island.

canton.fait: The largest atoll in the Phoenix Islands, it takes its name from the whaler Canton, which ran aground there in 1854.

malden.fait: This arid, uninhabited island holds “mysterious” prehistoric ruins; it is also a protected area for birds.

abaiang.fait: Its name means “land to the north” or “land of the wind” in Gilbertese; Europeans had first named it Charlotte Island.

millenaire.fait: Located just past the International Date Line, this island is the first place on Earth, excluding the poles, where the day begins.

satawal.fait: Satawalese is spoken here, a language close to that of Woleai but very different from the language of Yap, the state to which the island belongs.

ngerchelchuus.fait: Located on the island of Babeldaob, on the border between the states of Ngardmau and Ngaremlengui, this mountain is the highest point in Palau.

hatohobei.fait: This island, called Tobi in English, gave its name to the State of Hatohobei, of which it is part, in southwestern Palau.

malakal.fait: Called Ngemelachel in Palauan, this island in Koror State is home to the port of Koror and the radio station T8AA-AM.

koror-ile.fait: This island is home to most of Koror, the country's largest city and its former capital; bridges connect it to three neighboring islands.

kutubu.fait: This mountain lake in the Southern Highlands drains into the Kikori River, which serves as its outlet.

ulawun.fait: This volcano on the island of New Britain has many names, including “The Father” and “North Son.”

nouvelle-bretagne.fait: Formerly named New Pomerania, this island in the Solomon Sea is the largest landmass in the Bismarck Archipelago.

louisiades.fait: Bougainville named this archipelago in the Solomon Sea in honor of King Louis XV of France, in 1768.

kula.fait: In this circuit of sea expeditions, necklaces were exchanged for armbands with no market value, around which society was organized.

giluwe.fait: This extinct shield volcano, the country's second-highest peak after Mount Wilhelm, is also the highest volcano in Oceania.

manam.fait: This volcano, one of the most active in the country, forced the complete evacuation of the island in 2005; some of the inhabitants later returned.

karkar.fait: The roughly 50,000 inhabitants of this volcanic island speak Takia or Waskia, and are mostly Catholic or Lutheran.

savaii.fait: Formerly called Salafai, this island is the larger of the two main islands of Samoa, in the South Pacific.

manono.fait: This small island lies between Savai'i and Upolu, within the very coral reef that surrounds Upolu.

apolima.fait: A single village occupies this volcanic island, which can only be reached by boat through a small bay on its north coast.

silisili.fait: This summit, located in the middle of the island of Savai'i, is the highest in the entire Samoan archipelago.

siva-tau.fait: This dance inspired by traditional war dances is performed by Samoa's rugby teams before every match.

detroit-apolima.fait: A government ferry crosses this strait in about 1 hour 30 minutes to link Upolu and Savai'i, the two largest islands of Samoa.

funafuti.fait: This atoll is the country's capital: the government sits in Vaiaku, its largest town, and the international airport is located there.

nanumea.fait: This atoll is the northwesternmost in Tuvalu, a country made up of nine coral atolls and islands just south of the equator.

niutao.fait: On this island, three wells draw the fresh water that floats above the salt water; the others were destroyed by the sea.

majuro.fait: This atoll is home to the capital, Delap-Uliga-Darrit, whose name combines three islands and is often shortened to D-U-D.

ailinglaplap.fait: Its name means “the largest atoll”; the main Marshallese legends are said to come from there.

arno.fait: It is the atoll closest to the capital: on a clear day, it can be seen from Majuro by looking east.

maloelap.fait: This atoll has several names, including Kaven and Calvert; when Europeans discovered it, it was called Arakcheyev.

carte-batonnets.fait: Made of coconut palm ribs and shells, these charts showed islands and swells; often, only their maker knew how to read them.

atabaque.fait: This percussion instrument of African or Arab origin was one of the first to be introduced into the playing of capoeira.

caxixi.fait: This small closed basket filled with seeds is shaken like maracas; according to one belief, it attracts good spirits and drives away bad ones.

reco-reco.fait: This percussion instrument is played by scratching or scraping it, like the güiro; it is also called caracaxá or querequexé.

pukao.fait: These red volcanic rock headdresses, all carved from a single quarry on Easter Island, were placed on the heads of the moai.

rano-kau.fait: The flat floor of this Easter Island volcano's crater is covered with small lakes; the Orongo site overlooks its cliffs.

huaca-sol.fait: This stepped pyramid built by the Moche near Trujillo probably served as a large administrative center; its neighbor is the Huaca de la Luna.

tambomachay.fait: Its Quechua name means “resting place”: this archaeological site in the Sacred Valley of the Incas lies a short walk from that of Puca Pucará.

manu.fait: In this park, thousands of parrots gather on clay cliffs to eat the soil and absorb its mineral salts.

cathedrale-caracas.fait: This cathedral dedicated to Saint James the Great stands on Plaza Bolívar, in the heart of the historic center of Caracas.

pic-humboldt.fait: This summit of the Sierra Nevada de Mérida, in the Venezuelan Andes, is only the second-highest peak in all of Venezuela.

glacier-tasman.fait: This glacier has a dual name, Haupapa and Tasman, and it is the largest of all the glaciers in New Zealand.

waiheke.fait: This island near Auckland has eight thousand year-round residents, many more in summer; vines and olive trees are also grown there.

jiu-jitsu-gracie.fait: This martial art derived from judo, developed by the Gracie family, takes the fight to the ground, where the weight difference between opponents matters less.

goiabada.fait: This guava paste replaced the quince paste of the Portuguese colonists; served with cheese, it becomes the dessert “Romeu e Julieta.”

telepherique-pain-sucre.fait: This cable car links the foot of Sugarloaf Mountain to its summit, in Rio de Janeiro, and has carried passengers since 1912.

salchipapas.fait: This street food dish announces its recipe in its name, formed from “salchichas” and “papas”: sausages and fries, sold late at night.

sauce-caruso.fait: This Montevideo sauce pays tribute to the tenor Enrico Caruso; it combines cream, ham, cheese, walnuts and mushrooms to coat cappelletti.

festival-vina.nom: Viña del Mar International Song Festival
festival-vina.fait: This six-day Chilean festival, which pits pop songs against folk songs in competition, is considered the most important in Latin America.

tramway-melbourne.fait: Melbourne has had the largest tram network in the world since Saint Petersburg dismantled a large part of its lines.

sydney-hobart.fait: This sailing race leaves Sydney every December 26; in the Bass Strait, with its difficult winds and seas, retirements are not uncommon.

wondjina.fait: These Kimberley paintings depict Aboriginal deities of the Dreamtime; their name, Wandjina, literally means “near the water.”

bathurst-1000.fait: This touring car race has been held every October since 1963 at the Mount Panorama Circuit in Bathurst.

larvotto.fait: This district, once part of Monte Carlo, gained a new sector in 2024, Le Portier, created to extend its residential area.

gare-cite-vatican.fait: This station, opened in 1934, is mainly used for freight: its passenger platform is only used occasionally, during events.

pinacotheque-vaticane.fait: This department of the Vatican Museums opened its current building to the public in 1932, under the pontificate of Pope Pius XI.

casina-pio-iv.fait: This Renaissance-style villa, in the Vatican Gardens, serves as the seat of the Pontifical Academies of Sciences and of Social Sciences.

galerie-cartes.fait: Commissioned by Pope Gregory XIII, this long corridor in the Vatican Museums took Ignazio Danti three years of work to complete its panels.

scala-regia.fait: This staircase at the ceremonial entrance of the Vatican connects the Apostolic Palace to St. Peter's Basilica; Bernini extensively restored it in the 17th century.

appartement-borgia.fait: These six rooms, the private residence of Pope Alexander VI and his family, decorated with frescoes by Pinturicchio, were abandoned after his death.

tombeaux-rois-paphos.nom: Tombs of the Kings of Paphos
tombeaux-rois-paphos.fait: These rock-cut tombs owe their royal name to the impression their size made on 20th-century visitors.

aqueduc-wignacourt.fait: This early 17th-century aqueduct was part of the network built to bring water to Valletta, then the island's new capital.

theatre-manoel.fait: This theater is Malta's national stage and the home of the country's philharmonic orchestra, the Orkestra Filarmonika Nazzjonali.

upper-barrakka.fait: Below these gardens in Valletta, a restored battery that once saluted foreign ships fires its cannon every day at 12:00 and 16:00.

ramla-bay.fait: Its golden sand with reddish tints gives this Gozo beach its Maltese name: Ir-Ramla l-Ħamra, “the red beach.”

konigsberger-klopse.fait: These meatballs are served coated in a white sauce seasoned with capers; they are also called Soßklopse.

spaghettieis.fait: This dish of spaghetti with tomato sauce is actually ice cream, invented in Mannheim in the 1960s.

cathedrale-ulm.fait: Despite its nickname, this church is not a cathedral: Ulm has never been a bishop's seat. Its steeple was the tallest Christian building in the world until 2025.

chateau-eltz.fait: Never destroyed, this castle still belongs to the same family; its turrets abound because three lines of heirs each built there.

marienplatz.fait: This square, the most famous in central Munich, was originally called Schrannen before becoming “St. Mary's Square.”

chateau-schwerin.fait: The residence of the Dukes of Mecklenburg for centuries, this castle now houses the regional parliament, which owns it.

roland-breme.fait: Erected in 1404 facing the cathedral, this statue of Roland, protector of Bremen, bears witness to the autonomy the city enjoyed.

watzmann.fait: This Bavarian ridge peaks at 2,713 m, the highest point in the Berchtesgaden area; its silhouette forms the backdrop to the town.

heligoland.fait: Although part of Germany, this North Sea archipelago lies outside the European Union's customs territory and the German tax system.

hofbrauhaus.fait: This 16th-century Munich beer hall belongs to the Hofbräu München brewery, which produces the beers of the same name.

biergarten.fait: Born in Munich, this place where people drink beer outdoors, in a shady garden, can have up to 8,000 seats.

khm.fait: Opened in 1891, this Viennese museum is considered one of the world's foremost museums of old art.

route-grossglockner.fait: This road, which crosses the highest road pass in the Austrian Alps, is lined with parking areas for admiring the Pasterze Glacier.

ambras.fait: This Renaissance-style castle, south of Innsbruck, has a history tied to that of Archduke Ferdinand II of Austria.

secession.fait: Built in Vienna in 1897, this building was an architectural manifesto and the exhibition hall of artists rebelling against the old conception of the arts.

carbonade.fait: In this dish, pieces of beef or pork are slowly braised, covered, in beer; in Dutch, it is called stoofvlees.

saint-bavon.fait: A simple parish church dedicated to St. John in the 13th century, this Gothic building in Ghent only became a cathedral in the 16th century.

agneau-mystique.fait: This altarpiece shows a different scene depending on whether it is open or closed; begun by Hubert van Eyck, it was completed by his brother Jan.

saint-sang.fait: This chapel in Bruges was enlarged in the 12th century to house a relic of the Holy Blood brought back from the Holy Land by Thierry of Alsace.

orval.fait: Destroyed and burned during the conquest of Belgium by the French revolutionary armies, this abbey only regained monks in 1927: Trappists.

chateau-bouillon.fait: Godfrey of Bouillon sold this fortified castle to the Prince-Bishop of Liège to finance his departure on the First Crusade.

palais-royal-bruxelles.fait: This palace belongs not to the king but to the State, which places it at his disposal; facing the Palace of the Nation, it symbolically links the king and Parliament.

saxophone.fait: This instrument, usually made of brass, nonetheless belongs to the woodwind family; its Belgian inventor, Adolphe Sax, patented it in Paris.

emmental.fait: Its wheels are huge for a tax reason: in the 19th century, customs duties were paid per exported wheel, not by weight.

pilate.fait: Visitors go up on the world's steepest rack railway, the Pilatusbahn, whose gradient reaches 48%.

staubbach.fait: This waterfall forms a mist of fine droplets, hence its German name, “dust stream”; it inspired a poem by Goethe.

reichenbach.fait: Sherlock Holmes fights Moriarty there in fiction; in reality, these falls run dry from fall to spring, because of a dam upstream.

quatre-cantons.fait: This glacial lake in central Switzerland is called Vierwaldstättersee in German; in Italian, it is also called “Lake Lucerne.”

saint-gothard.fait: This pass is named after Godehard of Hildesheim; it carried most of the direct traffic between northern Switzerland, Ticino and Italy.

jamon-serrano.fait: This dry-cured ham is processed in Spain, but from the legs of pigs that may have been raised anywhere in the world.

fabada.fait: This specialty is one of the most typical dishes of the Principality of Asturias, hence its full name, fabada asturiana.

cocido.fait: This typical dish of the Madrid region is a kind of pot-au-feu, made with meats and vegetables.

pulpo-gallega.fait: In Galicia, this octopus with olive oil and paprika is eaten at fairs and pilgrimages, hence its local name, “polbo á feira.”

ensaimada.fait: This pastry from Majorca takes its name from lard, “saïm,” which goes into its dough along with flour, sugar and eggs.

tarta-santiago.fait: This almond cake from Santiago de Compostela is enjoyed especially in Galicia and along the pilgrimage routes.

pimientos-padron.fait: This pepper variety comes from crops grown at a convent: that of St. Anthony of Herbón, in the parish of Padrón, in Galicia.

palais-royal-madrid.fait: Nicknamed the “Palace of the East,” this palace nonetheless stands in the westernmost part of Madrid: it owes this name to the Plaza de Oriente.

prado.fait: This Madrid museum mainly displays paintings collected by the Habsburgs and the Bourbons; Velázquez, Goya and Hieronymus Bosch are the most represented there.

alcazar-seville.fait: Until recently, the royal family still used the upper floor of this palace; when it is present, the flag at the visitors' entrance is lowered.

compostelle.fait: The destination of one of the greatest pilgrimages of medieval Europe, this Galician cathedral is dedicated to the Apostle James, patron saint of Spain.

montserrat.fait: Located on a mountain massif in Catalonia, this Benedictine abbey established itself as early as the Middle Ages as the region's foremost Marian shrine.

caminito-del-rey.fait: This path fixed to the side of a cliff was built in the early 20th century for the construction of two hydroelectric dams.

puente-nuevo.fait: This bridge is the newest and most imposing of the three that span the Guadalevín gorge, which cuts the town of Ronda in two.

rambla.fait: This Barcelona avenue links Plaça de Catalunya to Port Vell, where the Columbus Monument stands.

cathedrale-palma.fait: This cathedral, known locally as the Catedral de Mallorca, is the largest religious building on the island of Majorca.

tour-hercule.fait: This Roman lighthouse still works: it is the oldest lighthouse in service in the world, and it gave its name to the city of A Coruña.

misteri-elx.fait: The Council of Trent banned theater in churches, but it made an exception for this mystery play performed every year in Elche.

sevillanas.fait: This folk dance born in Seville is performed in pairs and can express approach, confrontation, flight and love all at once.

carnaval-tenerife.nom: Carnival of Santa Cruz de Tenerife
carnaval-tenerife.fait: This Canary Islands carnival includes the election of a queen, murga contests and a “Burial of the Sardine.”

quiche.fait: This savory tart from Lorraine fills its shortcrust pastry with lardons and a “migaine,” a mixture of eggs and crème fraîche.

blanquette.fait: In this dish, veal is cooked in a broth of carrot, leek and onion, then coated with a white sauce with button mushrooms.

pot-au-feu.fait: In this dish, beef simmers for a long time over very low heat in a broth of leek, carrot, turnip, celery and cabbage.

tartiflette.fait: This Savoyard gratin with Reblochon was only invented in the 1980s; its name comes from “tartifle,” the Savoyard word for potato.

eclair.fait: This choux pastry descends from the “pain à la duchesse”; its miniature version is called a “caroline.”

mille-feuille.fait: This cake stacks three layers of puff pastry and two layers of pastry cream, all topped with fondant icing or powdered sugar icing.

brie-meaux.fait: This raw-milk cheese takes its name from the Brie region and the town of Meaux, but its production area extends as far as the Meuse.

comte.fait: About 450 liters of raw milk are needed per wheel: farmers therefore pooled their milk in cooperatives, the fruitières.

armagnac.fait: This brandy is made from distilled dry white wines; the age it displays corresponds to the time spent in oak barrels.

salade-nicoise.fait: Born in the cuisine of Nice, this composed salad has spread around the world; it is served as a starter, or even as a meal in itself.

soupe-oignon.fait: This soup topped with melted cheese, often served with croutons, even has its own international day, celebrated on July 27.

gratin-dauphinois.fait: This dish of potatoes cooked in milk is said to have originated in the Pays des Quatre Montagnes, around Villard-de-Lans, in the Dauphiné.

fontainebleau.fait: Francis I wanted to create a “new Rome” there and brought in Italian artists; Napoleon I called it the “house of the centuries.”

palais-papes.fait: In the 14th century, this fortress-palace was the seat of Western Christendom: the popes resided there and several were elected there.

pont-avignon.fait: This bridge no longer leads anywhere: the Rhône swept away most of the structure, of which only four arches and two chapels remain.

chartres.fait: This Gothic cathedral houses a relic that tradition presents as the Virgin's veil, which makes it a major place of pilgrimage.

reims.fait: From the 11th century onward, almost all the kings of France were crowned in this Gothic cathedral, whose statuary numbers 2,303 statues.

sainte-chapelle.fait: Saint Louis had this almost entirely glazed chapel built, designed like a reliquary, to house Christ's Crown of Thorns.

opera-garnier.fait: This opera house is named after its architect, Charles Garnier: it was called the “Paris Opera” until the Opéra Bastille opened.

moulin-rouge.fait: This Pigalle cabaret, known for its French cancan, has been imitated, right down to its name, by other cabarets around the world.

champs-elysees.fait: This Paris avenue originated as a tree-lined walk laid out by André Le Nôtre, the landscape architect of King Louis XIV.

fontaine-wallace.fait: These cast-iron drinking fountains are named after Richard Wallace, a British philanthropist who paid for their installation in Paris.

saganaki.fait: This specialty is nothing more than cheese, made from sheep's milk or sometimes goat's milk, fried in oil.

acropole.fait: This rocky plateau served as Athens' citadel from Antiquity until the Ottoman occupation, and it can only be reached from its west side.

vikos.fait: Guinness World Records ranks this canyon in Epirus as the deepest gorge in the world relative to its width.

samaria.fait: At the narrowest point, nicknamed “the Gates,” the vertical walls of this gorge in Crete leave only a passage a few meters wide.

odeon-herode.fait: Herodes Atticus had this theater built at the foot of the Acropolis in memory of his wife Regilla; it still hosts performances.

delos.fait: As soon as the wind picks up, this tiny island in the Cyclades becomes inaccessible, because its harbor has always been exposed to the winds.

mistra.fait: Founded by the Franks near Sparta, this city later became the second city of the Byzantine Empire, after Constantinople.

irish-stew.fait: This stew, once made with mutton, is a traditional St. Patrick's Day dish, often accompanied by the beer used to make its sauce.

dun-aonghasa.fait: This archaeological site on the Aran Islands has been described as “the most magnificent barbaric monument in Europe.”

clonmacnoise.fait: Nicknamed “the Seven Churches,” this monastery on the banks of the Shannon was founded by St. Ciarán, counted among the apostles of Ireland.

saint-patrick-dublin.fait: This Dublin cathedral is the seat of Anglican worship of the Church of Ireland; it stands on an ancient place of worship.

burren.fait: On this barren limestone plateau, Mediterranean and alpine plants grow side by side, such as the blue gentian, its emblematic flower.

gelato.fait: This artisanal ice cream is made with milk rather than cream; it is generally lower in fat and less sweet than other ice creams.

focaccia.fait: This flatbread made with olive oil is eaten at any time of day: in Genoa, people even have it with their cappuccino at breakfast.

bruschetta.fait: This traditional appetizer served with aperitifs was born of a very practical concern: farmers needed to preserve their bread.

jambon-parme.fait: This ham is only entitled to its name if it is produced solely in the province of Parma, a protected designation since 1996.

mortadelle.fait: The name of this cold cut from Bologna comes from a Latin word meaning “seasoned with myrtle.”

burrata.fait: This cheese from Apulia is a shell of mozzarella filled with cream, best enjoyed between May and August.

tortellini.fait: These stuffed and folded pasta, similar to ravioli, originate from Bologna and Modena, in Emilia-Romagna.

vitello-tonnato.fait: In this Piedmontese dish served chilled, slices of veal are coated with a sauce of tuna, anchovies and capers.

cassata.fait: This Sicilian cake, traditionally made for Easter, combines sweetened ricotta, sponge cake, marzipan, candied fruit and sugar icing.

sfogliatella.fait: This shell-shaped pastry from Campania, filled with ricotta, is enjoyed warm at breakfast with a coffee.

chianti.fait: This red wine from Tuscany is named after its production area, Chianti, and its history dates back to the 13th century.

negroni.fait: This cocktail made with gin, red vermouth and Campari was invented in Florence in 1919.

bellini.fait: This cocktail invented in Venice mixes prosecco, or champagne, with white peach purée.

cappuccino.fait: This coffee is an espresso mixed with milk and topped with steamed milk foam, sometimes decorated with latte art.

arc-constantin.fait: The last triumphal arch in Rome, this monument stands out for its systematic use of spolia: pieces taken from older monuments.

piazza-navona.fait: This square in Rome has kept the exact shape of the Stadium of Domitian, on whose ruins it was built.

chateau-saint-ange.fait: Also called the Mausoleum of Hadrian, this castle in Rome is linked to the Vatican by a fortified corridor, the Passetto di Borgo.

basilique-saint-marc.fait: Much older than its title, this basilica on St. Mark's Square has only been the cathedral of Venice since 1807.

santa-maria-fiore.nom: Cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore
santa-maria-fiore.fait: Its dome, the work of Brunelleschi, is the largest masonry dome ever built and marks the beginning of Renaissance architecture.

pont-soupirs.fait: This covered bridge led from the prisons to the interrogation rooms; its name evokes the sigh of prisoners seeing Venice one last time.

herculanum.fait: Buried by Vesuvius, this Roman town has yielded wooden objects and, in the Villa of the Papyri, previously unknown literary works.

cote-amalfitaine.fait: This very rugged coastline takes its name from Amalfi, its historic heart; it is also home to the villages of Positano and Ravello.

grotte-bleue-capri.fait: This sea cave on the island of Capri is famous for the luminous cobalt-blue reflections on its walls and for its crystal-clear water.

portofino.fait: Since the late 19th century, this municipality in Liguria has attracted European aristocracy; today it is a vacation spot for the international elite.

lac-come.fait: This lake is shaped like an inverted “Y,” and each of its branches has its main town: Como, Lecco and Colico.

stromboli.fait: This volcanic island in the Aeolian Islands, north of Sicily, shares its name with its volcano and belongs to the municipality of Lipari.

opera-pupi.fait: The puppets of this Sicilian theater mainly portray medieval knights, but sometimes also Romeo and Juliet or Macbeth.

hutspot.fait: This dish of traditional Dutch cuisine is a mash that combines potatoes, carrots and onions.

het-loo.fait: The residence of the House of Orange-Nassau until 1962, this palace has French formal gardens designed by a nephew of André Le Nôtre.

muiderslot.fait: Thanks to a chain stretched across the Vecht near this castle, Count Floris V made boats pay a toll.

hoge-veluwe.fait: This park of dunes and forests, bought by Helene Kröller-Müller and Anton Kröller and then bequeathed to the State in 1935, has the Kröller-Müller Museum at its center.

amsterdam-centraal.fait: This station was designed by Pierre Cuypers, who was also the principal architect of the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam, opened in 1885.

ronde-de-nuit.fait: Despite its name, this Rembrandt painting shows a daytime scene: a bitumen-based primer gradually darkened it.

laitiere.fait: It is the only Vermeer painting whose main subject is a woman of humble station, here pouring a thin stream of milk.

bolo-caco.fait: This wheat bread typical of Madeira is eaten as a starter or as a side dish, or even as a main course.

poncha.fait: This cocktail typical of Madeira combines sugarcane brandy, honey and lemon or orange juice, sometimes passion fruit juice.

alcobaca.fait: Founded by King Afonso I, this Cistercian monastery reflects the ideal of ascetic simplicity championed by St. Bernard.

temple-evora.fait: Also called the Temple of Diana, this 2nd-century temple stands right in the center of Évora and symbolizes the Roman presence in the country.

mont-pico.fait: This volcano in the Azores is the highest point in Portugal, and even of the entire Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

aqueduc-eaux-libres.fait: This Lisbon aqueduct is more than its 127 arches: it is an entire network for collecting and distributing the city's water.

palais-monserrate.fait: Built in the 19th century in Sintra, this neo-Moorish palace is surrounded by lush parks and botanical gardens.

almendres.fait: This ring of standing stones near Évora is the largest megalithic complex in the entire Iberian Peninsula.

sunday-roast.fait: This roast, eaten on Sundays, is served with Yorkshire pudding, roast potatoes, vegetables and a meat-juice sauce, gravy.

clotted-cream.fait: This thick cream, made by heating cream and then letting it rest, accompanies scones at teatime.

bitter.fait: Its name means “bitter”: this British pale beer, an ale, ranges in color from gold to dark amber.

saint-paul-londres.fait: Four places of worship preceded this cathedral on Ludgate Hill; the current one, by Christopher Wren, was built after the Great Fire of London.

trafalgar.fait: Every year, Oslo donates this square's Christmas tree to thank the United Kingdom for its support of Norway during the war.

piccadilly.fait: The statue nicknamed “Eros” that tops the fountain in this square actually represents an Angel of Christian Charity.

caernarfon.fait: The English king Edward I had this fortress built to assert his authority over Wales, which he had just conquered.

ben-nevis.fait: Its Gaelic name means “malicious,” because of the very harsh climate at its summit, the highest point in the British Isles.

forth-bridge.fait: Reserved for trains, this Scottish bridge more than 2.5 kilometers long was the first large cantilever bridge ever built.

balmoral.fait: This Scottish castle does not belong to the Crown: it is the king's private property, and the royal family has stayed there since 1852.

hyde-park.fait: It is one of London's royal parks, and the largest of all those in the center of the capital.

skara-brae.fait: These eight Neolithic houses in Orkney have survived the centuries almost intact because sand had covered them.

burns-supper.fait: Every January 25, the birthday of the poet Robert Burns, Scots gather for a dinner that serves as a national celebration.

tartan.fait: This checked cloth associated with the Scottish clans saw its wearing banned by the English conqueror in 1747, then allowed again.

penny-black.fait: The first stamp in history came with a postal reform: from then on, the sender, no longer the recipient, paid for the mail.

saucisse-francfort.fait: This smoked, precooked sausage, which comes from Germany, is called Frankfurter Würstchen in German; it is also simply called a “frankfurter.”

sbrinz.fait: This strong hard cheese, made from raw cow's milk, comes from central Switzerland, where it is produced according to a centuries-old tradition.

sobrasada.fait: This cured meat from the Balearic Islands, presented like a sausage, is also made in France, a legacy of pied-noir cooking.

papas-arrugadas.fait: Originally boiled in seawater, these small potatoes from the Canary Islands cook in their skins until they wrinkle.

clafoutis.fait: In this cake from Limousin, the cherries are traditionally left whole, without removing the pits.

broche-tara.fait: Found on a beach by a peasant woman, this brooch was sold to a Dublin jeweler who named it “Tara,” a more marketable name.

orecchiette.fait: Their name means “little ears”; in Apulia, they were pressed one by one with the thumb to give them their curve.

bistecca.fait: This Tuscan cut of beef, shaped like a T like the American T-bone, is eaten barely cooked, always red inside.

carpaccio.fait: This dish consists of raw beef cut into very thin slices, seasoned with olive oil and lemon, sometimes with shavings of Parmesan.

mascarpone.fait: This creamy cheese, originally from Lombardy, goes into many Italian desserts, including tiramisu.

amaretto.fait: This bitter almond-flavored liqueur can be made with apricot or peach pits; it comes from Saronno, in Lombardy.

vue-delft.fait: This painting by Vermeer shows his hometown; it is the painter's only cityscape, kept at the Mauritshuis in The Hague.

mince-pie.fait: Served at Christmas, this sweet tartlet is said to date back to the Crusaders, who supposedly brought back from the Middle East recipes mixing meat, fruit and spices.

up-helly-aa.fait: At the end of January, in Shetland, residents dressed as Vikings parade with torches, then throw them to set a replica longship ablaze.

musees-pontificaux.fait: These museums bring together the works collected by the popes over the centuries; of about 70,000 pieces, only part is on display.

palais-verdala.fait: This country residence was built in 1586 at the request of a Grand Master of the Order of Saint John of Jerusalem, Hugues Loubens de Verdalle.

gateau-battenberg.fait: This pink and yellow checkerboard cake was created by the royal family's cooks to celebrate the marriage of a princess to the Prince of Battenberg.

jambon-foret-noire.fait: This name is protected in the European Union, but in Canada and the United States, hams of varying types and quality are sold under this name.

bollenhut.fait: Now a symbol of the Black Forest, this hat was worn in only three villages: red pompoms for young girls, black for married women.

sauce-bolognaise.fait: In Bologna, this sauce is mostly served with tagliatelle or lasagna; it is in the rest of the world that it is served with spaghetti.

brunello.fait: This red wine from Montalcino, in the province of Siena, owes its name to brunello, a variety of the Sangiovese grape, and not to the town of Brunello.

bubble-squeak.fait: This dish uses up the vegetables left over from the Sunday roast; its name, “bubble and squeak,” is said by one theory to imitate the sound of the cooking.

champ-mets.fait: This mashed potato dish with chopped scallions, simple and cheap, has a variant made with nettle shoots.

munster.fait: This soft cow's milk cheese, made in northeastern France, has been protected by a designation of origin since 1969.

obatzda.fait: Served in the beer gardens of Bavaria, this spicy cheese spread was originally a way to use up old leftover cheese, mostly Camembert.

saint-nectaire.fait: This cheese is best enjoyed from September to November; the know-how of its makers has been on the French inventory of intangible heritage since 2019.

spotted-dick.fait: This English suet pudding owes its name to the raisins scattered through it, which make it “spotted.”

chardonneret.fait: Painted by Carel Fabritius in 1654, this small painting is kept at the Mauritshuis in The Hague, in the Netherlands.

toad-hole.fait: Its name refers to a toad in a hole: these sausages baked in batter are said to look like a toad poking its head out of a hole.

place-sukhbaatar.fait: This square in the center of Ulaanbaatar, the capital of Mongolia, was formerly named Sükhbaatar Square.

lac-khyargas.fait: This salt lake in western Mongolia lies in the middle of a desert steppe and is protected by a national park.

cafe-dalgona.fait: Instant coffee, sugar and hot water are whipped in equal parts until creamy, and the mixture is then poured over hot or cold milk.

gonggi.fait: This children's game was played with small pebbles the size of a grape; today, people often buy colored plastic stones.

sinseollo.fait: The name of this dish first referred to its vessel, the “immortal's pan,” in the center of which a fire burns to keep it warm.

gujeolpan.fait: Its name means “nine-section plate”: each filling has its own compartment, and the center holds a stack of small wheat pancakes.

changgyeonggung.fait: This palace in Seoul, South Korea, served as a royal palace for the rulers of the Joseon dynasty.

cheonggyecheon.fait: This stream in central Seoul was redeveloped into a promenade almost 6 km long, opened in 2005.

dabotap.fait: This stone pagoda at Bulguksa Temple embodies yin, facing its neighbor Seokgatap, of a different style, which represents yang.

seokgatap.fait: The oldest printed text in the world was found in the reliquary enclosed in this stone pagoda at Bulguksa Temple.

hunminjeongeum.fait: This document presented a new script, hangul, created so that the common people, who could not read Chinese characters, could write Korean.

chawanmushi.fait: Its name means “steamed in a tea bowl”: this savory egg custard is made with dashi, not with milk like flan.

curry-jp.fait: This curry is eaten over rice, in udon noodles or stuffed in bread, with a milder, less spicy taste than Indian curry.

ochazuke.fait: Its name means “soaked in tea”: green tea, or dashi, is poured over a bowl of rice topped with, for example, grilled salmon.

zoni.fait: This broth with glutinous rice cakes, usually eaten at New Year, is eaten with unlacquered willow chopsticks.

ekiben.fait: These boxed meals sold at train stations used to be sold through train windows, until the windows were locked to install air conditioning.

monjayaki.fait: This typical Tokyo dish, especially from Tsukishima, is a runnier variant of okonomiyaki.

kushikatsu.fait: These bamboo skewers topped with meat, seafood or vegetables are breaded then fried, and often served with Worcestershire sauce.

champon.fait: This Chinese-inspired noodle dish from Nagasaki is cooked entirely in a single pan, noodles included.

furikake.fait: This seasoning for sprinkling on rice is often sold in small packets featuring manga heroes: it is the main seasoning for young children.

ponzu.fait: This citrus sauce may owe its name to the Dutch word “pons,” meaning punch, but the origin of the word is still debated.

chirashi.fait: Its name means “scattered sushi”: a cold topping, such as sashimi, nori or cucumber, is laid on vinegared rice.

warabimochi.fait: This jelly-like mochi is not made from glutinous rice but from bracken starch, coated in roasted soybean flour.

manju.fait: Since they traditionally do not have dessert at the end of a meal, the Japanese instead eat these small steamed cakes filled with red beans as an afternoon snack.

imagawayaki.fait: This cake filled with azuki beans was first sold near the Imagawabashi bridge, in Tokyo, during the Edo period.

monaka.fait: These wafers filled with sweet azuki beans, sometimes shaped like a cherry blossom, are traditionally served at the tea ceremony.

konpeito.fait: This small ball-shaped sugar candy covered with spikes takes its name from the Portuguese “confeito,” a kind of rock candy.

amazake.fait: This fermented rice drink, with a naturally sweet taste, is drunk during the Doll Festival, Hina Matsuri.

gyokuro.fait: Unlike most teas, this green tea is grown in the shade; rich in theanine, it has a very sweet, umami taste.

ramune.fait: The name of this fizzy soda comes from the English word “lemonade”; it is drunk during matsuri and even has its own festival.

hichiriki.fait: This short bamboo oboe, with a nasal and very powerful sound, is wrapped in lacquered cherry bark and used in gagaku music.

tsuzumi.fait: Before playing this drum, the musician blows on its skin, or even puts a little saliva on it: it must be moist to sound right.

kokyu.fait: This small fiddle, which resembles a shamisen, is the only Japanese musical instrument played with a bow.

kanzashi.fait: Some of these hair ornaments, such as the long metal pins, could also be used as weapons for self-defense.

toro-jp.fait: These lanterns of stone, wood or metal came from China, and their first use was Buddhist.

noren.fait: This short split curtain, hung at the entrance of shops and restaurants, serves as a sign and is seen as a symbol of respectability.

byobu.fait: Their name means “wind walls”: these painted folding screens protect against drafts and, when covered in gold, reflect candlelight.

fusuma.fait: These sliding partitions are the size of a tatami mat, but their height has been increasing since the late 20th century, because the Japanese are getting taller.

tenugui.fait: This thin cotton towel, most often white, sometimes bears the family name or printed traditional patterns.

wakizashi.fait: Wealthy merchants, who were not allowed to carry the katana, were however permitted to carry this shorter sword.

tanto.fait: This short sword, which appeared in the Heian period, has a blade of less than 30 cm, or one shaku, a Japanese unit of length.

naginata.fait: This curved-blade weapon was used to cut horses' hamstrings, before becoming the favorite martial art of samurai daughters.

kunai.fait: This shinobi weapon could also serve as a climbing aid, a splint or a tool for picking locks.

shimenawa.fait: This sacred rice-straw rope marks off a pure place: wrapped around a rock or a tree, it indicates the domain of a kami.

kagami-mochi.fait: This New Year “mirror cake,” made of stacked mochi topped with a bitter orange, is believed to protect the house from fire.

omamori.fait: These amulets, sold at Shinto shrines and Buddhist temples, are believed to bring luck and protection.

temari.fait: This ball was originally a child's toy, made from scraps of silk from old kimonos.

shishi-odoshi.fait: The clack of this bamboo tube, which tips over when it fills with water, is meant to scare away deer that come to graze in the garden.

tokonoma.fait: This small alcove with a raised floor is used to display calligraphy, prints, bonsai or ikebana in the traditional room.

machiya.fait: These wooden town houses served their occupants as both home and workshop, especially in Kyōto.

kemari.fait: The name of this game means “kicked ball”: this form of football was popular in Japan during the Heian period.

awa-odori.fait: This dance festival in Tokushima takes place in August, during O-Bon, and is considered the liveliest festival of its kind in Japan.

sanja.fait: This Tokyo festival honors the founders of Sensō-ji temple, and its most famous parades carry three portable shrines.

aoi-matsuri.fait: This festival in Kyōto, one of the most important in the city, takes place every year on a fixed date, May 15.

jidai-matsuri.fait: This “Festival of the Ages” in Kyōto was created in 1895, the year of the 1,100th anniversary of the city's founding, when it was called Heian-kyō.

ama-jp.fait: These free-diving women catch abalone, octopus and sea urchins; they once searched for pearls, but no longer do.

yosakoi.fait: The name of this energetic dance means “come at night” in the Tosa dialect, of what is now Kōchi Prefecture.

parc-nara.fait: More than 1,200 wild sika deer roam freely in this park, where they are classified as a “natural treasure.”

kenroku-en.fait: This Japanese garden in Kanazawa, in Ishikawa Prefecture, has a name that means “garden of six attributes.”

korakuen.fait: This stroll garden in Okayama, created at the request of a daimyo, is one of the three most famous gardens in Japan.

lac-ashi.fait: This lake formed inside a volcano about 3,000 years ago, when an explosion caused part of Mount Kami to collapse.

lac-kawaguchi.fait: This lake north of Mount Fuji serves all year round as a starting point for those who want to climb the mountain.

amanohashidate.fait: Its name means “bridge to heaven,” and this site in the north of Kyoto Prefecture is considered one of the three most famous views in Japan.

hikone.fait: The construction of this Edo-period castle was ordered in 1603 by Ii Naokatsu; it is designated a National Treasure of Japan.

inuyama.fait: This castle overlooks the Kiso River and is one of the twelve Edo-period castles still standing in Japan.

matsue.fait: A symbol of a lakeside city, this castle completed in 1611 is the only one in the San'in region, in northern Chūgoku.

hirosaki.fait: Former seat of the Tsugaru clan, this castle built on a low hill or plateau is one of the last twelve original castles in Japan.

chion-in.fait: This vast temple in Kyoto is the headquarters of the Pure Land sect and includes the site where its founder, Hōnen, died.

sanjusangendo.fait: The gilded Kannon statues in this temple are said to have “a thousand arms,” but each actually has only 21 pairs.

to-ji.fait: The name of this Buddhist temple in Kyōto means “East Temple,” but its official name is Kyō-ō-gokoku-ji.

heian-jingu.fait: This Shinto shrine in Kyoto is classified among the first-rank shrines by the Association of Shinto Shrines.

yasaka.fait: This Shinto shrine, also called Gion Shrine, stands at the end of Kyōto's Fourth Avenue and borders Maruyama Park.

zenko-ji.fait: This temple is much older than the city of Nagano: when the city was founded, it was first built around the temple.

chuson-ji.fait: This Buddhist temple in Hiraizumi is the first temple of the Tendai sect in Tōhoku, in northeastern Japan.

kumano-kodo.fait: These ancient pilgrimage routes cross the Kii Peninsula and lead to the three grand shrines of Kumano, still visited by pilgrims.

dotonbori.fait: This street in Osaka runs along a canal; this former pleasure district is known for its illuminated signs, including one of a runner crossing the finish line.

kamikochi.fait: This remote valley in the Hida Mountains, whose name means “Highlands,” is sometimes nicknamed the “Japanese Yosemite Valley.”

yoshino.fait: This mountain in Nara Prefecture is part of the sacred sites and pilgrimage routes of the Kii Mountain Range, on the Kii Peninsula.

lac-biwa.fait: Close to the former capitals of Nara and Kyoto, this lake often appears in Japanese literature, especially poetry and accounts of battles.

dunes-tottori.fait: These sand dunes, an unusual geological formation in Japan, are one of the tourist sites of the Tottori region.

nikko-futarasan.fait: This Shinto shrine in Nikkō was founded in 767 by a Buddhist monk, the mountain ascetic Shōdō Shōnin.

samourai-armure.fait: Made of several pieces, this armor was assembled so as to hinder the wearer's movements as little as possible.

edamame.fait: These still-green soybeans are often served in their pods, as an appetizer, to go with beer in Japanese restaurants.

shiokara.fait: These pieces of seafood steep in a sauce made from their own salted, fermented viscera: a strong flavor that is an acquired taste, even in Japan.

kakiage.fait: This fritter of thinly sliced vegetables, sometimes with shrimp or oysters, is fried and then served with the same sauce as tempura.

sakuramochi.fait: This pink rice cake is wrapped in a salted cherry leaf, thought to be antiseptic and reputed to drive bacteria out of the mouth.

mikoshi.fait: This “divine palanquin” carries the kami through the streets: the priests place the relic inside wearing masks and gloves so as not to defile it.

riz-cantonais.fait: Its French name, “riz cantonais,” seems to have been introduced into French by the French in Vietnam: the recipe does not appear in French texts until the 1960s.

keemun.fait: This black tea is named after Qimen County, in Anhui Province, where it comes from along with the Huangshan region.

vin-shaoxing.fait: This rice wine, with a taste close to sherry, is usually drunk warm, but it is mainly used for cooking and also goes into traditional remedies.

pipa.fait: This pear-shaped lute gave its name to the loquat: in Chinese, its fruit is the “pipa-shaped fruit.”

konghou.fait: This ancient harp had disappeared since the Ming dynasty; it quietly reappeared in the 20th century, in a rather different form.

gaohu.fait: This bowed instrument was born when a master of Cantonese music tuned the erhu higher and replaced its silk strings with metal strings.

yueqin.fait: Its name means “moon-shaped stringed instrument”: this short-necked Chinese lute is also called the moon guitar.

double-neuf.fait: On this day, people climb a high place for a picnic; and since “nine” is pronounced like “long time,” it is also a day for the elderly.

peinture-shanshui.fait: In this “mountain-water” painting, the landscape always bears calligraphed inscriptions: without an inscription, it is not shan shui.

bund.fait: Its Anglo-Urdu name means “muddy embankment”: this Shanghai boulevard is lined with European-style buildings from the 1930s.

hongcun.fait: This village is shaped like an ox: a hill forms the head, two trees the horns, four bridges the legs and the lakes its stomach.

xidi.fait: This village owes its prosperity to the Hu family, merchants whose influence moved from trade to politics.

tianmen.fait: A road with 99 bends climbs up to “Heaven's Gate,” a natural arch pierced through the rock of this mountain.

hukou.fait: The largest waterfall on the Yellow River, it is also described as the largest yellow waterfall in the world.

zhangye.fait: This geological park is known for its colorful rocks, which Chinese media rank among the most beautiful landscapes in the country.

pagode-fer.fait: This Buddhist pagoda is not made of iron: it is made of stone and owes its name to its color, which resembles that of the metal.

yinxu.fait: These ruins are those of Yin, the last capital of the Shang dynasty, with many royal tombs and palaces, near present-day Anyang.

lac-tai.fait: Its name means “the greatest of lakes”: this lake lies near the Yangtze River Delta, mostly in Jiangsu Province.

lac-dian.fait: This vast lake, whose name means “Yunnan pond,” is also called Kunming Lake: it stretches south of that city.

xiangsheng.fait: Originally, the performer imitated sounds with their voice; this comedy show has become an exchange of jokes, as a monologue or a dialogue.

douhua.fait: Its name means “tofu flower,” but it is also called “tofu brain”: it is a snack made with very soft tofu.

congyoubing.fait: This unleavened flatbread made with scallions and oil is fried, crispy on the outside and soft on the inside; it is sold at street stalls.

doubanjiang.fait: People in Sichuan nickname this paste of fermented broad beans and soybeans “the soul of Sichuan cuisine.”

huajiao.fait: Its Chinese name means “flower pepper,” but this spice comes from the husk of the fruit of shrubs in the Rutaceae family.

mijiu.fait: This glutinous rice beer is drunk warm; bottles intended for cooking have salt added.

lac-boon-tsagaan.fait: This salt lake, whose name means “white lake,” is part of a protected wetland called the “Valley of the Lakes.”

manzushir.fait: Founded in 1733, this Buddhist monastery housed 20 temples and 300 monks; most of the site was later destroyed.

tonyukuk.fait: Located near Ulaanbaatar, these 8th-century inscriptions are the oldest written records of the Turkic language family.

onon-balj.fait: This park, where the Siberian forests meet the steppe, is also linked to the history of Genghis Khan.

hwachae.fait: These traditional cocktails combine fruit and edible flower petals, soaked in honey or omija berry juice.

muk.fait: These jelly-like dishes are made with grain flour, mung bean flour or even acorn flour.

namsadang.fait: These traveling troupes, a kind of circus, were made up only of men: their name comes from “nam,” which means man.

hwajeon.fait: These small sweet rice cakes, whose name means “flower cake,” are made with edible petals, such as azalea or chrysanthemum.

namul.fait: This name refers to a whole family of side dishes made from seasoned plants, served among the banchan.

hwangnyongsa.fait: This Buddhist temple of the “Golden Dragon,” built in Gyeongju during the Silla period, was destroyed in 1238 during the Mongol invasions.

yangnyeom.fait: This fried chicken coated in a sweet and spicy gochujang sauce is often eaten as an accompaniment to alcoholic drinks.

kimchi-buchimgae.fait: Kimchi brine is often added to this pancake: it gives the batter its red color but is not spicy in itself.

dosirak.fait: It is the Korean lunchbox: rice and side dishes, often prepared at home but also sold at train stations or in convenience stores.

magoksa.fait: This temple is built on a river bend shaped like a taegeuk; its stone pagoda, considered unstable, keeps visibly warping despite its restoration.

maeuntang.fait: This Korean fish soup gets its heat from gochujang, a red chili paste, and from ground chili added during cooking.

chimaek.fait: Its name blends “chicken” and “maekju,” the Korean word for beer: it is fried or spicy chicken served with beer in the evening.

jjim.fait: This word refers to a whole range of Korean dishes that are boiled or steamed, served among the banchan, the side dishes.

dubu-kimchi.fait: Despite its name, the tofu is not fermented: it is served next to stir-fried kimchi, often to go with a glass of soju.

buseoksa.fait: Founded in 676 by Uisang, this Buddhist temple belongs to the Huayan school; several of its features are protected as national treasures.

ganghwa.fait: This island in the Yellow Sea, part of the city of Incheon, lies very close to the border with North Korea.

jindo.fait: This island in South Jeolla Province is the birthplace of the Korean Jindo, a medium-sized dog breed with a light-colored coat.

bukhansan-parc.fait: Its name means “the mountain north of the Han River”: this national park spans Seoul and Gyeonggi Province.

biangbiang.fait: Their name is written with a 57-stroke character, so rare on computer keyboards that it is often replaced by another one.

shaomai.fait: These dumplings from traditional Chinese cuisine, filled with meat or fish and vegetables, are steamed.

cha-siu-bao.fait: This Cantonese bun filled with char siu pork is served as part of dim sum or bought in Chinese bakeries.

tofu-fermente.fait: Inoculated with mold, then salted and aged, this tofu becomes a creamy, strong-smelling paste used as a condiment.

gunpowder.fait: Its leaves, rolled into pellets, earned it its English name of “gunpowder”; the Maghreb imports it to make mint tea.

delice-bouddha.fait: This vegetarian dish was originally eaten by Buddhist monks; its Chinese name means “Buddhist's vegetarian food.”
