opera-yue.fait: Born in Zhejiang, this opera was shaped by 20th-century Shanghai; its troupes are made up almost exclusively of women.

canard-zhangcha.fait: This marinated duck is then smoked over tea leaves and camphor twigs; its complex preparation makes it more of a festive dish.

re-gan-mian.fait: These “hot dry noodles” coated in sesame sauce are often served in small paper bowls at Wuhan's food stalls.

qingtuan.fait: This filled treat made from glutinous rice flour is prepared for Qingming, the Chinese festival of the dead, and is also eaten as street food.

barbe-dragon.fait: This peanut confection owes its name to its cottony threads; very sensitive to humidity, it melts easily in hot weather.

lo-mai-gai.fait: This “glutinous rice chicken,” a dim sum classic served at yum cha, is steamed wrapped in lotus leaves.

cifantuan.fait: This glutinous rice ball, filled with pickled vegetables, pork and fried dough in its savory version, is eaten for breakfast in Shanghai with soy milk.

huangshan-maofeng.fait: This green tea from the Yellow Mountains is harvested only once a year, in spring; its name means “downy peak of the yellow mountains.”

yakiniku.fait: Its name means “grilled meat”: it mainly involves marinated beef, cooked over charcoal, on gas or on a hot plate.

los-glaciares.fait: This park in Patagonia includes two large glacial lakes and legendary mountains such as Fitz Roy and Cerro Torre.

punta-tombo.fait: This reserve on the Atlantic coast is one of the main mainland colonies where the Magellanic penguin breeds.

route-40.fait: It is the longest road in the country: it crosses Argentina from north to south, from the Bolivian border to the tip of Patagonia, along the Andes.

lujan.fait: This basilica welcomes about six million pilgrims every year; it is often mistakenly believed to be a cathedral.

phare-eclaireurs.fait: This lighthouse on the Beagle Channel, near Ushuaia, is often mistakenly confused with the Lighthouse at the End of the World, located on Isla de los Estados.

gp-australie.fait: Held on a circuit that partly uses ordinary streets of Melbourne, this race traditionally opens the Formula 1 season.

arbol-piedra.fait: This tree-shaped rock was carved by wind erosion in the Siloli Desert, at the entrance to an Andean wildlife reserve.

chacaltaya.fait: Its glacier was home to the highest ski run in the world, closed after the glacier's rapid retreat and near disappearance.

isla-luna.fait: It is said that only women lived there, devoted to crafts such as weaving, and that only the Inca emperor could access the island.

lac-poopo.fait: This large salt lake on the Altiplano virtually disappeared in 2015, due to the use of its waters for farming and mining.

carretera-austral.fait: This Patagonian road is particularly narrow: about 4.5 meters wide over most of its route.

chiloe.fait: This island is known for its houses on stilts, the palafitos, and its wooden churches, witnesses to the Christianity brought by the Jesuits.

glacier-grey.fait: This glacier in Torres del Paine park flows southward, and its meltwater forms a lake that bears the same name.

cathedrale-santiago.fait: Its construction stretched over more than half a century; it is now the seat of the Archdiocese of Santiago de Chile.

geant-atacama.fait: This human figure is a geoglyph drawn on the slopes of Cerro Unita, in the heart of the Atacama Desert.

pukara-quitor.fait: This 12th-century pre-Inca fortress, built on a hillside near San Pedro de Atacama, was protected by a defensive wall.

mompox.fait: This town with a well-preserved colonial look bears the name of its founder, Juan de Santa Cruz, governor of Cartagena, who established it in 1540.

baie-des-iles.fait: It is the first region of the country settled by Europeans; Charles Darwin also stopped there aboard the Beagle.

tipon.fait: This Inca site is made up of large agricultural terraces irrigated by a network of canals, all fed by a natural spring.

tucume.fait: These many adobe pyramids, clustered around a rock, remained in use until the Spanish conquest.

winay-wayna.fait: The name of these Inca ruins, set along the Inca Trail above the Urubamba River, means “forever young” in Quechua.

ferrocarril-central.fait: Designed by engineer Ernest Malinowski, this railway, which climbs from the port of Callao to an altitude of 4,781 meters, is the second highest in the world.

lihir.fait: This volcanic island in the Pacific Ocean, also called Niolam, lies north of New Ireland, an island in the Bismarck Archipelago.

mont-lamington.fait: Because its summit was covered in forest, no one had recognized it as a volcano before its devastating eruption in 1951.

umboi.fait: This volcanic island, also called Rooke or Siassi, is separated from New Britain only by the Dampier Strait.

ngardmau.fait: The Empire of Japan operated a bauxite mine there: it was the only major one available to it during the first half of the 20th century.

shortland.fait: These volcanic islands near Bougainville were named after Lieutenant John Shortland, who discovered them in 1788.

sikaiana.fait: This Polynesian atoll was offered to Hawaii in 1856; some inhabitants even tried, in vain, to register on the Hawaiian electoral rolls.

tetepare.fait: Its inhabitants left it in the early 19th century for reasons that are not precisely known: it is the largest uninhabited island in the South Pacific.

coppename.fait: This river, which rises in the Wilhelmina Mountains, shares its estuary with the Saramacca, but sandbanks hinder navigation there.

fonuafoou.fait: This submarine volcano, also called Falcon Island, has formed an island several times over the course of its history.

vaiaku.fait: This locality houses the administration without being a capital: the concept does not exist in law. It is home to the country's only hotel.

aeroport-funafuti.fait: When no plane is expected, residents play sports on this runway, and the national football team trains there.

piriapolis.fait: At once a bay, a town and a seaside resort, it ranks among the country's main resorts, alongside Punta del Este.

el-avila.fait: This national park, created in 1958 and also known as El Ávila, extends across the states of Miranda and La Guaira and the Capital District of Caracas.

lac-valencia.fait: This natural lake, straddling the states of Aragua and Carabobo, is the second largest in the country by area, after Lake Maracaibo.

roques-gran-roque.fait: This small island in the Los Roques archipelago is home to all the hotels, the airport and the school, as well as most of the inhabitants.

sierra-nevada-ve.fait: The second protected area created in the country, this park protects the Cordillera de Mérida and the highest-altitude ecosystem in Venezuela.

mota-lava.fait: In the Mwotlap language, the name of this island in the Banks Islands is written M̄otlap, with a bar over the m.

vanua-lava.fait: With an area of 334.3 km², this island is, along with Gaua, one of the largest in the Banks Islands archipelago, in northern Vanuatu.

branza-burduf.fait: This sheep's milk cheese matures in a sheep's stomach or skin, or in pine bark that gives it a resinous taste.

sainte-couronne.fait: This crown, named after the first king of Hungary, is still kept under the dome of the Parliament by the Republican Guard.

telemark.fait: This way of skiing, with a free heel and the inside leg bent in turns, was invented by a Norwegian carpenter, Sondre Norheim.

stanczyk.fait: This painting by Matejko shows a court jester; seized by the Germans during World War II, it was not returned to Poland until 1956.

casque-cotofenesti.fait: This Geto-Dacian gold helmet, stolen in 2025 during a heist at a Dutch museum that was exhibiting it, has since been put back on public display.

sambo.fait: This combat sport, born in the USSR, combines judo, boxing and wrestling; in its “combat” form, kicks and punches are allowed.

bateliers-volga.fait: Repin painted burlaks, the day laborers who hauled barges by rope along the Volga.

matin-pins.fait: The bears in this painting are by Savitsky, but the collector Tretyakov erased his signature: the work is attributed to Shishkin alone.

venus-moravany.fait: This prehistoric statuette of a woman is called a “Venus” merely by convention: the function of these figurines is still hotly debated.

epopee-slave.fait: Mucha told the history of the Slavs on twenty giant canvases, presented in Prague for the anniversary of Czechoslovakia.

esrom.fait: This cheese takes its name from Esrum Abbey, where it was produced; its making, long forgotten, was rediscovered in 1951.

fromage-jani.fait: This caraway cheese is traditionally made for Jāņi, the summer solstice festival, from which it takes its name.

paprikas.fait: This paprika and cream stew is often lumped together with pörkölt under the single name “goulash” in Western Europe.

garash.fait: This chocolate and walnut cake bears the name of its inventor, Kosta Garash; it is presented as the Bulgarian Sachertorte.

meggyleves.fait: This slightly sweet soup made with whole sour cherries and sour cream is served cold, as a main course or dessert, on summer evenings.

limpa.fait: This sweet rye bread made with molasses owes much of its flavor to the wort added to the dough; it is served at the Christmas Eve buffet.

cosaque-mamai.fait: This hero of Ukrainian folklore is one of the regular characters of the Vertep, the traditional traveling puppet theater.

ded-moroz.fait: This “Grandfather Frost” brings gifts at New Year rather than at Christmas, and travels by horse-drawn troika rather than by reindeer sleigh.

princesse-cygne.fait: Vrubel painted here a female character from an opera by Rimsky-Korsakov, The Tale of Tsar Saltan, itself based on a poem by Pushkin.

inconnue-kramskoi.fait: No one knows who posed for this portrait of a woman in a carriage; some critics saw her as a prostitute, others likened her to Anna Karenina.

boyarine.fait: This painting by Surikov depicts a scene from the schism of the Russian Orthodox Church; the Tretyakov Gallery bought it for 25,000 rubles.

ostromir.fait: The oldest illuminated manuscript of Kievan Rus', this book was copied by a deacon for Ostromir, the posadnik of Novgorod.

situle-vace.fait: This bucket made of sheet bronze, covered with figurative scenes, dates from the 5th century BC; it was found in a Slovenian village.

flute-divje-babe.fait: This pierced cave bear femur is thought to be the oldest known flute, but some researchers see carnivore bite marks in it.

tartaria.fait: These terracotta tablets bear signs that some archaeologists regard as proto-writing; others doubt their authenticity.

flateyjarbok.fait: This 14th-century manuscript, named after the island of Flatey, is the longest and most richly decorated of the Icelandic manuscripts.

danse-vie.fait: This painting, regarded as the centerpiece of the “Frieze of Life,” Munch's great thematic cycle, is held at the National Gallery in Oslo.

jeune-fille-peches.fait: For this portrait, Savva Mamontov's daughter posed every day for nearly two months, at the family estate of Abramtsevo.

champ-seigle.fait: Shishkin painted here a village field near Yelabuga, in present-day Tatarstan, the region he came from.

procession-hardanger.fait: This wedding party in boats on the Hardangerfjord was painted by two Norwegian artists, not in Norway but in Düsseldorf, Germany.

baiser-munch.fait: In this painting by Munch, the faces of the kissing couple merge into one another to symbolize their unity.

inger-plage.fait: The model for this canvas, painted by Munch one summer in Åsgårdstrand, is Inger, the painter's youngest sister.

nuit-etoilee-munch.fait: Munch painted here the coast of Åsgårdstrand as seen from the window of the hotel where he had first experienced love.

karl-johan.fait: Munch painted here the crowd on Karl Johan Street in Kristiania, today's Oslo; the canvas would become part of his Frieze of Life cycle.

soir-plage-kroyer.fait: Krøyer painted himself here with his wife Marie and his dog Rap, strolling in the moonlight on Skagen beach.

femme-oranges.fait: This painting by Gierymski, looted by the Nazi regime during World War II, was not recovered by Poland until 2011.

vadersolstavlan.fait: This painting shows a sun dog observed over Stockholm in 1535: it is the oldest known color depiction of the city.

moldavite.fait: This green natural glass was formed by a cosmic impact whose crater lies in Germany; it is found mainly in Bohemia and Moravia.

amandina.fait: This Romanian chocolate sponge cake, filled with almond cream, takes its name from the French word for almond, “amande.”

socata.fait: This traditional sweet Romanian drink is made with black elderflowers and contains no alcohol.

fromage-tcherkesse.fait: This fresh cow's milk cheese, called “basket cheese” in Adyghe, is made by the Circassians of Adygea, in southern Russia.

hallongrotta.fait: This jam-filled cookie, whose name means “raspberry cave,” is one of the seven kinds of cookies of the Swedish tradition.

paquet-maternite.fait: This cardboard box filled with clothes and bedding is given by Finnish social security to expectant parents, who may choose a cash allowance instead.

palacsinta-hortobagy.fait: These Hungarian pancakes are filled with a meat stew, often veal, fried with onions and spices like pörkölt.

rugbraud.fait: This rye bread used to be baked underground, near a hot spring; its effects on digestion have earned it the nickname “thunder bread.”

greve.fait: This cheese with a slightly nutty taste resembles a softer Emmental; its name belongs to the Swedish dairy association.

skagen-soiree.fait: The two women seen from behind on this Skagen beach are Anna Ancher and Marie Krøyer, painted from a photograph taken by the artist.

union-mal-assortie.fait: Painted by Vasily Pukirev just after his studies, this canvas made him one of the most prominent Russian painters and earned him the title of professor.

procession-koursk.fait: Ilya Repin painted here the annual procession of an icon; when it was shown, one critic praised the painting, while another saw in it “an inept lie.”

vladimirka.fait: The dirt road painted here by Isaac Levitan is the one taken by exiled prisoners on their way to penal servitude.

hdv-chisinau.fait: Almost destroyed during World War II, this Italian Gothic-style building was rebuilt using the surviving original images and plans.

cetinje.fait: The historic capital of Montenegro, nicknamed the “throne capital,” this town is now home to the president's main residence.

kotor.fait: Long dependent on Venice, this walled town still bears its imprint in its layout and architecture.

nevski-tallinn.fait: This Orthodox cathedral in Tallinn was built from 1895 to 1900, as part of the policy of forced Russification of Estonia launched by Alexander III.

ulcinj.fait: The southernmost town in Montenegro, on the Adriatic, it is called Ulqin in Albanian; its municipality is mostly populated by Albanians.

universite-vilnius.fait: Founded in 1578 from a Jesuit college, this university remained under Jesuit direction until their order was suppressed.

pont-latin.fait: It was just north of this bridge in Sarajevo, built in 1798 and 1799, that the attack on Archduke Franz Ferdinand took place, on June 28, 1914.

kuldiga.fait: This town in western Latvia was among the winners of a European competition rewarding sustainable tourism, the EDEN project.

rovinj.fait: Nicknamed the “little Croatian Venice,” this Istrian town has bilingual status: it is also called Rovigno, in Italian.

pont-mes.fait: Its Albanian name means “middle bridge”: this Ottoman bridge, one of the longest in the region, spans the Kir River near Shkodër.

saint-casimir.fait: The oldest Baroque church in Vilnius, it was built by the Jesuits, passed to the Augustinians, then returned to the Jesuits in 1991.

gerlach.fait: This peak changed its name six times after triangulation measurements revealed that it was the highest point in all the Carpathians.

cathedrale-zagreb.fait: This Catholic cathedral is dedicated not to a single patron but to three: Our Lady of the Assumption, Saint Stephen and Saint Ladislaus.

knez-mihailova.fait: Belgrade's main pedestrian street, it is protected for its architectural heritage, notably its buildings from the 1870s.

porto-palermo.fait: Built by Ali Pasha in a bay near Himarë, this castle is the best preserved of all the garrisons he erected in the region.

kursumli-an.fait: This caravanserai in Skopje owes its name to its lead roof; it served as a prison, then as an arms depot, before housing a lapidarium.

aglona.fait: This Baroque basilica is the center of Catholicism in Latvia, a country that is nonetheless Protestant by tradition.

skadarlija.fait: This neighborhood is considered the bohemian quarter of Belgrade, somewhat like Montmartre in Paris.

theth.fait: This small village in Shkodër County, in the heart of a national park, has been declared a protected historic center by the Albanian government.

vrsic.fait: The road over this pass, the highest in Slovenia, is called the “Russian Road”; it was originally built for military purposes.

hekla.fait: The locals believed this volcano was the gateway to Hell: its summit, though fairly easy to reach, was not climbed until 1750.

eglises-ivanovo.fait: Here, churches, chapels and monasteries were carved directly into the rock; the oldest of these churches dates from the 12th century.

bauska.fait: First a hill fort, then a castle of the Teutonic Knights, the site later had a palace added: today it combines ruins and palace.

karlovy-vary.fait: This spa town is famous for its hot springs and its hot-water river; Becherovka liqueur is also produced there.

lesnovo.fait: This still-active monastery hosts an artists' colony; its frescoes notably depict the Serbian emperor Stefan Dušan and his wife.

saint-donat.fait: This pre-Romanesque church with a circular plan, now deconsecrated, serves as a performance venue for concerts of sacred and medieval music.

myvatn.fait: Its name means “the lake of flies”; ornithologists know it for the fifteen or so species of ducks that come to nest there.

grotte-magoura.fait: This cave contains rock paintings dated to the Mesolithic and the Neolithic; it is now fitted out for visitors.

villa-tugendhat.fait: This villa in Brno, now a museum, was designed by the German architects Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich.

ston.fait: Nicknamed the “European Great Wall of China,” this stone enclosure surrounds the town of Ston, which was part of the Republic of Ragusa.

chateau-turku.fait: A former prison turned history museum, this medieval castle is one of the oldest buildings still in use in Finland.

landmannalaugar.fait: Its Icelandic name means “the hot baths of the local people”; it is a volcanic region located east of Hekla.

monastere-troyan.fait: Its icon of the Virgin, considered miraculous by the faithful, is known as the “Three-Handed”: a severed hand, that of Saint John of Damascus, appears at the bottom.

holasovice.fait: This hamlet brings together farmhouses built in the 1770s in a style the Czechs call “rural Baroque.”

cathedrale-roskilde.fait: A royal burial site for centuries, this brick cathedral holds the tombs of twenty-one kings of Denmark.

vysehrad.fait: The cemetery of this Prague fortress holds the remains of Dvořák, Smetana, Alphonse Mucha and Karel Čapek, among others.

hortobagy.fait: This park protects the puszta, a steppe of wild horses and great bustards, but also pastoralism and the local culture.

tyn.nom: Church of Our Lady before Týn
tyn.fait: This Gothic church overlooking Prague's Old Town Square was one of the symbols of the struggle between Catholics and Protestants.

christiansborg.fait: Nicknamed “Borgen,” this palace houses the Danish Parliament, the Prime Minister's Office and the Supreme Court.

sarmizegetusa.fait: This ancient city was the capital of the Dacians under King Decebalus; the Roman emperor Trajan laid siege to it.

eglises-paix.fait: The Peace of Westphalia allowed Lutherans to build these churches out of wood, clay and straw, without a bell tower or bells, within one year at most.

maison-chimeres.fait: This Art Nouveau house in Kyiv, lived in by its architect, a passionate hunter, is decorated with exotic animals and hunting scenes.

holloko.fait: In this village, the 16th-century wooden church was used as a granary until 1889; at Easter, residents put on their colorful regional costumes.

zelena-hora.fait: This church is the last masterpiece of the architect Santini-Aichel, who combined Baroque architecture with Gothic elements.

rosenborg.fait: This castle started out as a two-story summer house in the king's garden; it now houses the Danish crown jewels.

sphinx-bucegi.fait: No one carved this rock in the Carpathians: it is a natural sculpture which, from certain angles, recalls the head of the Sphinx of Giza.

wilanow.fait: The facades of this palace, built for King John III Sobieski, use ancient symbols to celebrate his military triumphs.

saint-andre-kiev.fait: This Baroque church on Volodymyrska Street in Kyiv is sometimes wrongly called a cathedral: it is only a church.

place-heros.fait: This vast square in Budapest was built to celebrate a thousand years since the Magyars settled in the plain of Hungary.

sainte-barbe.nom: St. Barbara's Church in Kutná Hora
sainte-barbe.fait: This Gothic church is dedicated to Saint Barbara, patron saint of miners, because the town lived off silver mining in the Middle Ages.

frederiksborg.fait: Kings were crowned here when Denmark was an absolute monarchy; its splendor has earned it the nickname “Danish Versailles.”

curtea-arges.fait: This former monastery houses the necropolis of the first kings of Romania, and its church is featured on the 1 leu banknote.

ksiaz.fait: The most important castle in Lower Silesia, near Wałbrzych (Waldenburg before 1946), it also has a German name: Schloß Fürstenstein.

basilique-saint-etienne.fait: This Budapest church keeps in a reliquary the right hand of Stephen, the first king of Hungary, known as the Holy Right.

ruelle-or.fait: These low, colorful houses within the walls of Prague Castle were built to house the guards of Rudolf II and their families.

egeskov.fait: This castle on the island of Funen, surrounded by water, is the best-preserved moated castle in Europe.

sucevita.fait: This monastery, built by the Movila family, is often considered “the testament of Moldavian art.”

slowinski.fait: On this Baltic coast, between Łeba and Rowy, the sand does not stay put: Słowiński National Park is best known for its shifting dunes.

kamianets.fait: This fortress stands in the former capital of Podolia and ranks among the most important architectural monuments of Ukraine.

pannonhalma.fait: Founded in 996, this Benedictine abbey also houses a school and a boys' boarding high school, alongside the monks' quarters.

tour-poudre.fait: This tower, one of the best-known buildings in Prague, marks the boundary between the Old Town and the New Town.

stevns-klint.fait: The name of these white chalk cliffs on the island of Zealand means “the cliffs of Stevn”; they contain fossils.

stavropoleos.fait: The name of this Orthodox church in Bucharest comes from a Greek expression that can be translated as “city of the cross.”

sarcophage-ahiram.fait: This sarcophagus of a king of Byblos bears the oldest known text of significant length written in the Phoenician alphabet.

tapis-kouba-chirvan.fait: In the past, finished rugs were spread out in front of the house: the weight of passersby's footsteps tightened their knots even further.

bastani.fait: This Persian ice cream flavored with saffron and rose water often hides flakes of frozen clotted cream.

daria-e-nour.fait: Its name means “sea of light”: this pale pink diamond, one of the rarest hues, is kept in the basement of a bank in Tehran.

tapis-heriz.fait: Its artisans do not knot curves: starting from the same cartoon as a Tabriz rug, they turn the arabesques into straight lines.

kahve.fait: This coffee was not necessarily invented in Turkey: its name mainly recalls that the Ottoman world spread this way of preparing it.

cay-tulipe.fait: This tea grows on the southern coast of the Black Sea, with its mild, rainy climate; in 2016, the country consumed 4 kg per person per year.

arnavut-cigeri.fait: Literally “Albanian-style liver,” this Turkish dish combines fried liver and potatoes, spiced with chili pepper and served with onion and parsley.

beyaz-peynir.fait: This salty white cheese, kept in brine, is the most popular in the country: it is eaten mainly at breakfast or with rakı.

kapuska.fait: This cabbage stew takes its name from the Slavic word kapusta; a Turkish poet admitted to having hated it during the war, when it was a poor man's meal.

sira.fait: This non-alcoholic drink is a barely fermented, very sweet grape juice; it is most often served with Iskender kebap.

tulum-cornemuse.fait: This powerful bagpipe was originally made by shepherds, from sheepskin and wood; it is mostly played outdoors.

rubab-afghan.fait: This national instrument, traditionally made of mulberry wood, is played by plucking the strings, but its waisted body suggests that it was once played with a bow.

stele-tel-dan.fait: This basalt stele was not erected by a king of Israel but by an Aramaean king; it was found in two fragments in the north of the country.

pyramidion.fait: The ancient Egyptians called this small pyramid, placed at the very top of a pyramid or an obelisk, a benben.

kudurru.fait: Their name means “boundary” in Akkadian: these Babylonian stelae record land grants and are among the few Kassite works of art.

clou-de-fondation.fait: This clay nail inscribed in cuneiform was driven into the walls of a temple to symbolically dedicate the building to a deity.

otrar.fait: The ancient Turks called it Keñü Tarman: this ancient city in southern Kazakhstan stood on the banks of the Syr Darya.

lac-zaissan.fait: This freshwater lake on the course of the Irtysh lies between the Altai Mountains and the Tarbagatai range, near the Chinese border.

desert-karakoum.fait: Its name means “black sands”; this Central Asian desert alone covers more than half of Turkmenistan.

mosquee-vendredi-herat.fait: Babur called it the “mosque of Kings”: destroyed and rebuilt several times, this mosque is adorned with rich decoration of glazed tiles.

corridor-wakhan.fait: This narrow corridor in eastern Afghanistan, in Badakhshan province, is nicknamed the “duck's bill.”

jabal-al-lawz.fait: This mountain in northwestern Saudi Arabia is the highest point of the Midian Mountains; it overlooks the Gulf of Aqaba.

mosquee-al-haram.fait: This mosque in Mecca houses the Kaaba, toward which Muslims all over the world pray, including those inside the mosque itself.

tarim-yemen.fait: This town in the Hadhramaut valley is a center of Islamic learning, home to a large concentration of descendants of Muhammad.

qalhat.fait: Of this former trading port on the Gulf of Oman, only a few remains survive, the main one being the mausoleum of Bibi Maryam.

djebel-akhdar-oman.fait: Its name means “the green mountain”: this central massif of the Hajar Mountains is crisscrossed by trails popular with hikers.

masirah.fait: This island in the Indian Ocean, off the sultanate's eastern coast, has been home to a US military air base since 1980.

vieux-dongola.fait: Capital of Makuria for centuries, this city of medieval Nubia was the starting point for caravans heading to Darfur.

lac-gaberoun.fait: This extremely salty lake borders an oasis in the Libyan Desert, whose Bedouin village was abandoned in the 1980s.

vallee-qadisha.fait: Its name comes from Syriac, the language spoken in Lebanon before Arabic; the valley is a World Heritage Site together with the Forest of the Cedars of God.

citadelle-amman.fait: This L-shaped hill in the heart of Amman was one of the seven hills of the ancient city; today it is an open-air museum.

qasr-al-azraq.fait: Its name means “blue fortress”; in 1917, Lawrence of Arabia set up his headquarters there during the Arab Revolt.

capharnaum.fait: In French, the name of this former fishing village in Galilee also refers to a very messy place, a meaning Balzac used a great deal.

ebla.fait: Excavations of this ancient city uncovered an archive room holding more than 17,000 clay tablets and fragments.

ak-saray.fait: Its name means “white palace”: this palace in Shahrisabz was built during the reign of Tamerlane, at the start of the Timurid era.

medracen.fait: This stone tumulus, decorated with half-columns and false doors, is the oldest surviving ancient royal mausoleum in North Africa.

ananouri.fait: This 16th-century fortress on the Georgian Military Road contains two churches and an Orthodox monastery.

lac-ulken-almaty.fait: This natural mountain lake, whose name means “Big Almaty,” nestles in the Trans-Ili Alatau mountains, south of the city.

mausolee-aisha-bibi.fait: This mausoleum near Taraz is covered in terracotta decoration; the same site holds that of Babazhi Khatun, according to tradition someone close to Aisha Bibi.

bourabay.fait: This lakeside spa resort mainly treats tuberculosis and respiratory diseases, with a sanatorium and mud baths.

mosquee-shah-do-shamshira.fait: Its name means “mosque of the king with two swords”: this two-story yellow mosque stands on the Kabul River, in the city center.

mes-aynak.fait: This site with Buddhist monasteries, the country's main archaeological discovery in more than forty years, is threatened by a copper mining project.

tillia-tepe.fait: This “hill of gold” yielded a treasure of more than 21,000 pieces, mixing steppe art, Indian objects and Chinese mirrors.

grotte-de-hira.fait: According to Islam, it was in this cave that Muhammad is said to have received his first revelations, through the angel Gabriel.

fort-nakhal.fait: This fort follows no standard plan: it was built around an irregular rocky outcrop, with which it forms a single whole.

musawwarat.fait: The Meroites called this large temple complex Aborepi; it was built in the 3rd century BC, northeast of present-day Khartoum.

notre-dame-harissa.fait: On a hill overlooking the sea, a monumental statue of the Virgin, patron and protector of Lebanon, stands atop a chapel from 1908.

temple-echmoun.fait: This temple of the Phoenician god of healing, forgotten and then used as a quarry, was rediscovered in 1900 by treasure hunters.

mshatta.fait: The facade of this Umayyad palace was given by the Ottoman sultan to the German emperor: it is now on display in Berlin.

qasr-al-hallabat.fait: This Jordanian desert castle forms a single site with a mosque, the Hammam as-Sarah baths and a few outbuildings.

vallee-houla.fait: This valley, now drained and farmed, held a lake surrounded by many marshes in biblical times.

bet-guvrin.fait: In these bell-shaped caves, where limestone was quarried for building, concerts are now held thanks to their good acoustics.

theatre-bosra.fait: This 2nd-century Roman theater, the best preserved in the Middle East, still has its stage wall.

palais-azem.fait: This palace, built in Damascus for an Ottoman governor, now houses the museum of popular arts and traditions.

arouad.fait: It is the only inhabited island in Syria; the Phoenicians called it Arwad and the ancient Greeks Arados.

resafa.fait: In Roman times, this city, now an archaeological site southwest of Raqqa, was called Sergiopolis.

qalat-jabar.fait: This citadel overlooked the Euphrates valley from the top of a hill; the filling of a dam reservoir turned the hill into an island.

medersa-koukeldach.fait: Its name means “foster brother”; this madrasa in Tashkent later served as a caravanserai, a fortress and then a prison.

chashma-ayub.fait: Its name means “Job's spring”; this mausoleum is among the most enigmatic buildings in Bukhara.

hippone.fait: Augustine was the bishop of this Roman port city and died there in 430, while the Vandals were besieging the city.

mosquee-sidi-boumediene.fait: First a tomb and later given a mosque, this building in Tlemcen honors a Sufi saint born near Seville and regarded as a patron saint of the city.

parc-gouraya.fait: In the forests of this park in Kabylia, on the Mediterranean shore, live Barbary macaques and golden jackals.

sevanavank.fait: Once called the “black monastery,” this site built on a peninsula of Lake Sevan retains only two churches, now part of the neighboring seminary.

gochavank.fait: This monastery bears the name of its founder, Mkhitar Gosh, who was at once a fabulist, a jurist and a theologian.

saghmosavank.fait: Also called the “monastery of psalms,” this site perched above the Kasakh valley includes a library among its buildings.

aqueduc-zaghouan.fait: This Roman aqueduct linked springs to Carthage; part of it is listed as an Important Bird Area, because lesser kestrels nest there.

nimroud.fait: This site owes its name to the Nimrod of the Bible, but its ruins are those of Kalhu, which was the capital of Assyria.

dur-kurigalzu.fait: These ruins are those of Dur-Kurigalzu, a city founded around 1400 BC by a Kassite king; the tell of Aqar Quf was its religious center.

medersa-ben-youssef.fait: This Quranic school in Marrakesh housed students who came from elsewhere: it had 132 rooms for them.

tombeaux-saadiens.fait: This royal necropolis in Marrakesh, linked mainly to the reign of Ahmad al-Mansur, lies in the royal quarter of the kasbah.

volubilis.fait: This Roman city lived off the olive oil trade: many presses can still be found in its ruins.

chellah.fait: This Marinid necropolis in Rabat, built on an ancient city, has hosted a jazz festival every year since 2005.

tombe-hafez.fait: In this garden in Shiraz, poems from Hafez's Divan are written on tiles and marble, on the walls of the north courtyard.

damavand.fait: This semi-active volcano, the highest in Iran, has not erupted for more than 7,300 years.

dasht-e-lut.fait: Its Persian name means “desert of emptiness”: temperatures there are among the hottest in the world, and only its edges are inhabited.

mosquee-lotfallah.fait: Nicknamed the “king's oratory,” this mosque was the first built in Isfahan under the Safavids, before the Shah Mosque.

yakhtchal.fait: This ancient stone structure, whose name comes from Persian, served in Iran as a natural refrigerator.

khan-el-khalili.fait: This large souk lies in the heart of Islamic Cairo, between the Al-Azhar Mosque and the gates “of conquest” and “of victory.”

oasis-siwa.fait: In this oasis near Libya, the population is mostly of Berber origin and still speaks a Berber dialect, Siwi.

monastere-sainte-catherine.fait: This Orthodox monastery in Sinai holds the world's second library of ancient manuscripts, after that of the Vatican.

pyramide-rhomboidale.fait: Its unusual shape comes from an abandoned attempt at a smooth pyramid; yet it remains the best preserved in Egypt, with most of its casing.

pyramide-rouge.fait: Its color comes from inner blocks rich in iron and manganese, exposed since its white casing disappeared.

tour-de-leandre.fait: The Turks call it the “maiden's tower”; it is built on an islet in the Bosphorus, off the Üsküdar district of Istanbul.

citerne-basilique.fait: Its Turkish name means “the cistern sunk underground”: this giant reservoir of Constantinople can still be seen in Istanbul.

mosquee-selimiye.fait: Commissioned by Sultan Selim II, this mosque in Edirne is considered the masterpiece of the architect Sinan.

mont-heha.fait: This highest point of Burundi, at 2,684 meters, rises in Bujumbura province, about twenty kilometers from Lake Tanganyika.

bwiti.fait: This initiation rite combines music, art, architecture and masks to ensure the link between the world of the living and that of the spirits.

bubaque.fait: This island in the Bijagós archipelago, in Guinea-Bissau, shares its name with the main town located on it.

mont-moco.fait: This summit, the highest point in Angola, rises in Huambo province, between the cities of Huambo and Lobito.

gorges-riviere-noire.fait: These gorges in southwestern Mauritius have formed a national park since 1994, called Black River Gorges National Park in English.

ehotile.fait: These islands set on the Aby Lagoon, in eastern Côte d'Ivoire, together form a national park.

marahoue.fait: This national park in Côte d'Ivoire is crossed by the Marahoué River, also called the Red Bandama.

lagune-ebrie.fait: Part of Abidjan, including Treichville and Marcory, is built on an island in this brackish lagoon.

fako.fait: This active volcano is only mildly explosive: its eruptions open fissures from which lava flows pour out.

parc-benoue.fait: Created in 1968, this national park became a biosphere reserve and is one of the richest in species in Cameroon.

monte-verde-cv.fait: This volcanic mountain is the highest point of São Vicente, an arid island but the most populous in the north of the archipelago.

ilheu-raso.fait: This uninhabited islet of Cape Verde lies between Branco Islet, slightly smaller, and the island of São Nicolau.

kirinyaga.fait: Scholars long doubted that there could be snow at these latitudes: the existence of this mountain was only confirmed in 1883.

elmenteita.fait: This saltwater lake lies in the Great Rift Valley, in Kenya, northwest of the capital, Nairobi.

thimlich.fait: These stone enclosures, built without mortar, were inhabited until 1981; in Luo their name means “the great forest frightens me.”

musee-nairobi.fait: The largest of Kenya's museums has as its motto the English phrase “A place of discovery.”

pangalanes.fait: This canal, built in the 20th century, runs along eastern Madagascar and links Farafangana to the port of Toamasina.

nosy-komba.fait: Nicknamed “lemur island,” this small volcanic island is home to lemurs that its inhabitants consider sacred.

andringitra.fait: This park is home to Pic Boby, the highest accessible peak in Madagascar; it was originally a strict nature reserve.

ankarafantsika.fait: The lakes of this park are the last refuges of species such as the Madagascar fish eagle and Coquerel's sifaka.

lac-anosy.fait: This artificial lake in southern Antananarivo has a Malagasy name meaning “lake with its islet.”

maromokotro.fait: According to popular belief, the spirits of the dead come to wander on this mountain, the highest in Madagascar.

chutes-gouina.fait: Mali, Senegal, Mauritania and Guinea began building a hydroelectric dam at the site of these falls in 2013.

chutes-felou.fait: Below these falls, the Senegal River narrows sharply as it crosses a mass of rocks; a hydroelectric plant is installed there.

lac-faguibine.fait: During floods, the waters of this lake in the inner Niger delta, in northern Mali, can spread out very widely.

lac-otjikoto.fait: In the Herero language, Otjikoto means “deep hole”: this small karst lake even gave its name to its entire region.

lac-guinas.fait: This Namibian lake is the larger of the two karst lakes located near Etosha National Park.

cross-river-np.fait: This national park consists of two protected areas that do not touch: Okwangwo and Oban.

igbo-ukwu.fait: These lost-wax bronzes were discovered by chance in 1939 by a villager who was digging a well.

rwenzori-np.fait: Located in the Rwenzori Mountains, this national park in Uganda has been a World Heritage Site since 1994 and a Ramsar site since 2008.

bunyonyi.fait: This lake in southwestern Uganda lies near the town of Kabale, not far from the border with Rwanda.

mosquee-touba.fait: This building dominates the city of Touba: it is the largest mosque in Senegal and one of the most imposing in Africa.

almadies.fait: This rocky headland on the Cap-Vert peninsula, in Senegal, is the westernmost point of the entire African continent.

saint-louis-ile.fait: This island forms the historic heart of the city of Saint-Louis, also known for the richness of its intangible heritage.

ile-bird.fait: The island owes its name to a colony of about 700,000 pairs of sooty terns, which arrive there at the end of March to lay their eggs.

maison-merveilles.fait: This building in Stone Town, Zanzibar, also bears an Arabic name, Beit-al-Ajaib, and that of “Palace of Wonders.”

lac-eyasi.fait: This salty soda lake in northern Tanzania has no outlet to the sea: its waters flow nowhere.

simien.fait: The strange shapes of the rocks in this park are due to erosion; gelada baboons and Ethiopian wolves can be seen there.

harar.fait: Sometimes described as the fourth holy city of Islam, this city owes its nickname of Jugol to the walls that surround it.

tiya.fait: This megalithic site in southern Ethiopia, dated to the 12th or 13th century, brings together 46 stelae and associated tombs.

trinite-addis.fait: This Orthodox cathedral in Addis Ababa is European in style, but its interior walls and stained-glass windows bear works in Ethiopian style.

sof-omar.fait: The Weyib River sinks into these caves and resurfaces farther on; the site is sacred to Muslims and to Oromo followers of traditional religion.

cango.fait: These caves can only be visited in small groups with a guide, and one of the tours goes through narrow, dimly lit passages.

lions-head.fait: Dutch settlers saw a lion's head in it, but the British first called this Cape Town peak the “Sugar Loaf.”

addo.fait: This park near Port Elizabeth is reserved for African elephants; it is the third largest in the country, after Kruger and Kgalagadi.

tugela.fait: These waterfalls are the highest in Africa and the second highest in the world; their name is sometimes spelled Thukela.

va-waterfront.fait: On this Cape Town waterfront, the most visited site in South Africa, a hotel occupies a former 19th-century prison.

pilgrims-rest.fait: The name of this museum village, a small town declared a national monument, literally means “the pilgrim's rest.”

tsitsikamma.fait: This park in the Eastern Cape includes a marine protected area created in 1964, the oldest in the world.

droewors.fait: This thin sausage dries quickly in warm air, without any curing agent: it must therefore be kept away from moisture.

pierre-livingstone.fait: This stone does not mark the place where Livingstone and Stanley met, which was in Ujiji, but a spot where they stopped.

lagune-ndougou.fait: This lagoon in southwestern Gabon has about 350 islands, and barracuda and tarpon are fished near its mouth.

parc-ntringui.fait: This park protects, in the center of Anjouan, one of the last remnants of the island's natural forest, as well as Lake Dzialandzé.

sapitwa.fait: In Chichewa, the name of this peak, the highest in Malawi, means “don't go there”; the area is known to be dangerous, with sometimes very changeable weather.

chutes-chisimba.fait: These falls, considered “one of the most sacred places of power,” also feed a hydroelectric plant.

crane-kabwe.fait: This skull was found in a lead and zinc mine in Zambia; kept in London, it is the subject of a repatriation request.

palais-gouverneur-asmara.fait: This building, commonly called the Governor's Palace, actually serves as the city hall of Asmara, the capital of Eritrea.

lac-ihema.fait: It is the largest and southernmost body of water in Akagera National Park, near the Tanzanian border.

tarso-tousside.fait: This volcanic massif in northwestern Chad marks the western end of the Tibesti Mountains.

barrage-nangbeto.fait: This dam on the Mono River was meant to supply electricity to Togo and Benin, create fisheries and provide irrigation.

pieter-both-2.fait: The summit of this mountain bears a rock resembling a human head; its name honors a governor of the Dutch East Indies.

enfant-taung.fait: This skull of a child of about three allowed Raymond Dart to define a new genus of hominid: the australopithecines.

mrs-ples.fait: This fossil australopithecine skull, discovered in 1947, is the most complete of its species found to date in South Africa.

os-ishango.fait: These notched bones were first seen as tally sticks; some even read mathematics in them, a hotly disputed thesis.

liemba-2.fait: Built by German colonists, this ferry served as a warship and was then scuttled; today it sails on Lake Tanganyika.

protea.fait: This flower is the national plant of South Africa; it grows in the Western Cape province.

strelitzia.fait: This flower native to South Africa is the best known of the birds of paradise, because it is easy to find at florists.

ravenala.fait: Its drinkable sap, easy to extract with a stroke of a machete, quenches the traveler's thirst; its fan of leaves, roughly oriented east-west, serves as a rudimentary compass.

shotel.fait: This curved sword from Abyssinia was used mainly on foot, to hook the opponent from behind his shield.

koba-2.fait: This dessert from the Malagasy highlands, also called koba ravina, combines ground peanuts, brown sugar and rice flour.

isi-ewu.fait: This Igbo dish, whose name means “goat head,” is a soup made precisely with a goat's head, sometimes cooked whole.

ogbono-2.fait: Ground fruit seeds thicken this Igbo soup and turn it black; it is eaten with cassava or yam fufu.

potbrood.fait: This “pot bread” of the Boer settlers was baked in a cast-iron pot set in a pit lined with glowing coals.

hertzoggie.fait: This cookie filled with jam and coconut is enjoyed with tea; in Cape Town, the Malay community eats it during Eid.

homo-naledi.fait: First judged very old based on its morphology, this hominin from the Rising Star caves turned out to be much more recent, which has reopened debate.

au-sediba.fait: Its fossils come from Malapa, a site interpreted as an ancient natural death trap: a long vertical shaft into which animals fell by accident.

orchidee-comete.fait: This orchid, nicknamed the star of Madagascar, grows naturally nowhere else but on this island.

trochetia.fait: Its flower, nicknamed “earring,” is the floral emblem of Mauritius; on the island, the shrub survives only on the slopes of Le Morne.

medusagyne.fait: This tree was thought to be extinct until a few specimens were discovered; its fruits recall the shape of a jellyfish.

mine-jwaneng.fait: This open-pit mine, whose name means “a place of small stones,” is the richest diamond mine in the world.

baie-maputo.fait: Its former name, Delagoa Bay, comes from the fact that it was the first port of call for ships coming from Goa, in India.

pont-dona-ana.fait: Once the largest railway bridge in Africa, this structure over the Zambezi was used by cars before being returned to trains alone.

chapelle-baluarte.nom: Chapel of Nossa Senhora de Baluarte
chapelle-baluarte.fait: This chapel stands on the northernmost artillery bastion of Fort São Sebastião, on the Island of Mozambique.

lac-kossou.fait: The largest lake in Ivory Coast is artificial: created by a dam on the Bandama, it forced some 75,000 Baoulé people to leave.

cosmoledo.fait: This uninhabited atoll is home to the largest colony of sooty terns in the Seychelles, as well as boobies.

morne-seychellois-2.fait: This highest point of the Seychelles, covered in tropical forest, is home to the country's largest terrestrial national park.

parc-sainte-anne.fait: This marine park, very close to Victoria, brings together eight islands and islets; fishing and overly invasive water sports are banned there.

serra-malagueta.fait: This mountain range of volcanic origin, in the north of Santiago Island, has been made a natural park.

monte-estancia.fait: On the flat island of Boa Vista, this bare, almost circular rise can be seen from any point on the island.

topo-coroa.fait: Its name means “summit of the crown”: this volcano is the highest point on the island of Santo Antão.

lac-debo.fait: The largest lake in Mali sees its surface area vary with the floods of the Niger and the Bani, whose overflow it collects.

cap-skirring.fait: This cape at the southwestern tip of Senegal, in Casamance, is also a seaside resort and a village.

takamanda.fait: This park was created to protect an endangered species, the Cross River gorilla; it borders a neighboring national park in Nigeria.

baie-ambas.fait: Also called Amboise Bay, this bay on the Gulf of Guinea opens south of Mount Cameroon and is home to the port of Limbe.

mont-speke.fait: This peak in the Rwenzori Mountains, near the Congolese border, is the fifth highest in Africa.

mont-moroto.fait: This volcano towers over the town of Moroto, in Karamoja, and is part of a chain of volcanoes running along the Kenyan border.

mont-baker.fait: Together with Mounts Stanley and Speke, this peak forms a triangle in the “Mountains of the Moon”; its highest summit is Edward Peak.

nalubaale.fait: This dam on the White Nile was formerly called the Owen Falls Dam; Nalubaale is the Luganda name for Lake Victoria.

lac-kompienga.fait: This lake is artificial: it was created by the filling of the Kompienga Dam, which feeds a hydroelectric power station.

dendrosenecio.fait: This species of giant groundsel, in the Asteraceae family, grows in Tanzania, notably in Kilimanjaro National Park.

clivia.fait: Native to South Africa, this plant, also called the Natal lily, grows well indoors in countries with cold winters.

agapanthe.fait: Native to South Africa, this perennial is recognizable by its blue umbels, visible throughout the summer.

flamboyant.fait: Native to Madagascar, this red-flowering tree now graces the entire intertropical zone.

kalanchoe.fait: Native to Madagascar, this plant of the Crassulaceae family is grown as a houseplant in temperate countries.

pachypodium.fait: This flowering plant of the Apocynaceae family grows naturally only in the tropical forests of Madagascar.

nepenthes-pervillei.fait: This insectivorous plant, which grows only in the Seychelles, lives on the summits of the archipelago's granite mountains.

palmier-bouteille.fait: This small palm, also called the gargoulette or bonbonne palm, is native to Round Island, an islet that is a dependency of Mauritius.

saintpaulia.fait: Despite its name, this plant has no connection to true violets; it was discovered in the Usambara Mountains.

baie-luderitz.fait: This bay also has a Portuguese name, Angra Pequena, “little cove”; the town of Lüderitz stretches along its edge.

dame-blanche.fait: Among tens of thousands of paintings in the Brandberg, this one is the best known, because its origin was long debated.

parc-bui.fait: This park, a refuge for hippos, has seen much of its territory flooded by the reservoir of the Bui Dam.

parc-bia.fait: This park is home to some of the largest trees still intact in West Africa, in one of Ghana's last remnants of relatively untouched forest.

kyabobo.fait: This park is home to Mount Dzebobo, Ghana's second-highest peak, from which Lake Volta can be seen.

cascades-kintampo.fait: Hidden in the forest, this waterfall consists of three main drops; in colonial times, it was called Sanders Falls.

plateau-kwahu.fait: This plateau in southern Ghana forms the divide between the basin of the Pra River and that of the Volta.

barrage-kpong.fait: The low head of this dam on the Volta required turbines that are unusually large for their power output.

desert-chalbi.fait: This small desert in northern Kenya was formed by the drying up of a lake, Lake Chalbi, about 10,000 years ago.

longonot.fait: This volcano in the Great Rift Valley is crowned by a vast caldera; its last eruption dates back to around 1863.

menengai.fait: This Great Rift Valley volcano has the largest caldera in Kenya, and its volcanic soils enrich the surrounding farmland.

kakamega-2.fait: This reserve is part of a larger forest area, Kenya's last primary tropical rainforest.

arabuko.fait: On the Kenyan coast, this forest reserve is protected as a national park over only a very small part of its area.

chutes-thomson.fait: The mist from this waterfall supplies water to the dense forest below; the Scotsman Joseph Thomson discovered it in 1883.

musee-blixen-2.fait: This museum occupies the former home of Karen Blixen, author of “Out of Africa,” at the foot of the Ngong Hills, in a suburb of Nairobi.

musee-train-nairobi.fait: This museum mainly displays railway equipment from the defunct East African Railways and Harbours Corporation.

kitum.fait: Elephants enter this cave to dig into the rock and extract mineral salts; two visitors reportedly contracted the Marburg virus there.

lac-logipi.fait: This salty soda lake attracts many flamingos, which feed there on cyanobacteria such as spirulina.

songo-mnara.fait: The ruins on this island are a World Heritage Site together with those of Kilwa Kisiwani; in 2004, they were listed as “in danger.”

roc-kondoa.fait: In these rock shelters, elongated human figures and perhaps hunting scenes were painted; some works are said to be more than 50,000 years old.

parc-arusha.fait: This park, the smallest national park in Tanzania, covers Mount Meru, a volcano; it had two other names before receiving its current one in 1967.

kitulo.fait: It is the 14th and last national park established in Tanzania, in the far south near Malawi; it is still largely being set up.

cathedrale-dar.fait: In this Catholic cathedral in Dar es Salaam, dedicated to Saint Joseph, Mass is celebrated sometimes in Swahili, sometimes in English.

mine-williamson.fait: Started by a Canadian geologist in 1940, this mine has operated without interruption ever since: one of the oldest continuously operating diamond mines.

sainte-marie-sion.nom: Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion
sainte-marie-sion.fait: According to tradition, this church in Aksum houses the Ark of the Covenant, which is said to have been stolen by King Menelik I.

lac-abaya.fait: The Italian explorer Vittorio Bottego, the first European to come to the region, had named it Lake Margherita in honor of the Queen of Italy.

cathedrale-saint-georges-addis.fait: This octagonal Orthodox church houses works by Afewerk Tekle, the artist known for the stained-glass windows of Africa Hall.

lac-afrera.fait: This lake in the Danakil Depression is so salty that it allows dozens of salt pans to be worked.

marojejy.fait: The summit of this massif bears Madagascar's last cloud forest, made up of shrubs, which gives way to tall trees lower down.

baie-diego.fait: This bay owes its name to two Portuguese navigators, Diogo Dias and Admiral Suarez; it is actually a group of several bays.

phare-ile-aux-prunes.fait: Standing 60 meters tall, this reinforced concrete lighthouse on an uninhabited islet is considered the tallest in Africa.

musee-lagos.fait: This museum on Lagos Island brings together archaeology, traditional African art and contemporary art; its renovation made it possible to digitize its objects.

cathedrale-christ-lagos.fait: Built on Lagos Island, this cathedral is the oldest Anglican cathedral in the entire Church of Nigeria.

eredo.fait: This network of defensive walls and ditches near Ijebu Ode was built in honor of a Yoruba noblewoman, Bilikisu Sungbo.

cathedrale-sainte-croix-lagos.fait: This Neo-Gothic cathedral in Lagos was built at the end of the 19th century, mainly at the initiative of French missionaries.

lesatima.fait: This 4,001-meter peak, also called Mount Satima, is the highest point of the Aberdares; it lies in the national park of the same name.

lac-karoum.fait: Salt has been extracted from this lake for centuries; in late September, it merges into Lake Assale, which breaks up again into pools in the dry season.

yangudi-rassa.fait: This park was proposed in 1977 to protect the African wild ass; it is also home to the beisa oryx, the gerenuk and Grévy's zebra.

arbre-argent.fait: This endangered tree grows naturally only in a small area of the Cape Peninsula, mostly in and around the city of Cape Town.

bismarckia.fait: This blue palm, the only one of its genus, grows wild only in Madagascar, but it is cultivated to decorate tropical regions around the world.

alluaudia.fait: This plant looks so much like the American ocotillo that it is nicknamed the “Madagascar ocotillo”: a case of convergent evolution.

cat-island-bs.fait: Cascarilla bark is harvested here and exported to Italy, where it is used notably in Campari.

iles-berry.fait: Freed slaves settled here in 1836; today, many seasonal residents, reputed to be very wealthy, own private islets here.

mayaguana.fait: The easternmost island of the archipelago, it is among the first lands where Christopher Columbus landed on his voyage to the New World.

acklins.fait: This island shares a single atoll with Crooked Island, Long Cay and Castle Island, but forms a separate district on its own.

cerros.fait: Built beside a navigable river well suited to trade, this Preclassic Maya city dug canals to increase its harvests.

turneffe.fait: It is one of the three atolls of the Belize Barrier Reef, along with Glover Reef and Lighthouse Reef.

louisbourg.fait: This former French fortress on Cape Breton Island has been rebuilt: visitors today tour a partial reconstruction of the original site.

casa-loma.fait: Its owner had to leave this mansion in 1923 for lack of money; the city of Toronto then seized it for unpaid taxes.

capilano.fait: This rope bridge stretched over the Capilano River belongs to a private establishment: you have to pay an admission fee to cross it.

haida-gwaii.fait: Its name means “islands of the Haida people”; this archipelago off British Columbia was formerly called the Queen Charlotte Islands.

gros-morne.fait: Here, a piece of the floor of the ancient Iapetus Ocean and of the Earth's mantle can be seen in the open air, a good example of plate tectonics.

manicouagan.fait: This reservoir fills a meteorite crater flooded by a dam; with the island that formed at its center, it is sometimes nicknamed the “Eye of Quebec.”

mont-robson.fait: Its summit is visible only about 14 days a year, and only a few ascents succeed each year on this highest point of the Canadian Rockies.

fjord-saguenay.fait: This river is actually a fjord: it rises in Lac Saint-Jean and flows into the tidal section of the Saint Lawrence River.

santa-rosa-cr.fait: Costa Rica's first national park, it takes its name from a battle fought in 1856 at the Santa Rosa hacienda.

braulio-carrillo.fait: It is reached through the Zurquí Tunnel, the only one in the country; its highland jungle hides hundreds of waterfalls and an extinct volcano.

humboldt-cu.fait: Located in the provinces of Holguín and Guantánamo, this park has been a World Heritage Site since 2001 for its biological and geological richness.

cayo-guillermo.fait: On this small island in northern Cuba, the beach of Playa Pilar inspired a book by the writer Ernest Hemingway.

parc-la-visite.fait: This park, created to protect the flora from deforestation, is home to Haiti's largest pine reserve, but tree clearing continues there.

zaculeu.fait: This city was the capital of the Mam Maya, before being captured and destroyed by the conquistador Gonzalo de Alvarado in 1525.

uaxactun.fait: Its modern name, “eight stone,” comes from an archaeologist; in the past, the city was reportedly called K'an Kok, “precious turtle.”

kaminaljuyu.fait: This archaeological site in the Highlands lies on the continental divide between the Atlantic and the Pacific.

acatenango.fait: This volcano has Volcán de Fuego as its neighbor to the south and Volcán de Agua to the southeast, not far from Guatemala City.

aguateca.fait: This Maya site built on the shores of Lake Petexbatún was not discovered until 1957, by chicleros.

lac-amatitlan.fait: A dam cuts this volcanic lake into two very different parts: the northwestern one receives some of the waste from Guatemala City.

santiaguito.fait: This volcano, which takes this name from its lava dome, has been erupting since 1922 and often produces pyroclastic flows.

san-cristobal-ni.fait: The highest volcano in Nicaragua, it constantly releases large amounts of volcanic gases and water vapor.

cosiguina.fait: In 1835, one of the most violent eruptions in history decapitated this volcano, whose elevation, estimated at 2,300 meters beforehand, dropped to 872 meters.

bosawas.fait: Its name combines three natural sites: the Bocay River, Mount Saslaya and the Waspuk River; this tropical forest reserve covers 21,815 km².

volcan-san-salvador.fait: Its Nahuatl name means “mountain of the quetzal bird”; part of the capital, San Salvador, spreads over its slopes.

chinchontepec.fait: Its Nahuatl name means “mountain of the two breasts”; at its base gush hot springs nicknamed “little hell.”

chinampa.fait: These “floating gardens” created in lake areas covered more than half the food needs of Tenochtitlán, the great capital of the time.

orizaba.fait: The highest point in Mexico, this volcano is also the tallest in North America; its last eruption dates back to 1846.

mitla.fait: Its name comes from “Mictlan,” “place of the dead” in Nahuatl; its geometric friezes are made of stones cut with great precision.

xochicalco.fait: Its name means “house of flowers” in Nahuatl; the site is listed by UNESCO for its very well-preserved architecture and sculptures.

yaxchilan.fait: This Maya city, enclosed in a bend of the Usumacinta River, is renowned for its hieroglyphic inscriptions carved on lintels and stelae.

pena-bernal.fait: This rock is presented as the third-largest monolith in the world, behind two Australian giants, including Uluru.

sian-kaan.fait: Its name means “origin of the sky” in Maya; this reserve combines marshes, mangroves and tropical forest, and is home to more than 300 bird species.

iztaccihuatl.fait: Its name means “white woman” in Nahuatl; it is the third-highest mountain in the country, after Pico de Orizaba and Popocatépetl.

cathedrale-metropolitaine-mx.fait: Its construction stretched over more than two centuries: begun in the 16th century, the cathedral was not completed on the outside until 1813.

tlacoyo.fait: This snack of pre-Hispanic origin is a thick oval corn tortilla filled with frijoles, fava beans or other ingredients.

huitlacoche.fait: These corn kernels, transformed by a fungus into misshapen tumors, are a prized delicacy in Mexico, sold in markets.

zocalo.fait: A UNESCO World Heritage Site, this square in the historic center of Mexico City is Constitution Square; only part of it is popularly called the Zócalo.

long-island-iced-tea.fait: This cocktail owes its name to its resemblance to iced tea, though it contains none: it mixes tequila, gin, vodka, rum, orange liqueur and cola.

chicken-fried-steak.fait: This Southern dish is a tenderized beef steak, rolled in flour and then fried, similar to Wiener schnitzel.

cioppino.fait: This fish and seafood stew, originally from San Francisco, California, is eaten like a soup.

hot-rod.fait: Its name means “hot connecting rod”: these old cars, often early Fords, are restored and fitted with souped-up engines.

mesa-verde.fait: Among hundreds of cliff dwellings, this park is home to Cliff Palace, considered the largest cliff dwelling in North America.

independence-hall.fait: It was in this Philadelphia building that the Declaration of Independence was signed, and later the U.S. Constitution adopted.

crater-lake.fait: This lake occupies the caldera of the Mount Mazama volcano, in Oregon; a small uninhabited island, Wizard Island, rises from it to the west.

denali.fait: This highest point of North America, covered in glaciers and with an extreme climate, was not climbed for the first time until 1913.

zion.fait: Its name comes from Mormon culture, where it refers to a refuge or sanctuary; its deep canyons were carved by the Virgin River.

mammoth-cave.fait: This cave has nothing to do with the mammoth: it owes its name to its size and is part of the largest underground network in the world.

fallingwater.fait: The architect Frank Lloyd Wright built this house directly over a waterfall in the Allegheny Mountains, in Pennsylvania.

old-faithful.fait: Its name means “old and faithful”: this Yellowstone geyser produces one of the largest jets of hot water and steam in the world.

mont-rainier.fait: This active volcano near Seattle is named after a friend of the explorer George Vancouver, Rear Admiral Peter Rainier.

glacier-np.fait: This Montana park is home to dozens of glaciers and, together with a neighboring Canadian park, forms an “International Peace Park.”

meteor-crater.fait: This Arizona crater was formed about 50,000 years ago by an iron-nickel meteorite, much of which was vaporized or scattered on impact.

grand-teton.fait: The name of these Wyoming mountains comes from French Canadians who were exploring the region on behalf of the North West Company.

succotash.fait: This dish of Indigenous cuisine combines beans and corn; its name comes from the Narragansett word “sohquttahhash.”

gros-piton.fait: This mountain is one of the two that tower over Soufrière Bay; it is the second-highest peak in Saint Lucia after Mount Gimie.

petit-piton.fait: This mountain rises in the middle of Soufrière Bay, between the town of Soufrière and its taller neighbor, Gros Piton.

harbour-island.fait: Its inhabitants nickname this small island “Briland”; its town, Dunmore Town, prospered thanks to shipbuilding and sugar.

cockscomb.fait: This reserve in the Maya Mountains is considered the first wildlife sanctuary dedicated to the jaguar; more than 100 jaguars live there.

lighthouse-reef.fait: This group of small coral islands, known in French as the récif du Phare, is one of the three atolls of the Belize Barrier Reef.

real-fuerza.fait: This 16th-century fortress, which now houses a museum in Havana, is among the oldest stone fortresses in the Americas.

valle-ingenios.fait: Its name means “valley of the sugar mills”: this valley stretches east of the town of Trinidad, on the island of Cuba.

cafecito.fait: This espresso is sweetened with brown sugar during the extraction itself; it was born in Cuba with the arrival of Italian espresso machines.

timbales.fait: These percussion instruments were invented in Cuba in the early 20th century to accompany the danzón; most salsa bands use them.

hotel-nacional.fait: Perched on Taganana Hill facing the sea, this grand hotel opened in 1930 is considered the most luxurious establishment in Havana.

labadee.fait: This seaside resort in northern Haiti is private; it is also called Labadee, an English name intended for English-speaking tourists.

volcan-agua.fait: This volcano is inactive, but in the 16th century a major mudflow destroyed an entire city; its fertile slopes are heavily cultivated.

lac-izabal.fait: Nicknamed Golfo Dulce, this lake, the largest in Guatemala, flows into the Caribbean Sea via the Río Dulce and gave its name to a department.

piedras-negras.fait: It was by studying the inscriptions at this site that Tatiana Proskouriakoff laid the foundations for deciphering Maya writing.

swan-islands.fait: These islands in the Caribbean Sea, called the Swan Islands in English, are the northernmost in the Honduran department of Islas de la Bahía.

concepcion-ni.fait: This active volcano forms the northwest of Ometepe Island, in Lake Nicaragua; faults sometimes let its magma emerge quite low on its slopes.

maderas.fait: With no known historical activity, this volcano on Ometepe Island hides a crater near its summit occupied by a small freshwater lake.

chemin-fer-panama.fait: Opened in 1855 for traffic to California, this line between the Atlantic and the Pacific has been described as the first transcontinental railroad.

palacio-garzas.fait: Located in the historic center of Panama City, this “Palace of the Herons” is the official residence of the President of the Republic.

parc-chagres.fait: The rivers in this park supply enough water to keep Gatún Lake, the main lake of the Panama Canal, operating.

conchagua.fait: This volcano towers over the small peninsula that marks the southern side of the Gulf of Fonseca, on the Pacific; its slopes are a nature reserve.

al-pastor.fait: Its spit recalls that of shawarma, but the meat is almost always pork; the dish was brought over by Lebanese immigrants.

ofrenda.fait: For the Day of the Dead, the portrait of the deceased, their favorite foods, cempasúchil flowers, candles and papel picado are placed on it.

volcan-colima.fait: This volcano in the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt goes by many names: Fuego de Colima, Volcán de Fuego, or Tzapoltlan.

cookie.fait: In Quebec and New Brunswick, this small round cookie from American cuisine is simply called “biscuit aux pépites de chocolat.”

egg-cream.fait: Despite its name, this New York drink contains neither cream nor egg: just syrup, milk, and soda water.

submarine.fait: This sandwich on a baguette-style roll, nicknamed a “sub,” is the specialty of Subway, the most widespread restaurant chain in the United States.

chess-pie.fait: In the Southern United States, this pie often replaces pumpkin pie on Thanksgiving and Christmas tables.

applejack.fait: In the 18th century, this apple brandy was used as currency to pay road construction crews in New Jersey.

mason-jar.fait: The metal lid of this jar lets you check, with a simple touch of a finger, that the preserves are properly vacuum-sealed.

carlsbad.fait: This New Mexico park has 83 separate caves; Carlsbad Cavern contains one of the largest underground chambers.

nahanni.fait: At Virginia Falls, this park's river plunges twice the height of Niagara; in practice, it can only be reached by floatplane or helicopter.

columbia-icefield.fait: This icefield in the Rockies caps a triple divide; in summer, tourists travel across its Athabasca Glacier in snowcoaches.

ranch.fait: This dressing made with mayonnaise and dried herbs seasons salads in the United States, but also serves as a dip.

fudge.fait: Grainier than caramel, this confection made with butter, sugar, and milk has the advantage of not sticking to your teeth.

devils-food.fait: This “devil's” chocolate cake is seen as the counterpart of angel food cake; it too was born in the United States in the early 20th century.

chiffon-cake.fait: This very airy cake, originally from the United States, is made with vegetable oil, eggs, sugar, flour, and baking powder.

blt.fait: Its name sums up its recipe: B for bacon, L for lettuce, and T for tomato, all between two slices of bread.

chicken-nuggets.fait: These croquettes were invented by a Cornell University professor, who published his recipe without a patent, long before McNuggets.

oysters-rockefeller.fait: These baked oysters are topped with a butter and parsley sauce, sometimes with spinach, to give them their famous green color.

zombie-cocktail.fait: This tiki cocktail blending fruit juices, liqueurs, and rums was born in late 1934 in Hollywood, at Donn Beach's restaurant Don the Beachcomber.

dry-martini.fait: This cocktail of gin and dry vermouth, not to be confused with the Italian brand Martini, is James Bond's favorite.

aviation.fait: This gin cocktail owes its sky-blue color to crème de violette; it was reportedly created in 1916 by the head bartender of a New York hotel.

autoharp.fait: It was with this stringed instrument that Nikola Tesla carried out his first wireless telegraphy experiments, at Pikes Peak in 1896.

washboard.fait: This instrument, born in New Orleans, is a repurposed laundry tool, played by rubbing it with thimbles.

tiffany-lamp.fait: The glass in these lampshades is assembled with copper foil, not with lead as in the classic stained-glass technique.

conestoga.fait: This seatless wagon forced the driver to ride on a left-hand horse; it is credited with the habit of driving on the right.

covered-wagon.fait: Its canvas cover, reminiscent of a sail, earned it the nickname “prairie schooner”; thousands of pioneers took it West.

muscle-car.fait: Unlike the rare powerful cars of the prewar era, bought mainly by the well-off, these cars sold at prices young people could afford.

zoot-suit.fait: During the shortages of World War II, this suit, popularized by jazz singers, was considered unpatriotic because it wasted fabric.

rose-parade.fait: The floats in this Pasadena parade are decorated exclusively with natural materials, such as flowers or wood.

kentucky-derby.fait: Nicknamed the “Run for the Roses,” this race for 3-year-old horses is the first leg of the American Triple Crown.

pickleball.fait: This racket sport was born in 1965 as a children's game in a backyard on Bainbridge Island, in Washington State.

barbacoa.fait: Nicknamed “barbacha,” this way of cooking meat dates back to pre-Hispanic times; its most famous version comes from the state of Hidalgo.

queso-oaxaca.fait: This semi-hard cheese, also called quesillo, is named after the Mexican state where it originated.

banane-flambee.fait: Hailing from New Orleans, this caramelized banana, served with vanilla ice cream, is flambéed with rum.

piment-poblano.fait: This large chili pepper from Puebla is fairly mild; once dried, it changes its name and becomes the ancho chili, “wide chili.”

kin-ball.fait: This sport created in Quebec pits three teams against each other at once around a very large ball that must not be allowed to touch the ground.

pizza-sushi.fait: Invented in Toronto, this pizza has a fried rice patty as its base, topped with avocado and then salmon, tuna, or crab.

detroit-pizza.fait: In Detroit, this rectangular pizza was originally baked in steel trays designed for the automotive industry or for factory parts.

turducken.fait: This dish is a turkey stuffed with a duck, itself stuffed with a chicken; its name blends the English words for the three birds.

hot-brown.fait: This hot sandwich was invented at the Brown Hotel in Louisville to replace the eggs and ham served at late-night dinners.

krump.fait: Born in Los Angeles, this dance looks aggressive but rules out any physical confrontation: the rage on the faces expresses effort and unsettles the opponent.

popping.fait: This funk dance, popularized by a Californian group, rests on one basic principle: contracting and then releasing your muscles to the beat.

jigme-dorji.fait: About 6,500 people live in this park, from subsistence farming and herding, and it covers all three of Bhutan's climate zones.

lac-manchar.fait: The Mohana people traditionally live here on boats that form floating villages; according to legend, they are descended from Noah.

nagarkot.fait: It is the only place in the Kathmandu Valley from which the Everest range can be seen during the monsoon season.

tilicho.fait: This high-altitude lake was only discovered in 1950, by the French Annapurna expedition that was looking for a route to the summit.

namche-bazar.fait: Nicknamed the “Sherpa capital,” this town is the last one that would-be Everest climbers pass through before the first base camp.

kala-patthar.fait: It is not a true summit but a viewpoint over Everest; in 2009, a cabinet meeting was held at its base to raise the alarm about global warming.

bardia.fait: This park is what remains of the royal family's former hunting grounds, once sparsely populated because of malaria epidemics.

rani-pokhari.fait: In the center of this artificial pond in Kathmandu stands the Ghanta Ghar, Nepal's first public clock tower.

vat-phnom.fait: This pagoda, whose name means “temple hill,” is among the oldest in Phnom Penh, even though the current building dates from 1926.

ta-keo.fait: This state temple was never completed: work stopped when a rival king took the throne, hence its rough appearance.

pre-rup.fait: Its name supposedly refers to a funeral rite, “changing the form” in Khmer, but it more likely comes from a Sanskrit word meaning “having various forms.”

banteay-kdei.fait: The name of this Buddhist temple, built by King Jayavarman VII at the Angkor site, means “the citadel of monastic cells.”

bakong.fait: A model for many Khmer temple-mountains, this pyramid was rebuilt in the 20th century from a mere heap of stones.

kbal-spean.fait: Lingas were meticulously carved into the very bed of this river, deep in the jungle; the area remained inaccessible until 1998 because of land mines.

bako.fait: At the foot of this park's cliffs, the waves have carved arches and sea stacks, colored by iron deposits.

khao-soi.fait: Somewhere between curry and soup, this dish from northern Thailand is said to come from Muslim traders; its noodles are traditionally cut with scissors.

wat-saket.fait: The gilded chedi of this Bangkok temple, set on an artificial hill, gives it its nickname; it is said to house a relic of the Buddha.

wat-mahathat-ayutthaya.fait: In this Ayutthaya temple, a Buddha head is entwined in the roots of a strangler fig.

phanom-rung.fait: This Khmer temple was built on top of an extinct volcano, whose crater was turned into a drinking water reservoir.

phimai.fait: This Buddhist sanctuary is the most important Khmer temple in present-day Thailand; an inscription from Angkor places it on an imperial road.

ko-tao.fait: This small island in the Gulf of Thailand, roughly half of whose inhabitants are Burmese, has become a world-renowned scuba diving hotspot.

khao-sok.fait: This national park includes Cheow Lan Lake, held back by the Ratchaprapha Dam, which produces electricity for the region.

wat-traimit.fait: This gold statue, described as the largest in the world, stands in a temple in Bangkok's Chinatown.

chao-phraya.fait: This river bears the name of the highest Thai noble title; in Thai, “river” is “maenam,” literally “mother” and “water.”

khao-phing-kan.fait: Since its appearance in “The Man with the Golden Gun” in 1974, this pair of islands has been nicknamed James Bond Island.

wai.fait: This greeting gesture, linked to Buddhism and Hinduism, is also found elsewhere in Asia: in Cambodia, it is called sampeah.

pagode-tran-quoc.fait: This pagoda, the oldest in Hanoi, was built in the 6th century on a small peninsula of West Lake.

pagode-parfums.fait: During its festival, hundreds of thousands of pilgrims travel to this temple complex, whose heart is nestled in a cave.

mui-ne.fait: The name of this seaside resort means “Cape Né”; it is a popular destination with Russian and Chinese tourists.

tam-coc.fait: This system of flooded limestone caves is the main boat landing for what is nicknamed “Ha Long Bay on land.”

montagnes-marbre.fait: These five marble hills are each named after an element: metal, water, wood, fire, and earth; they hide caves and shrines.

po-nagar.fait: This Cham temple in Nha Trang is dedicated to the goddess Yan Po Nagar, the legendary founder of the kingdom of Champā.

col-hai-van.fait: This “Pass of the Clouds” separates Huế from Đà Nẵng and even marks a difference in accent between their inhabitants.

vovinam.fait: This martial art, known for its acrobatic scissor kicks, has as its symbol the bamboo, which “bends but does not break.”

jeepney.fait: Originally, these public transport vehicles were jeeps abandoned by the U.S. Army after World War II, then converted.

mont-pulag.fait: This mountain is the highest point on Luzon, the largest island of the Philippines, and the third-highest peak in the country.

croix-magellan.fait: This wooden cross, erected in 1521 when Magellan's explorers arrived in Cebu, is now protected by a chapel.

tongkonan.fait: In original Toraja society, only nobles could build these houses on stilts with boat-shaped roofs.

dieng.fait: This volcanic plateau, still active, preserves small Hindu temples that are among the oldest stone architecture on Java.

goa-gajah.fait: This temple in Bali, nicknamed “Elephant Cave,” may first have been Buddhist before becoming a Hindu sanctuary.

mendut.fait: This Buddhist temple near Borobudur houses a Buddha seated “in the European style,” accompanied by two statues of bodhisattvas.
