trifle.fait: This English dessert layers custard, fruit, sponge cake and whipped cream; Quebec has a cousin of it, the bagatelle.

charrette-foin.fait: This painting, known in English as “The Hay Wain,” was completed by John Constable in 1821 and hangs in the National Gallery in London.

banoffee.fait: Its name blends “banana” and “toffee”: this English pie combines banana, dulce de leche and whipped cream on a biscuit base.

temeraire.fait: In it, Turner shows HMS Temeraire, a ship that played a crucial role at Trafalgar, being towed by a steam tug toward the place of its destruction.

eton-mess.fait: This traditional English dessert is simply a mix of strawberries, meringue and cream, sometimes with banana added.

bara-brith.fait: This Welsh fruit bread, whose name means “speckled bread,” is also popular in Argentina, where Welsh settlers brought it.

punch-judy.fait: This puppet show was first transcribed by John Payne Collier, who had come to watch Giovanni Piccini perform in a tavern.

cullen-skink.fait: This thick smoked haddock soup comes from the town of Cullen, in Scotland; it is served as an appetizer at formal dinners and in everyday meals alike.

casque-sutton-hoo.fait: On its mask, the eyebrows, nose and mustache form a dragon; the helmet was found shattered into more than 500 fragments.

palais-westminster.fait: The British Parliament sits in this palace, which was almost entirely destroyed by fire in 1834: only Westminster Hall escaped.

cathedrale-canterbury.fait: This cathedral was extended eastward to accommodate the pilgrims coming to the shrine of Thomas Becket, the archbishop murdered within its walls.

lake-district.fait: This region of lakes and mountains, linked to the poet William Wordsworth, is home to the highest point in England, Scafell Pike.

kew-gardens.fait: These London gardens also house one of the largest herbaria in the world, with more than seven million specimens.

blenheim.fait: This palace was given to the Duke of Marlborough for his victory at Blenheim, a Bavarian village that gave it its name.

loch-lomond.fait: This loch south of the Highlands belongs to three Scottish regions at once: Stirling, Argyll and Bute, and West Dunbartonshire.

royal-albert-hall.fait: In 1941, General de Gaulle gave a speech here to the French people in Great Britain, broadcast by the BBC.

holyrood.fait: Originally a monastery founded by King David I, this Edinburgh palace houses British monarchs during their official stays in Scotland.

chateau-stirling.fait: Built on a volcanic crag bordered by cliffs on three sides, this Scottish castle was contested between the Scots and the English from the very beginning.

york-minster.fait: The seat of the Archbishop of York, second in the Anglican hierarchy, this cathedral is the largest Gothic building in Northern Europe.

royal-pavilion.fait: The future King George IV had this seaside residence built in Brighton in an Anglo-Indian style, then very widespread in India.

machine-anticythere.fait: Recovered from the wreck of a Roman galley, this bronze mechanism with toothed wheels made it possible to calculate astronomical positions.

masque-agamemnon.fait: Schliemann believed he had found the body of Agamemnon, but this gold mask is thought to predate the supposed date of the Trojan War by several centuries.

aurige-delphes.fait: Buried by a landslide, this bronze spent twenty-four centuries underground, hence its brownish-green color.

dieu-artemision.fait: The sinking of the ship carrying it saved this statue from being melted down, the fate bronzes suffered at the end of Antiquity.

deesse-serpents.fait: These figurines of a Minoan goddess linked to the underworld were found during the excavations of the palace of Knossos, on Crete.

ephebe-anticythere.fait: This bronze young man was discovered in 1900 by divers in the Antikythera wreck, off the island, in the Aegean Sea.

jockey-artemision.fait: This bronze young boy on horseback escaped melting down, the fate of most ancient bronzes, thanks to the shipwreck that swallowed it.

cratere-derveni.fait: This volute vase was found in a tomb in the Derveni necropolis, near Thessaloniki, in whose museum it is kept.

temple-hephaistos.fait: This Doric temple in Athens, also wrongly called the Theseion, served as an Orthodox church dedicated to Saint George from the 7th century until 1834.

lycabette.fait: You can climb this Athens hill by funicular; on its two summits stand a Chapel of Saint George and an amphitheater.

plaka.fait: This old Athens neighborhood, at the foot of the Acropolis, is a maze of little streets full of restaurants and souvenir shops.

achilleion.fait: Empress Sisi had this palace in Corfu built in honor of Achilles; Kaiser Wilhelm II later bought it.

livre-durrow.fait: This illuminated gospel book from the late 7th century long belonged to the treasury of Durrow Abbey; it is now at Trinity College.

chateau-dublin.fait: Until 1922, this castle housed the seat of the British administration in Ireland; it is built on an old castle mound.

killarney.fait: Founded in 1932, it is Ireland's first national park; it lies in County Kerry, on the “Ring of Kerry” route.

christ-church-dublin.fait: This Anglican cathedral is the older of Dublin's two medieval cathedrals, the other being St. Patrick's Cathedral.

phoenix-park.fait: Its name comes from the Gaelic “fionn uisce,” “clear water”; this vast Dublin park is home to a herd of wild fallow deer.

croagh-patrick.fait: On the last Sunday of July, more than 25,000 pilgrims climb this holy mountain, many of them barefoot, in honor of Saint Patrick.

benbulben.fait: This mountain rises in County Sligo, in an area known as “Yeats Country.”

knowth.fait: In this Neolithic tomb, the cremated remains of the dead were placed in stone basins at the back of a cross-shaped chamber.

gallarus.fait: Scholars disagree about this small stone building: an early Christian church, a private chapel or a shelter for pilgrims.

chateau-cahir.fait: Built on an island in the River Suir, this castle surrendered to Cromwell in 1650 without a single shot being fired.

cene-vinci.fait: Leonardo da Vinci painted this scene on the wall of the refectory of a Dominican convent in Milan, Santa Maria delle Grazie.

david-michel-ange.fait: This statue comes from a block of marble abandoned by other sculptors; Michelangelo carved out the space between the arm and the torso in a crack in the block.

homme-vitruve.fait: This drawing by Leonardo da Vinci inscribes a man's body both in a circle, centered on the navel, and in a square.

naissance-venus.fait: This painting by Botticelli was revolutionary: it showed a nude body without any religious justification, on a mythological theme.

louve-capitoline.fait: This bronze she-wolf, linked to the legend of Romulus and Remus and to the founding of Rome, has been in the Capitoline Museums since 1471.

printemps-botticelli.fait: This painting brings together mythological figures in a garden, but no known story explains why this group is gathered.

extase-therese.fait: Bernini sculpted this marble group and designed the entire Roman chapel around it, from the architecture to the decoration.

pizza-margherita.fait: This pizza in the colors of Italy, born in Naples, is topped with tomato sauce, mozzarella and fresh basil.

gressin.fait: This small, dry, elongated bread from Piedmont is usually no thicker than a pen; its creation dates back to the 14th century.

sambuca.fait: This sweet, strong star anise liqueur was created in Civitavecchia, in the province of Rome, and is usually 40% alcohol.

pandoro.fait: Its name means “golden bread”: this Christmas cake from Verona is shaped like a star-shaped truncated cone, dusted with powdered sugar.

grana-padano.fait: This cooked, pressed cow's milk cheese comes from the valleys of northern Italy; it is best enjoyed from May to August.

marsala.fait: This fortified wine from Sicily, dry or sweet, is named after the town of Marsala, around which it is produced.

moise-michel-ange.fait: This statue by Michelangelo is part of the tomb of Julius II, in the Basilica of San Pietro in Vincoli in Rome.

saltimbocca.fait: Its name means “jumps in the mouth”: this Roman-style veal cutlet is topped with cured ham and sage, then cooked in butter.

amatriciana.fait: This sauce, born in Amatrice, derives from a shepherd's dish made from dried products; tomato and chili pepper were only added later.

bicerin.fait: This Piedmontese drink, born in Turin, combines espresso, hot chocolate and milk or cream in a single glass.

cacio-e-pepe.fait: This pasta from Rome and Lazio is made with black pepper and pecorino romano cheese.

caponata.fait: This Sicilian dish was first made with fish, which was gradually replaced by cheaper eggplant; it is sweetened with raisins or honey.

piadina.fait: In the words of Giovanni Pascoli, this flatbread from Romagna is “the bread, indeed the national food, of the Romagnoli.”

nduja.fait: The name of this spicy pork sausage, born in Calabria, comes from the French word “andouille.”

castel-del-monte.fait: With no drawbridge or moat, this castle built in Apulia by Emperor Frederick II may never have had a defensive role.

arenes-verone.fait: This Roman amphitheater is still used as a performance venue: every summer since 1913, it has hosted the Verona festival.

trinite-des-monts.fait: Funded by the bequest of a French diplomat, this Rome staircase links a church then under the patronage of the kings of France to the square of the Spanish embassy.

burano.fait: This island in the Venetian Lagoon is known for its lace and for its canals lined with brightly colored houses.

ta-hagrat.fait: These Neolithic megalithic temples serve as the reference site for an entire period of Maltese prehistory, the Mġarr phase.

fort-rikasoli.fait: Built by the Knights of the Order of Saint John, this fort in Malta has a film studio, Malta Film Studios, as its immediate neighbor.

skorba.fait: The finds made in this Neolithic village, later crowned by two temples, made it possible to define the “Grey Skorba” and “Red Skorba” phases.

fort-manoel.fait: Standing on an island in Marsamxett Harbour, north of Valletta, this fort commands the entrance to the harbor and the anchorage of Sliema.

tour-sainte-agathe.fait: This coastal tower built in the 17th century in Mellieħa is better known as the “Red Tower,” because of its color.

mangeurs-pommes-terre.fait: Van Gogh painted this canvas in Nuenen after many studies: he said he felt this painting so well that he could “literally see it in a dream.”

champ-ble-corbeaux.fait: Kept at the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam, this canvas painted a few days before the painter's death was long thought to be his last, an idea since disproved.

fiancee-juive.fait: Van Gogh said he would give ten years of his life to sit for two weeks in front of this Rembrandt canvas, with only dry bread to eat.

petite-rue-vermeer.fait: This Delft street corner is, along with the View of Delft, one of only two outdoor paintings by Vermeer that have come down to us.

syndics-drapiers.fait: Completed in 1662, this canvas on display at the Rijksmuseum has been described as Rembrandt's “last great group portrait.”

amandier.fait: Van Gogh painted this blossoming tree in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence in February 1890, but the canvas is kept at the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam.

lettre-amour.fait: Seen through a doorway, a maid has probably just brought her mistress a letter, which the mistress is still holding sealed.

victory-boogie.fait: Painted in New York, this last painting by Mondrian was left unfinished at his death; it is now kept at the municipal museum of The Hague.

palais-paix.fait: This palace in The Hague houses the United Nations' International Court of Justice, the Permanent Court of Arbitration and an academy of law.

palais-royal-amsterdam.fait: This palace on Dam Square was built to serve as a town hall; it has only been used as a royal palace since 1808.

westerkerk.fait: Built between the Prinsengracht and the Keizersgracht, this Protestant church in Amsterdam is one of the best-known landmarks of the Grachtengordel.

vondelpark.fait: Opened in 1865, this Amsterdam park is named after the poet Joost van den Vondel, to whom it pays tribute; it lies near the Museumplein.

acorda.fait: This soup or bread panada is made with bread, garlic, herbs and olive oil; each region of the country has its own recipe.

se-lisbonne.fait: The oldest church in Lisbon, this cathedral was built on the orders of King Afonso I, some time after he had retaken the city from the Moors.

cap-saint-vincent.fait: This cape marks the southwestern tip of the Iberian Peninsula and even of the Eurasian continent; a monastery and later a lighthouse were built there.

mafra.fait: This baroque palace was born of a vow: King John V had it built after Queen Maria Anna of Austria gave him heirs.

couvent-carmo.fait: Collapsed in the earthquake of 1755, the church of this convent was never rebuilt: its ruins house an archaeological museum.

sanctuaire-fatima.fait: Among the monuments of this major Catholic pilgrimage center, in Fátima, is a piece of the Berlin Wall, added over time.

algar-carvao.fait: This “coal cave” is actually an ancient lava tube, or volcanic vent, located in the center of Terceira Island, in the Azores.

lagunes-sete-cidades.fait: These lakes lie at the bottom of the caldera that crowns the Sete Cidades volcano, on São Miguel Island, in the Azores archipelago.

dispute-saint-sacrement.fait: This fresco by Raphael owes a somewhat inaccurate name to Vasari: its upper part glorifies the Church in heaven more than it shows a debate.

liberation-st-pierre.fait: Pope Julius II, who commissioned this fresco, rests in the Basilica of San Pietro in Vincoli, which keeps the chains said to have bound Saint Peter.

messe-bolsena.fait: Painted in 1512 by Raphael and his assistants, this fresco in the Apostolic Palace depicts the Eucharistic miracle of Bolsena.

jardins-pontificaux.fait: These gardens cover more than half of the Vatican's territory and even house Vatican Radio, a monastery and the Saint John's Tower.

chapelle-nicoline.fait: Pope Nicholas V had this chapel built for his personal use, and Fra Angelico painted its frescoes in the mid-15th century.

chapelle-pauline.fait: Reserved for the pope, this chapel is not open to visitors; its walls bear Michelangelo's last two paintings.

hulhumale.fait: This island was extended out into the sea to provide a solution to the overcrowding of Malé, the nearby capital.

meghna.fait: This river receives the waters of the Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna basin, then flows into the Bay of Bengal.

sukkur-barrage.fait: This barrage on the Indus was built under the British Raj; it was originally called the Lloyd Barrage.

sri-ksetra.fait: Its Sanskrit name means “city of splendor”: it was a kingdom in the Irrawaddy basin between the 7th and 9th centuries.

ta-som.fait: This small Buddhist temple at Angkor, built in the Bayon style, has gates topped with four-faced towers.

thommanon.fait: Its enclosure is broken on the north and south sides: gates were probably planned there, but only the east and west ones exist.

banteay-chhmar.fait: This massive temple, surrounded by eight satellite temples, is one of the most important and least understood sites of the Angkor era.

phimeanakas.fait: It was said that the king joined there at night with a protective goddess, who then left her serpent body for that of a young woman.

preah-ko.fait: Its name means “the sacred bull”: it is the first Khmer temple in the Angkor region, and its towers honor deified kings.

srah-srang.fait: The name of this large Angkor basin means “the royal bath”; its terrace and surrounds are made of sandstone.

baray-occidental.fait: This reservoir, the largest at Angkor, has at its center an artificial islet on which a Hindu temple was built.

island-peak.fait: An expedition gave it this name, comparing it to an island in an ocean of ice; from its summit, Everest remains hidden by Lhotse.

mera-peak.fait: From this summit, accessible to trekkers, you can see Everest, Lhotse, Cho Oyu, Makalu and Kangchenjunga.

langtang.fait: This park was the first national park in the Himalayas; its northern and eastern boundaries coincide with the border of Tibet.

san-sebastian-manille.nom: San Sebastian Basilica, the Steel Church
san-sebastian-manille.fait: This Neo-Gothic basilica in Manila is notable for being built of steel, a unique example in Asia.

kanlaon.fait: This volcano, the highest point on the island of Negros, is one of the most active in this region of the Philippine archipelago.

hamiguitan.fait: Its pygmy mossy forest is unique; there you can see the Philippine eagle and pitcher plants, some of which exist only in this region.

fort-san-pedro.fait: This fort in Cebu was built in 1565 by the Spanish conquistadors led by Miguel López de Legazpi.

pad-thai.fait: This national dish, pad thai, blends sour, sweet, salty and spicy flavors around rice noodles stir-fried in a wok.

nuad-thai.fait: This ancient therapy is inscribed on the list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity; the state has coordinated its revival since the 1980s.

maison-jim-thompson.fait: This Bangkok museum brings together six old houses acquired by an American who wanted to revive the country's silk, before mysteriously disappearing.

wat-suthat.fait: This temple in the Phra Nakhon district of Bangkok is one of the six royal temples of the country.

wat-phra-si-sanphet.fait: This temple takes its name from a bronze Buddha covered with gold plates, 16 meters tall, which King Rama Thibodi II had placed there.

ko-chang.fait: Its name means “elephant island”; mountainous, with several waterfalls, it is the largest island in a park that has dozens of islands and islets.

riviere-parfums.fait: It owes its name to the blossoms of fruit trees that fall into it in autumn and then perfume the city of Hue.

candi-sukuh.fait: This 15th-century Javanese temple is still a place of worship: Balinese people still come here on pilgrimage.

tirta-gangga.fait: This former royal palace in eastern Bali owes its reputation to its water palace, owned by the royal family of Karangasem.

gunung-kawi.fait: This temple brings together ten shrines carved into the cliff, believed to be dedicated to King Anak Wungsu and his wives.

tangkuban-perahu.fait: The name of this volcano in western Java, just north of Bandung, literally means “upturned boat.”

maninjau.fait: This lake in Sumatra actually lies in a caldera, and its name comes from a word meaning “observation.”

nusa-penida.fait: This island, separated from Bali by the Badung Strait, has two small neighbors: Nusa Lembongan and Nusa Ceningan.

lorentz.fait: This park in Papua is the only reserve in the Asia-Pacific region to cover the full range of environments, from marine areas to glaciers.

way-kambas.fait: This park in Sumatra is home to a breeding center where Sumatran rhinos sent from zoos come to acclimatize.

baluran.fait: This park in eastern Java, with a drier climate than the rest of the island, combines forest, savanna and mangrove and is named after the Baluran volcano.

kulfi.fait: To make this ice cream, the Mughal emperors are said to have brought ice from the Himalayan mountains.

victoria-memorial.fait: The bronze angel at the top of its dome is mounted on ball bearings: it turns like a weather vane when the wind is strong.

buland-darwaza.fait: This “high gate” was built by the Mughal emperor Akbar to celebrate his victory over Gujarat.

fort-agra.fait: This former Mughal imperial residence, surrounded by red sandstone walls, is the largest fort in the country.

gol-gumbaz.fait: This mausoleum of a sultan of Bijapur is topped by a dome with an inner diameter of 38 meters.

jama-masjid-delhi.fait: Its Persian name means “world-reflecting mosque”; built under Shah Jahan, it can hold 25,000 people.

palais-mysore.fait: This palace is illuminated on Sundays, on public holidays and every evening during the ten days of the Navratri festival.

city-palace-jaipur.fait: Here you can see two enormous silver jars that carried Ganges water to England for a maharaja who refused to drink English water.

lake-palace.fait: This former summer residence of the maharanas, on an island in Lake Pichola, has become a hotel reached by boat.

fort-jaisalmer.fait: This fort is still home to nearly a quarter of the old city's population, and its yellow sandstone walls take on a honey hue at sunset.

brihadesvara.fait: This temple in Thanjavur, one of the largest in the country, also bears the name of its builder: the Rajarajesvaram temple.

temple-rivage.fait: This temple owes its name to its location: it was built at the edge of the sea, on a promontory jutting into the Bay of Bengal.

vallee-des-fleurs.fait: There are more than 500 species of flowering plants in this Himalayan park, which is associated with Nanda Devi National Park.

ranthambore.fait: This park in Rajasthan, made up of lakes and cliffs, is considered one of the best places to observe the country's wildlife.

kanha.fait: The sal and bamboo forests of this tiger reserve inspired Rudyard Kipling's novel The Jungle Book.

nanda-devi.fait: Its name means “goddess of Bliss”; it is the highest mountain located entirely within the country's territory.

padma.fait: This river is fed mostly by the Ganges, so much so that one could say it is the Ganges changing its name as it crosses the border.

jamuna.fait: The sandbars of this river, called chars, disappear and re-form with the seasons, blurring the boundaries of districts.

makli.fait: This necropolis in Sindh, built mostly under the Mughal Empire, is said to contain up to a million tombs.

tombe-anarkali.fait: This Mughal tomb stands in Lahore, in the province of Punjab; it was built in 1615 by Jahangir.

lal-suhanra.fait: This national park in Punjab, in the Bahawalpur district, has also been declared a biosphere reserve by UNESCO.

knuckles.fait: These mountains in the center of the country, in the Matale and Kandy districts, once had a completely different name: Dumbara Kanduvetiya.

mebon-oriental.fait: This 10th-century Angkor temple was built on what was an artificial island, in the middle of a now-dry reservoir: the East Baray.

west-mebon.fait: A bronze reclining Vishnu more than five meters long was unearthed here, the largest ancient statue of its kind found in Cambodia.

thorong-la.fait: At 5,416 meters, this pass is the highest point of the Annapurna Circuit; besides trekkers, many Nepalis traditionally use it.

shivapuri.fait: This park in the hills north of the Kathmandu Valley takes its name from Mount Shivapuri, over which it extends.

hibok-hibok.fait: This volcano, also called Catarman, rises on the small island of Camiguin, just north of the large island of Mindanao.

santa-maria-ilocos.fait: Instead of occupying the central plaza as Spanish tradition dictated, this church stands on a hill surrounded by defensive walls.

lumpini.fait: This public park in Bangkok is linked to Benjakitti Park by the “Green Bridge,” an elevated walkway for pedestrians and cyclists.

vimanmek.fait: This former royal palace in Bangkok is the largest teak residence in the world; it was dismantled from the Dusit royal estate in 2019.

ko-samet.fait: This narrow T-shaped island attracts tourists and Thais alike thanks to its proximity to Bangkok and its white sand beaches.

tarutao.fait: This marine park groups together 51 islands in the Strait of Malacca, off Satun province; the sea covers most of its area.

kaeng-krachan.fait: The largest national park in Thailand, it lies in the border zone with Myanmar and adjoins a nature reserve on the other side.

sam-roi-yot.fait: Its name means “mountain of three hundred peaks”; it is the oldest marine national park in Thailand.

muang-tam.fait: No inscription has been found there yet: it is the style of the lintels that makes it possible to date this Khmer temple dedicated to Shiva.

ping-river.fait: This river in Thailand is, along with the Nan, one of the two main tributaries of the Chao Phraya River.

long-bien.fait: This bridge that crosses the Red River in Hanoi was once called the Paul Doumer Bridge.

phat-diem.fait: Built by Father Six at the end of the 19th century, this cathedral is the largest Catholic architectural complex in Vietnam.

candi-sewu.fait: Its Javanese name means “the thousand temples”; this Buddhist sanctuary is older than Prambanan, its Shaivite neighbor.

candi-plaosan.fait: This Buddhist sanctuary in Central Java, located not far from Prambanan Temple, is thought to date from the 9th century.

penataran.fait: On the slopes of the Kelud volcano, this sanctuary is the last still-visible example in Java of a type of temple from the Majapahit era.

wakatobi.fait: This name is a portmanteau formed from the first letters of the four main islands: Wangi-Wangi, Kaledupa, Tomia, and Binongko.

bunaken.fait: This marine park, renowned for diving, is home to almost every species of giant clam in the world.

lac-batur.fait: This crater lake, nestled in the Batur caldera between two mountains, is the largest lake on the island of Bali.

karimunjawa.fait: This archipelago of 27 rocky islands in the Java Sea should not be confused with the island of Karimun, in the Riau Islands.

kepulauan-seribu.fait: This string of islands, also called the “thousand islands,” stretches 45 km across the Java Sea, off Jakarta, the capital.

kebun-raya-bogor.fait: Founded in 1817 by the government of the Dutch East Indies, this garden was meant to bring together, for study, the plants the Javanese used as remedies.

kota-tua.fait: This district, the original heart of Jakarta, was called “Old Batavia” in Dutch; it includes the Chinatown of Glodok.

istana-bogor.fait: This presidential palace, next to the botanical garden, once served as the residence of the governor-general of the Dutch East Indies.

fort-rotterdam.fait: Built in the 17th century by the Dutch VOC on the site of the old Jum Pandan fort, the origin of “Ujung Pandang,” for a time the name of Makassar.

trowulan.fait: This site is believed to have been the capital of the kingdom of Majapahit, whose palace is described in an epic poem written in 1365.

gedong-songo.fait: Its Javanese name means “nine buildings”: these groups of Hindu temples are numbered from the lowest to the highest on the volcano.

muara-takus.fait: Its great stupa has the unusual shape of a tower, rather than the bell shape typical of Buddhist architecture.

gunung-padang.fait: This megalithic site in West Java keeps its mystery: its dating is still a subject of controversy.

bibi-ka-maqbara.fait: This mausoleum, built by a son of Aurangzeb for his mother, is nicknamed the “Taj of the Deccan” because it so closely resembles the Taj Mahal.

chittorgarh.fait: More than a fort, it is a fortified city: the former capital of the kingdom of Mewar, with its palaces, temples, and victory towers.

kumbhalgarh.fait: On clear days, from this fort in Rajasthan, you can see beyond the Aravalli Range to the distant dunes of the Thar Desert.

pont-howrah.fait: Renamed in honor of the poet Rabindranath Tagore, this Kolkata bridge is nevertheless still commonly called Howrah Bridge.

jim-corbett.fait: The oldest national park in India, it is known for its wildlife and for serving as the launch site of Project Tiger.

gede-pangrango.fait: This park nestled between two volcanoes was created by merging several protected areas, including the Cibodas Botanical Gardens.

demak.fait: This mosque in Central Java is said to be the oldest in Indonesia; Demak was once a Muslim kingdom.

itimad-ud-daulah.fait: Nicknamed the “Baby Taj,” this older mausoleum laid the architectural groundwork for the Taj Mahal; Nur Jahan had it built for her father.

phnom-krom.fait: This Hindu temple crowns a natural hill southwest of Angkor; it is uncertain which of two kings of the same name built it.

roi-lepreux.fait: This 12th-century terrace, next to the Terrace of the Elephants, faces the great royal square of Angkor Thom.

yak-loum.fait: This almost perfectly round lake fills an old volcanic crater; hill tribes believe it is inhabited by protective spirits.

ream.fait: This park near Sihanoukville combines beaches, mangroves, and tropical jungles, and it is well known for its monkey population.

virachey.fait: The largest park in Cambodia, it remains largely unexplored, in thick jungle in one of the most isolated regions of the country.

makalu-barun.fait: Created as an extension of Sagarmatha park, this park protects both very high peaks and the Arun Valley.

shukla-phanta.fait: This reserve, made up mostly of grasslands, is famous for its barasingha deer; it is also home to a few tigers.

shey-phoksundo.fait: The largest park in Nepal, its main attraction is Phoksundo Lake, now listed as a Ramsar site.

poon-hill.fait: This summit near the village of Ghorepani is a viewpoint popular with tourists, facing Annapurna and Dhaulagiri.

aloo-gobi.fait: This “dry” curry of potatoes and cauliflower has a prominent place in the film “Bend It Like Beckham.”

balushahi.fait: Called badusha in the south of India, this pastry may look like a glazed doughnut, but it differs in texture and taste.

sankirtana.fait: In Manipur, these ritual songs, accompanied by drums and dance, mark religious ceremonies and the stages of the faithful's lives.

salt-range.fait: This mountain range in Punjab is made of vast deposits of rock salt and includes the Khewra, Warcha, and Kalabagh salt mines.

monts-kirthar.fait: This range marks the border between two provinces, Balochistan and Sindh, and contains a large part of a national park.

sacre-coeur-lahore.fait: This Romanesque-Byzantine cathedral, consecrated in 1907, is the main Catholic place of worship in Lahore.

lac-beira.fait: This artificial lake in the heart of Colombo has kept its Portuguese name, even though the Dutch and then the British also used it.

crocker.fait: This range in northern Borneo culminates at Mount Kinabalu, the highest point of both Malaysia and the entire island.

bukit-larut.fait: Formerly called Maxwell Hill, this “hill station,” or high-altitude town, is nestled in the Bintang Range of Perak.

ile-gaya.fait: This island in the state of Sabah, very close to the city of Kota Kinabalu, is protected: it is part of Tunku Abdul Rahman National Park.

sisters-islands.fait: These two islands are separated by a narrow channel whose currents can be very dangerous for swimmers and divers.

hotel-de-ville-sg.fait: This building was simply called the “Municipal Building” until 1951, when King George VI granted Singapore city status.

ile-bhola.fait: The largest island in Bangladesh, it was half swallowed by the waters in 2005; its inhabitants have been described as among the world's first climate refugees.

bulusan.fait: This volcano in southern Luzon rises at the boundary between the Philippine and Eurasian plates, which makes it a subduction volcano.

lac-taal.fait: This lake on the island of Luzon fills a crater, and it once had another name: it was called Lake Bombon.

sibuyan.fait: This very wild island in the province of Romblon is home to endemic plant species; its highest point is Mount Guiting-Guiting.

cerro-pero.fait: This mountain in the department of Guairá, also called Cerro Tres Kandú, is the highest point in Paraguay.

grande-mosquee-paramaribo.fait: Also called the Great Mosque of Paramaribo, this mosque in Suriname is a place of worship of the Ahmadiyya Muslim community.

chemin-fer-nauru.fait: This single line makes up the entire rail network of Nauru: it carries only phosphate, the country's sole resource in the 20th century.

kukenan.fait: This tepui in the Sierra de Pacaraima rests on the Precambrian shield of the Guiana Highlands, in Venezuela.

lac-tota.fait: This natural lake in Boyacá is the largest body of water in Colombia; one of the municipalities on its shores is also called Tota.

san-francisco-lapaz.nom: Basilica of San Francisco, La Paz
san-francisco-lapaz.fait: This church in La Paz, dedicated to Francis of Assisi, gave its name to the downtown square where it stands.

pumapunku.fait: In Aymara, the name of this vast ceremonial complex at Tiwanaku, near Lake Titicaca, means “the Gate of the Puma.”

tunupa.fait: This volcano bears the name of an Aymara deity linked to the origin of the Salar de Uyuni; its slopes hold a cave with Inca mummies.

alpamayo.fait: This peak in the Cordillera Blanca was proclaimed the “most beautiful mountain in the world” by the magazine Alpinismus in 1966.

ausangate.fait: This mountain holds a place in Inca mythology; nearby, the Qoyllurit'i festival, “snow star,” draws thousands of pilgrims every year.

ascenseur-lacerda.fait: This public elevator, one of the symbols of Salvador, Bahia, was built in the 19th century; its current concrete structure is much more recent.

ibera.fait: These marshes take their name from the Guarani Y vera, “shining water,” and form a wetland of international importance.

cathedrale-ste-marie-sydney.nom: St. Mary's Cathedral in Gothic Revival sandstone
cathedrale-ste-marie-sydney.fait: This Gothic cathedral in Sydney is at once a national shrine, a basilica, and the seat of the city's archbishop.

glacier-fox.fait: This glacier honors William Fox, a former prime minister of the country; its Māori name, Te Moeka o Tuawe, was only officially added to it in 1998.

medanos-coro.fait: This national park in the state of Falcón, in Venezuela, is also recognized as an important bird area.

desert-dali.fait: This desert owes its name to its arid ridges and isolated rocks, which recall the landscapes painted by Salvador Dalí.

amboro.fait: This park lies at the “Elbow of the Andes,” where the Bolivian Eastern Cordillera changes direction to run straight south.

guagua-pichincha.fait: This 4,776-meter volcano, located about ten kilometers west of Quito, towers over the capital of Ecuador.

bartolome.fait: This island in the Galápagos archipelago is uninhabited; it lies very close to Santiago Island, to the southeast.

arche-darwin.fait: This natural arch in the Galápagos collapsed due to erosion in 2021: only the side columns remain.

illiniza.fait: This volcano has two summits: Illiniza Sur, heavily snow-covered and popular with Andean climbers, and Illiniza Norte, much less white.

pululahua.fait: The giant crater of this extinct volcano, the largest in South America, is now an inhabited and cultivated valley.

palais-carondelet.fait: According to tradition, it was Simón Bolívar who named this presidential palace, after the baron who had its facade built.

cerro-catedral-uy.fait: This “cathedral hill” is the highest point in Uruguay, quite modest compared with the peaks of other Latin American countries.

plaza-cagancha.fait: Also called Plaza Libertad, this square in Montevideo is just as busy as Independence Square, which has become the main one.

santa-teresa-parc.fait: This national park on the Atlantic coast contains a fortress and has the distinction of being managed by the Uruguayan army.

cerro-animas.fait: Long thought to be the highest point in Uruguay, this hill flew the national flag atop the tallest flagpole in South America.

cathedrale-florida-uy.nom: Cathedral of Our Lady of Luján, Florida
cathedrale-florida-uy.fait: This church in Florida serves as the shrine of the Virgin of the Thirty-Three and holds the status of cathedral, basilica, and national shrine.

owen-stanley.fait: Sighted in 1849 by Captain Owen Stanley, who gave it his name, this range offers few passages, the easiest being the famous Kokoda Track.

ancohuma.fait: The name of this glaciated peak comes from the Aymara Janq'u Uma; it is the third-highest peak in Bolivia.

uturuncu.fait: Despite its altitude and isolation, part of this volcano can be climbed by motor vehicle; it still emits fumaroles.

laguna-hedionda.fait: Its Spanish name means “fetid lagoon”: this salt lake in the high Andes lies in the department of Potosí, in Bolivia.

isla-pescado.fait: This hill is surrounded not by water but by salt: on the flat, white Salar de Uyuni, it looks like an island.

tunari.fait: This park in the department of Cochabamba, created in 1962, covers 3,090 km² at altitudes between 2,200 and 4,400 meters.

jayu-khota.fait: Its Aymara name means “salt lake,” but it is a volcano in Bolivia, made up of a volcanic cone and two maars.

pic-cristobal-colon.fait: Named in honor of Christopher Columbus, this summit, probably the highest in Colombia, rises on the traditional territory of the Arhuaco people.

ritacuba.fait: If melting continues at its current pace, this summit's glacier will have disappeared by 2055; the Indigenous U'wa people live at its foot.

los-nevados.fait: This park dominated by the Nevado del Ruiz volcano was, in 2009, the third most visited national park in Colombia, with more than 50,000 visitors.

cocuy.fait: This sierra, whose highest point is Ritacuba Blanco at 5,330 meters, contains the largest glacier in Colombia as well as many lakes and waterfalls.

purace-parc.fait: This park's main attraction is an active volcano, and four of Colombia's most important rivers, including the Magdalena and the Cauca, rise in its region.

cathedrale-medellin.fait: This cathedral, the main church of Medellín, is also a basilica; it is also nicknamed the Villanueva Cathedral.

el-abra.fait: This name refers to a whole group of prehistoric sites, nestled in a valley that stretches between Zipaquirá and Tocancipá, in Colombia.

altar-volcan.fait: This extinct volcano in Ecuador forms a cirque crowned with many peaks, whose floor is occupied by a lake.

wolf-volcan.fait: The highest point of the Galápagos, this volcano is named after Theodor Wolf, a German geologist who studied the archipelago in the 19th century.

carihuairazo.fait: This volcano topped by a caldera has as its neighbor Chimborazo, the highest mountain in Ecuador.

cotacachi.fait: This probably extinct volcano has as its most beautiful crater Cuicocha, which has become a lake visited by tourists.

llanganates.fait: The name of this national park, which spans four provinces of Ecuador, comes from Quechua and means “beautiful mountain.”

sumaco.fait: Far from any inhabited area and any drivable road, this volcano covered in thick vegetation requires a week-long trek to climb.

pasochoa.fait: This extinct volcano has the shape of a semicircular collapsed crater, created by an eruption that destroyed the old crater and the western flank of the cone.

cascade-san-rafael.fait: This waterfall, once the highest in Ecuador, disappeared in 2020 according to NASA's Earth Observatory.

cueva-tayos.fait: This cave in the Ecuadorian Andes owes its name to the tayos, or oilbirds, birds that live in it.

lac-junin.fait: It is the largest lake located entirely in Peru: Titicaca, which is larger, is shared with Bolivia.

mismi.fait: Expeditions have concluded that the source of the Amazon is on the slopes of this mountain in the Peruvian Andes.

ubinas.fait: Fumaroles and ash emissions have followed one another here since the 16th century: this stratovolcano is the most active in Peru.

siula-grande.fait: This mountain is known for the terrible descent of Joe Simpson and Simon Yates, told in the book and film “Touching the Void.”

huandoy.fait: This snow-covered mountain in Peru has four peaks, arranged in relation to one another in the shape of a furnace.

artesonraju.fait: Its pyramid shape is said to be that of the star-ringed mountain in the logo of Paramount Pictures, the oldest studio in Hollywood.

chachani.fait: Despite its altitude, snow is very rare at the summit of this volcano, which lost its last glaciers in 2008.

jirishanca.fait: Its Quechua name means “hummingbird's beak”; it is one of the highest peaks in the Cordillera Huayhuash.

chacraraju.fait: Its Quechua name literally means “snowfield”; this summit rises in Huascarán National Park.

guitarrero.fait: This cave was occupied by nomadic hunters, then at the beginnings of agriculture: its layers preserve the record of this evolution.

mont-hudson.fait: This glacier-covered volcano in southern Chile was the site of one of the largest eruptions of the 20th century.

lac-ranco.fait: Its name means “running waters” in Mapudungun; on its main island, Huapi Island, there is a Mapuche reserve.

fray-jorge.fait: Very close to the Atacama Desert, this coastal park nevertheless shelters lush vegetation, an ecosystem unique in the world.

lascar.fait: This volcano in northern Chile is considered the most active in the region; it is surrounded by other volcanoes, including Acamarachi.

conguillio.fait: This park in Araucanía is, along with the Alto Bío-Bío National Reserve, part of the Araucarias Biosphere Reserve of Chile.

perez-rosales.fait: It is the oldest national park in Chile; it includes in particular Lake Todos los Santos and the Osorno volcano.

cerro-armazones.fait: This summit was chosen to host the European Extremely Large Telescope, which at its inauguration will be the largest optical telescope in the world.

monte-pissis.fait: This dormant volcano in Argentina is the third-highest summit in the Andes, behind Aconcagua and Nevado Ojos del Salado.

mercedario.fait: It is not known whether the altitude of this summit, the highest in the Cordillera de la Ramada, has been measured correctly.

calilegua.fait: This park in Jujuy protects the yungas, humid subtropical forests clinging to the eastern slopes of the Andes.

lago-puelo.fait: Glacial sediments carried by rivers give Lake Puelo, at the heart of this park, an opaque turquoise color.

los-cardones.fait: Dinosaur eggs and rock paintings left by pre-Hispanic cultures have been found in this park.

los-arrayanes.fait: This park protects forests of arrayanes, trees with golden bark that grow extremely slowly.

el-leoncito.fait: This park in the province of San Juan hosts an astronomical complex, including the Félix Aguilar Observatory.

salinas-grandes-centre.fait: Once called the “Salt Flats Desert,” this salt flat in central Argentina is one of the largest salt deserts in the world.

jardin-botanique-ba.fait: This garden in the Palermo neighborhood of Buenos Aires brings together more than five thousand five hundred plant species and various sculptures.

gondwana.fait: These rainforests bring together eight distinct areas, grouped on either side of the border between New South Wales and Queensland.

naracoorte.fait: The roof of these caves can give way underfoot: animals that fell into the holes could not get out, hence their many fossils.

petit-desert-sable.fait: This desert owes its name to its resemblance, except in size, to its neighbor, the Great Sandy Desert.

parc-royal.fait: The first national park in Australia, it was renamed “Royal” after Elizabeth II passed through it during her 1954 visit.

mont-ossa.fait: Tasmania's highest point is named after Mount Ossa in Greece, a mountain from Greek mythology.

zoo-taronga.fait: This zoo on the shore of Sydney Harbour, home to more than 2,600 animals, is the second park where platypuses have bred.

lac-gairdner.fait: This salt lake, north of the Eyre Peninsula, is endorheic: its waters drain to no sea.

mont-wellington.fait: This summit overlooking the city of Hobart, in Tasmania, has officially had a dual name since 2014.

mont-bogong.fait: This summit shares its name with the bogong, a moth of the region whose caterpillar the Aboriginal people ate.

wolfe-creek.fait: This meteorite crater was only discovered in 1947, during an aerial survey; the Jaru Aboriginal people call it Kandimalal.

boodjamulla.fait: The Waanyi Aboriginal people have lived in this “Rainbow Serpent country” for at least 17,000 years; its gorges are sacred to them.

hyde-park-sydney.fait: It is the oldest public park in Australia; it is home to about 580 trees, including figs and palms.

fiordland.fait: It is the largest of New Zealand's fourteen national parks; it occupies the southwest of the South Island.

westland.fait: This park runs from the highest peaks of the Southern Alps to a wild coast where the remains of gold rush mining towns survive.

lacs-nelson.fait: This park is centered on two large lakes, Rotoiti and Rotoroa, where New Zealanders come to camp, hike and fish.

mont-tasman.fait: Called Rarakiora in Māori, this second-highest summit in the country is the neighbor of Aoraki/Mount Cook, the highest.

arthurs-pass.fait: A state highway crosses this park through Arthur's Pass, in the Southern Alps; it is the country's third national park.

te-urewera.fait: This traditional land of the Tuhoe, difficult to reach, was one of the last regions brought under British control.

mont-aspiring.fait: The Māori call it Tititea, “glistening peak”; its pyramidal shape has earned it the nickname “Matterhorn of the Southern Hemisphere.”

lac-ohau.fait: This lake marks the natural boundary between the Otago and Canterbury regions; its Māori name may mean “windy place.”

taupo-volcan.fait: This supervolcano produced two of the most violent eruptions of recent geological times; a lake now fills its caldera.

pic-mitre.fait: This 1,683-meter summit rises west of Milford Sound, a fjord at its base, in Fiordland National Park.

one-tree-hill.fait: Its English name comes from a solitary tree that stood atop this volcanic hill in Auckland before being cut down by settlers in 1852.

frying-pan-lake.fait: This volcanic lake in the Waimangu Valley is the largest hot spring in the world: its water is between 50 and 60 °C.

waikaremoana.fait: Its Māori name means “sea of rippling waters”; it is the deepest lake on the North Island, in the heart of Tuhoe country.

waipoua.fait: This Northland forest is home to two giant trees of the species Agathis australis, named Tāne Mahuta and Te Matua Ngahere.

serra-capivara.fait: This region of Piauí is rich in prehistoric sites, for which early dates have been proposed.

emas.fait: This park in Goiás is named after the greater rheas that live there, called “ema” in Portuguese.

tumucumaque.fait: This park in Amapá, close in size to Switzerland, is the largest park protecting tropical rainforest in the world.

ibirapuera.fait: This park is the green lung of São Paulo: it is compared to Central Park in New York or the Bois de Boulogne in Paris.

tijuca.fait: This Rio forest is the result of reforestation, decided when deforestation caused by coffee was harming the drinking water of the Empire's capital.

lagoa-rodrigo.fait: This lagoon surrounded by Ipanema and Leblon receives salt water from the ocean through a small canal that crosses the Jardim de Alah.

itatiaia.fait: Created in 1937, it is Brazil's oldest national park, surrounded by the mountains of the Mantiqueira range.

matosinhos.nom: Sanctuary of Bom Jesus de Congonhas
matosinhos.fait: Twelve soapstone prophets, carved by Aleijadinho and his assistants, adorn the terraced staircase of this sanctuary in Congonhas.

sao-miguel-arcanjo.fait: Founded in 1632, this Guaraní Jesuit mission left ruins listed as a World Heritage Site in 1984, which a town completely surrounds.

peruacu.fait: This park protects more than 140 caves, rock paintings and part of the reserve of the Xakriabá Indigenous people.

aparados-serra.fait: This canyon in the Serra Geral is protected by Aparados da Serra National Park, created in 1959 partly to preserve it.

anavilhanas.fait: This vast archipelago is not at sea but on a river: its islands dot the Rio Negro, in the state of Amazonas.

theatro-sp.nom: Municipal Theater on Ramos de Azevedo Square
theatro-sp.fait: It was in this São Paulo theater that the Modern Art Week took place in 1922, revolutionizing the arts in Brazil.

agulhas-negras.fait: Its name means “peak of the Black Needles”; it is the fifth-highest summit in Brazil, in Itatiaia park.

mont-pascoal.fait: It is said to be the first land sighted by Pedro Álvares Cabral; its name comes from the landing, which took place just after Easter.

jardin-curitiba.fait: In 2007, this Curitiba garden was the most chosen place in an online vote to elect the “Seven Wonders of Brazil.”

jardin-botanique-rio.nom: Botanical Garden and Avenue of Imperial Palms
jardin-botanique-rio.fait: Founded in 1808 by John VI of Portugal, this garden was first meant to acclimatize imported species, such as the nutmeg tree, pepper and the cinnamon tree.

candelaria-rio.fait: Built and decorated over more than a century, this Rio church combines a Baroque facade with a Neoclassical interior.

canoa-quebrada.fait: This beach in Ceará, very popular with tourists, stretches at the foot of a cliff with sands of various colors.

kahal-zur-israel.nom: Kahal Zur Israel Synagogue of Recife
kahal-zur-israel.fait: The first synagogue in the Americas: refugees from Recife who attended it founded the first Jewish community in New York.

arpoador.fait: Fishermen used to fish with harpoons from this Rio promontory: “arpoador” means “one who harpoons” in Portuguese.

acamarachi.fait: This volcano with very steep slopes contains a lake ranked as the third highest in the world.

chopicalqui.fait: Its name comes from the Quechua Chawpikallki, “center” and “ravine”; it rises near Huascarán, in the Cordillera Blanca.

aracar.fait: This 6,095-meter stratovolcano, in Salta Province, is considered active, even though it is currently dormant.

parc-chaco-ar.fait: This park protects woods of red quebracho, a tree so overexploited in the 20th century that its survival was endangered.

galeras.fait: This volcano, also called Pasto volcano, rises west of San Juan de Pasto, the capital of Nariño Department.

nevado-tolima.fait: This volcano in the Colombian Andes is mostly reached from the city of Ibagué, in Tolima Department.

nevado-huila.fait: This volcano in the Andes mountain range, in Huila Department, is the highest active volcano in Colombia.

salto-tequendama.fait: Next to this waterfall on the Bogotá River stands a former hotel, now a museum of biodiversity and culture.

santa-cruz-islote.fait: This island in the San Bernardo archipelago, in the Caribbean Sea, is not natural at all: it is an artificial island.

place-bolivar-co.fait: This square is the plaza mayor of Bogotá, the capital of Colombia; a statue of Simón Bolívar stands at its center.

calbuco.fait: After decades of calm, this volcano with a glacier-covered summit suddenly erupted in 2015, without any warning sign.

llaima.fait: This volcano, considered one of the most active in South America, is surrounded by araucaria woods; a ski resort lies on its western slope.

lac-villarrica.fait: This lake, Mallalafquén in the Mapuche language, has as its southern neighbor the Villarrica volcano, ranked among the ten most active in the world.

cerro-paranal.fait: For the purity of its sky, this mountain in the Atacama hosts the VLT telescopes; the surrounding land was donated to protect it.

chaiten.fait: This volcano, thought to be extinct, erupted in 2008 and destroyed the nearby town, whose residents were evacuated to a new town.

misti.fait: This volcano with a symmetrical cone, near Arequipa, reawakened in 1985 after nearly two centuries without a documented eruption.

chandelier-paracas.fait: This candelabra-shaped geoglyph is dug into the very sand of a dune, on the Paracas Peninsula, in Peru.

huaca-luna.fait: This adobe pyramid was the most important place of worship of the Moche; some of its murals have survived looting.

qenqo.fait: The name of this Inca shrine near Cusco comes from the Quechua q'inqu, which means “zigzag.”

vilcabamba.fait: This region north of Cusco, also called Espíritu Pampa, was the last refuge of the Incas after the Spanish conquest.

yerupaja.fait: Peru's second-highest summit and one of the hardest to climb in the Andes, it is said to be nicknamed “the Butcher” for its sharp ridges.

desert-sechura.fait: This coastal desert runs along the Pacific Ocean in the Piura region and extends to the foothills of the Andes.

cahuachi.fait: This Nazca ceremonial center had few permanent residents: it may have been a place of pilgrimage that filled up during ceremonies.

cathedrale-buenos-aires.nom: Metropolitan Cathedral of the Holy Trinity
cathedrale-buenos-aires.fait: With no towers, this Neoclassical cathedral looks more like a Greek temple than a church; the future Pope Francis was its archbishop.

el-palmar.fait: This park was created to safeguard an area populated by yatay palms, on the banks of the Uruguay River, in Argentina.

loreto-mission.fait: These ruins are those of a Jesuit reduction founded in 1633, when the missions of Paraguay were moved south.

santa-ana-mission.fait: The ruins remain of this Jesuit reduction, founded when the Jesuit missions of Paraguay were moved south.

domuyo.fait: The Mapuche name of this volcano means “That which trembles and resounds,” probably because of its geysers and hot springs.

desert-tanami.fait: This rocky desert, one of the most isolated and arid places on Earth, was only explored in the 20th century.

riversleigh.fait: This fossil site has yielded the ancestral forms of kangaroos, koalas and wombats: several hundred new species have been described there.

lac-burley-griffin.fait: This artificial lake, created in 1963 in the center of Canberra, is named after the architect who won the competition to lay it out.

taumata.fait: This 85-letter name, one of the longest in the world, comes from a Māori legend; its oversized sign attracts tourists.

mont-tarawera.fait: This North Island volcano is made up of eleven aligned lava domes, cut through the middle by a wide eruptive fissure.

chutes-sutherland.fait: This waterfall drops in three leaps; long believed to be the highest in the country, it is in fact surpassed by Browne Falls.

pico-bandeira.fait: This summit was considered Brazil's highest point until 1965, when two higher peaks were discovered and measured.

cerro-batovi.fait: The Guaraní name of this butte, inspired by its shape, means “a virgin's breast”; it serves as the emblem of Tacuarembó Department.

papyrus-rhind.fait: This scroll copied by the scribe Ahmes contains 87 solved mathematical problems, some of which repeat older results.

afrasiab.fait: This Sogdian mural came to light in 1965, when a road was to be built through the middle of the Afrasiab hill, ancient Samarkand.

burney.fait: This terracotta plaque shows a goddess in high relief: it was thought to be Lilith, but several specialists lean toward Ishtar, Ereshkigal or Inanna.

lelo.fait: This Georgian ball game is considered the historical ancestor of rugby union, which it closely resembles.

angora-turc.fait: This very old breed is the origin of all long-haired and semi-long-haired cat breeds in Europe and America, such as the Persian or the Maine Coon.

papyrus-edwin-smith.fait: It is the oldest known document on surgery; some see in it a rational approach to medicine, in which magic plays little part.

code-ur-nammu.fait: This Sumerian tablet bears the oldest law code to have come down to us; some historians think it could be the work of Shulgi, son of Ur-Namma.

table-abydos.fait: Seti I had his predecessors engraved on it, but deliberately left some out, such as Hatshepsut or Tutankhamun, deemed illegitimate.

lettres-amarna.fait: In these diplomatic tablets, the great kings call each other “my brother” and often discuss at length the quantity of gifts to offer.

liste-royale-sumerienne.fait: According to this text, kingship “descended from heaven,” and the first kings each reigned several thousand years before the Flood.

mont-sinai.fait: According to the biblical account, Moses saw the burning bush there and received the Ten Commandments; in Arabic, it is called “Mountain of Moses.”

elephantine.fait: This Nile island, a former provincial capital, is now a district of Aswan that is home to two Nubian villages.

mykerinos.fait: The smallest of the three great pyramids of Giza shows signs of being unfinished: the pharaoh died during construction.

vallee-reines.fait: Its ancient name meant both “the place of beauty” and “the place of the royal children”: princes were also buried there.

chora.nom: Church of the Holy Savior in Chora
chora.fait: Its Greek-cross plan served as a model for all the Orthodox churches of Istanbul until the 18th century.

kv62.fait: Famous for its treasure, this tomb in the Valley of the Kings took Howard Carter ten years to explore and to inventory its furnishings.

aphrodisias.fait: When archaeologists arrived, a village covered the city: sarcophagi were used as goat pens.

derinkuyu.fait: Dug on several levels, this underground city could shelter up to 20,000 people with their livestock and provisions.

hatta.fait: This town in the Hajar Mountains, part of the emirate of Dubai, was a former stopover on the route between the northern emirates and Oman.

grande-mosquee-sanaa.fait: According to Islamic history, its oldest walls date from Muhammad's lifetime; manuscripts were discovered there during a restoration.

jaffa.fait: As early as antiquity, this port was a stop on the trade route between the Mediterranean and East Asia; Tel Aviv was founded in 1909 north of the town.

qornet-sawda.fait: This mountain is the highest point of Lebanon, but also of the whole Mount Lebanon range and of the entire Levant.

aragats.fait: This extinct volcano is the highest point of Armenia and of the Lesser Caucasus; it overlooks the Armenian Highlands that stretch at its feet.

mosquee-bleue-mazar.fait: Its local name, Rawze-i-Sharif, means “the mosque of the Saint,” in reference to Ali Ibn Talib; it stands in the center of Mazar-i-Sharif.

farasan.fait: This Red Sea archipelago, off the southwest coast of Saudi Arabia, is made up of coral islands.

mahram-bilqis.fait: This Sabaean temple dedicated to the god Almaqah, nicknamed “Mahram Bilqis” by archaeologists, was a famous place of pilgrimage.

deir-el-qamar.fait: Its name means “the convent of the Moon”: a Roman temple dedicated to the Moon stood where a convent and a church are today.

shahdag.fait: At the foot of this Greater Caucasus summit, prehistoric cave dwellings occupied more than 9,000 years ago have been found.

jibla.fait: This town at the foot of Jabal At-Taʿkar is home to the palace and mausoleum of a queen, Arwa al-Sulayhi.

alakol.fait: This lake lies at the heart of a closed basin, whose waters do not reach the sea, and which it shares with Lake Sasykköl and Lake Balkhash.

yusif-kuseyir.fait: One of the oldest buildings in Nakhchivan was designed by an architect whose name is known: Ajami ibn Abubakr Nakhchivani.

musalla-herat.fait: These Timurid buildings date from the time when Herat was the capital of the empire; despite looting and earthquakes, their remains are still impressive.

chateau-byblos.fait: This castle was built by the Crusaders in the 12th century on Phoenician and Roman foundations, in Byblos.

djerba.fait: Ulysses is said to have passed through this island, which keeps one of the last Berber languages of Tunisia, the Tamazight of Djerba.

aydarkul.fait: This artificial salt lake has only existed since 1970: it occupies a depression in the Kyzylkum Desert and is fed by overflows from the Syr Darya.

djanet.fait: This oasis, the capital of the Tassili n'Ajjer, is inhabited mainly by Kel Ajjer Tuaregs; it was formerly called Fort Charlet.

hazor.fait: In 2013, the paws of an Egyptian sphinx bearing the name of the pharaoh Menkaure were discovered there, which puzzled specialists.

hajar-hibla.fait: This stone block in Baalbek ranks, with two other ancient blocks close by, among the longest monoliths ever cut by humans.

sanahin.fait: This monastery in northern Armenia, in Lori Province, took shape gradually between the 10th and 13th centuries.

timimoun.fait: This town is the main oasis of Gourara, set between the dunes of the Grand Erg Occidental to the north and the Tademaït Plateau to the south.

pella.fait: This ancient city, once called Pella and Berenice, is now named Tabaqat Fahil; it lies 5 km east of the Jordan River.

chouf.fait: This reserve includes the cedar forests of Barouk, Maaser el Chouf and Ain Zhalta, and is home to 200 species of birds.

toprak-kala.fait: Its name means “fortress covered with earth”: in this presumed capital of Khwarezm, a palace with 150 painted and sculpted rooms was found.

kazbek.fait: This dormant, glacier-covered volcano is the second-highest summit in Georgia, and its ascent presents only moderate difficulties.

apamee.fait: This ancient site near the Orontes, which the Greeks called Apameia, now bears the name Qal'at al-Madhiq.

zenkov.fait: This Russian Orthodox church in Almaty, officially the Cathedral of the Ascension, stands in the middle of Panfilov Park.

mont-arbel.fait: This mountain in Lower Galilee overlooks Lake Tiberias and features high cliffs, a cave fortress and the ruins of an ancient synagogue.

ad-deir.fait: This rock-cut monument is the largest in the ancient city of Petra; its Arabic name means “the monastery.”

charvak.fait: This lake in Tashkent Province is artificial: its Russian name literally means “Charvak water reservoir.”

citadelle-tripoli.fait: Despite its name, the Crusader Raymond of Saint-Gilles did not build it, and an Ottoman governor largely rebuilt it in the 19th century.

taghit.fait: This oasis in the Saoura, with its ksar on the edge of the Zousfana valley, is known for combining desert, recreational and archaeological tourism.

tekkiye.fait: This Ottoman-era Sufi monastery, built in the 16th century, stands in Damascus on the right bank of the Barada.

aksu-zhabagly.fait: Created in 1926 in southern Kazakhstan, this protected area is the oldest nature reserve in Central Asia.

lyab-i-hauz.fait: This square in Bukhara, grouped around a pool, was one of the few open spaces in a very densely built city.

grande-mosquee-tlemcen.fait: Built in 1136 by an Almoravid emir, this mosque combines in its decoration marble, carved and pierced plaster, ceramics and wood.

qasr-al-abd.fait: Its name means “castle of the slave,” but this vast palace is said to have been built by the Tobiads, a prominent Jewish family.

sbeitla.fait: Ancient Sufetula was the entry point of the Arab conquest of North Africa and retains an important archaeological site.

shymbulak.fait: This winter sports resort in the Trans-Ili Alatau range lies upstream of the Medeu dam, south of Almaty.

hazrat-khizr.fait: This Samarkand mosque, built on the site of an older one, bears the name of the legendary immortal prophet Khizr.

qasr-hayr-gharbi.fait: Its name means “castle of the western reservoir”: this Umayyad castle was built at the request of Caliph Hisham, west of Palmyra.

lac-ourmia.fait: This salt lake has no outlet; with Lakes Van and Sevan, it was one of the “three seas” of the ancient kingdom of Armenia.

lac-tonga.fait: This freshwater lake in El Kala National Park is the most important nesting area for birds in North Africa.

kok-tobe.fait: Its name means “blue mountain”: this mountain in southeastern Almaty is considered a symbol of the city.

kara-tepe.fait: This Buddhist site near Termez reached its peak under the Kushans before declining, probably during the Kushano-Sasanian invasion.

ghriba2.fait: According to tradition, this synagogue in Djerba contains remains of Solomon's Temple; several thousand pilgrims visit it every year.

nippur.fait: This city was the great sanctuary of the god Enlil: in cuneiform writing, the same signs are read NIBRU and EN.LÍL.

sioni-tbilissi.fait: This cathedral overlooking the Kura, in the historic center of Tbilisi, is a key site of Georgian national identity.

akhtala.fait: This fortified monastery has a church renowned for its frescoes; its name is said to be of Turkic origin and to mean “white clearing.”

medina-sousse.fait: This medina retains its kasbah, ramparts and ribat, and a lighthouse has been installed atop the Khalef tower since 1890.

ayaz-kala.fait: These two ruined citadels, built of dried mud on top of promontories, are surrounded by the Kyzylkum Desert, which stretches to the Aral Sea.

citadelle-damas.fait: Rebuilt by Saladin's brother to withstand the counterweight trebuchet, it was taken by force only once during the Ayyubid struggles, in 1239.

shatili.fait: This historic village in Upper Khevsureti clings to the northern slope of the Greater Caucasus, very close to the border with Chechnya.

mantashyants.fait: This monastery in Tsaghkadzor was an important center of medieval learning, built gradually by several Armenian noble families.

tamerza.fait: Some scenes from the film “The English Patient” were shot in this mountain oasis area of Tozeur Governorate.

serjilla.fait: Very well preserved, the 5th- and 6th-century houses of this ancient village have barely changed since they were examined in the 1860s.

gonio.fait: This fortress on the Black Sea, near the mouth of the Chorokhi, was called Apsaros in antiquity.

hovhannavank.fait: This Monastery of Saint John in the Kasakh valley, a neighbor of Saghmosavank, has been under restoration since the 1980s.

hormuz.fait: This island owes its strategic importance to its position at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, in the strait that bears the same name.

fort-ghar-el-melh.fait: Its name means “salt cave,” because of the nearby salt pans; this coastal town was once called Porto Farina.

cap-spartel.fait: It is at this headland, at the southern entrance to the Strait of Gibraltar, that the Mediterranean and the Atlantic meet.

odzun.fait: This 6th-century church, also called Odzun Monastery, stands in the village of the same name, in Lori Province.

rabati.fait: This 9th-century fortress was completely rebuilt under the Ottoman Empire, in the town of Akhaltsikhe.

soltaniyeh.fait: This imperial city became the capital of the Ilkhanate of Persia under Öljaitü, who had a notable mausoleum built there.

borsippa.fait: This ancient city, now the site of Birs Nimrud, was the city of Nabu, the god of knowledge and wisdom.

lixus.fait: According to ancient sources, this Phoenician city on the banks of the Loukkos River is said to have been founded long before Carthage and Cádiz.

alaverdi.fait: This Orthodox monastery in Kakheti is older than its current cathedral: some of its parts date back to the 6th century.

harichavank.fait: Looted and then refounded, this monastery on the slopes of Mount Aragats became a summer residence of the catholicoi of Armenia in the 19th century.

jameh-ispahan.fait: Begun in the 10th century and heavily remodeled under the Safavids, this “old mosque” is linked to the new city by the Grand Bazaar.

thuburbo-majus.fait: Much of this ancient site remains to be uncovered, but excavations have already yielded mosaics and fragments of a colossal statue of Jupiter.

amadiya.fait: This former capital of the Kurdish principality of Bahdinan looks like an eagle’s nest perched on a mountain plateau.

menara.fait: The large pool of this olive grove is fed by a hydraulic system more than 700 years old that brings water down from the mountains.

caravanserail-selim.fait: Built in 1332 in Vayots Dzor, this stopover for caravans is the best-preserved caravanserai in Armenia.

alamut.fait: Once reputed to be impregnable, this fortress built around 840 bears a name said to mean “eagle’s nest” in the local dialect.

chebika.fait: Its name means “little trickle” in Tunisian Arabic: the water running down the oasis’s waterfalls forms liquid trickles.

el-badi.fait: This “palace of the incomparable” was stripped of its riches by Moulay Ismail to build Meknes; only an esplanade remains.

ateni-sioni.fait: This 7th-century church, in the Tana valley near Gori, owes its name “Sioni” to Mount Zion in Jerusalem.

pergame.fait: Its Greek name means “citadel”; this ancient city of Asia Minor is now called Bergama.

bazar-tabriz.fait: This bazaar prospered thanks to trade along the Silk Road, but it was entirely rebuilt in the 18th century.

mar-mattai.fait: Founded in the 4th century on Mount Alfaf, this Syriac Orthodox monastery is renowned for its collection of Syriac manuscripts.

bab-mansour.fait: Nicknamed the “Renegade’s Gate,” it is the most important of the gates of Meknes; it faces Lahdim Square.

anchiskhati.fait: Built in the 6th century, this Georgian Orthodox basilica is among the oldest churches in Tbilisi.

mardin.fait: The Romans called it Marida, an Assyrian name meaning “fortress”: the town crowns a steep hill overlooking the Tigris.

bab-agnaou.fait: This Almohad gate opens onto the royal kasbah of Marrakesh, home to the El Badi Palace and the Saadian Tombs.

imam-reza.fait: This shrine in Mashhad, built in honor of the 8th imam of Twelver Shiism, is the largest mosque in Iran.

harran.fait: Two villages survive here, with houses of stone and mud brick topped by beehive-shaped domes.

temple-biyun.fait: This Buddhist temple in Beijing was founded in 1331 under the Mongol Yuan dynasty; it notably houses a five-pagoda temple.

mont-heng-shanxi.fait: Rising to 2,016 meters, this mountain in Shanxi is one of the country’s five sacred mountains, also known as the “Northern Mountain.”

zhujiajiao.fait: This water town attached to Shanghai has kept 36 stone bridges over its many rivers, amid old buildings.

xitang.fait: This town in Zhejiang is built entirely around canals: its rivers divide it into sections linked to one another by more than a hundred bridges.

lac-lugu.fait: The shores of this lake, on the border between Yunnan and Sichuan, are inhabited by minorities such as the Mosuo, the Yi, the Pumi and Tibetans.

lac-hulun.fait: This lake in Inner Mongolia usually has no outflow: only in very rainy years does a river connect it to the Argun.

huai-he.fait: This river is often regarded as the boundary between North and South China, and it marks the southeastern limit of the Mandarin dialects.

badain-jaran.fait: This desert has the highest dunes in the world, up to 500 meters; the hundred or so lakes nestled between them earn it its Mongolian name of desert of “mysterious lakes.”

taotie.fait: This animal mask often adorns Chinese ritual bronzes of the Shang and Zhou dynasties, but also funerary ceramics and jade discs.

har-gow.fait: This traditional Cantonese dumpling is served as part of dim sum, and its name is spelled in many ways: ha kao, ha gow or haukau.

nakdong.fait: This river, the longest in South Korea, passes near Daegu and Busan, two of the country’s major cities.

muraille-seoul.fait: King Taejo had this wall built around Hanyang, the old name of Seoul; a good part of the wall and most of its gates survive.

cheongju-alcool.fait: This rice liquor, the Korean equivalent of sake, differs from makgeolli in its clarity: it is filtered through a bamboo sieve.

chateau-kanazawa.fait: The famous Kenroku-en garden, right next door, was once the outer private garden of this castle in Ishikawa Prefecture.

chateau-kochi.fait: Built in the Edo period in the former Tosa Province, this castle is notable for having kept most of its original buildings.

ritsurin.fait: This garden in Takamatsu, begun in the early 17th century, combines a Japanese-style garden to the south and a Western-style garden to the north.

kairaku-en.fait: Created in Mito by Tokugawa Nariaki, this garden forms, with Kenroku-en and Kōraku-en, the trio of the country’s most famous gardens.

shinjuku-gyoen.fait: Once the residence of the Naito family, this Tokyo park was managed by the Imperial Household Agency before coming under the Ministry of the Environment.

villa-katsura.fait: Japanese modernist architects saw in this Kyoto villa a parallel to their theories; the German Bruno Taut made it known as early as 1934.

lac-towada.fait: This lake in northern Honshū was formed 55,000 years ago by a period of activity of the Towada volcano, and it is the source of the Oirase River.

mont-zao.fait: The caldera at the summit of this volcano holds a lake whose water changes color depending on weather conditions.

mii-dera.fait: At the foot of Mount Hiei, near Lake Biwa, this temple has forty buildings and serves as a kind of sister temple to Enryaku-ji, built on the summit.

kongobu-ji.fait: Perched on Mount Kōya, in Wakayama Prefecture, this temple is the head temple of Shingon Buddhism on Kōyasan.

eihei-ji.fait: Its name means “temple of eternal peace”; it was founded in 1244 by Dōgen, who had brought Sōtō Zen over from China.

kotohira-gu.fait: To reach this shrine, pilgrims climb 785 steps, and many more are needed to get to the inner shrine.

dogo-onsen.fait: This hot spring bath in Matsuyama, already mentioned in the 8th century in the Man’yōshū, has a bath reserved for the imperial family.

laba.fait: This winter festival opens the Chinese New Year celebrations; offerings used to be made to heaven, earth, the gods and the ancestors.

xun.fait: On this terracotta flute, you blow across an open hole rather than into a duct; with its very soft sound, it is played mostly solo.

lap-cheong.fait: These dried, smoked and moderately sweet sausages come in pairs tied together with string; they used to be prepared for the New Year.

gateau-navet.fait: It is sometimes mistakenly called “carrot cake”: in Chinese, the word luobo can mean either white radish or carrot.

baihao-yinzhen.fait: Its name means “white downy silver needles”: this rare and expensive white tea is produced in Fujian Province, in southeastern China.

oolong.fait: Its name means “dragon-crow tea”: halfway between green tea and black tea, it is only partially oxidized.

pagode-fogong.fait: Built in 1056, this pagoda has survived several major earthquakes; it is so well known that it is simply called “the wooden pagoda.”

petite-pagode-oie.fait: This pagoda was built in Xi’an when the city, then called Chang’an, was the most populous in the Empire.

temple-lingyin.fait: Its name translates as “temple of the soul’s retreat”; it is surrounded by caves and religious sculptures carved into the rock.

palais-mukden.fait: Before moving into the Forbidden City in Beijing, the first emperors of the Qing dynasty lived in this palace in Shenyang.

qianling.fait: This funerary complex holds Emperor Gaozong of Tang and his wife, Empress Wu Zetian, not far from Xi’an, the former Chang’an.

passe-jiayu.fait: This fort marks the western end of the Great Wall; it is nicknamed the “first and greatest pass under heaven.”

passe-shanhai.fait: Here the Great Wall meets the Bohai Sea: the spot is nicknamed “the old dragon’s head.”

pagode-songyue.fait: Built in 523, it is the oldest known Chinese brick pagoda; most buildings of that period, made of wood, have not survived.

lac-qiandao.fait: This “lake of a thousand islands” is not natural: it was created by a hydroelectric station built on the Qiantang River.

tongli.fait: This old town crisscrossed by canals, in the Wujiang District of Suzhou, has more than 1,000 years of history.

kabayaki.fait: These eels grilled over a wood fire are basted with a sauce whose stock is traditionally made from their heads and bones.

chanko-nabe.fait: This stew is eaten in large quantities by sumo wrestlers: it is part of their high-calorie diet.

nabemono.fait: This winter dish simmers on the table, and the leftover soup can be used at the end to make an egg rice dish, zōsui.

inarizushi.fait: This pouch of fried tofu filled with rice is named after the Shinto god Inari, said to have a weakness for fried tofu.

makizushi.fait: Its name means “rolled sushi”: a sheet of dried nori seaweed wraps around the vinegared rice and its filling.

mirin.fait: This very sweet, syrupy sake, pale yellow to amber in color, is now used almost exclusively to season dishes.

somen.fait: These very thin white noodles cook very quickly and are usually eaten cold, in soup, in summer.

tsukemen.fait: These noodles are dipped in a bowl of broth before being eaten; the dish was born in Tokyo in 1961.

korokke.fait: Its name comes from the Dutch kroket, itself taken from the French “croquette”: it is a potato croquette, usually with ground beef.

donburi.fait: Its name means “large bowl”: a bowl of rice topped with all kinds of ingredients, meat, fish or vegetables.

tamago-kake-gohan.fait: Often eaten for breakfast, this popular dish mixes boiled rice with a beaten raw egg, with or without soy sauce.

ohagi.fait: This autumn sweet made of rice and red bean paste takes its name from hagi, a plant that blooms in autumn.

kanda-matsuri.fait: This Tokyo festival takes place only in odd-numbered years, because it alternates with another one, the Sannō Matsuri.

yabusame.fait: This horseback archery began as a form of training: a shogun was worried about his samurai’s shortcomings in archery.

gagaku.fait: This “refined music” was once played at the imperial court; it is often contrasted with so-called popular music.

kyogen.fait: This comic form of theater often appears in the middle of a Noh play, while the lead actor changes costume and mask.

manzai.fait: This comedy duo pits a serious character, the tsukkomi, against an outrageous one, the boke; it used to be performed in the street.

sashiko.fait: This embroidery was first used to patch and reinforce clothing, before also being used for decoration.

shibori.fait: The fabric is bound before dyeing so that certain areas stay light: this is also known as “tie-dye.”

haori.fait: This jacket worn over the kimono was reserved for men until geishas from Fukagawa adopted it in the early 1800s.

happi.fait: This straight-sleeved cotton coat, often indigo or brown, is recognizable by the distinctive crest printed on it.

shinai.fait: This kendo weapon is made of four bamboo slats held together by leather; it is used in training for its flexibility and resistance to impact.

yumi.fait: This traditional bow has an asymmetrical shape; it is used for kyūdō and for horseback archery, yabusame.

chawan.fait: Its name means “tea bowl”: this rustic bowl is used to prepare matcha during the tea ceremony.

raku.fait: Its name means “happy firing”: these hand-shaped ceramics, fired at low temperatures, accompany the tea ceremony.

imari.fait: This porcelain is named after the port of Imari, from which it was exported, although it was mostly made in Arita.

shisa.fait: On these pairs of Okinawan guardians, the male opens its mouth to ward off evil spirits, while the female keeps it closed to hold in happiness.

komainu.fait: These guardian lions watch over Shinto shrines in pairs; some, kept in the inner sanctuary, remain hidden from the public.

tsukubai.fait: This basin is placed low so that one must bend down as a sign of humility before purifying oneself for the tea ceremony.

irori.fait: Unlike the kamado, placed in the doma, this hearth is built into the main living room of traditional minka houses.

genkan.fait: Shoes are removed in this entrance hall, found in homes as well as in temples and baths.

chateau-okayama.fait: Its main keep, destroyed in 1945, was rebuilt in concrete; two watchtowers, however, survived the bombing.

daitoku-ji.fait: This Zen temple in Kyoto, whose name means “temple of great virtue,” actually brings together several subtemples.

ninna-ji.fait: Its founder, Emperor Uda, retired there as a priest; from 888 to 1869, custom required the emperors to send one of their sons there as head priest.

saiho-ji.fait: It is nicknamed the “moss temple”: this Zen temple on the outskirts of Kyoto is home to 120 species of moss.

atsuta-jingu.fait: This shrine in Nagoya houses the legendary sword Kusanagi, one of the three Imperial Regalia of Japan.

sumiyoshi-taisha.fait: This Osaka shrine gave its name to a style of Shinto architecture; large crowds flock there on New Year’s Day.
