dazaifu-tenmangu.fait: According to legend, a tree that the exiled Michizane longed for was uprooted and carried all the way to this shrine built over his grave.

lac-mashu.fait: This crater lake, set in the caldera of a volcano, is reputed to have some of the clearest water in the world.

gion.fait: This Kyoto district first served as a stopping place for visitors to Yasaka Shrine, before becoming the geisha district.

rinno-ji.fait: This temple in Nikkō, at the foot of Mount Nantai, houses the mausoleum of the shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu.

budae-jjigae.fait: This “army base” stew combines Spam, sausage, instant noodles and American cheese; the city of Uijeongbu claims to have invented it.

kumgangsan.fait: These “Diamond Mountains” owe their name to the sparkle of the peaks at sunrise; they are sacred to Koreans.

taedong.fait: This river, which rises in the northern mountains, flows through Pyongyang and has given its name to a beer.

taedongmun.fait: The former east gate of the Pyongyang fortress, it was rebuilt in 1635 after being destroyed by fire.

jeongol.fait: Unlike the jjigae of commoners, this multi-ingredient dish was originally a delicacy of the upper class and the royal court.

sungnyung.fait: This drink made from scorched rice is usually drunk after meals, but some Koreans have it for breakfast.

jian-dui.fait: As it puffs up during frying, this sesame-coated glutinous rice ball becomes hollow, and the cavity holds a lotus or bean filling.

soupe-suanla.fait: In France, it is often served under the name “Peking soup,” although its variants come from Sichuan, Hunan and Shandong.

jingisukan.fait: This lamb dish is named after Genghis Khan: its grill imitates a Mongol soldier’s helmet, and lamb is almost absent from the rest of Japanese cuisine.

hoto.fait: This soup from Yamanashi simmers flat udon noodles and vegetables in a miso soup.

sekihan.fait: This glutinous rice owes its reddish color to azuki beans; it is eaten at celebrations, or offered to the kami.

tokoroten.fait: This seaweed jelly is pressed into noodle shapes with a dedicated tool, the tentsuki, then most often seasoned with vinegar.

tonjiru.fait: Its name means “pork soup”: it is a richer variation of miso soup, with pork, vegetables and a greater number of ingredients.

hanabiramochi.fait: This small rice-paste cake is eaten mainly at the start of the year: it is served at the New Year tea ceremony.

pain-melon.fait: This bread does not necessarily contain melon: its name comes from its cookie crust, whose texture is reminiscent of a cantaloupe.

hibachi.fait: Its name means “fire bowl”: rooms were heated with this container, open at the top and filled with glowing charcoal.

bonsho.fait: These temple bells have no clapper: they are struck from the outside with a mallet or a beam hung from ropes.

asazuke.fait: Marinated for only 30 minutes to a few hours, these vegetables generally lack the sharpness of longer pickles but keep their fresh taste.

akashiyaki.fait: This egg and octopus dumpling is dipped in a fish broth; it inspired takoyaki, which is better known today.

sata-andagi.fait: Originally from southern China, these round fritters are part of Okinawan cuisine, where their name means “sugar” and “fried.”

aburaage.fait: Old tales say foxes are drawn to this fried tofu: udon noodles topped with it are therefore called “fox udon.”

teppanyaki.fait: Its name means “grilled on an iron plate”: a chef cooks meat, noodles or shrimp on a hot plate, the teppan.

hannya.fait: This Noh mask shows a demon woman consumed by jealousy; yet its name comes from a Sanskrit word meaning “great wisdom.”

maki-e.fait: In this lacquer art, the surface is sprinkled with gold or silver powder; first designed for court nobles, its objects became a symbol of power.

sumi-e.fait: Brought over from China, this black ink painting plays on dilution and on the force and speed of the brush to obtain shades of gray.

the-jaune.fait: This green tea undergoes a light post-fermentation; it is produced only in very small quantities, by a handful of growing areas.

kung-fu-shaolin.fait: This martial art is named after the Shaolin Monastery, where it is said to have been created; hundreds of Chinese styles claim its legacy.

lac-hongze.fait: Fed by the Huai River, this lake in Jiangsu Province is the fourth largest freshwater lake in China.

riviere-perles.fait: In the most common sense, this river is formed by the meeting of two others: the Xi Jiang, “West River,” and the Bei Jiang, “North River.”

karatsu-kunchi.fait: During this festival, there is no school in Karatsu, and fourteen lacquered wooden floats parade in the shape of samurai helmets, sea bream or dragons.

obi-ceinture.fait: Since no jewelry is worn with a kimono, this sash with no buckle or clasp is richly decorated to stand out against the fabric.

geta.fait: These traditional shoes are still worn with the yukata, but also with Western clothing, especially at festivals.

sailor-fuku.fait: This sailor uniform, sometimes called a “marinière” in French, is commonly worn by Japanese schoolgirls.

jinbei.fait: This traditional summer garment is worn at any age in Japan: men, women, children and even babies wear it.

kosode.fait: This garment with “small sleeves” is the direct ancestor of the kimono; the word “kimono” was first used to refer to it.

junihitoe.fait: Its name means “twelve layers,” but the number of stacked robes varies; the imperial family still wears it on major occasions.

gakuran.fait: This uniform is one of the typical uniforms worn by boys in middle school and high school in Japan; girls wear its counterpart, the sailor fuku.

sai-arme.fait: Similar to a trident that does not cut but stabs, this weapon was used by the Okinawa police; a third one was sometimes tucked into the belt as a spare.

yari.fait: A favorite weapon of the samurai, this spear was used in particular to slash horses' hamstrings and unseat their riders.

kusarigama.fait: This sickle attached to a weighted chain originated among peasants who were not allowed to use the katana and had to defend themselves.

jitte.fait: With no cutting edge, this police weapon made it possible to subdue without killing; it resembles the sai but has only one “claw.”

chute-nachi.fait: This waterfall, one of the most impressive in Japan, is also a sacred site for both Shinto and Buddhism.

jigokudani.fait: This hot spring in Nagano Prefecture is known for the population of Japanese macaques that settles there in winter.

jardin-sec.fait: This garden is made up of sand, rocks, gravel and moss: as a rule, no other plants are found there.

hama-rikyu.fait: Bordered by seawater moats, this Tokyo garden, once part of a Tokugawa villa, contains a lagoon that fills at high tide.

kamigamo-jinja.fait: This Shinto shrine in Kyoto, founded in 678, is dedicated to the kami of thunder; it is one of the Kamo shrines, believed to protect the city from evil influences.

iwami-ginzan.fait: At its peak, this mine in Shimane Prefecture alone supplied one third of the silver produced in the world.

filature-tomioka.fait: The Japanese state built this silk mill with machinery imported from France, a sign of the country's entry into the industrial world.

chateau-nakijin.fait: These ruins were the fortress of the Hokuzan kingdom, in northern Okinawa; they are known for their cherry trees, which bloom as early as mid-January.

chateau-nakagusuku.fait: This ruined fortress, one of the oldest in the Ryūkyū Islands, is the second-largest castle in Okinawa after Shuri Castle.

iriomote.fait: The main road only goes about halfway around this island covered in mangroves and forest: some villages can only be reached by water.

amami.fait: On this island in the East China Sea, people speak Northern Amami and Southern Amami, two languages of the Ryukyuan family.

dotaku.fait: These bronze bells were decorated with animals that are enemies of rice pests: according to historians, they were used to pray for a good harvest.

tangsudo.fait: Its founder, Hwang Ki, said he created it by reading old texts on subak, an older Korean martial art.

yangdong-village.fait: This Joseon dynasty village was laid out according to Korean geomancy; it has more than 160 houses with tiled or thatched roofs.

dadohaehaesang.fait: This national park is unusual in being both a land and a marine park; it is also the largest in South Korea.

jian-epee.fait: In Shaolin kung fu, this long sword is nicknamed “the gentleman of weapons”; it is one of the four basic weapons.

crochet-tigre.fait: This hook sword is traditionally associated with the martial arts of northern China; today it is often found in Southern styles.

dao-sabre.fait: In China, the word dao also refers to everyday knives; in Shaolin kung fu, this saber is nicknamed “the general of weapons.”

yuki-tsumugi.fait: This silk weaving is practiced mainly around Yūki, in Ibaraki Prefecture; it is designated an Important Intangible Cultural Property.

tachi.fait: This curved-blade sword, a forerunner of the classic Japanese sword, was above all a cavalryman's weapon.

odachi.fait: To deserve its name, this great sword must have a blade of about 90 cm, but there is no exact definition of its size.

nodachi.fait: This long sword is wielded with both hands; its name means “field sword,” but it has become almost synonymous with ōdachi.

chokuto.fait: Its name means “straight blade”: this weapon, worn hanging from the belt, was used on foot for stabbing or cutting.

kasa-chapeau.fait: This word refers to any old-style Japanese hat, from the straw amigasa of folk dances to the jingasa of the samurai.

ceramique-bizen.fait: This reddish-brown pottery receives no glaze: its exterior bears the marks left by its firing in the kiln.

canal-lingqu.fait: This canal was dug on the orders of the first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, to supply the armies sent to conquer the land of the Yue.

cangshan.fait: These mountains just west of Dali are renowned for the diversity of their flora: the plant Pilea peperomioides is endemic to the region.

temple-tanzhe.fait: This Buddhist temple in the hills west of Beijing is about 1,700 years old: it is one of the oldest in the city.
